> |---|---|

Explain the term ‘mission statement’.
parts.solutionMd:
A mission statement is a short statement that defines a business's purpose and core values, communicating what it stands for to its stakeholders **[1]**. MC's mission - 'to be the world leader in delivering quality motorcycle components to our customers' - tells employees, customers and shareholders that quality and global market leadership are central to everything the business does **[1]**. Explain the term ‘triple bottom line’.
parts.solutionMd:
The triple bottom line is a framework that measures business performance **[1]** across three areas: people (the social impact on employees and communities), planet (the environmental impact of operations) and profit (financial performance) **[1]**. For UC, the recall of faulty components would damage all three,  harming its reputation with stakeholders, potentially wasting materials and reducing its profit **[1]**

> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks

> 
> AO1
> 
> - People - the social impact of a business on its employees, local communities and other stakeholders
> - Planet - the environmental impact of the business's operations, including waste, pollution and resource use
> - Profit - the financial performance of the business, measured through revenue, costs and profitability
> 
> AO2
> 
> - UC's training scheme for the long-term unemployed demonstrates its commitment to the people element of its triple bottom line
> - The recall of 2000 faulty components generated waste and may have increased UC's environmental impact, damaging its planet performance
> - The \$200,000 cost of the recall will reduce UC's profit in 2020, directly affecting the financial element of its triple bottom line

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'social enterprise'.

A social enterprise is a business that trades in order to achieve social or environmental aims **[1]**, reinvesting most of its profit into those aims rather than paying it to owners **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
>

> - An organisation that sells goods or services and reinvests the majority of its surplus into its social purpose instead of distributing it to shareholders

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Quill (QL)**
> 
> Quill (QL) runs private language schools in country J. It teaches English and Mandarin to adults and employs 60 teachers across four schools.
> 
> QL's owner, Dieter, has told staff that his objective is "to grow the business and improve teaching quality". Managers at each school have interpreted this differently. One has spent money on new classroom equipment, another has reduced class sizes, and a third has advertised heavily for new students.
> 
> At a recent meeting, Dieter's finance manager suggested replacing this with a SMART objective: to increase student numbers from 900 to 1,100 by the end of next year, while keeping the proportion of students who pass their final examination above 85%.

Explain **one** benefit to QL of setting SMART objectives.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit is that a SMART objective tells everyone exactly what QL is trying to achieve **[1]**. At present Dieter's aim to "grow the business and improve teaching quality" has been understood differently by each school manager, so one has bought equipment while another has advertised **[1]**. Replacing it with a target of 1,100 students and an 85% pass rate would give all four schools the same measurable goal, so their spending and effort pull in the same direction instead of against each other **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - SMART objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-limited, making clear exactly what must be achieved and by when
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Dieter's current aim has been interpreted differently by each of the four school managers, so a specific target removes that ambiguity and aligns their decisions
> - A measurable target of 1,100 students lets QL check progress during the year rather than discovering at the end that the aim was missed
> - Setting a deadline of the end of next year creates urgency, so managers act now instead of treating growth as something to address eventually
> - Including the 85% pass rate stops managers reaching the student target by lowering standards, since both parts of the objective must be met together
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common weakness is to write out what SMART stands for and stop there. Listing the acronym is knowledge, not explanation - the marks come from showing what one of those features actually does for this business. Pick the letter that matters most here and develop that one.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Torque (TQ)**
> 
> Torque (TQ) services and repairs cars in country H. It began in 2010 as a single garage owned by Elif, whose objective at the time was simply to earn enough to keep the business open.
> 
> By 2018 TQ was well established and Elif set a new objective of opening ten garages within five years. TQ now has twelve.
> 
> Electric vehicles have grown quickly in country H.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Electric vehicles in country H**
> 
> | Share of new cars sold that were electric, 2018 (%) | 4 |
> |---|---|
> | Share of new cars sold that were electric, 2025 (%) | 31 |
> | TQ mechanics qualified to service electric vehicles (%) | 15 |
> 
> Electric vehicles need less routine servicing than petrol cars, and most of TQ's mechanics are not yet qualified to work on them. Elif's objective for the next three years is to have every mechanic trained to service electric vehicles.

Explain **one** reason why TQ's objectives have changed over time.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that TQ's circumstances have changed as the business has developed **[1]**. In 2010 Elif's objective was survival, because a new garage with no reputation could easily fail; once TQ was established she was able to aim for growth instead, reaching twelve garages **[1]**. The objective has changed again because the market has moved, as electric vehicles rose from 4% to 31% of new car sales while only 15% of TQ's mechanics can service them, making training staff more urgent than opening further garages **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Objectives change as a business moves through different stages of its development, and as market conditions, technology, competition or regulation change around it
> 
> AO2
> 
> - In 2010 TQ was a single new garage with no reputation, so survival was the realistic objective; a new business that pursues rapid growth before it has customers is likely to fail
> - By 2018 TQ was established and had the reputation and cash flow to support expansion, so growth to ten garages became an achievable aim
> - Electric vehicles have risen from 4% to 31% of new car sales and need less routine servicing, so TQ's existing repair work will decline regardless of how many garages it operates
> - Only 15% of TQ's mechanics can service electric vehicles, so training has become more urgent than expansion - opening further garages staffed by mechanics unable to service a third of new cars would not help TQ
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks why something has changed, your answer must show both the before and the after. Naming only the current objective describes the situation rather than explaining the change, so use the dates and figures in the case to show what shifted and what caused it.

parts.problemMd: Analyse the** **ways in which ethics may influence the activities of a business.
parts.solutionMd:
One way ethics may influence business activities is through sourcing and supply chain decisions **[K]**. A business committed to ethical behaviour may refuse to use suppliers that employ child labour or pay extremely low wages, even if this would reduce costs significantly **[An]**. While this places the business at a cost disadvantage compared to less scrupulous competitors, it builds a positive reputation with consumers who increasingly choose brands that align with their values **[An]**. Over time, this trust generates greater customer loyalty and protects the business from reputational damage that could prove far more costly than the savings it forfeited **[An]**

Ethics may also influence a business's environmental decisions **[K]**. A business may reject production methods that pollute the environment, such as cheap waste disposal or high-emission processes, and instead invest in more sustainable alternatives **[An]**. This increases short-term operating costs but reduces the risk of legal penalties from regulators and reputational damage from pressure groups or negative media coverage **[An]**. It can also attract ethically minded customers and investors, improving long-term financial performance. In industries where environmental standards are tightening, early adoption of ethical practices can give a business a significant competitive advantage **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of ways in which ethics may influence the activities of a business |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of ways in which ethics may influence the activities of a business |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the ways in which ethics may influence the activities of a business |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of ways in which ethics may influence the activities of a business |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A business may refuse to source materials from suppliers that use child labour or pay poverty-level wages, even though this increases production costs. This builds consumer trust and a strong ethical reputation, which can drive brand loyalty and long-term revenue growth - particularly as consumers increasingly choose businesses that reflect their values
> - A business may reject production methods that pollute the environment, such as cheap waste disposal or high-emission processes, in favour of more sustainable but costlier alternatives. This reduces the risk of regulatory fines, protects the business from reputational damage caused by pressure groups or negative media coverage, and can attract ethically minded customers and investors
> - A business may avoid misleading or exploitative advertising - such as making false health claims or targeting vulnerable consumers - even if such tactics would increase short-term sales. Maintaining honest communication builds long-term customer relationships and reduces the risk of legal action or loss of consumer confidence
> - A business may develop fairer, more transparent relationships with suppliers rather than exploiting its buying power to force down prices. Stronger partnerships based on mutual trust tend to improve supply chain reliability and quality, reducing disruption and long-term costs
> - Ethical decisions across all areas of the business are likely to build a positive organisational culture, improving employee motivation and reducing labour turnover, which lowers recruitment and training costs while raising productivity
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **reasons why it is important for a business to set SMART objectives.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason SMART objectives are important is that they are measurable **[K]**, meaning a business can track its progress and assess whether it is on course to achieve its goals. Without a measurable target, such as 'increase market share by 5% within 12 months', there is no way of knowing whether the business is succeeding or falling short **[An]**. This allows managers to identify problems early and take corrective action before significant resources are wasted **[An]**. Consistently hitting measurable targets also builds confidence among shareholders and stakeholders, improving the business's ability to attract investment and support over time **[An]**

SMART objectives are also important because they are specific and achievable **[K]**, giving employees a clear sense of direction and realistic targets to work towards. Vague objectives such as 'do better this year' offer no clarity about what employees should prioritise or how success will be defined, leading to wasted effort and inconsistent decision-making **[An]**. Specific objectives focus effort on the activities that matter most. Achievable targets also maintain employee motivation - if targets are set too high, employees may become disengaged and productivity will fall **[An]**. Setting objectives that stretch but do not overwhelm is therefore essential for sustaining long-term business performance **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of why it is important for a business to set SMART objectives |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of why it is important for a business to set SMART objectives |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of why it is important for a business to set SMART objectives |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of why it is important for a business to set SMART objectives |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - SMART objectives are measurable, meaning a business can track its progress and assess whether it is on course to meet its goals. This allows managers to identify problems early and take corrective action before resources are wasted, making it far more likely that the business achieves what it set out to do.
> - SMART objectives are specific, giving employees and managers a clear sense of what needs to be achieved and why. Vague objectives such as 'improve performance' offer no direction, leading to wasted effort and inconsistent priorities. Specificity focuses the whole business on the activities that will deliver results.
> - SMART objectives are time-limited, which creates discipline and ensures that important longer-term goals are not sacrificed for short-term pressures. A deadline also provides a clear point at which performance can be reviewed, making accountability easier to enforce across departments and teams.
> - SMART objectives are achievable and realistic, which helps maintain employee motivation. Targets that are set too high can demoralise employees if they feel success is impossible; targets that are too easy provide no incentive to improve. Objectives that stretch but do not overwhelm employees help sustain productivity and engagement over time.
> - However, an over-reliance on SMART objectives could make a business inflexible and stifle creativity, particularly in fast-changing markets where rigid targets may become outdated before the time limit is reached
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two** reasons why a business should set SMART objectives.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason a business should set SMART objectives is that time-specific targets give employees a clear deadline to work towards **[K]**, allowing them to plan and organise their work more effectively. For example, a target to 'reduce operating costs by 20% over three years' makes it clear when performance will be judged **[An]**. This allows managers to monitor progress throughout the period and take corrective action if the business is falling behind **[An]**. Without a time limit, there is no urgency and employees may consistently prioritise short-term tasks at the expense of more important longer-term goals **[An]**

A business should also ensure objectives are realistic and agreed with employees rather than simply imposed on them **[K]**. If targets are perceived as unachievable - for example, demanding a large increase in productivity without providing additional resources or training - employees are likely to become demotivated **[An]**. This can lead to increased absenteeism and higher labour turnover, raising recruitment and training costs while reducing productivity further **[An]**. Objectives that are discussed and mutually agreed are more likely to gain employee commitment, creating a shared sense of purpose and significantly improving the chances that the business achieves what it set out to do **[An]**

> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of why a business should set SMART objectives |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - SMART objectives are time-specific, giving employees a clear deadline to work towards. This allows them to plan and organise their work effectively, and gives managers a defined point at which to assess whether the business is on track. Without a time limit, there is no urgency and longer-term goals may be continually delayed in favour of short-term priorities
> - SMART objectives are measurable, meaning progress can be monitored throughout the period, not just at the end. For example, if the operations department is targeting a 20% cost reduction over three years, managers can check progress annually and take corrective action if the business is falling behind, avoiding a much larger problem at the deadline
> - SMART objectives are realistic and, where possible, agreed with employees rather than simply imposed on them. Targets that are mutually discussed are more likely to be accepted and embraced, increasing employee commitment and the probability of success
> - If objectives are unrealistic - for example, demanding a 50% increase in output with no additional resources - employees may feel the targets are impossible and become demotivated. This can lead to increased absenteeism and higher labour turnover, raising recruitment and training costs and reducing overall productivity
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Analyse why mission statements are important to many businesses.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason mission statements are important is that they communicate the overall purpose and core values of a business to both internal and external stakeholders **[K]**. Internally, a mission statement provides a strategic backdrop against which managers can set objectives and make decisions. When all departments understand what the business ultimately stands for, their activities are more likely to be consistent and aligned**[An]**. For example, a business with a quality-focused mission will recognise that cutting costs in ways that compromise standards directly contradicts its purpose **[An]**. This reduces the risk of conflicting decisions across the organisation and ensures day-to-day operations support the business's long-term direction **[An]**

Mission statements can also motivate employees by giving them a shared sense of purpose beyond simply earning a wage **[K]**. When employees identify with the values expressed in a mission statement, they are more likely to feel engaged and committed to the success of the business **[An]**. This can reduce labour turnover, lower recruitment and training costs, and improve productivity **[An]**. A business that clearly communicates its purpose - for example, a commitment to sustainability or innovation - may also find it easier to attract like-minded candidates during recruitment, further strengthening its workforce over time **[An]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A mission statement communicates the core values and overall purpose of a business to internal and external stakeholders. Internally, it provides a strategic backdrop against which managers can set objectives and make decisions, ensuring that activities across different departments are consistent and aligned with the business's long-term direction
> - By clearly defining what the business stands for, a mission statement helps managers avoid decisions that contradict the business's stated purpose — for example, a business with a quality-focused mission will recognise that cutting costs in ways that compromise standards is inconsistent with its values
> - Mission statements can motivate employees by giving them a shared sense of purpose beyond simply earning a wage. When employees genuinely identify with the values expressed in the mission statement, they are more likely to feel engaged and committed, reducing labour turnover and improving productivity
> - A clearly communicated mission statement can also attract new employees who share the same values, strengthening the workforce and making recruitment easier — particularly relevant for businesses competing for skilled or specialist staff
> - However, mission statements have significant limitations. They are often criticised for being bland, vague and overly general, functioning as cynical public relations exercises rather than meaningful management tools. Marketing Marketing products made from recycled materials can be a major challenge in country A. Many consumers think these products are of inferior quality. However, C4T’s brand image is strong. Its products have featured in premium magazines and on websites aimed at consumers who are ‘socially responsible’. Kris works hard to keep the C4T website up-to-date and maintain its social media presence, as part of the company’s attempt to establish good customer relationships. An ambitious new idea Plastic water bottles have become a real environmental problem over recent years as more are bought and thrown away when empty. Jan Guiding Service (JGS) Jan loves being in the countryside. Many years ago, he visited country P, where mountains take up 80% of the land area. Country P is one of the poorest countries in the world, with very low income per head. Jan made his home there and took a job assisting with walking groups. He gained a certificate as a professional mountain walking guide. The start of JGS Five years ago Jan set up JGS, in partnership with Gorl, another professional mountain walking guide. JGS offers mountain walking tours. JGS organises and promotes these tours. Originally, Jan and Gorl guided most of the walking tours themselves. JGS has always outsourced all its travel and accommodation. Jan and Gorl are spending more time on managing the business and less time guiding as the demand for JGS tours increases. JGS now outsources most of its mountain guiding. Customers stay with host families in mountain villages, most of which cannot be reached by road. Host families are paid by JGS to provide food and accommodation for its customers. Many families compete to provide these services to JGS. Using outsourcing in this way gives JGS many benefits. JGS employs an administrator to organise outsourcing. JGS is one of the few businesses operating in this market. However, Jan knows that other businesses are becoming interested in offering mountain walking tours. Demand for JGS services JGS has not increased its prices for three years. Over 95% of JGS customers are visitors from country K. Demand for JGS tours is increasing and Jan thinks that income levels in country K are an important factor. Average income in country K rose by 5% in 2019. Demand for JGS tours from residents of country K increased by 20% in the same period. Jan currently believes that there is still time to get more bookings for quarters 3 and 4 in 2020. He also knows that increasing the effectiveness of the JGS Internet presence is important. Gorl has analysed sales figures for the last three years. Table 1 shows his results. He has used the moving average method and has forecast the centred moving average (trend) sales figure for Quarter 3 2021 of \$86560.

Jan and Gorl are planning to increase the number of employees for two main reasons: • The rapid growth of JGS means that three regional managers and additional administrative employees will be needed. • The government of country P has introduced new, stricter employment regulations. It has stated these will apply to all businesses. This now means that businesses using outsourcing must insist that outsource providers keep to these stricter employment regulations. Jan and Gorl think that providing guiding and accommodation services through direct employment of workers is the best way of meeting these requirements. They are unsure whether to offer flexible temporary contracts or part time permanent positions. Jan suggested to Gorl that: ‘Our rapidly expanding business and external environment changes mean that a clear effective organisational structure will be very important.’ Jan wishes to keep control and is reluctant to give responsibility to employees who might not be reliable. He added: ‘Centralising decision making enables rapid decisions and is key to success. We must have authority and make employees accountable to us.’ Gorl replied: ‘Employees can be trusted to take decisions. They are closer to the problems and find solutions faster. Delegation is essential for success.’ They think JGS might need a marketing department. This would be responsible for the planned increase in marketing activities necessary to maintain expansion.

Costing each tour Gorl and Jan have different views on the minimum number of customers needed before each tour can take place. This is because they have different views about how to deal with the fixed and variable costs. JGS policy is to provisionally confirm that a tour will take place once customer numbers reach six. The business then hopes to get at least two more customers before the tour starts. However, Jan now thinks that a tour should go ahead with just two customers. Gorl is not happy about this. They discuss the financial information in Table 2. Table 2: Cost and price information (\$) Fixed costs per tour: administration, marketing, guide, transport 550 Variable costs per customer: accommodation, food 370 Price per customer 480 Corporate social responsibility issues JGS has a business model based on attracting customers who wish to experience the culture of people who live in country P’s high mountains. Jan and Gorl are aware that this culture is under threat from too many tourists, cheap souvenir production, corruption and increasing environmental damage. JGS tries to operate to the highest standards, which can result in high costs. However, other businesses do not. Consequently, there is irresponsible forestry, litter, inappropriate payments by tourists, bribes for local authorities and businesses not paying villagers a fair price for services. Pressure groups in country K and country P are increasing their demands that tourist businesses provide for the needs of the various communities in country P. Some customers might be willing to pay higher prices to ethical and responsible travel businesses. The government in country P has set up an official enquiry into the corporate social responsibility of the tourism industry. Additional opportunities for growth Jan and Gorl are always aiming to expand JGS. They are enthusiastic about the future and are considering two growth options. They know it is very important to make an assessment of the risk involved in each option.

Option 1: a partnership with KrazyTours Jan has held initial talks with KrazyTours; a large multinational tourist operator that is considering expanding into country P. KrazyTours is only interested in a partnership with a business already operating. In effect this would be a franchise agreement. The two businesses agreed the following points: • JGS would arrange mountain walks in country P with agreed costs that would need to be paid in advance. • KrazyTours market these holidays in over 120 countries, providing JGS with client lists. JGS would pay a fee for each tour. This arrangement offers the possibility of increased revenue and profit for JGS but carries risks. KrazyTours may fail to deliver customers and may pressure JGS to lower prices significantly. Option 2: guided walks for tourists Expanding into the general tourist market by offering guided visits and/or walks to attractions. These include historical sites, temples, markets and a wildlife park. This would require JGS to: • research and identify suitable venues with appropriate transport and accommodation arrangements • employ suitably qualified guides to take charge of the groups • engage in additional targeted marketing. The risks are that several businesses from country P already offer such holidays and competition is higher than for mountain walks. Jan presented Gorl with a completed decision tree calculation shown in Table 3. They discuss the risks involved in each option as well as the forces that might make them choose one option rather than the other. The strongest reason JGS should maintain high CSR standards is that its business model depends entirely on the culture and environment it is selling **[K]**. Customers visit country P to experience authentic mountain life **[Ap]**. If irresponsible tourism - such as environmental damage, litter and unfair payments to villagers - destroys this culture, the reason for visiting disappears entirely. For JGS, maintaining CSR is not just an ethical decision but a commercial one; it is protecting the product that generates all of its revenue **[An]** High CSR standards also give JGS a clear marketing advantage **[K]**. Pressure groups in both country K and country P are demanding more responsible behaviour from tourist businesses **[Ap]**. Some customers are already willing to pay higher prices to ethical operators, which could help JGS charge a premium and stand out from cheaper competitors entering the market. Treating local host families fairly also ensures they deliver good quality service, which is essential to customer satisfaction **[An]** The main challenge is cost **[K]**. Evaluate the benefits to SC of having corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit of making CSR a business objective is that it could protect SC from losing customers over its use of plastic packaging **[K] [Ap]**. A similar food manufacturer in country T recently lost many customers due to negative media reports about plastic. SC's target market - people interested in nature, sports, health and travel **[Ap] **- is particularly likely to care about environmental issues. A clear commitment to CSR would show these customers that SC takes their concerns seriously, helping to protect its \$51m revenue and keep existing customers loyal **[An]**

CSR could also help SC grow its market share **[K]**. SC currently holds 34% of the market compared to OK's 40% **[Ap]**. If a strong CSR reputation attracts environmentally conscious customers away from OK, SC could close this gap. Customers who care about sustainability are often willing to pay higher prices for products that match their values, meaning SC could improve its profit margins even if changing its packaging increases costs in the short term **[An]**

Overall, SC should make CSR a business objective **[E]**. The most important reason is that plastic packaging is already a known risk - doing nothing could lead to the same damaging customer losses seen by the other food manufacturer **[Ap]**. Although new packaging will cost more in the short term, the long-term benefits of protecting SC's reputation and growing its market share make this the right decision for a business whose target customers care deeply about environmental issues **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Evaluate the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business.
parts.solutionMd:
There is a strong argument that a mission statement is only valuable if it genuinely influences how a bank operates. A bank's strategy covers long-term decisions such as which markets to enter and how to manage risk **[K] [Ap]**. Tactics are the day-to-day departmental decisions - such as lending policy and customer service standards - that support this strategy **[K] [Ap]**. If a mission statement shapes neither, it is just a slogan. Many banks produce statements so vague that they provide no practical guidance. A mission statement that changes nothing adds cost without adding value** [An]**

However, mission statements also have external value beyond strategy and tactics. They communicate the bank's values to customers, investors and regulators **[K] [Ap]**, making it more accountable to stakeholders. After the 2008 financial crisis, many banks were criticised for abandoning their stated values **[Ap]**, causing serious reputational damage. A clear mission statement gives stakeholders a standard to hold the bank to, and that external accountability can indirectly shape behaviour even without formal strategic influence **[An]**

Mission statements can also support recruitment and employee motivation **[K]**. Staff who believe in the purpose of their organisation tend to be more engaged and productive. A bank committed to ethical lending may attract employees who share those values, improving morale and reducing staff turnover without the mission statement needing to directly dictate specific tactical decisions **[An]**

Overall, the view is largely correct - the primary value of a mission statement lies in whether it genuinely shapes how the bank behaves **[E]**. A vague statement that changes nothing is of little practical worth. However, its external impact on customer trust and stakeholder accountability means it retains some value even without direct strategic influence **[E]**. The most important test is whether the bank actually lives by its mission. If it does, the statement adds real value; if it does not, it becomes little more than a public relations exercise **[E]**

> - A mission statement that does not change how the bank actually operates is essentially just a slogan. If it does not shape the bank's long-term strategy - such as which markets to enter, how to manage risk, or what products to develop - it adds cost without adding value. Many banks produce statements so vague ("we put customers first", "we deliver excellence") that they provide no practical guidance and have no measurable effect on decisions
> - Banks are primarily driven by the objective of profit maximisation. If the mission statement conflicts with or simply exists alongside this goal without influencing it, senior managers are likely to ignore it when making real strategic decisions, rendering it meaningless
> - A rigid mission statement could actually harm the bank by locking it into a fixed direction and preventing it from responding to new market opportunities or changes in the economic environment, reducing strategic flexibility rather than improving it
> 
> Arguments that mission statements have value beyond direct strategic influence
> 
> - Mission statements communicate a bank's values externally to customers, investors and regulators. After the 2008 financial crisis, banks that abandoned their stated values faced severe reputational damage. A published mission statement makes a bank accountable to its stakeholders - this external pressure can indirectly shape behaviour even without the statement being embedded in formal strategy
> - A well-crafted mission statement can improve employee motivation and support recruitment, particularly of staff who share the bank's stated values. Employees who believe in the purpose of their organisation tend to be more engaged and productive, reducing labour turnover and improving service quality - benefits that do not require the statement to dictate specific tactical decisions
> - Mission statements can also reassure investors and regulators that the bank has a clear ethical framework, which may reduce scrutiny and the cost of compliance over time
> 
> Evaluation
> 
> - The view is largely correct. The primary value of a mission statement lies in whether it genuinely influences the bank's behaviour. A statement that changes nothing is of limited practical worth, regardless of how well-worded it is
> - However, its external value in building customer trust and stakeholder accountability means it is not entirely worthless even if internal strategy is mainly profit-driven. The two are connected: a credible mission statement can attract customers and investors in ways that ultimately do affect strategy
> - The key judgement is whether the mission statement is genuine or just a PR exercise. If the bank actually lives by it, the statement delivers value both internally and externally. If it does not, it risks damaging credibility when the gap between stated values and actual behaviour becomes apparent
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

parts.problemMd:
‘Ethics should always influence the human resource management (HRM) activities of a mining business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
The strongest reason ethics should always influence HRM in a mining business is health and safety **[K]**. Mining is one of the most dangerous industries in the world - workers face risks including underground collapse, flooding and toxic gas **[Ap]**. Ethical HRM requires rigorous safety training, proper protective equipment, and clear safety procedures for all employees. Without this, accidents are more likely, and in mining they can be fatal. A business that ignores safety ethics not only harms its workers but risks legal action, government investigation, and reputational damage that could threaten the entire operation **[An]**

Ethical HRM is also important in how mining businesses recruit and manage workers **[K]**. Mines are often in low-income areas where workers have few alternatives **[Ap]**, making exploitation easier. Unethical practices, such as below-minimum wages or unsafe conditions, may reduce costs in the short term but damage morale and increase labour turnover, reducing productivity. Fair pay and transparent dismissal procedures build a more stable and motivated workforce **[An]**

However, "always" is a demanding standard. Fully ethical HRM - better equipment, higher wages, more training - increases costs significantly **[K]**. In an industry where international buyers demand low raw material prices **[Ap]**, ethical businesses can be undercut by rivals in countries with weaker labour laws. If costs become too high and the business closes, the resulting job losses are themselves harmful to workers **[An]**

Overall, I largely agree with the view. Health and safety ethics should always apply **[E]**. No financial saving justifies workers dying or being seriously injured, and the legal and reputational consequences of ignoring safety are too severe **[E]**. Other ethical standards, such as fair pay and working conditions, are important but may be more constrained by competitive pressures. Mining businesses that commit to ethical HRM tend to be more sustainable in the long run - a safer, better-treated workforce is also a more productive one **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **5** | 17-20 | - Effective evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a mine if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **4** | 15-16 | - Limited evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of the extent to which you agree with the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the view that a mission statement is only important to a bank if it significantly influences the strategy and tactics of that business |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of mission statements, strategy and/or tactics |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> **Arguments that ethics should always influence HRM in a mining business**
> 
> - Mining is one of the most dangerous industries in the world. Workers face risks including underground collapse, flooding, toxic gas and heavy machinery. Ethical HRM requires rigorous safety training, protective equipment and clear safety procedures for all employees. Without this, accidents are more likely and in mining they can be fatal. A business that ignores safety ethics faces legal action, government investigation and severe reputational damage, all of which threaten the long-term survival of the business
> - Mines are often located in low-income regions where workers have few employment alternatives, making exploitation easier. Unethical HRM practices - such as paying below the minimum wage, using zero-hours contracts, or demanding excessive overtime - reduce short-term costs but damage morale and increase labour turnover. A demotivated, unsafe workforce is less productive and more likely to make costly mistakes. Ethical treatment, fair pay, and clear dismissal procedures build a more stable and committed workforce.
> - Poor workforce planning in a mining business can lead to understaffing, overworking employees, and increased rates of accidents and absenteeism. Ethical workforce planning ensures the business has sufficient trained workers for each role, protecting both safety and productivity
> - Management that communicates openly and involves workers in decisions improves trust and reduces the risk of industrial disputes - which can be extremely costly in an industry where stopping production even briefly has major financial consequences
> 
> **Arguments against "always" - challenges and limits**
> 
> - Fully ethical HRM significantly increases costs - better safety equipment, higher wages, more training, and better working conditions all reduce profit margins. In a globally competitive raw materials market, businesses in countries with stricter ethical standards may be undercut by rivals in countries with weaker labour laws and less enforcement
> - If ethical HRM costs make the business uncompetitive and it is forced to close, the resulting job losses could be argued to cause more harm to workers than the original ethical compromises - a difficult trade-off with no simple answer
> - The extent to which a mining business can afford to be fully ethical may depend on its size and profitability. A large, profitable multinational can absorb higher ethical costs more easily than a small mining operation in a developing economy
> - In some countries, governments are unwilling to enforce ethical standards in mining because of the tax revenues and employment the industry provides, reducing external pressure on businesses to act ethically
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - The word "always" is key. Health and safety ethics should always apply - the human cost of ignoring them is too great and the legal and reputational consequences too severe. No short-term saving on safety equipment or training is worth the risk of worker deaths or serious injuries
> - Other ethical standards - such as fair wages and working conditions - are important but may be more constrained by competitive and financial pressures. The degree to which these can be applied may depend on the country of operation and the regulatory environment
> - The strongest argument for ethics "always" influencing HRM is the long-term commercial one: safer, better-treated workers are more productive, less likely to leave, and less likely to cause costly accidents. Ethical HRM is therefore not just a moral obligation - it is sound business practice
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

parts.problemMd: Discuss why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason shareholders of a plc might not support CSR is that it increases costs without directly increasing profit **[K]**. Shareholders invest in a plc mainly to receive dividends, which depend on the business making a profit. CSR activities - such as paying workers more than the legal minimum or reducing pollution at extra cost - use up money that could otherwise be paid to shareholders as dividends **[An]**. Many shareholders, especially large investment funds **[Ap]**, are focused purely on financial returns and will oppose anything that reduces profit without a clear financial benefit in return **[An]**

Shareholders in a plc also tend to think short term **[K] **because they can sell their shares quickly if the business underperforms. The benefits of CSR, such as a better reputation and greater customer loyalty, can take several years to improve profits. A shareholder who plans to sell their shares within the next couple of years **[Ap]** is unlikely to support spending money now on CSR programmes that may only pay off long after they have sold up **[An]**

However, not all shareholders think this way **[E]**. A growing number of investors specifically choose to invest in businesses with strong CSR records **[Ap]**, and they recognise that poor CSR can damage a brand and reduce the value of their shares **[An]**. Overall, shareholder opposition to CSR is most likely when investors are focused on short-term profits **[E]**. If a business can show that CSR will improve profits in the long run, even profit-focused shareholders may change their minds **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 9-12 | - Effective evaluation of why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective |
> | **3** | 7-8 | - Limited evaluation of why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective |
> | **2** | 3-6 | - Analysis and application of why the shareholders of a public limited company might not support corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a business objective. |
> | **1** | 1-2 | - Knowledge and understanding of shareholders / public limited companies / CSR / business objectives |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> Why shareholders might not support CSR
> 
> - Shareholders in a plc primarily invest to earn dividends and capital growth, both of which depend on profit. CSR activities - such as paying above-minimum wages, donating to community projects, or investing in cleaner production methods - increase costs without directly generating revenue, reducing profit margins and the dividends available to shareholders
> - Many shareholders, particularly institutional investors managing pension or savings funds, have a short-term investment outlook and measure success by near-term financial returns. The benefits of CSR - improved reputation, greater brand loyalty, reduced regulatory risk - may take years to generate financial gains, making CSR a poor use of resources in the eyes of a shareholder who may sell their shares within two or three years
> - Some shareholders hold the view that the purpose of a business is to generate profit, and that social good is the responsibility of governments rather than companies. From this perspective, CSR represents an inappropriate use of shareholder funds
> - Shareholders may also feel that legal compliance and basic ethical behaviour are sufficient, without the additional cost and management time required for a formal CSR programme
> 
> Why some shareholders might support CSR — evaluation
> 
> - Not all shareholders oppose CSR. The growth of ESG (environmental, social and governance) investing means an increasing number of shareholders actively seek businesses with strong CSR credentials, particularly long-term institutional investors and ethical investment funds
> - Poor CSR can generate damaging press coverage, consumer boycotts, or regulatory action - all of which destroy shareholder value in ways that far outweigh the short-term cost savings of ignoring social responsibility
> - The extent of shareholder opposition depends on the composition of the shareholder base. A plc with a high proportion of short-term, profit-focused institutional investors is more likely to face resistance to CSR than one whose shareholders take a longer-term view of value creation
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'business strategy'.
parts.solutionMd:
Business strategy is a long-term plan setting out how a business intends to achieve its objectives **[1]**, covering the whole organisation and the resources it will use to get there **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A long-term plan of action designed to achieve a business's overall objectives
> - The direction a business chooses to take, together with the way it intends to use its resources to compete successfully
> - A whole-organisation plan covering where the business wants to be in the long run and how it will get there

> **[exam-tip]**
> Strategy and tactics are easily confused. Strategy is long-term and covers the whole business; tactics are the short-term actions that carry it out. If your definition would also describe running a weekend promotion, it is describing a tactic rather than a strategy.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'PEST analysis'.
parts.solutionMd:
PEST analysis is a framework used to examine the political, economic, social and technological factors outside a business **[1]**, so that it can judge how those factors may affect its plans **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A framework for examining the political, economic, social and technological influences in a business's external environment
> - A tool that identifies outside factors a business cannot control, so their likely effect on its strategy can be assessed
> - An analysis of the external conditions surrounding a business, grouped under political, economic, social and technological headings

> **[exam-tip]**
> Naming what the letters stand for shows you have learned the acronym, but a definition also needs to say what the tool is for. Add the purpose: judging how outside factors may affect the business. Frameworks produce something useful, and the second mark usually sits in what they produce.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'blue ocean strategy'.
parts.solutionMd:
Blue ocean strategy is an approach in which a business creates a new, uncontested market rather than competing in an existing one **[1]**, so that it faces little or no direct competition **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A strategy of creating new market space where no competitors currently operate, rather than fighting for share in a crowded market
> - An approach that makes competition largely irrelevant by offering something for which there is not yet an established market
> - Seeking growth by opening up untapped demand instead of competing directly with rivals in a saturated market

> **[exam-tip]**
> Some strategy names are metaphors, and blue ocean is one of them. The examiner is not looking for the image but for the idea behind it: creating a market with no competitors, as opposed to fighting in a crowded one. Explain the idea rather than the picture.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'market penetration'.
parts.solutionMd:
Market penetration is a growth strategy in which a business sells more of its existing products **[1]** to customers in the markets it already serves **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Selling more of a business's current products in the markets it already operates in, for example by attracting more customers or increasing purchase frequency
> - The lowest-risk strategy in the Ansoff matrix, combining existing products with existing markets
> - Growth achieved by winning a larger share of a market the business is already in, rather than by launching new products or entering new markets

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Ansoff matrix sets product against market, so every strategy within it has two halves. Market penetration means existing product and existing market, and an answer naming only one of those leaves a mark behind. Whenever a term comes from a matrix, check you have covered both dimensions.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'contingency planning'.
parts.solutionMd:
Contingency planning is the process of preparing in advance for events that might disrupt a business **[1]**, setting out what the business would do if such an event actually happened **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Preparing plans in advance for possible emergencies or disruptions, so the business can respond quickly if they occur
> - Identifying risks that could seriously affect operations and deciding beforehand how each one would be handled
> - Planning for events that may never happen, so the business is not forced to react without preparation if they do

> **[exam-tip]**
> A contingency plan exists for something that might happen, not something that will. Your definition needs that conditional element: preparing now for an event that may occur later. A definition describing ordinary forward planning misses what makes contingency planning distinct.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Slate (SL)**
> 
> Slate (SL) owns 26 DIY and hardware stores in country F, selling tools, paint and building materials. It employs 900 people.
> 
> SL's sales to trade customers such as builders have grown by 19% over three years, while sales to household customers have fallen by 8%. Two large online retailers now deliver tools and materials to homes across country F within a day.
> 
> SL owns all 26 of its stores rather than renting them, and has no long-term borrowing.
> 
> SL's board has never carried out a formal review of the business's position. A new managing director has asked for a SWOT analysis before deciding what SL should do next.

Explain **one** benefit to SL of conducting a SWOT analysis.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit is that a SWOT analysis would show SL where its real strengths lie **[1]**. SL owns all 26 of its stores outright and has no long-term borrowing, which many of its competitors could not say **[1]**. Setting that alongside the threat from next-day online delivery would help the new managing director see that SL can actually afford to invest in changing its stores, so the decision about what to do next rests on SL's real position rather than on guesswork **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A SWOT analysis sets out a business's internal strengths and weaknesses alongside the external opportunities and threats it faces, giving a structured basis for decisions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Owning all 26 stores outright with no long-term borrowing is a financial strength giving SL capacity to fund change, which the board may not have recognised
> - Trade sales up 19% against household sales down 8% identifies both an opportunity and a weakness that SL has not yet responded to
> - Two online retailers offering next-day delivery is a clear external threat, and setting it against SL's strengths shows which responses are realistic
> - Since SL has never conducted a formal review, the analysis gives the new managing director a shared starting point with a board used to deciding without one
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A SWOT analysis only earns marks if you say what the business does with it. Listing what goes in each of the four boxes describes the tool; explaining how the findings change a decision is what earns the development marks. Always finish with the decision the analysis informs.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** of Porter's generic strategies.
parts.solutionMd:
One of Porter's generic strategies is cost leadership **[1]**. A business following this strategy aims to produce at a lower cost than any of its competitors, usually by producing on a large scale or by using highly efficient processes **[1]**. Because its costs are lower, it can either charge the same price as rivals and earn a wider margin, or charge less and win customers while still making a profit, which higher-cost competitors cannot match for long **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Porter identified three generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation and focus, applied either to a broad market or to a narrow segment
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Cost leadership means producing more cheaply than rivals, allowing either a wider margin at the same price or a lower price competitors cannot match profitably
> - Differentiation means offering something customers value that rivals do not provide, supporting a higher price and reducing the need to compete on cost
> - A focus strategy concentrates on a narrow segment and serves it better than firms treating the whole market as one, which suits smaller businesses without scale advantages
> - Porter argued that a business failing to commit to one of these becomes stuck in the middle, competing effectively on neither cost nor distinctiveness
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks about a named theory, choose one element and name it correctly. Porter's generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and focus. An answer gesturing at "being cheap or being different" without using the terms is unlikely to convince the examiner you know the model.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Nimbus (NB)**
> 
> Nimbus (NB) installs solar panels on homes and small businesses in country A. It employs 120 people and has grown quickly.
> 
> Around 55% of NB's orders come from customers claiming a government grant that covers a quarter of the cost of installation. The government has said the grant will be reviewed next year but has not said what it will decide.
> 
> The price NB pays for solar panels has fallen by 30% in four years, but two of its three panel suppliers are based in one country, which has recently introduced new export controls.
> 
> NB's owner has begun preparing plans for several different possible futures.

Explain **one** benefit to NB of scenario planning.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit is that NB can prepare for outcomes it has no way of predicting **[1]**. The government has said it will review the grant that supports 55% of NB's orders, but has not said what it will decide **[1]**. By planning for both the grant continuing and the grant being withdrawn, NB can work out in advance how it would cut costs or find new customers, so it could act immediately rather than losing months of sales while it decided what to do **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Scenario planning involves preparing for several possible futures rather than forecasting a single most likely outcome, so the business is ready whichever occurs
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The grant supports 55% of NB's orders and its future is genuinely unknown, so a single forecast would be a guess whereas planning for both outcomes covers either result
> - Export controls in the country where two of NB's three suppliers are based create a second uncertainty that scenario planning can address alongside the grant question
> - Agreed responses prepared in advance mean NB can act at once if the grant is withdrawn, instead of losing sales while its board works out a reply
> - Working through the scenarios may itself reveal how exposed NB is, prompting it to reduce its reliance on grant-supported orders or on suppliers in one country before anything changes
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Scenario planning does not predict the future, and answers claiming that it does tend to lose marks. Its value is preparedness: the business decides in advance what it would do under each outcome. Frame your explanation around being ready, not around knowing what will happen.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** feature of transformational leadership.
parts.solutionMd:
One feature of transformational leadership is that the leader sets out a clear vision of what the business could become **[1]**. Rather than simply telling employees what to do, the leader explains why the change matters and how each person contributes to it **[1]**. Employees who understand and share that vision are more willing to accept difficult changes and to put in effort beyond what their job strictly requires, which is what allows a business to change direction quickly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Transformational leadership involves inspiring employees to commit to a shared vision and to perform beyond normal expectations, rather than managing them through instructions and rewards alone
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Setting out a clear vision gives employees a reason to accept change, which matters most when a business is altering direction and staff would otherwise resist
> - Leading by example builds trust, so employees are more willing to persist through difficult periods when the benefits are not yet visible
> - Paying attention to individuals and developing them raises capability as well as motivation, so the business is better able to deliver the change it wants
> - Encouraging employees to question existing methods generates ideas from the people closest to the work, which an instruction-based approach would never surface
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Leadership questions reward description of what the leader does, not what kind of person they are. Words such as inspiring or charismatic describe personality; setting a vision, explaining why change matters and developing individuals are actions. Write about behaviour and the development marks follow naturally.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Prism (PR)**
> 
> Prism (PR) is an architecture practice in country D, employing 240 people across four offices.
> 
> PR was founded by two architects who still lead it. Every design must be approved personally by one of them before it is shown to a client, and junior architects are expected to follow the practice's established style closely.
> 
> PR has won awards for the quality and consistency of its work. However, three of its largest clients have recently asked for more unusual and experimental designs, and two junior architects have left saying their ideas were never considered.
> 
> PR has never won work in the growing market for timber-framed buildings.

Explain **one** way PR's corporate culture could affect its decision-making.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is that PR's culture concentrates decisions in very few hands **[1]**. Every design must be approved personally by one of the two founders before a client sees it, and junior architects are expected to follow the established style **[1]**. Ideas that do not match the founders' preferences therefore never reach a client at all, which helps explain both why two junior architects left saying their ideas were never considered and why PR has never won work in the growing timber-framed market **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Corporate culture is the set of shared values, beliefs and ways of working within a business, and it shapes which decisions are made, who makes them, and which options are considered at all
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Requiring personal approval from one of the two founders concentrates decision-making, so options not matching their preferences are filtered out before anyone else sees them
> - Expecting junior architects to follow an established style produces the consistency PR has won awards for, but narrows the range of designs the practice is willing to propose
> - Three large clients now want more experimental work, which PR's culture makes it slow to supply, so the culture that built its reputation may now be costing it business
> - Two junior architects have already left because their ideas were never considered, so the culture affects not only which decisions are taken but whether PR keeps the people who could widen its options
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Culture is invisible, so show the route by which it reaches an actual decision. Here that route runs through who is allowed to approve a design and which ideas therefore reach a client. Answers describing what a culture is like, without tracing it to a decision, rarely get past the first mark.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Reed (RD)**
> 
> Reed (RD) manufactures woodwind and brass instruments in country J. Founded forty years ago, it employs 260 people and sells mainly to schools and to specialist music shops.
> 
> School music programmes in country J have been cut as education budgets have tightened, and RD's revenue has fallen steadily as a result.
> 
> **Table 1.1: RD selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in 2020 (\$m) | 38 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 31 |
> | Employees | 260 |
> | Cost of entering the audio speaker market (\$m) | 9 |
> | Share of the speaker market held by the three largest brands (%) | 71 |
> 
> RD's board has proposed diversifying into the manufacture of high-end audio speakers, a market RD has never entered. The \$9m needed would be raised by borrowing.
> 
> RD's sales team has always sold to schools and music shops. It has no experience of selling consumer electronics.

Analyse **two** risks to RD of diversifying into the audio speaker market.
parts.solutionMd:
One risk is that RD has no experience of the market it plans to enter **[K]**. RD has spent forty years making instruments for schools and music shops, and its sales team is built around those customers rather than around consumer electronics **[Ap]**. Selling speakers would mean reaching retailers and buyers RD has never dealt with, so it could easily misjudge which features customers want or how much they are willing to pay **[An]**. Mistakes of that kind are expensive here, because RD would already have spent the \$9m setting up production before discovering that the product does not sell as expected **[An]** A second risk is that RD would be entering a market already dominated by established brands **[K]**. Three companies hold 71% of the speaker market, and they have recognised names and existing shelf space that RD does not **[Ap]**. To win customers RD would probably have to price low or spend heavily on marketing, and either choice reduces the profit the new venture returns **[An]**. Because the \$9m is borrowed, RD must meet interest payments whether or not the speakers sell, so a slow start would put real pressure on a business whose revenue has already fallen from \$38m to \$31m **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

**Background**

Kopara Beverages (KB) is a private limited company based in country P. It manufactures and sells premium fruit juices and plant-based drinks, including cold-pressed juices, coconut water blends, and protein smoothies. Founded 15 years ago by entrepreneur Lily Sato, KB now employs 400 workers in one large production facility in country P.

KB sells its products domestically and has recently begun exporting to country Q, where demand for healthy, natural drinks is growing rapidly. KB's mission is 'to bring nutritious, sustainably produced beverages to customers across the world'.

**Organisational Structure**

Two years ago, KB moved from a centralised management structure to a decentralised one, giving production and marketing managers greater autonomy over day-to-day decisions. Lily believes the change has increased innovation and improved employee morale.

However, KB's Finance Director has raised concerns about inconsistent financial decisions being made across departments and a lack of coordinated budgeting.

**Competitive Pressures**

The domestic market for beverages in country P has become increasingly competitive. Several large multinational companies (MNCs) have entered the market with similar healthy drink products, often at significantly lower prices than KB. KB's share of the domestic market has fallen from 18% to 14% over the past two years.

KB's Marketing Director is recommending that KB invests in product innovation — developing new flavours, new formats, and stronger branding — to differentiate its products from MNC rivals and justify its premium price.

The Finance Director disagrees, believing that KB must reduce prices to remain competitive and maintain market share.

Read the [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2026/04/45237-Insert%20-%20CIE%20A%20Level%20Business%20Paper%203%20Insert%20Practice%20Set%202.pdf)before answering this question.

'Investing in product innovation and stronger branding is the most effective way for KB to respond to increased competition from multinational companies in its domestic market.'

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Product innovation involves developing new or improved products to meet customer needs. Branding creates a distinct identity that customers associate with a business. Porter's differentiation strategy argues that businesses can compete effectively by making their products stand out in ways that justify a premium price, rather than competing purely on cost **[K]**

The Marketing Director's view has strong strategic logic. The MNCs entering KB's domestic market are likely to have significant economies of scale **[K]** and lower costs than KB, meaning that trying to match their prices would compress KB's margins without necessarily winning back customers **[An]**. KB's domestic market share has already fallen from 18% to 14% **[Ap]**, suggesting that competing on price is not a viable path. By contrast, KB has a genuine USP - its commitment to natural, sustainably sourced ingredients **[Ap]** - which larger MNCs with mass-production processes cannot easily replicate. Investing in innovation and branding that builds on this USP could attract health-conscious consumers who are willing to pay more for a product they trust, reducing the impact of price competition **[An]**

A stronger brand also increases customer loyalty **[K]**. Consumers who identify with KB's values - natural ingredients, sustainability, premium quality **[Ap]** - are less likely to switch to a cheaper MNC alternative. This makes brand investment a long-term protection against competitive pressure, not just a short-term marketing tool **[An]**

However, there are significant limitations to this approach. Brand investment and product innovation take time to influence consumer behaviour **[K]**, and KB's market share is already falling. KB's net profit declined from \$576,000 in 2022 to \$510,000 in 2023 **[Ap]** despite rising revenue, and long-term borrowings have increased significantly, suggesting limited finances for large-scale R&D or marketing spending **[An]**

KB should also consider expanding further into country Q, where export revenue has already grown by 35% **[Ap]** and the market conditions are more favourable, as an alternative route to growth that reduces reliance on the increasingly competitive domestic market

Overall, I partially agree with the statement **[E]**. Product innovation and stronger branding is the right strategic direction for KB; competing on price with MNCs is unlikely to succeed. However, it is not sufficient on its own, and the speed of KB's market share decline **[Ap]** means that faster, complementary actions,  such as a customer loyalty programme or faster investment in country Q, are also needed alongside any long-term innovation strategy  **[E]**
