Marco would like advice on which strategic direction SES should pursue. > > **Appendix 1: The renewable energy market in country T (2016)** > > - The government of country T has committed to generating 50% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030. > - Solar energy is the fastest-growing renewable energy source in country T, with installations rising by 22% per year. > - Growing public awareness of climate change is driving strong demand from residential and commercial customers. > - Government subsidies for residential solar installations are generous but are scheduled to be reduced from 2021. > - Competition for government contracts is intense; however, profit margins on public sector contracts are higher than on private sector work. > - MNCs from Europe and Asia are beginning to establish operations in country T, benefiting from economies of scale and established brand recognition. > > **Appendix 2: HR Director's report following SES's acquisition of EcoGrid (2018)** > > EcoGrid was a family-run business of 45 employees. It had a flat organisational structure, a culture of autonomy and flexible working, and a strong reputation for technical innovation in energy storage systems. > > SES operates with a more hierarchical management structure. Following the acquisition, SES standardised HR practices across both companies. EcoGrid employees were moved from flexible contracts to fixed-hours annualised contracts. A third of EcoGrid's specialist engineers chose to leave within twelve months. > > Recruiting qualified energy storage engineers in country T is difficult. Training new engineers to the required standard takes an average of 18 months. Productivity in the EcoGrid division has fallen significantly since the acquisition. Several planned product development projects have been delayed. > > **Appendix 3: SES AI energy management software (2020)** > > - Software is integrated into all new SES solar systems and is compatible with EcoGrid storage units. > - Optimises energy use in real time, reducing customer energy bills by an estimated 15–20%. > - Revenue model: customers pay an annual subscription fee of \$120 per year. > - 12,000 customers are currently subscribed to the platform; subscription revenue is growing at 8% per year. > - Development cost: \$2.5m, funded entirely from SES's retained profit. > - The platform is widely regarded within the industry as technically advanced, but requires ongoing investment to maintain and update. > > **Appendix 4: Analysis of SES's financial accounts between 2018 and 2022** > > | | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | > |---|---|---|---|---|---| > | Current ratio | 1.8 : 1 | 1.6 : 1 | 1.4 : 1 | 1.3 : 1 | 1.2 : 1 | > | Acid test ratio | 1.2 : 1 | 1.0 : 1 | 0.8 : 1 | 0.7 : 1 | 0.6 : 1 | > | Return on capital employed (%) | 18 | 15 | 13 | 11 | 9 | > | Gearing (%) | 12 | 22 | 28 | 32 | 38 | > | Profit for the year (\$m) | 2.1 | 1.8 | 1.6 | 1.4 | 1.2 | Advise Marco on which strategic option - Option A or Option B - SES should pursue to secure its long-term future.
parts.solutionMd:
Using Ansoff's Matrix, Option A is a market development strategy. Option B  is related diversification, given the technological overlap between solar energy, battery storage, and EV charging** [K]**

The case for Option A is that country U's government incentives have created rapid demand for solar energy** [Ap]**, and entering early could give SES a first-mover advantage** [K]** before MNCs move in. However, SES's financial position makes this very risky. ROCE has fallen from 18% to 9% between 2018 and 2022, profit has declined every year, gearing has risen to 38%, and the acid test ratio has fallen to 0.6:1** [Ap]**,  well below the safe benchmark of 1:1. The Finance Director has already warned that any new strategy must be carefully costed. Taking on the additional capital required for international expansion - market research, regulatory compliance, building an installation team in a new country - when SES is already financially stretched would be extremely high risk** [An]**

Option B is more strategically sound. SES already has the building blocks for a strong position in EV charging: EcoGrid's energy storage expertise, the AI software platform with 12,000 paying subscribers, and an established customer base in country T** [Ap]**. Offering customers an integrated package - solar generation, energy storage, AI energy management, and EV charging - would be highly differentiated and difficult for competitors to replicate. This bundled proposition could justify premium pricing and reduce the impact of MNC price competition, rather than trying to fight MNCs on cost** [An]**

Cross-selling EV charging to existing software subscribers also reduces marketing costs, making Option B more financially efficient than winning entirely new customers** [K]**. However, the EcoGrid acquisition shows that SES can struggle when taking on new areas of expertise. Mismanaging the integration caused a loss of specialist engineers and a fall in productivity** [Ap]**. SES must ensure that EV charging investment is introduced gradually, starting with cross-selling to existing customers, rather than committing all available capital upfront **[E]**

Overall, I advise Marco to pursue Option B** [E]**. SES's financial constraints make international expansion too risky at this stage, and Option B builds on existing strengths in a way that offers genuine competitive advantage. Option A could be reconsidered once SES's finances have stabilised** [E]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Using Ansoff's Matrix, Option A (existing solar product in new geographic market) is a market development strategy. Option B (EV charging in country T using SES's existing customer base and related technology) is related diversification
> - Core competencies are the unique capabilities that give a business competitive advantage
> - First-mover advantage is the competitive benefit gained by entering a market early before rivals
> - Country U's government incentives for solar energy create a genuine first-mover opportunity for SES; if SES enters country U before MNCs establish themselves there, it could build brand recognition, win key contracts, and develop local installation teams that would be difficult for later entrants to replicate quickly
> - First-mover advantage could be especially valuable given that government contracts in country T have historically delivered higher profit margins than private sector work, suggesting similar contracts in country U could help reverse SES's declining ROCE
> - However, international expansion is operationally complex for a business that relies on skilled local installation teams; unlike a product that can be manufactured and shipped, SES's core competency - designing and physically installing solar systems - is location-dependent
> - SES would need to recruit and train engineers in country U, navigate unfamiliar regulations and supply chains, and manage operations at a distance, all while its domestic financial position continues to weaken; the EcoGrid acquisition showed that SES can struggle to manage integration challenges effectively, suggesting that adding international complexity is particularly risky at this point
> - Option B offers a compelling bundled proposition that competitors would find difficult to replicate — if SES can offer customers a single integrated system covering solar generation, battery storage (via EcoGrid), AI-powered energy management software, and EV charging, it creates a highly differentiated product that pure solar companies and pure EV charging providers cannot match; this aligns with Porter's differentiation strategy and could allow SES to justify premium pricing despite increased competition from MNCs in country T
> - SES's 12,000 AI software subscribers already represent an established customer base with a proven interest in energy management technology; cross-selling EV charging solutions to these customers would have significantly lower marketing and customer acquisition costs than winning entirely new customers, making Option B more financially efficient, an important consideration given that SES's acid test ratio has fallen to 0.6:1 and gearing has risen to 38%, indicating real constraints on its ability to fund large-scale investment
>

> 
> - SES's deteriorating financial position is the most important factor in this decision; with ROCE at 9%, profit declining for five consecutive years, gearing at 38%, and a Finance Director warning about financial weakness, taking on the capital requirements of international expansion (Option A) would carry significant risk that SES may not be able to absorb if the strategy does not deliver results quickly
> - Option B's synergies with EcoGrid's battery expertise and the existing AI software platform mean that SES is not starting from zero — it has genuine technical foundations for the EV charging market that competitors would struggle to replicate
> - However, the EcoGrid acquisition is a warning: SES took on a new area of expertise and then mismanaged the integration, losing a third of EcoGrid's specialist engineers; SES must avoid repeating this by ensuring that any EV charging investment is carefully managed, phased to match available capital, and integrated with existing operations rather than treated as a separate venture
> - Option A could remain a medium-term ambition once SES has stabilised its finances and fully integrated EcoGrid; country U's incentive-driven growth may still be accessible in two or three years

Use the financial data in Appendix 4 to support your argument; for example, citing the declining acid test ratio or rising gearing strengthens your analysis considerably.
> 
> Avoid sitting on the fence. The command word "advise" requires you to make a clear recommendation. You can acknowledge the merits of the option you reject, but your conclusion must come down firmly on one side.
>

>

Cash4Trash (C4T) C4T is located in the capital city of country A in Africa. This private limited company was started six years ago by Andy and Kris, who both had experience working for a large international charity. C4T is a social enterprise, initially financed by international charities and a grant from the government of country A. The government also provided land to C4T for its factory. C4T’s corporate objectives include two social objectives which are to: • improve the environment of the city • provide jobs for the unemployed. C4T collects and cleans all types of recyclable materials that have been discarded as trash (rubbish). The clean materials are then used to create products for sale, such as bags made from woven plastic. A local artist volunteers her services to help with product designs. C4T has grown and now manufactures a range of products from recycled materials, including bags and jewellery. Cases for laptops and smartphones are currently its most popular products. Products are sold to local people and tourists in its shop next to the factory. C4T also sells via its website. C4T employs 90 people in its factory, who were previously unemployed. It runs training courses for 16 to 18 year olds to teach them basic skills. All profit is re-invested to expand and improve the business. C4T has won awards for being a sustainable social enterprise. Operations problems Factory employees work in teams and are rewarded with bonus payments if they exceed targets. Each team collects materials and other resources needed for production from a central store. However, sometimes this store runs out of resources, halting production. Products are checked for quality at the end of the production process and many are rejected and faults have to be corrected. Employees have been trained to specialise in one task within one team. Andy and Kris feel that time and resources are being wasted and would like to reorganise the factory and improve employee flexibility. Marketing Marketing products made from recycled materials can be a major challenge in country A. Many consumers think these products are of inferior quality. However, C4T’s brand image is strong. Its products have featured in premium magazines and on websites aimed at consumers who are ‘socially responsible’. Kris works hard to keep the C4T website up-to-date and maintain its social media presence, as part of the company’s attempt to establish good customer relationships. An ambitious new idea Plastic water bottles have become a real environmental problem over recent years as more are bought and thrown away when empty. Kris is planning to introduce a new type of product. He thinks there is a market for durable, reusable plastic drinking bottles. These will be made from recycled plastic and marketed as souvenirs for tourists. Demand will be highest during holiday periods. They will be produced in a range of colours, with country A’s name and flag on them. A new C4T slogan ‘Protecting the environment’ will be printed on each bottle. A factory extension will be required to recycle the plastic materials to be used and to manufacture the bottles. Kris is planning to recruit the new employees required on part-time flexible contracts. C4T’s objective for the bottles would be to make a profit, so labour costs will need to be kept low. The recruitment of skilled employees able to achieve high productivity levels will be important.

Finance The factory extension will cost \$1.5m to build and equip with machinery. The government of country A will provide a grant of \$1m. Andy and Kris are hoping to raise the remaining \$0.5m from a bank loan. However, a local venture capitalist has offered to invest \$0.5m in return for 30% of the profit from the new product and substantial involvement in future decision making. C4T’s latest accounts valued its non-current liabilities at \$3m and its capital employed at \$5m. Forecast annual data for the reusable bottles is shown in Table 1. Table 1: Forecast annual data for the reusable bottles Forecast data for 2021 (\$000) Revenue 390 Material and recycling costs 130 Labour costs 100 Marketing, management and administration costs 60 A special order C4T has been approached by a design company in country A with a one-off special order. This company specialises in computer and phone accessories. The order is for 5000 cases for laptops, which would be branded with the design company logo. The design company will pay \$5 per case. C4T sells similar cases for \$7. C4T would need to move employees and resources from other product teams to increase capacity if the order is accepted. Average material and labour costs are not expected to change. The design company requires the laptop cases to be delivered during 2021. Financial and capacity data is shown in Table 2. Table 2: Special order data Special order number of units 5000 Annual capacity for laptop cases 12000 Forecast output of laptop cases in 2021 without the special order 9000 Usual price per unit \$7 Proposed special order selling price \$5 Total raw material variable cost at annual output of 9000 laptop cases \$18000 Total labour variable cost at annual output of 9000 laptop cases \$13500 The economy Country A has a relatively young population with an average age of 28 years. It is one of the fastest growing economies in Africa. The government is stable and incomes are rising, especially in the cities. Unemployment is falling which has led to some worries about increasing inflation which means the central bank may raise interest rates.

Further options for growth In addition to the reusable bottles, Andy and Kris are looking for other growth opportunities for C4T. They are both committed to their original social enterprise, but have different ideas of how to move the business forward. Two possible options are: Option 1 – favoured by Kris Increase recycling facilities further, using additional new machinery at the current site. Manufacture low-cost reusable shopping bags which would be branded ‘Bag4Ever’. These would be mass-produced and sold in bulk to supermarkets and shops. They would be sold at a low price, as an alternative to single-use plastic carrier bags which the government will ban in 2022. Option 2 – favoured by Andy Enter into a joint venture with a well-known African design company to launch a range of luxury travel cases. These would combine recycled materials with other materials, such as leather and traditional African designed cloth. These cases would be made in a new factory. They would be promoted to high income consumers and sold through outlets in shopping centres (malls) and airports in many countries. C4T will only be able to afford one of these options and it is clear that they both take the company in different strategic directions. Further information about the two options is in Table 3. Assume option 2 is chosen. Evaluate the importance of a strategic business plan to the successful implementation of this option.
parts.solutionMd:
A business plan sets out a company's goals and explains how it will achieve them. It usually covers marketing, finance, human resources and operations **[K]**. For C4T, Option 2 means entering a new market, building a new factory, and working with a partner business for 18 months **[Ap]**. This makes a clear business plan very important

Marketing is one area where the plan is essential **[E]**. C4T currently sells affordable recycled products to local people and tourists. Option 2 means selling luxury travel cases to wealthy customers through airports and shopping malls in many countries **[Ap]**. C4T has no experience doing this. The business plan needs to identify the target customers, set a marketing budget, plan how products will be distributed, and show how C4T will compete against established luxury brands. Without this, C4T would not know how to reach the right customers or how to stand out in a very competitive market **[An]**

The plan is also important for managing the joint venture **[K]**. C4T and the design company will be working closely together for at least 18 months **[Ap]**. They may have different ways of working and different goals. The plan must make it clear from the start who makes decisions, how profits are shared, and what each partner must do. If this is not agreed before the project starts, disagreements could cause delays and make it harder to implement Option 2 successfully **[An]**

However, the plan will only be useful if the information in it is accurate **[E]**. C4T has no experience in the luxury goods market **[Ap]**, so its sales and profit forecasts may not be correct. The plan needs to be reviewed and updated regularly as the project moves forward **[An]**

The most important issue is whether Andy and Kris both support Option 2 **[E]**. This option moves C4T away from its original social enterprise goals towards making profit from luxury products **[Ap]**. If the two directors disagree about this, the business plan will be very difficult to carry out, no matter how detailed it is. A strong plan is vital, but only if both directors are fully committed to making it work **[E]**

Evaluate whether the data in Table 3 is sufficient for the managers of C4T as they make the strategic choice between option 1 and option 2.
parts.solutionMd:
A strategic choice is a decision about the long-term direction of a business **[K]**. Table 3 includes two tools to help with this decision: decision tree analysis, which shows the probability of success and the expected monetary value (EMV), and force field analysis, which lists the key driving and restraining forces for each option **[K]**

Table 3 does provide some useful information. The EMV figures show that Option 2 is likely to generate much more profit - \$3m compared to \$1.5m for Option 1 **[Ap]**. This matters because C4T reinvests all its profit to fund its work and achieve its social objectives, so higher profit could help C4T do more to improve the environment and create jobs **[An]**. Table 3 also shows that Option 1 has a higher chance of success (80% compared to 65%), which tells Andy and Kris that Option 1 carries less risk. Option 1 is also cheaper (\$500,000 compared to \$800,000) and can be completed eight months earlier, which would help C4T's cash flow **[Ap]** **[An]**

However, Table 3 is not sufficient on its own **[E]**. The probabilities used in the decision tree are estimates, not facts. If the actual probability of success for Option 2 turns out to be lower than 65% **[Ap]**, the expected monetary value will also be lower, and the option may not be worth the investment **[An]**. Andy and Kris cannot rely too heavily on figures that might be inaccurate **[E]**

Table 3 also does not show what happens if an option fails. Andy and Kris need to know whether a failed Option 2 would result in a loss, not just a smaller profit. parts.solutionMd:
Strategic implementation means putting a strategy into action in a planned way **[K]**. Strategy 2 involves buying Abila for \$1.5m and spending a further \$0.5m on refurbishment and rebranding. This is a major decision that will affect every part of GR's business

The first step in implementing this strategy is to secure the finance **[K]**. The total cost is \$2m. GR has low gearing, which is listed as a strength in the SWOT analysis, meaning it does not have large existing debts **[Ap]**. This makes it easier for Leff to borrow money **[An]**. However, taking on a large loan will increase GR's gearing and make the business more financially risky. Leff must make sure the finance is in place before the takeover begins, as delays could slow down the refurbishment and hold back the reopening of Abila's restaurants **[Ap] [An]**

Managing the redundancies is another key part of the implementation. Strategy 2 involves rationalisation, which means cutting costs - and Leff believes this will lead to many job losses **[Ap]**. This must be handled carefully. If employees feel they are being treated unfairly, morale across both Abila and GR could fall **[An]**. GR already has high labour turnover and low motivation at many of its restaurants. A poorly managed redundancy process could make these problems much worse and increase recruitment and training costs at a time when GR is already spending a large amount of money on the takeover **[Ap] [An]**

GR will also need to rebrand and refurbish the Abila restaurants to match GR's standards. This includes changing menus, training staff, and building the GR brand across 10 new sites. This takes time, and Leff will need a clear timetable for each restaurant **[Ap] [An]**

Overall, the most important factor is that Leff plans the implementation carefully before the takeover happens **[E]**. He also needs to consider whether he can realistically make all the key decisions for 25 restaurants on his own. Delegating more responsibility to restaurant managers may be needed for this strategy to succeed **[Ap] [E]**

> - Leff may also need to accept that he cannot manage 25 restaurants in the same centralised way he manages 15; delegating more responsibility to restaurant managers would help GR grow, but this would be a significant change for Leff, who has always kept control of all key decisions
> - Overall, a detailed plan covering finance, communication, HR, and operations — worked out before the takeover happens — will be essential; without this, the risks of the strategy could outweigh the potential benefits

parts.solutionMd:
A SWOT analysis identifies a business's internal strengths and weaknesses, and the external opportunities and threats it faces. It helps a business understand where it is now and what options might be available for the future **[K]**

There are several ways the SWOT helps Leff choose between Strategy 1 and Strategy 2. The SWOT identifies low gearing as a strength, which means GR has limited existing debt **[K]**. This tells Leff that the business is in a good position to borrow money if needed to fund either strategy **[An]**. The SWOT also identifies the growth in chilled meal sales (10% per year) as an opportunity **[Ap]** - a much faster rate of growth than the restaurant market (3% per year). This information points towards Strategy 1 being a better fit for the current market conditions **[An]**

The SWOT also highlights weaknesses that Leff needs to think about. High labour turnover and demotivated employees are listed as weaknesses **[Ap]**. These problems could be especially damaging if Leff chooses Strategy 2, because adding 10 more restaurants means managing more staff at a time when GR already struggles to keep and motivate its employees. A SWOT analysis helps Leff see this risk before making the decision **[An]**

However, SWOT analysis has clear limitations. It does not provide any financial information to compare the two strategies - there are no cash flow forecasts, no payback periods, and no return on capital figures **[Ap]**. For a decision involving \$2m or \$3m of investment, this is a major gap. Leff would need to use investment appraisal alongside the SWOT to properly compare the two options **[An]**

SWOT analysis is also subjective **[K]**. Leff carried out this analysis himself, which means he might not have been fully honest about GR's weaknesses. For example, his limited experience of manufacturing is not mentioned in the SWOT but could be a serious problem for Strategy 1  **[Ap]** **[An]**

Evaluate the importance of core competencies as a framework for business strategy when NH carries out strategic analysis.
parts.solutionMd:
Core competencies are the unique strengths that give a business a competitive advantage over its rivals. A true core competency must be valued by customers, give access to a range of markets, and be hard for competitors to copy **[K]**. NH has identified three core competencies: outstanding customer service, professional standards focused on efficiency, and clear leadership.

Using core competencies as a framework for strategic analysis helps NH decide which strategies are a good fit **[K]**. For example, if NH considers expanding into country Q or taking over EatBest, the core competency framework asks whether NH's strengths will transfer into these new areas. Running restaurants (EatBest) and managing hotels both require similar hospitality and operational skills, which suggests that the takeover could be a reasonable match for NH's existing capabilities **[Ap]** **[An]**

However, there is a serious problem with using NH's stated core competencies as a strategic framework. The data does not support the idea that NH currently provides outstanding customer service **[K]** **[Ap]**. Customer complaints went up by 7–9% across all hotel types in 2019, and customers often say staff are too busy to help them. Labour turnover for non-management employees doubled from 14% to 26% in one year, and job satisfaction scores are falling. This evidence suggests that NH's stated core competencies may be what Jolin hopes the business will be, rather than what it actually does well right now **[An]**

Core competency analysis is also subjective and cannot stand alone **[K]**. NH should use it alongside SWOT analysis, PEST analysis, and Porter's Five Forces to build a complete picture **[E]**

Overall, core competencies are a useful framework in principle, but for NH they are currently unreliable as a basis for major strategic decisions **[E]**. The fact that customer complaints are rising and labour turnover has nearly doubled makes it very hard to argue that "outstanding customer service" is a genuine strength that can support new strategies. If Jolin bases the decision to take over EatBest - a \$70m commitment **[Ap]** - on these flawed competencies, he risks choosing a strategy that NH does not actually have the capability to deliver. Before pursuing either the EatBest takeover or the country Q expansion, NH must first use tools like SWOT analysis **[K]** to be honest about its real weaknesses and address the HR and customer service problems that the data clearly shows. Only then will core competency analysis give Jolin a reliable framework for strategic decision-making **[E]**

> - Core competencies are the unique strengths or capabilities that give a business a competitive advantage. To be a true core competency, a capability must give access to a wide range of markets, be valued by customers, and be difficult for competitors to copy

> - NH is considering taking over EatBest, a restaurant chain; using core competencies as a framework helps NH assess whether this strategy makes sense - if NH's main strengths are in hospitality, customer service, and efficient operations, these skills could transfer to managing restaurants, which would make the EatBest takeover a lower-risk strategy than entering a completely unrelated industry; however, the takeover would involve \$20m in cash plus 0.5m NH shares and an additional \$50m in borrowing, so it is important that core competencies alone are not the only factor considered

Pizza Adventure Company (PAC) PAC is a private limited company which owns restaurants. It was started ten years ago in a large city in country X, which is located in Asia. In addition, competition is increasing with several multi-national pizza companies starting up in country X. Alice would like PAC to serve a wider range of vegetarian options and many more salads, as well as the pizzas. She has noticed increasing numbers of online articles about the need to eat a healthy diet, with pizzas often mentioned as examples of unhealthy food items. Alice wants to launch a new ‘healthy life’ range of meals at two of the biggest restaurants to test the market. The target market for the new range will be young professionals trying to lead a healthy lifestyle. Alice has used her skills as an ICT graduate to build a website for PAC, which she now maintains on a daily basis, including news on new products, special offers and customer reviews. PAC restaurants have received many excellent reviews on travellers’ websites as well as in local newspaper articles and tourism guides.

Finance PAC’s profits have increased every year. Paulo has always reinvested most of the profit back into the company, after paying dividends to himself and other family shareholders. Paulo has also financed the purchase of some of PAC’s restaurants through loans from banks. Financial data for PAC is shown in Appendix 1. A new project Paulo has identified the rising popularity of ‘street food’ being sold by mobile vendors at events and markets. He would like to import four pizza vans in 2020, equipped with ovens. Pizzas can then be prepared and sold wherever the vans are taken. The total investment will be \$50000 per van. Each van will cost \$2000 per year to maintain. Paulo plans to purchase the vans using a bank loan. However, Gio is worried about PAC taking on further non-current liabilities. The data for the proposed pizza van project is shown in Appendix 2 and Appendix 3. Evaluate the importance to PAC of contingency planning as part of strategic implementation if Option 2 is chosen.
parts.solutionMd:
Contingency planning means identifying risks in advance and preparing a plan for how to deal with them if they happen. It is different from crisis management, which only starts after a problem has already occurred **[K]**

If PAC chooses Option 2, one of the biggest risks is that franchisees in countries Y and Z do not follow PAC's food quality and service standards **[K] ** **[Ap]**. PAC has no experience of running franchises and no knowledge of conditions in countries Y and Z. Franchisees could change ingredients, lower cooking standards, or change how the food is served - all without Paulo or Gio knowing. PAC already has evidence that quality problems can go unreported: the food poisoning complaint in one of its own restaurants was not passed on to the directors. If this happened in a franchised restaurant overseas, it would be much harder to detect and much slower to resolve **[An]**. A contingency plan for food safety incidents, including a clear communication process, instructions for dealing with the media and steps to compensate affected customers, would help PAC respond quickly and limit the damage to its brand **[An]**

Option 2 also carries significant financial risk **[E]**. The probability of success is only 55%, and PAC already has non-current liabilities of \$4.9m. If Option 2 fails, PAC will have spent \$0.5m with little return **[Ap]**. A contingency plan that includes financial triggers - for example, setting a point at which PAC would stop the strategy if revenue targets are not met - would help protect the rest of the business **[An]**

However, contingency planning takes time and money, and it is impossible to plan for every risk **[K]**. Paulo and Gio must focus their planning on the risks most likely to cause serious damage **[An]**

Overall, contingency planning is more important for Option 2 than it would be for Option 1 **[E]**. Option 1 costs more but has an 85% chance of success and is in a familiar market. Option 2, by contrast, takes PAC into two countries it does not know, with a business model - franchising - it has never used before **[Ap]**, and a probability of success of only 55%. Given PAC's existing financial pressures and the fact that its brand depends on consistent food quality **[Ap]**, failing to plan for what could go wrong with Option 2 could put not just the new strategy but the entire business at risk **[E]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Contingency planning means identifying risks in advance and preparing a plan for how to respond if those risks happen. It is different from crisis management, which happens after a problem has already occurred. A well-prepared contingency plan reduces the damage a business suffers when things go wrong
> - Option 2 has a probability of success of only 55%, which is lower than Option 1 (85%); this means there is a 45% chance the strategy will not deliver the expected returns; PAC already has non-current liabilities of \$4.9m, and if Option 2 fails, the business would have spent an additional \$0.5m with limited return; a contingency plan that includes a financial exit strategy, such as clear terms in franchise agreements that allow PAC to withdraw if targets are not met, would help protect the rest of the business from serious financial damage
> - PAC has no experience of operating in countries Y and Z; local conditions such as food regulations, ingredient availability, and consumer preferences may be very different from country X; a franchisee might change the menu or use lower-quality ingredients without telling PAC; contingency planning would help PAC prepare responses to these risks in advance - for example, by including quality checks and inspection rights in the franchise agreement, and having a clear process for ending contracts with franchisees who do not meet standards
> - The case study already shows that a PAC restaurant manager did not report a food poisoning complaint to Paulo and Gio; this shows that quality problems can occur and go unnoticed when managers are not supervised closely; when PAC's franchises are operating in other countries, this risk becomes much greater; a contingency plan for food safety incidents, including who to contact, how to communicate publicly and how to compensate affected customers, would be essential to protect PAC's brand if this happened in country Y or Z
> - However, contingency planning takes time and money to prepare properly; writing detailed plans for every possible risk that could occur across multiple countries over a 1–2 year implementation period could slow PAC down and use resources that are needed elsewhere; it is also impossible to plan for every risk, especially in unfamiliar markets
> - Contingency planning is important for any business implementing a new strategy, but it is especially important for PAC choosing Option 2, because the risks here are both high and unfamiliar; PAC has no experience of franchising, no knowledge of countries Y and Z, and already struggles to detect quality problems in its own restaurants, as the food poisoning incident shows
> - The most important contingency plans for PAC are those that protect its brand; if a franchised restaurant in country Y or Z is linked to food poisoning or poor service, this could damage PAC's reputation not just in those countries but back in country X as well; the whole value of Option 2 - building an international brand - would be at risk
> - The cost of contingency planning must also be considered; PAC is already carrying nearly \$5m of non-current liabilities, and with a \$0.5m investment in Option 2, the business cannot afford to lose money on a failed strategy without careful financial preparation
> - Overall, contingency planning is very important for PAC - more so for Option 2 than it would be for Option 1, which is simpler, faster to implement, and has a much higher probability of success; the combination of an unfamiliar international market, no franchising experience, and a low probability of success means that Paulo and Gio must plan carefully for what they will do if things go wrong, particularly around protecting food quality standards and the PAC brand across borders

Evaluate the usefulness of the information in Appendix 4 for the directors of PAC as they make the strategic choice between Option 1 and Option 2.
parts.solutionMd:
A strategic choice is a decision about the long-term direction of a business **[K]**. Appendix 4 contains probability of success data, cost and timescale figures, a force field analysis, and Ansoff Matrix positions for both options

Some of the information in Appendix 4 is useful **[E]**. The probability of success data allows Paulo and Gio to compare risk directly: Option 1 has an 85% chance of success compared to 55% for Option 2 **[Ap]**. This is important because PAC already has \$4.9m in non-current liabilities - a large amount of existing debt. If a strategy fails, PAC could face serious liquidity problems **[An]**. The probability data clearly points towards Option 1 being the lower-risk choice. The timescale data adds to this: Option 1 can be implemented in three months, while Option 2 takes one to two years **[Ap]**. Starting to earn returns from Option 1 much sooner would help PAC manage its finances while reducing debt **[An]**

The Ansoff Matrix positions are also useful. Placing Option 1 as product development and Option 2 as market development helps Paulo and Gio understand why Option 2 is riskier - PAC would be entering unknown markets with a business model (franchising) it has never used before **[Ap]**

However, Appendix 4 has serious gaps **[E]**. Most importantly, it does not include any expected profit or cash flow data for either option. Paulo has said the goal of expansion is to increase return on capital employed **[Ap]**, but Appendix 4 does not give enough information to calculate what return either option might generate. Without this, Paulo and Gio cannot judge which option is actually more likely to achieve the goal they have set **[An]**

The force field analysis is also limited. It was most likely prepared by Paulo himself, which means it may not be fully objective **[K]**. It does not mention PAC's existing quality problems, including the food poisoning incident that was not reported to directors **[Ap]**, as a restraining force for either option. These problems would be much harder to manage in franchised restaurants in other countries **[An]**

Overall, Appendix 4 is a useful starting point that makes Option 1 look like the safer and faster choice **[E]**. However, it is not enough on its own to make a well-informed strategic decision. Paulo and Gio need financial forecasts showing the expected profit from each option before they can decide which will best help PAC increase return on capital employed **[Ap]**. Without this data, even the clearest risk comparison from Appendix 4 cannot answer the question that matters most to the directors **[E]**

Historic Buildings and Gardens (HBG) HBG was started in 1965 as a social enterprise in country R. HBG’s main objective is to protect the country’s heritage through conserving buildings and gardens of historic interest. HBG now owns over 200 historic buildings and gardens throughout country R. These are open to the public and HBG receives most of its income from the two million members who pay an annual subscription to visit the historic buildings and gardens. HBG charges admission fees to non-members. Gift shops and cafés also provide a source of income. HBG needs sufficient income to cover costs and finance expansion in new conservation projects. However, it is also aware of a responsibility to provide social benefits to local communities such as employment and education. HBG appointed Eusebio Alves as Managing Director in October 2018 with the objective of increasing membership, admissions and income as they had been falling in recent years. Strategic Review Eusebio started by conducting a strategic analysis of HBG. He completed a SWOT analysis. Table 1 is an extract from the results of the analysis. Table 1: SWOT Analysis 2018 Strengths • High brand awareness • Highest membership of any organisation in country R • High levels of customer satisfaction among the over 50 age group Opportunities • Increasing levels of international tourism to country R • Rising gross domestic product (GDP) per head • New technologies to improve the customer experience and marketing • Falling cost of renewable energy sources such as wind power Weaknesses • Average annual labour turnover of 11% in the last 5 years • 10% reduction in membership since 2015 • Limited access for disabled people at 40% of properties • 70% of members are over 50 • Narrow hierarchical organisational structure • Corporate culture unwilling to accept change Threats • Minimum wage legislation proposed for 2021 • Laws to protect the rights of disabled people being considered by the government • Increasing consumer awareness of social responsibility

Eusebio used this analysis to identify four strategic changes required in order to achieve the objectives he had been set: • making the business more responsive to market changes • improving social responsibility • targeting younger customers • improving financial control by establishing profit centres. Eusebio recognised that these four strategic changes would need to be supported by developing a change culture within HBG to be successful. Centralised control At the end of 2018, Eusebio told his Board of Directors that: ‘HBG is bureaucratic with a centralised organisational structure. It is essential to change the way the business is organised and make it more responsive.’ He proposed the following changes. • remove three layers of middle management • delegate greater authority to managers of buildings and gardens to make decisions about local marketing and operations • operate buildings and gardens as individual profit centres • encourage two way communication with employees. However, the Board of Directors would retain control of national marketing, purchase of new buildings, IT infrastructure and strategic decision making. The Human Resources Director expressed concerns about the implications of decentralisation and the need for training. However, in early 2019 HBG began to implement the organisational changes proposed by Eusebio. This followed a two-month employee consultation. Social responsibility Eusebio thinks that HBG should focus more on its corporate social responsibilities. He told the Board of Directors that: ‘we can gain a competitive advantage over other businesses in the leisure industry if we focus on increasing our positive social and environmental impact. Target market Country R has an ageing population. HBG has used a consistent marketing strategy for targeting its core customers. Evaluate the significance of contingency planning for HBG as it prepares to implement its future strategies.
parts.solutionMd:
Contingency planning means identifying risks in advance and preparing a response plan so that if something goes wrong, the business can act quickly and limit the damage **[K]**

Contingency planning is significant for HBG because it is implementing several major strategies at the same time. One important risk comes from Project Alderly. HBG has a fixed target of opening the gardens in 23 weeks, in time for the holiday season **[Ap]**. The network analysis shows a series of activities that depend on each other, leaving little room for delays. If planning permission takes longer than expected, or building materials arrive late, the project could miss the holiday season deadline entirely. This would mean a significant loss of income that HBG was counting on **[An]**. A contingency plan that identifies which activities have no float, and that prepares backup suppliers and alternative timelines, would help HBG respond quickly if delays occur **[K]**

Decentralisation also creates risks that need contingency planning **[K]**. HBG is removing three layers of middle management and giving local property managers new authority over marketing and operations **[Ap]**. Some of these managers may not yet have the skills to handle these responsibilities well. If poor decisions are made at individual properties - for example, spending the local marketing budget on ineffective promotions - it will be hard for Head Office to detect and fix the problem quickly **[An]**. A phased approach to decentralisation, with clear training and regular check-ins from Head Office, would help manage this risk  **[K]**

HBG also faces the threat of new minimum wage and disability legislation. These could significantly increase HBG's costs, particularly since 40% of its properties already have limited access for disabled people  **[Ap]** **[An]**

Overall, contingency planning is very significant for HBG - more so than for many businesses - because HBG is implementing multiple major changes at once **[E]**, in an organisation that its own SWOT analysis describes as having a culture "unwilling to accept change" **[Ap]**. This combination of ambitious strategic change and internal resistance makes things going wrong much more likely. The most important contingency plans are those that protect Project Alderly's deadline and support the managers taking on new responsibilities through decentralisation **[Ap]**, because if either of these fail, HBG's income and its ability to fulfil its mission of conserving historic buildings and gardens will both be put at risk **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **5** | 17-20 | - Effective evaluation of the significance of contingency planning for HBG |
> | **4** | 15-16 | - Limited evaluation of the significance of contingency planning for HBG |
> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of  the significance of contingency planning for HBG |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the significance of contingency planning for HBG |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of  the significance of contingency planning for HBG |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Contingency planning means identifying risks in advance and preparing a plan for how to respond if those risks become reality. A contingency plan reduces the damage a business suffers when things go wrong.
> - HBG is removing three layers of middle management and giving local property managers much greater authority; there is a real risk that some managers will not have the skills or confidence to handle their new responsibilities well, leading to poor local decisions that damage the visitor experience or reduce income at individual properties
> - Acontingency plan - such as a phased rollout of decentralisation with clear training and mentoring support - would help HBG identify and support struggling managers before problems become serious
> - HBG faces two significant legal threats: minimum wage legislation proposed for 2021 and new laws to protect the rights of disabled people; either of these could increase HBG's costs significantly; HBG already has limited access for disabled people at 40% of its properties, meaning the cost of compliance with new disability laws could be very large; a contingency plan that sets aside a financial reserve and creates a phased plan for improving disabled access would help HBG manage these costs without putting pressure on its other budgets
> - Project Alderly has a fixed deadline of 23 weeks before the holiday season begins; the network analysis shows a tight schedule with several dependent activities; if any activity on the critical path is delayed — for example, if planning permission takes longer than expected or building materials are delivered late - the gardens will not open in time, and HBG will lose the income it was expecting from the first holiday season
> - A contingency plan that identifies which activities have float and which have no flexibility, along with backup suppliers and an alternative opening date strategy, would help HBG respond quickly to any delays
> - HBG is planning to target younger customers without losing its existing older members; if the new marketing strategy under Nelinha does not attract younger visitors, HBG risks spending a large part of its marketing budget without achieving the growth in membership it needs; a contingency plan that tests the new marketing approach at a small number of properties first, rather than rolling it out nationally all at once, would allow HBG to measure results and make changes before committing the full budget
> - Contingency planning is particularly significant for HBG because it is trying to implement several major changes at the same time - decentralisation, a new marketing strategy, a CSR programme, and Project Alderly - while also managing the risk of new legislation; this makes the overall risk much higher than if it were implementing just one change
> - HBG's existing culture is described as "unwilling to accept change," which means employee resistance to decentralisation is a genuine and specific risk; this is one of HBG's own identified weaknesses and will need to be directly addressed in any contingency plan
> - However, contingency planning has costs in time, money, and management attention, and HBG is a social enterprise that is already concerned about its income; spending too much time planning for every possible risk could slow down implementation at a time when urgent action is needed
> - The most significant contingency plans for HBG are those that protect its core income: ensuring Project Alderly opens on time, supporting the transition to profit centres so that local managers succeed, and preparing financially for the impact of new legislation; if any of these go wrong without a plan in place, HBG's income and mission could be seriously damaged

Explain the term ‘joint venture’.
parts.solutionMd:
A joint venture is when two or more businesses agree to work together on a shared project **[1]**, contributing resources such as finance or expertise and sharing the risks and rewards **[1]**. The arrangement is usually set out in a formal contract to show what each party will contribute and receive **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Two or more businesses agreeing to work together on a project or activity
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The businesses share resources, capital, expertise, risk or rewards
> - Each party contributes something to the arrangement, such as finance, facilities, skills or promotion
> - The arrangement is formalised in a legal contract
> - The businesses remain separate and independent - a joint venture is not a merger

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **problems a sole trader might have if they change the legal structure to a partnership.
parts.solutionMd:
Changing to a partnership means the sole trader has to share control with other partners **[1]**. If the partners have different objectives, this could lead to conflict that disrupts the business **[1]**. A second problem is that one partner might act irresponsibly **[1]** and damage the reputation of the business **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The sole trader would lose total control and have to share decision-making with partner(s)
> - A Deed of Partnership would need to be produced, adding legal cost and complexity
> - Partners may have different objectives or ideas about how to run the business
> - Conflict may arise between partners
> - A partner's actions could damage the reputation of the business
> - There may be difficulties if a partner wants to leave or dies
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Sharing control could slow down decision-making, as all partners must be consulted, and disagreements may disrupt how the business operates
> - Without a Deed of Partnership, disputes may arise over how profits are divided, how costs are shared, and what each partner's responsibilities are
> - If partners have conflicting objectives, reaching agreement on key decisions becomes difficult, which can harm the business
> - Conflict between partners may disrupt day-to-day operations and, in serious cases, require legal intervention to resolve
> - If one partner acts irresponsibly, the sole trader - now a partner - has little control over this and may suffer reputational damage as a result
> - If a partner leaves or dies, the partnership may have to be dissolved and reformed, causing significant disruption to the business
> 
> Accept any other valid response.
> 
> **[4 marks]**

Explain the term ‘private limited company’.
parts.solutionMd:
A private limited company is an incorporated business with limited liability, meaning shareholders cannot lose more than they have invested **[1]**. Unlike a public limited company, its shares cannot be traded on a stock exchange. They may only be sold privately to family, friends or selected investors **[1]**. This limits how much finance the business can raise, as it cannot access the wider investing public **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - An incorporated business
> - Shares can be sold/owners are shareholders
> - Shares cannot be sold on a public stock exchange - may only be sold to family, friends or private investors
> - Limited liability
> - Separate legal identity
> - Continuity
> - Must make accounts available to everyone
> - Do not need to publish accounts (just make available)
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Cannot sell shares on the stock exchange → limits the business's ability to raise large amounts of finance from the general public
> - Does not need to publish accounts → competitors cannot easily access financial information about the business
> - An independent example of a private limited company, e.g. Jaguar or Lifestyle International
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘limited liability’.

Limited liability means that the owners or shareholders of a business can only lose the amount they have invested **[1] **- their personal possessions cannot be taken to pay the business's debts **[1]**

> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
>

>

> - Owners cannot lose their personal wealth
> 
> A clear, correct definition earns 2 marks. A partial, vague or unfocused definition earns 1 mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure your definition addresses both sides of limited liability: what owners *can* lose (the amount they invested) and what they *cannot* lose (their personal assets). Avoid vague statements such as "they are not fully responsible for debts" without specifying the limit of their financial exposure.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **reason why a business might remain a private limited company rather than change to a public limited company.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason a business might stay private rather than become a plc is that the owners do not want to lose control **[1]**. If shares are sold to the general public, new shareholders may buy up a large number of shares, which reduces the original owners' ownership and voting power **[1]**. This means the owners could end up losing the ability to make important decisions without needing approval from outside shareholders, which may stop them running the business the way they originally intended **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Does not want to lose control - selling shares to the general public risks diluting the current owners' ownership
> - Does not want the cost and complexity of floating on a stock exchange
> - Does not want to publish accounts or face increased public scrutiny
> - Already has sufficient sources of finance (e.g. venture capital) so there is no need to go public
> - May not be ready to float - for example, if the business is making losses
> - Wants to retain the business's distinctive values, culture or family ownership
> - Current shareholders may be willing to accept postponed dividend payments, reducing pressure to list
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If control is diluted, the original owners may no longer be able to set the direction of the business or make key decisions without outside shareholder approval
> - The process of listing on a stock exchange involves significant legal and administrative costs, as well as management time that could be spent running the business
> - Publishing accounts means competitors can access detailed financial information, potentially undermining the business's competitive position
> - If finance needs are already being met, the risks and costs of going public - including loss of control and increased scrutiny - outweigh any benefits
> - If the business is making losses, a stock market listing could undervalue it or fail to attract enough investors
> - Once listed, pressure from shareholders for short-term profits may conflict with the long-term values or family culture the owners want to preserve
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'limited liability'.
parts.solutionMd:
Limited liability means that if a business fails, the owners or shareholders only lose the money they originally invested **[1]**, and their personal possessions and savings are protected from being used to pay off the business's debts **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Where the financial responsibility of owners/shareholders for a business's debts is limited to the amount they have invested in the business
> - Shareholders/owners can only lose the money they invested and their personal assets are protected if the business fails

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure your definition addresses two key ideas: that the owners' financial responsibility is capped at their investment, and that their personal assets cannot be seized to pay business debts. Many students only state one of these ideas and therefore receive only 1 mark. Avoid vague statements such as "they are not responsible for debts" without specifying the limit of their responsibility.

**[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'franchise'.
parts.solutionMd:
A franchise is a business arrangement where the owner of a brand (the franchisor) allows another person or company (the franchisee) to trade using its brand name, products and systems **[1]**, in exchange for an initial fee and ongoing royalty payments **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A business arrangement in which the owner of a brand/business model (the franchisor) licenses another party (the franchisee) to operate under the brand in return for a fee and/or a share of revenue
> - A licence granted by a business to an individual or company allowing them to trade using its brand, products and systems in return for an initial fee and ongoing royalty payments

> **[exam-tip]**
> When defining franchise, make sure you include two key elements: the nature of the relationship (one party allowing another to use its brand/business model) and the financial arrangement (fees or royalties paid in return). Many students lose the second mark by simply stating that "a business uses another business's name" without mentioning the payment involved. Try to use precise terminology such as "franchisor" and "franchisee" to demonstrate your understanding clearly.
