parts.problemMd: Explain **two **advantages to a business of being a social enterprise.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of being a social enterprise is that it may attract more customers, as the business is seen as ethical and community-focused **[1]**. Customers who share these values are more likely to choose it over a profit-driven competitor **[1]**

A second advantage is that employees may be easier to recruit and retain **[1]**. People motivated by social values are drawn to working for social enterprises, reducing recruitment costs **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - May attract more customers because the business is seen as ethical and community-focused
> - Customers may be willing to pay a higher price than they would to a profit-driven competitor
> - Employees may be easier to recruit, as people are drawn to working for a social enterprise
> - Employees may be easier to retain, leading to lower labour turnover
> - Government grants or subsidies may be available
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Being seen as ethical increases demand for the product or service, boosting sales and revenue
> - A higher price increases revenue and profit margin without needing to attract more customers
> - Lower recruitment costs and a larger pool of motivated candidates improve the quality of the workforce
> - Lower labour turnover reduces the cost of recruiting and training replacements, and maintains consistency of service
> - Grants or subsidies reduce costs, freeing up funds to invest in the business or its social mission
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you develop each advantage fully rather than simply listing them. A clear explanation means you identify the advantage and then link it to a positive outcome for the business - e.g. stating that a social enterprise attracts customers is only partial; explaining that this increases sales revenue makes it a clear explanation. Two well-developed points are needed for full marks, so aim to write a brief chain of reasoning for each advantage. Avoid repeating the same point in different words, as this will only be credited once.

**[4 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **advantages to a business of buying a franchise.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of buying a franchise is that the franchisee benefits from the franchisor's established brand and reputation **[1]**. Customers already know and trust the product, making it easier to attract sales from day one **[1]**

A second advantage is that marketing and advertising costs are shared across all franchisees **[1]**. This means the individual franchisee spends less on promotion while still benefiting from national or wider campaigns **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The franchisee benefits from the established reputation and brand of the franchisor
> - Marketing and advertising costs are shared across all franchisees
> - Help and advice is available from the franchisor
> - The product or service is already known by customers, increasing the chance of success
> - Competition may be limited by the franchisor restricting other outlets in the same area
> - Supplier relationships are already established by the franchisor
> 
> AO2
> 
> - An established brand means customers already trust the product, making it easier to attract sales from day one and reducing the risk of failure
> - Shared marketing costs reduce the individual franchisee's expenses while still providing national or wider coverage
> - Support from the franchisor is particularly valuable to someone new to business ownership, reducing the risk of costly mistakes
> - A known product or service builds a customer base more quickly than an unknown start-up business
> - Restricted competition gives the franchisee a protected market, helping to maintain stable revenue
> - Ready-made supplier relationships can mean better prices and a more reliable supply chain from the outset
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **limitations of partnership as a business structure.
parts.solutionMd:
One limitation of a partnership is that all partners have unlimited liability, meaning their personal assets - such as their home or savings - could be used to pay business debts if the partnership fails **[1]**. This is a significant risk, as each partner is liable for the debts of the whole business, not just their own share **[1]**

A second limitation is that all partners are legally bound by the decisions of any one partner **[1]**. This means that if one partner makes a poor business decision - such as signing an expensive contract - the other partners are responsible for the consequences **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - All partners have unlimited liability
> - Profits must be shared between partners
> - All partners share losses
> - All partners are bound by the decisions of any one partner
> - Compromises are necessary in decision-making, which can lead to conflict
> - Ability to raise capital is limited, as partnerships cannot sell shares
> - Continuity is not assured - the partnership must be reformed if a partner dies or leaves
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Unlimited liability means all personal assets - including savings and property - are at risk if the business cannot pay its debts
> - Sharing profits means each partner receives less than they would as a sole trader generating the same revenue
> - Each partner is personally responsible for losses, including those caused by the decisions of other partners
> - One partner's poor decisions bind all others, meaning the actions of a single partner could cause financial harm to the whole business without the others' agreement
> - Disagreements between partners can slow down decision-making or lead to poor compromises that damage the business
> - The inability to sell shares makes it harder to raise large amounts of finance compared to a limited company, restricting growth
> - If a partner dies or leaves, the partnership must be legally reformed, causing disruption to the business
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **advantages that a business in the public sector may have that a business in the private sector may not.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of being in the public sector is easier access to finance, as the business is funded by the government through taxation **[1]**. This means it does not need to attract private investors or take on commercial loans **[1]**

A second advantage is that public sector businesses are not under pressure to make a profit **[1]**. This means they can focus on providing essential services to all customers, including those in areas or situations that a private sector business would consider unprofitable **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Easier access to finance as the business is funded by the government
> - Not under pressure to make a profit, as it often provides essential goods or services
> - Does not have to pay dividends to shareholders
> - Often a large business that can benefit from economies of scale
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Government funding means finance can be raised through taxation or grants, without needing to attract private investors or take on commercial loans
> - Without the need to make a profit, the business can focus on providing quality services to all customers, including those in unprofitable areas that a private business would not serve
> - Not paying dividends means any surplus can be reinvested into improving services rather than being distributed to shareholders
> - Economies of scale allow the business to produce goods or services at a lower average cost, meaning it can offer better value than many private sector competitors
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **disadvantages to a private limited company of changing to a public limited company.
parts.solutionMd:
One disadvantage is that the original owners lose control of the business **[1]**. Once shares are freely available on the stock exchange, any member of the public can buy them without needing approval from existing shareholders and could outvote the founders on key decisions **[1]**

There is also a significantly higher risk of takeover **[1]**. Because shares can be freely bought and sold on the stock exchange, a rival company or investor could gradually acquire enough shares to gain control of the business entirely **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - High cost of preparing documentation and floating the company on the stock exchange
> - Any member of the public can purchase shares without needing approval from existing shareholders
> - Higher public profile means business problems are more visible and may attract greater media scrutiny
> - Divorce of ownership and control — original owners lose total control over the direction of the business
> - Higher risk of takeover by an outside individual or business
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The cost of floating can be substantial, diverting money away from investment in the business at a critical time
> - Without control over who buys shares, the original owners could find themselves outvoted on key decisions by new shareholders whose interests differ from their own
> - Greater public scrutiny means any negative news, poor financial results or controversies are more likely to become widely known, damaging the company's reputation
> - With ownership and control separated, professional managers may make decisions that conflict with the founders' original vision or values for the business
> - Once shares are freely traded on the stock exchange, a rival company or investor could acquire enough shares to take over the business against the wishes of the original owners
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership.
parts.solutionMd:
One disadvantage of changing to a partnership is that the sole trader loses sole control of decision-making **[K]**. Previously, they could make all decisions independently and act quickly when opportunities or problems arose. Once partners join the business, agreement must be reached before decisions can be made **[An]**. If the partners have different views on how the business should be run, this can cause conflict and slow down the decision-making process considerably **[An]**. As a result, the business may miss time-sensitive opportunities that it would previously have been able to act on quickly, weakening its competitive position **[An]**

Also, each partner is legally liable for the actions of all other partners **[K]**. This means that if one partner takes on a large debt or signs an expensive contract without the others' consent, all partners are equally responsible for that obligation **[An]**. For the original sole trader, this represents a significant new risk - previously they were only answerable for their own decisions, but now a partner's poor judgement could expose them to unlimited liability for debts they played no part in creating **[An]**. In the worst case, this could put their personal assets, such as their home or savings, at risk **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of sole trader or partnership |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - When a sole trader changes to a partnership, they lose sole control and must share decision-making with the new partner(s). Previously, the sole trader could act quickly and independently; now, agreement must be reached before decisions can be made. If the partners have different views on the direction of the business, this can cause conflict and significantly slow down decision-making, meaning the business may miss opportunities that require a fast response
> - In a partnership, each partner is legally bound by the actions of all other partners. If one partner takes on a large debt or signs an expensive contract without the others' consent, all partners are equally liable for that obligation. This is a significant risk for the original sole trader, who previously only had to answer for their own decisions - a partner's poor judgement could expose all partners to unlimited liability, putting their personal assets at risk
> - Changing to a partnership means profits must be shared between all partners. Previously, the sole trader kept all of the profit they generated; now, a portion goes to the new partner(s), reducing the original owner's financial reward even if their contribution to the business has not changed. This could reduce the sole trader's motivation, particularly if they feel they are working just as hard for a smaller return
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two** reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company is to gain limited liability **[K]**. As a sole trader, the owner has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets such as their home and savings are at risk if the business accumulates debts it cannot pay **[An]**. By incorporating, the owner can only lose the amount they have invested in the company. This significantly reduces the personal financial risk of running the business and may make the owner more willing to take calculated risks, such as expanding into new markets or investing in new equipment, that they might previously have avoided out of fear of losing personal assets **[An]**. As a result, incorporation can open up growth opportunities that are simply too risky to pursue as a sole trader **[An]**

A second reason is to make it easier to raise finance **[K]**. A sole trader cannot sell shares and must rely on personal savings or bank loans to fund the business, which limits how much capital they can access. By becoming a private limited company, the owner can sell shares to family, friends or private investors, providing a much larger pool of finance **[An]**. Unlike a bank loan, this does not create debt or require interest payments, which means the additional capital can be invested directly into growing the business - for example, by purchasing new equipment or hiring additional staff - without reducing profitability **[An]**. This makes incorporation particularly attractive to a sole trader who wants to expand but has exhausted their personal sources of finance **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of a sole trader and/or private limited company |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A sole trader has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets such as their home and savings are at risk if the business cannot pay its debts. By incorporating, the owner gains limited liability and can only lose the amount they have invested in the company. This significantly reduces personal financial risk and may encourage the owner to take calculated risks that they would have been too cautious to attempt as a sole trader
> - A sole trader cannot sell shares to raise finance and must rely on personal savings, bank loans or personal investment; by becoming a private limited company, the owner can sell shares to family, friends or private investors, accessing a much larger pool of capital. This finance can be used to fund expansion without taking on debt, avoiding interest payments that would reduce the business's profitability and making growth more financially sustainable
> - Incorporation gives the business a separate legal identity, meaning the company can continue to exist if the owner becomes ill or dies. This provides continuity that is not possible for a sole trader, protecting customers, employees and the value of the business from the disruption that would occur if it ceased to exist due to the owner's death or incapacity
> - A private limited company may be seen as more credible and established than a sole trader, making it easier to win contracts, attract investment and negotiate favourable terms with suppliers - none of which are as easily achieved when operating as an unincorporated business
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks on "Analyse" questions by simply identifying reasons without developing them. Make sure each reason follows a clear chain of argument: state the reason, apply it to a realistic business situation, and then explain the consequences or impact on the business.
> 
> A useful technique is to use connective phrases such as "this means that…", "as a result…" or "therefore…" to signal that you are moving from description into analysis. Aim to write two well-developed paragraphs rather than listing several undeveloped points.
> 
> Avoid spending time on evaluation (e.g. weighing up whether incorporation is the best option overall) - the command word is "Analyse", not "Evaluate", so marks are awarded for depth of reasoning rather than judgement.

**[8 marks]**

Plc status also brings pressure from shareholders to pay dividends and requires greater financial disclosure. The other two shareholders have already warned Amit that flotation costs will be very high. UBH paid dividends of \$0.2m even in 2020 when it made a loss. High flotation costs reduce the net finance actually raised, potentially making the exercise less worthwhile. Ongoing shareholder pressure for dividends could drain cash at a time when UBH needs funds for expansion
> - The decision depends primarily on whether UBH can realistically raise \$16m through debt alone. Given gearing of ~69% and rising interest rates, this appears both costly and risky, which strengthens the case for equity finance
> - A critical factor is investor demand for UBH shares. If demand is low, the flotation may not raise sufficient funds, yet the costs will still have been incurred
> - Amit's attitude to control is important. If retaining his majority stake matters more than growth, debt finance may be preferred despite the higher cost
> - The timing is worth weighing - UBH has only been trading since 2018, made a loss in 2020, and has returned to profit for just one year. Investors may view this as too short a track record, limiting demand for shares

parts.problemMd: Evaluate whether a joint venture is the best way for a business to enter a new international market.
parts.solutionMd:
A joint venture is an agreement in which two businesses set up a separate business together and share its costs, risks and profits **[K]**. Entering a new international market is expensive and risky, because a business may not understand local tastes, laws or distribution systems. A food manufacturer moving into a country where religious rules affect which ingredients are acceptable **[Ap]** could take years to learn this on its own. Working with a partner already established there gives the business that knowledge immediately, and the set-up costs are shared, so expansion becomes possible for a business that could not afford to enter the market by itself **[An]**

However, a joint venture also means giving up control **[K]**. Every major decision must be agreed with the partner, and the two businesses may want different things - one may want rapid growth while the other prefers steady profits **[Ap]**. Disagreements can slow decisions down at exactly the moment a new market needs a quick response to competitors, and any profit made has to be shared rather than kept in full **[An]**

Whether a joint venture is the best method depends on the circumstances **[E]**. Where the market is very different from the home market, or where a government requires foreign firms to work with a local partner, a joint venture may be the only realistic way in **[E]**. Where the business already understands the market and has enough finance, setting up its own operation would let it keep full control and all of the profit, which is likely to be better over time **[E]**. Much also depends on how well matched the partners are, since a joint venture between firms with similar aims is far more likely to work than one formed simply because a partner was available **[E]**. Overall, a joint venture is the best choice when risk and unfamiliarity are high, rather than in every case **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
> - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout
> - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
> - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
> - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **4** | - Shows understanding of two ways of entering a new international market in context |
> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one way of entering a new international market in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two ways of entering a new international market |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one way of entering a new international market |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two ways of entering a new international market in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one way of entering a new international market in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two ways of entering a new international market |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one way of entering a new international market |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A joint venture spreads the cost and risk of entering an unfamiliar market across two businesses, which may make expansion affordable for a firm that could not fund it alone, and if the venture fails each partner loses only its share rather than the full investment. However, profits are divided in the same proportion, so a successful venture returns less than a wholly owned operation would
> - A local partner brings knowledge that would otherwise take years and considerable expense to acquire, including established supplier and distributor relationships, consumer preferences, and familiarity with local employment and product regulations, shortening the time before the business earns revenue. However, sharing designs, technology or commercial knowledge carries the risk that the partner later becomes a competitor using what it has learned
> - Some governments restrict foreign ownership and require overseas firms to operate through a joint venture with a domestic company, so the choice becomes one between a joint venture and staying out of the market altogether rather than between a joint venture and a wholly owned subsidiary. However, where no such rule applies, a business with sufficient finance and market knowledge may do better setting up alone
> - Each partner can contribute what it does best, one providing brand recognition and product technology while the other provides manufacturing capacity and distribution, which may produce a stronger entry than either could achieve independently. However, control is shared, so decisions on pricing, marketing and reinvestment must be agreed, and disagreement slows response at exactly the point a new market demands speed
> - The business could instead enter by exporting, licensing, franchising or setting up a wholly owned subsidiary, each carrying a different balance of risk, control and commitment. However, the lower-risk options generally give less control over how the product is presented, while the higher-control options require considerably more capital and local knowledge
> 
> Accept any other valid response

Explain what is meant by ‘the business environment is dynamic’.
parts.solutionMd:
The business environment refers to the external factors outside a business's control that affect how it operates, such as competition, economic conditions, and market trends **[1]**. Dynamic means these factors are always changing, and businesses must adapt their strategies in response **[1]**. For CTV, the television market in country A illustrates this - market growth has declined from +2% in 2020 to a forecast of –3% in 2022, and rising competition has forced CTV to respond by launching the new lower-priced STV brand **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - External factors that affect how a business operates, such as economic conditions, competition, technology and market trends
> - Dynamic means these external factors are constantly changing rather than remaining stable or predictable
> - A dynamic environment requires businesses to adapt their strategies in response to shifting conditions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - For CTV, the television market in country A illustrates this — market growth has declined from +2% in 2020 to a forecast of –3% in 2022, showing that conditions are changing and forcing CTV to respond by launching the lower-priced STV brand
> - The increasingly competitive television market means CTV cannot rely on its existing strategy and must adapt, for example by introducing automation and targeting the mass market with STV
>

After defining both parts, give a brief example or further development to secure the third mark. For instance, you could mention that new competitors may enter the market, technology may change, or consumer tastes may shift. parts.problemMd: Explain **two **qualities of a successful entrepreneur.
parts.solutionMd:
One quality of a successful entrepreneur is a willingness to take risks **[1]**. An entrepreneur must be prepared to invest their own time and money into a business idea with no guarantee of success **[1]**. An entrepreneur is also self-motivated and determined **[1]**. Building a business involves setbacks and obstacles, so a successful entrepreneur must be able to persist and adapt after failure is essential **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires the clear identification of two entrepreneurial qualities (AO1), each supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded up to 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Ability to identify and develop innovative business proposals/projects / solve problems
> - Self-confident – energetic and driven
> - Self-motivated and multi-skilled
> - Ability to lead, inspire and motivate others
> - Good communicator/persuasive
> - Visionary
> - Creative
> - Passionate, resolute, optimistic
> - Future-centric
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A willingness to take risks allows an entrepreneur to commit personal capital to an untested business idea, essential for bringing new products or services to market
> - Being self-motivated and determined means an entrepreneur can persist through early setbacks such as low sales or cash flow problems, adapting their approach rather than giving up
> - Strong leadership and communication skills enable an entrepreneur to attract investors, recruit talented employees and build customer loyalty
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you do more than simply list qualities - the command word is "explain", so you need to develop each point by stating why or how that quality helps an entrepreneur succeed. A common mistake is to name several qualities without explaining any of them, which limits you to just 1 mark. Structure your answer clearly: identify the quality, then explain its importance. Two well-explained qualities will score much better than a long list of undeveloped ones.

**[4 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **reasons why many new businesses fail in their first year of operation.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason many new businesses fail in their first year is a lack of finance** [1]**. A new business may struggle to pay for premises, stock, and employees for several months before revenue is high enough to cover costs **[1]**

A second reason is poor or inadequate market research **[1]**. If the entrepreneur misjudges customer demand the business cannot may not be able to cover its costs and is unlikely to survive its first year **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires the clear identification of two reasons (AO1), each supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded up to 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The product or service is not wanted by enough consumers
> - Lack of business or management experience
> - Insufficient finance to sustain early operations
> - Poor or inadequate market research
> - An unexpected change in economic conditions
> - A strong competitive reaction from established businesses
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If the product has no real demand, sales will be too low to cover costs and the business will be unable to survive
> - Without experience, owners are likely to make poor decisions around pricing, staffing, or cash flow, which can quickly threaten the business's survival
> - A new business may have to fund its operations for months before revenue is sufficient to cover costs, and without enough capital it will run out of cash
> - Flawed market research produces inaccurate information about customer demand, meaning the business may invest in a product or service that the market does not actually want
> - A downturn in the economy may cause consumers to cut spending, reducing sales below the level needed for the business to break even
> - Established competitors may respond by cutting prices or increasing advertising, making it very difficult for a new business to attract enough customers

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two** ways marketing could be used to add value to a product.
parts.solutionMd:
One way marketing can add value is by building a strong brand through advertising **[K]**. When a business spends money on advertising to create a well-known and trusted brand image, customers begin to see the product as worth more than similar products from less well-known competitors **[An]**. For example, a clothing brand with a strong image can charge a higher price than an unbranded item that costs roughly the same to make **[Ap]**. This widens the gap between the selling price and the cost of production, which increases the added value the business creates **[An]** Another way marketing can add value is by promoting a clear unique selling point (USP) **[K]**. If a business highlights something that makes its product different from competitors, such as an eco-friendly ingredient or an exclusive feature **[Ap]**, customers who care about this difference are often willing to pay a higher price for it. This means the business can increase its selling price without a large rise in production costs, which increases added value **[An]**. As word spreads about this unique feature, the business may also attract new customers who specifically want that benefit, further growing sales at these higher, more profitable prices **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to a business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

> **[case-study]**
> **The Shop (TS) **
> 
> Thomas worked for 30 years as a manager of a factory. Although he was very good at his job he was recently made redundant.
> 
> Thomas always wanted to open a shop. He thinks he has the qualities an entrepreneur is likely to need for success. He has undertaken some primary market research to identify possible opportunities in city X where he lives (see Fig. 1.1).
> 
> ![Pie chart showing shop preference: sandwich shop 25%, bakery shop 20%, coffee and grocery shops 15% each, electronics and butcher shops 10% each, clothes shop 5%.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-business-23/business-and-its-environment/enterprise/assets/001-pie-chart-showing-shop-preference-sandwich-shop-.png)
> 
> **Fig. 1.1: Market research**
> 
> Thomas now needs to make a decision about which type of shop to open. He has used the data in Fig. 1.1 and some secondary market research to identify two options.
> 
> *Option 1: Coffee shop *
> The coffee shop would provide hot drinks that customers could take away and drink elsewhere. It would also sell some bakery items, such as biscuits and doughnuts. There are four other shops selling takeaway hot drinks and bakery items in the city, as well as five cafés. Thomas thinks that the profit margin would be 6% to 8%.
> 
> *Option 2: Sandwich shop *
> The sandwich shop would make sandwiches using job production. Customers can choose from a range of sandwich fillings, as well as cold drinks and snacks. There is only one competitor in the city. It is a well-known international franchise that spends a lot of money on promotion. Thomas thinks that the profit margin would be 10% to 15%.

Analyse **two **qualities that Thomas will need to be a successful entrepreneur.
parts.solutionMd:
One quality Thomas will need is risk-taking **[K]**. Opening TS requires Thomas to invest his own capital with no guarantee of success - city X already has several competitors in both the coffee and sandwich markets, and there is a real possibility the business could fail **[Ap]**. Without a willingness to accept this financial risk, Thomas would be unable to act on the opportunity at all; however, by carefully using his market research to choose the option with the strongest profit margin and least competition, Thomas can make an informed decision that reduces, but does not eliminate, that risk **[An]** A second quality Thomas will need is determination **[K]**. If he opens the sandwich shop, he will be competing directly against a well-known international franchise that invests heavily in promotion - a significant challenge for a new, unknown business **[Ap]**. Thomas is likely to face a slow start while he builds awareness of TS in city X, and without the resilience to persist through this difficult period rather than giving up, the business is unlikely to reach the point where it becomes profitable **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Kiln (KL)**
> 
> Priya worked for twelve years as a secondary school art teacher in country X. She has always made handmade ceramic tableware in her spare time and sells it at local craft markets. Last year she decided to leave teaching and set up Kiln (KL) as a sole trader, producing handmade plates, bowls and mugs to sell to homeware shops.
> 
> Priya has \$18,000 in personal savings. She estimates that KL needs \$45,000 before it can begin trading, as shown in Table 1.1. She approached two banks for a loan. Both refused, saying that KL has no trading record and no assets to offer as security.
> 
> **Table 1.1: KL estimated start-up costs**
> 
> | **Item** | **Cost (\$)** |
> |---|---|
> | Industrial kiln | 20,000 |
> | Workshop equipment and tools | 9,000 |
> | First three months' rent on workshop | 8,500 |
> | Raw materials (clay and glazes) | 5,000 |
> | Safety certification and licences | 2,500 |
> | **Total** | **45,000** |
> 
> The homeware market in country X is dominated by three established manufacturers. The largest holds 40% of the market and supplies plates to retailers at \$12 each. Priya has calculated that KL's cost of making one plate is \$9.
> 
> Before KL can begin production, its workshop must pass a safety inspection. Priya has been told that the certification process usually takes about four months.
> 
> Priya is confident about the quality of her designs. However, she has no experience of pricing, managing cash flow or negotiating with suppliers. A friend has advised her to write a business plan before going any further.

Analyse **two** barriers to entrepreneurship faced by Priya.
parts.solutionMd:
One barrier Priya faces is a lack of finance **[K]**. KL needs \$45,000 to begin trading but Priya has only \$18,000 in savings, and both banks have refused to lend because KL has no trading record **[Ap]**. This leaves a shortfall of \$27,000, so Priya may have to buy a smaller or second-hand kiln and cut back on raw materials, which would reduce the number of items KL can produce each month **[An]**. Producing fewer items means lower revenue at a time when Priya must still pay the \$8,500 workshop rent, so KL could run out of cash before it has built up a regular group of customers **[An]** A second barrier is strong competition from established manufacturers **[K]**. Three firms already dominate the homeware market in country X, and the largest supplies plates to retailers at \$12 each while KL's cost of making one plate is \$9 **[Ap]**. This leaves Priya a margin of only \$3 per plate if she matches the market price, which is very little to cover her rent and other fixed costs **[An]**. If she charges more than \$12 to protect her margin, retailers may simply buy from the larger manufacturers instead, so KL could struggle to win enough orders to survive its first year **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Lattice (LT)**
> 
> Lattice (LT) is a private limited company based in country Y. It was founded fourteen years ago and now employs 320 people. LT develops software that helps delivery companies plan their routes.
> 
> Almost all of LT's income comes from a single product, RouteMaster, which was launched eleven years ago. Two competitors have released newer route-planning software in the past eighteen months, and several of LT's customers have asked why RouteMaster has changed so little.
> 
> **Table 1.1: LT selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 24 |
> |---|---|
> | Share of revenue from RouteMaster (%) | 78 |
> | Labour turnover, software developers (%) | 22 |
> | Industry average labour turnover (%) | 14 |
> 
> Several of LT's software developers have suggested ideas for new products, but they have no time to work on them because they are fully occupied maintaining RouteMaster for existing customers.
> 
> LT's Managing Director, Anika, wants to encourage intrapreneurship. She has proposed that every developer is given one day each fortnight to work on their own project, and that LT sets aside an annual fund of \$200,000 to develop the most promising employee ideas.
> 
> LT's Finance Director disagrees. He estimates that the lost development time would cost LT around \$900,000 each year, and points out that most employee ideas never become products that customers will pay for.

Analyse **two** benefits to LT of encouraging intrapreneurship among its employees.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit is that intrapreneurship could help LT develop new products **[K]**. At the moment 78% of LT's revenue comes from RouteMaster, a product launched eleven years ago, and two competitors have released newer software in the past eighteen months **[Ap]**. Giving developers one day each fortnight to work on their own ideas would allow LT to test far more concepts than it does now, without the cost of hiring an outside development team **[An]**. If even one of these ideas became a product that customers were willing to buy, LT would earn income from a second source, so a future fall in RouteMaster sales would no longer put the whole business at risk **[An]** A second benefit is that intrapreneurship should improve staff retention **[K]**. Labour turnover among LT's software developers is 22%, which is much higher than the industry average of 14% **[Ap]**. Developers who are trusted to work on their own projects are likely to find their work more interesting and feel their ideas are valued, which makes them less willing to leave for a competitor **[An]**. Lower turnover would cut the money LT spends on recruiting and training replacements, and would keep hold of experienced staff who already understand how RouteMaster is built, meaning that customer requests are dealt with more quickly than they would be by a constant stream of new employees **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Thread (TH)**
> 
> Thread (TH) makes school uniforms in country Z. It was set up four years ago by Mariam, who had spent nine years working as a buyer for a large clothing retailer.
> 
> While working as a buyer, Mariam noticed that schools in her region were paying high prices for uniforms imported from overseas. She believed the same garments could be made locally for far less. She left her job, invested \$30,000 of her own savings, and formed a partnership with her sister, who contributed a further \$20,000.
> 
> Mariam rented a small factory unit and bought twelve industrial sewing machines. She recruited 60 workers from the local area, most of whom had never used industrial equipment before, and trained them herself over three months. She also negotiated directly with a fabric mill in a neighbouring country, cutting out the wholesalers that her competitors use.
> 
> TH now sells a hard-wearing cotton blend that Mariam developed with the mill. Schools report that the uniforms last around a year longer than the imported ones they replaced.
> 
> **Table 1.1: TH selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in year 1 (\$) | 180,000 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in year 4 (\$) | 940,000 |
> | Number of schools supplied | 34 |
> | TH price compared with imported uniforms | 25% lower |
> 
> Mariam is now considering whether TH should begin supplying schools in a neighbouring region.

Analyse **two** ways in which Mariam has carried out the role of an entrepreneur at TH.
parts.solutionMd:
One way Mariam has acted as an entrepreneur is by spotting an opportunity in the market **[K]**. While working as a buyer she noticed that schools in her region were paying high prices for imported uniforms, and her experience of the clothing trade told her the same garments could be produced locally for much less **[Ap]**. By setting TH's prices 25% below the imported alternatives, she gave schools a clear financial reason to change supplier, which explains why TH has won orders from 34 schools in only four years **[An]**. Those customers have lifted revenue from \$180,000 to \$940,000, giving TH the income it needs to fund further growth **[An]** A second way is by organising the factors of production **[K]**. Mariam rented a factory unit, bought twelve industrial sewing machines and recruited 60 local workers, most of whom had never used this kind of equipment before **[Ap]**. By training them herself over three months instead of paying to attract experienced machinists from rival firms, she kept TH's wage costs lower than a competitor would face, which is part of the reason TH can undercut imported uniforms and still make a profit **[An]**. Having a workforce she has trained also means TH can raise output fairly quickly when new schools place orders, so Mariam can take on customers in the neighbouring region without long delays that might send those schools to a competitor instead **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problemMd: Discuss the possible challenges for an entrepreneur in starting a new business selling only vegetarian food products.
parts.solutionMd:
An entrepreneur is a person who takes on financial risk to start and run a business **[K]**. Opening a business selling only vegetarian food products has some good opportunities, but there are also challenges of operating in such a niche market to consider **[Ap]**

One challenge is the higher cost of vegetarian ingredients. As a new business, the entrepreneur will not benefit from economies of scale, so costs per unit will be higher than for larger competitors **[K] [Ap]**. This means the entrepreneur must either charge higher prices and risk losing customers or accept lower profit margins, both of which make it harder to survive in the early months **[An]**

A second challenge is that vegetarian food may be a trend rather than a permanent change in consumer behaviour **[K]**. If demand slows or falls, a business that only sells vegetarian products cannot easily switch to meat or fish-based products **[Ap]**, which could lead to falling sales and business failure **[An]**

Overall, the biggest long-term challenge is competition **[E]**. In the short term, entering a growing market early is an advantage. However, as the market gets bigger, larger food businesses with more money and better supply chains will enter, making it harder for a small new business to compete on price or promotion **[An]**. The entrepreneur's best chance of success is to build a loyal customer base and a strong brand quickly, before this competition arrives **[E]**

> - A growing consumer interest in vegetarian lifestyles has expanded the potential market for vegetarian food products. A new business in this sector can target health-conscious consumers and those adopting plant-based diets as a permanent lifestyle choice. However, as the market grows, it will attract larger, well-funded competitors with greater economies of scale, making it progressively harder for a small new entrant to compete on price
> - Higher prices for vegetarian ingredients compared to conventional food products increase the cost base for a new business. A vegetarian food start-up will not yet benefit from bulk purchasing or economies of scale, meaning its prices may be higher than those of established rivals. This limits the size of the accessible market, slows customer acquisition, and puts pressure on already tight profit margins during the critical early months
> - Vegetarian food trends, while currently strong, carry the risk of being a short-term consumer preference rather than a permanent shift. A business built entirely around vegetarian products has no product diversification to fall back on if demand declines. If the trend fades or evolves, the entrepreneur faces falling revenue with limited options to adapt quickly, increasing the risk of business failure
> - Successfully targeting and reaching the right customers is a significant challenge for any new business. A vegetarian-only food business must identify and attract a specific consumer segment in a market where a well-known brand or international franchise may already hold consumer loyalty. Without an effective and affordable marketing strategy, the business may struggle to build awareness quickly enough to generate the sales needed to cover its fixed costs
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]** > **Seaside Hotel (SH) ** > > SH is a large hotel located in a tourist area of country H. SH has 120 rooms and employs 42 workers during the peak (busiest) season, which is from April to September. Table 2.1 shows employee data for SH’s peak season. > > **Table 2.1: Employee data for SH’s peak season** > > | **Type** | **Number** | **Main tasks** | > |---|---|---| > | Manager | 3 | - decision-making
- supervising other employees | > | Cleaner | 12 | - cleaning rooms, corridors and reception area to required standard
- maintaining a clean and safe working environment | > | Customer service | 16 | - greeting guests upon arrival
- making sure guests are satisfied | > | Marketing | 7 | - designing promotional materials
- promoting hotel to increase number of guests | > | Other | 4 | - various | > > SH makes half of the cleaners and customer service employees redundant at the end of the peak season. > > To break even, the hotel must sell 72 rooms per night. The hotel offers good views of the sea and it is very busy in the peak season when the weather is hot. Table 2.2 shows SH’s sales of rooms. > > **Table 2.2: SH’s sales of rooms 2021–2022** > > | **Time period** | **Average percentage of rooms sold per night** | > |---|---| > | April 2021 – September 2021 | 95% | > | October 2021 – March 2022 | 45% | > > SH does not have a restaurant. It has a joint venture with a restaurant close to the hotel where SH’s customers receive a discount on their food and drink. The hotel advertises the restaurant on social media and the restaurant advertises the hotel on its menu. > > Tia is one of the managers of SH. She has an autocratic leadership style and is responsible for the cleaners and marketing employees. > > The directors of SH aim to increase the value added to the service that SH provides. Recommend how SH could increase the value added to its service. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
SH could add its own restaurant to increase value added **[K]**. Currently, SH relies on a joint venture with a nearby restaurant **[Ap]**, meaning all food and drink revenue goes to another business **[An]**. If SH opened its own restaurant, guests would receive more as part of their stay, increasing the perceived value of the hotel and allowing SH to charge a higher room rate **[An]**. However, setting up a restaurant would require significant investment in equipment and the recruitment of new staff with catering skills, increasing costs considerably in the short term **[E]**

SH could also use its sea views as a USP and invest in stronger branding **[K]**. The hotel already benefits from good views and a popular tourist location, but off-peak occupancy is only 45% **[Ap]**, suggesting many potential guests are not aware of SH or are choosing competitors instead. By promoting the sea views more strongly through social media, SH could differentiate itself and justify charging a higher price **[An]**. However, other hotels in the same tourist area may also offer sea views, which could limit how much SH is able to stand out from its competitors on this basis alone **[E]**

I recommend that SH add its own restaurant **[E]**. Although the start-up costs are a risk, the restaurant would create an entirely new revenue stream from food and drink, something that stronger branding cannot do. Branding would mainly affect how many rooms are sold, but SH already sells 95% of its rooms in the peak season **[Ap]**, leaving little room to grow through attracting more guests **[E]**. A restaurant would allow SH to earn more from the guests it already has, making it the more effective and sustainable way to increase value added in the long run **[E]**

By bringing dining in-house, SH would retain this revenue and offer a more complete service, allowing it to charge a higher room rate and increase its profit margin. However, set-up costs would be significant, and SH would need to recruit and train new staff, which increases costs in the short term
> - SH could use its sea views as a USP by promoting them more strongly in its marketing. The risk is that other hotels in the same tourist area may also have sea views, limiting how much SH can differentiate on this basis alone

Off-peak occupancy is only 45% (below break-even of 72 rooms), so stronger branding could also attract more guests in the quieter months and help SH reach break-even year-round

Higher quality increases the perceived value of a stay, allowing SH to charge more per room. Since peak season occupancy is already 95%, even a modest price increase would significantly boost revenue without needing to attract more guests

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **The Shop (TS) **
> 
> Thomas worked for 30 years as a manager of a factory. Although he was very good at his job, he was recently made redundant.
> 
> Thomas always wanted to open a shop. He thinks he has the qualities an entrepreneur is likely to need for success. He has undertaken some primary market research to identify possible opportunities in city X where he lives (see Fig. 1.1).
> 
> ![Pie chart showing shop preference: sandwich shop 25%, bakery shop 20%, coffee and grocery shops 15% each, electronics and butcher shops 10% each, clothes shop 5%.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-business-23/business-and-its-environment/enterprise/assets/001-pie-chart-showing-shop-preference-sandwich-shop-.png)
> 
> **Fig. 1.1: Market research**
> 
> Thomas now needs to make a decision about which type of shop to open. He has used the data in Fig. 1.1 and some secondary market research to identify two options.
> 
> *Option 1: Coffee shop *
> The coffee shop would provide hot drinks that customers could take away and drink elsewhere. It would also sell some bakery items, such as biscuits and doughnuts. There are four other shops selling takeaway hot drinks and bakery items in the city, as well as five cafés. Thomas thinks that the profit margin would be 6% to 8%.
> 
> *Option 2: Sandwich shop *
> The sandwich shop would make sandwiches using job production. Customers can choose from a range of sandwich fillings, as well as cold drinks and snacks. There is only one competitor in the city. It is a well-known international franchise that spends a lot of money on promotion. Thomas thinks that the profit margin would be 10% to 15%.

Recommend which of the two options Thomas should choose for his new shop. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
Thomas could open a coffee shop, which targets two market segments and could attract up to 35% of potential customers in city X **[K] [Ap]**. The combination of hot drinks and bakery items creates synergy, as both tend to appeal to similar customers looking for a quick snack **[An]**. The presence of four takeaway shops and five cafés in the city **[Ap]** also confirms that demand already exists for this type of service **[An]**. However, competing against nine existing businesses would make it very difficult for Thomas to establish a USP, and the profit margin of only 6–8% **[Ap]** leaves very little room for a new business to absorb its start-up costs **[E]**

Alternatively, Thomas could open a sandwich shop. The sandwich market is the largest single segment **[K]** in city X at 25%, and there is only one competitor - an international franchise **[Ap]**. By using job production, Thomas could offer fully customised sandwiches, giving him a clear, attractive USP over the franchise, which relies on standardised production methods **[An]**. The profit margin of 10–15% is also significantly higher than Option 1. However, the franchise spends heavily on promotion, so Thomas may struggle to attract customers initially, as many people in city X may already be loyal to the existing brand **[E]**

I recommend that Thomas opens a sandwich shop **[E]**. Although the coffee shop targets a larger share of the market overall, the nine competitors would make it very hard for a new business to survive on a margin of only 6–8% **[Ap]**. The sandwich shop has far less competition and a higher profit margin, making it much more likely that Thomas can reach break-even and build a sustainable business **[E]**. The franchise's promotional spending is a challenge, but Thomas's use of job production gives him a genuine advantage that a large, standardised franchise cannot easily replicate **[E]**

> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two challenges in context |

> | **1** | - Analysis of one option |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Option 1 (coffee shop) targets two market segments from the research, meaning Thomas could potentially attract 35% of the market. The combination of hot drinks and bakery items creates synergy, as both tend to appeal to similar customers, and the presence of four takeaway shops and five cafés in the city confirms that demand already exists.
> - However, competing against nine existing businesses would make it very difficult for Thomas to establish a USP, and the profit margin of only 6–8% leaves little room for error in a new business
> - Option 2 (sandwich shop) targets 25% of the market — the largest single segment — with only one competitor. Using job production to make customised sandwiches would give Thomas a clear USP over the international franchise, which uses standardised production and cannot easily match a personalised service. The profit margin of 10–15% is significantly higher than Option 1
> - However, the franchise competitor spends heavily on promotion, which could make it difficult for Thomas to attract customers initially, as many people in city X may already have strong brand loyalty to the franchise.

The coffee shop reaches a larger overall market share but the intense competition (nine rivals) and low profit margin make survival much harder for a start-up with no established reputation.
>
