parts.problemMd: Define the term 'nationalisation'.
parts.solutionMd:
Nationalisation is when a government takes ownership of a business or industry **[1]** that was previously owned by private individuals or shareholders **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The transfer of a business or industry from private ownership into public ownership by the state
> - A government buying or taking control of a firm so that it is run by the public sector rather than for private profit
> - The process by which privately owned assets or industries come to be owned and operated by the government

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nationalisation and privatisation describe the same movement in opposite directions, so the mark depends on saying which way ownership travels. "The government gets involved with a business" is too vague; state that ownership moves from private hands into the public sector.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Fold (FD)**
> 
> Fold (FD) manufactures cardboard packaging in country M. It employs 190 people and supplies food producers and online retailers.
> 
> Three of FD's largest customers have told it that from 2028 they will buy only from suppliers whose packaging is made entirely from recycled material and who can show that their energy use is falling. Together these three customers provide 44% of FD's revenue.
> 
> FD currently uses 61% recycled material. Moving to 100% would cost around \$2.8m in new equipment.
> 
> Country M's government has also announced a tax on packaging containing less than 70% recycled content, starting in 2027.

Explain **one** reason why sustainability is important to FD.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that FD's largest customers now treat sustainability as a condition of doing business **[1]**. Three customers providing 44% of FD's revenue will buy only from suppliers using entirely recycled material from 2028, and FD currently uses 61% **[1]**. If FD does not invest the \$2.8m needed to reach 100%, it risks losing nearly half its sales at once, which would cost far more than the equipment, so sustainability has become necessary for FD's survival rather than a choice about its image **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Sustainability matters to a business because of customer requirements, legal and tax changes, cost savings, reputation, and access to finance
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Three customers worth 44% of revenue will require fully recycled packaging from 2028, so failing to invest puts almost half of FD's sales at risk
> - Country M's tax on packaging below 70% recycled content begins in 2027, and FD's current 61% falls below that threshold, adding a cost it does not face today
> - The \$2.8m investment is large, but it answers the customer requirement and the tax at the same time, so the two pressures reinforce one another
> - Being able to prove falling energy use may open opportunities with other buyers applying similar standards, turning compliance into a competitive advantage
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sustainability is a very broad idea, so narrow it to one strand before you start writing. Trying to cover environmental, social and financial sustainability at once produces a list rather than an explanation. One narrow reason, followed through to its effect on the business, will always score better.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'supply-side policy'.
parts.solutionMd:
Supply-side policy is government action intended to increase the productive capacity of the economy **[1]** by making markets work more efficiently and improving the quantity or quality of resources such as labour and capital **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Government measures aimed at raising the economy's ability to produce goods and services, rather than at influencing the level of demand
> - Policies designed to improve the efficiency of markets and the quality of labour and capital, such as training schemes, deregulation or tax incentives to invest
> - Action taken to increase long-run productive capacity by improving skills, competition and incentives across the economy

> **[exam-tip]**
> A policy definition must say what the policy is trying to achieve, not just that a government carries it out. Every government policy is government action, so that half earns very little. The mark lies in the purpose: raising the economy's capacity to produce.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'pressure group'.
parts.solutionMd:
A pressure group is an organisation formed by people with a shared concern **[1]** that tries to influence the decisions of businesses or governments without seeking to run them **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An organised group of people who campaign to influence the decisions of businesses or governments on a particular issue
> - A body that seeks to change the behaviour of firms or policymakers through campaigning, publicity or lobbying rather than by taking control of them
> - A group with a shared interest that applies public or political pressure in order to change how organisations act

> **[exam-tip]**
> A definition has to fit every example of the term, not just the best-known one. An answer built around a single famous campaign will not describe a local residents' group or a trade body, and both of those count too. Aim for wording that would cover any pressure group you can think of.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** benefit to a business of a trade agreement between countries.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit is that a trade agreement usually reduces or removes tariffs between the countries involved **[1]**. A tariff is a tax on imports, so removing it lowers the price at which a business can sell its products in the other country **[1]**. Cheaper products are likely to sell in greater numbers, so the business can raise its sales abroad without cutting its own profit margin, and producing those extra units may also lower its average cost **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Trade agreements can reduce tariffs and quotas, simplify customs procedures, standardise regulations, and give businesses more secure access to a partner country's market
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Removing tariffs lowers the selling price in the partner country without reducing the exporter's margin, so sales volumes are likely to rise
> - Simpler customs procedures cut delays and paperwork costs, which matters most for goods that are perishable or time-sensitive
> - Common product standards allow a business to sell the same version of a product in several countries, avoiding the cost of redesigning it for each market
> - More secure access reduces the risk of sudden trade barriers, making it safer to invest in production capacity aimed at export markets
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A benefit question needs you to identify who gains and by what route, not simply to assert that something is good for business. Here the route runs from a lower tariff, to a lower selling price, to higher sales volume. Making that path explicit is what separates a three-mark answer from a one-mark one.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Meadow (MW)**
> 
> Meadow (MW) processes milk into cheese and yoghurt in country K. It employs 340 people at one large plant, where staff work with heavy machinery, hot liquids and refrigerated storage rooms.
> 
> New health and safety laws in country K require all food processing businesses to fit machine guards, provide protective clothing, and give every employee eight hours of safety training each year.
> 
> MW estimates that meeting the new requirements will cost \$620,000 in the first year and \$180,000 a year afterwards.
> 
> In the year before the new law, MW recorded 34 workplace injuries, nine of which required time off work.

Explain **one** way health and safety law affects MW.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is that health and safety law increases MW's costs **[1]**. The new requirements mean MW must spend \$620,000 in the first year on machine guards, protective clothing and eight hours of training for each of its 340 employees **[1]**. That money cannot be spent on anything else, such as new production equipment, so in the short term the law reduces the profit MW has available to reinvest, although fewer injuries than last year's 34 should eventually mean less production lost to absence **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Health and safety law places duties on a business to protect its employees, which affects its costs, working practices, productivity and legal risk
> 
> AO2
> 
> - MW must spend \$620,000 in the first year and \$180,000 a year afterwards, money that cannot be used for other investment
> - Eight hours of annual training for 340 employees takes staff away from production while it happens, reducing output during those periods
> - Fewer than last year's 34 injuries should mean less time lost to absence, since nine of them required time off work
> - Failure to comply could bring prosecution, fines or forced closure, which for a single-site business would stop production altogether
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> With a question about law, name the duty the law places on the business first, then follow it through to a business consequence such as cost, output or risk. Answers that describe the legislation in detail but never reach a consequence for the business tend to earn the first mark only.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'migration'.
parts.solutionMd:
Migration is the movement of people from one country or region to another in order to live there **[1]**, which changes the size and make-up of the population in both the place they leave and the place they settle **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The movement of people between countries or regions in order to live and work there
> - People relocating permanently or semi-permanently, altering the population and labour supply of both the origin and the destination
> - Inward and outward movement of population, affecting the number and skills of people available to businesses in an area

> **[exam-tip]**
> Some terms work in both directions, and migration is one of them: people move in and people also move out. A definition mentioning only arrivals describes immigration rather than migration. Where a term is two-sided, check your wording covers both.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'environmental audit'.
parts.solutionMd:
An environmental audit is a check on the impact a business's activities have on the environment **[1]**, carried out so that the business can measure that impact and identify ways of reducing it **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An assessment of the effect a business has on the environment, covering matters such as emissions, waste and energy use
> - A systematic review of a firm's environmental performance, used to identify where improvements can be made
> - An internal or independent check on how far a business's operations meet the environmental standards it has set or is required to meet

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a term names a process, say both what is examined and what the examination is for. Here that means the effect of the business on the environment, and the purpose of measuring it. A definition that stops at "a check on the environment" leaves the second mark unearned.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way a government might intervene to help businesses.
parts.solutionMd:
One way a government might help businesses is by offering grants or subsidies **[1]**. A grant reduces the amount a business must fund itself when buying equipment or opening a new site, so projects that would otherwise be too expensive become affordable **[1]**. This matters most to smaller firms, which often struggle to borrow, and it can persuade businesses to invest in areas where the government wants new jobs created **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Governments can support businesses through grants and subsidies, tax reductions, training schemes, infrastructure investment, advice services, or reduced regulation
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A grant lowers the amount a firm must fund itself, so investment projects that would be unaffordable become viable
> - Reducing business taxes leaves more profit available for reinvestment, which may encourage expansion and job creation
> - Government-funded training raises the skills available in the labour market, reducing the cost each business must bear to train staff itself
> - Investment in roads, ports or broadband lowers distribution and communication costs for firms across the whole economy
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Without a case study, the development marks still have to be earned, and they come from a chain of reasoning rather than from naming an example. State the intervention, say what it changes for the business, then say what follows from that. Naming a real government scheme adds nothing on its own.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Folio (FL)**
> 
> Folio (FL) is a printing business in country W. It prints books, catalogues and packaging for around 200 customers, and employs 75 people.
> 
> Paper is FL's largest cost. FL buys all of its paper from just two mills, because only these two can supply the weights and finishes its customers require.
> 
> Last year one of the two mills raised its prices by 22% and reduced credit terms from 60 days to 30 days. FL had to pay more, and sooner, than it had planned.
> 
> FL's owner is now considering whether to hold larger stocks of paper or to look for a supplier in another country.

Explain **one** way FL's suppliers can influence its decisions.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is that FL's suppliers can dictate the terms on which it buys **[1]**. FL depends on only two mills, because they alone supply the paper weights and finishes its customers need, so when one raised prices by 22% and cut credit from 60 days to 30 days, FL had little choice but to accept **[1]**. Paying more and paying sooner both reduce the cash FL has available, which is exactly why its owner is now weighing up larger stock holdings or a supplier abroad **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Suppliers can influence a business through the prices they charge, their credit terms, their reliability, the quality they provide, and how easily they can be replaced
> 
> AO2
> 
> - FL buys from only two mills because of the specialist weights and finishes required, so its bargaining power is weak and it must largely accept the terms offered
> - A 22% increase on FL's largest cost either squeezes its margins or forces it to raise prices to its 200 customers
> - Cutting credit from 60 days to 30 halves the time FL has to collect money from customers before it must pay the mill, putting pressure on cash flow
> - Supplier behaviour is already reshaping FL's strategy, since the owner is weighing higher stock levels or an overseas supplier, both of which carry costs of their own
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Suppliers can influence a business helpfully or harmfully, and this question asks for one way, not a survey. Choose the direction the case supports, state it plainly, then develop it. Listing price, quality, reliability and delivery without developing any of them will not reach the second and third marks.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Pop Cool (PC) PC is a public limited company. Its head office is in Europe and it operates with centralised decision making. The company owns the Pop Cool brand name, logo and the distinctive bottle shape that is still used in some markets. PC operates its own bottling and canning factories in some countries. However, it also has joint venture agreements with packaging businesses in other countries. Much of the fruit and sugar used in producing the soft drinks is imported from African and Asian countries. 75% of PC’s sales and 90% of its profits are earned in the USA and Europe. The directors of PC are keen to develop other markets and other products so that the company becomes less dependent on a few key markets and products. Economic changes The economies of the USA and Europe have experienced very slow economic growth since 2008 – and some have even been hit by recession. Interest rates are very low as the monetary policy of these countries is aiming to boost demand. However, this has contributed to exchange rate depreciations of the US dollar and the European euro. Consumer spending has fallen due to declining real incomes. There are ageing populations in most of the countries where PC sells its products. More employees are now working from home rather than in offices. The populations of European capital cities include significant numbers of young, professional individuals who earn above average incomes. Marketing TK differentiates its meal service from the increasing number of competitors on the basis of choice, quality and packaging. The menu is varied and includes daily special offers. TK’s Operations Director has worked closely with a packaging company to research, develop and patent a range of recyclable packaging containers that ensure meals arrive hot and in excellent condition. Fashion Frames plc (FF) FF makes plastic frames for glasses (spectacles) in a factory in country W, in South East Asia. Improving quality Chang, the production manager, aims to reduce the high level of rejects by the wholesalers. He has identified a number of factors which make this difficult including: • employees know that rejected frames can be recycled • production targets are very difficult to meet • problems with suppliers of raw materials • breakdowns with machinery. Chang proposes introducing Total Quality Management (TQM). He thinks this will reduce the number of substandard frames and improve FF’s delivery times. Chang forecasts successful implementation of TQM will also increase output by 10% and average variable cost will fall by 5%. However, Chang is aware that there may be problems with TQM and forecasts can be inaccurate. Table 1 shows information on FF’s output, costs and prices, before TQM is implemented. Table 1: FF’s output, costs and prices Year ending September 2021 Maximum capacity 16 million frames Actual output 14 million frames Average variable cost \$20 Average selling price \$40 Communication challenges FF has a centralised organisational structure with a low degree of delegation. Directors make decisions, department managers plan how to implement these and supervisors give instructions. Employees have little responsibility or control. FF has provided good pay, good conditions of work and security of employment. However, employees are aware that the directors are considering significant changes to working conditions. All employees find it difficult to discuss this with their line managers. Many employees work alone so information is passed on informally and often inaccurately. Evaluate the likely impact on AC’s future profitability of the forecast economic changes in Appendix 1.
parts.solutionMd:
Rising inflation is likely to have a significant negative impact on AC's profitability **[K]**. Inflation in country K is forecast to rise from 6% to 10% over the three-year period **[Ap]**, which will push up AC's costs for raw materials, components, and energy used to manufacture its fitness equipment. If AC cannot pass these higher costs on to customers through price increases, its profit margins will be squeezed **[An]**. This is a particular concern in the consumer market AC plans to enter in 2022, where Khalil's research suggests price is important to buyers - meaning AC may have limited ability to raise prices without losing sales to cheaper competitors, including the foreign manufacturers already entering the market **[An]**

Rising interest rates from 6% to 8% also threaten AC's future profitability **[K]**, especially given Omar's expansion plans. AC already carries \$40m in non-current liabilities, suggesting it is heavily reliant on borrowing, and both growth options require large additional investment - \$15m for Option 1 and \$20m for Option 2 **[Ap]**. Higher interest rates will increase the cost of servicing this debt, raising expenses and reducing net profit. The planned rise in direct tax from 24% to 26% **[Ap] **will also reduce households' disposable income, potentially weakening demand in the consumer market AC is about to enter, as fitness equipment is likely to be seen as a discretionary purchase that consumers may delay or avoid when money is tighter **[An]**

Overall, the economic changes in Appendix 1 are broadly negative for AC's profitability **[E]**. The most significant threat is the combination of rising inflation and rising interest rates, which will increase both operating costs and borrowing costs at exactly the time AC needs to invest heavily in expansion **[Ap]**. GDP growth of 3–5% is a positive signal - rising incomes may support demand in the industrial sector and the new consumer market - but this benefit is likely to be outweighed by the pressure from higher costs and lower disposable income **[E]**. The accuracy of these forecasts is uncertain; if inflation rises less sharply than predicted, the impact could be more manageable **[E]**. However, the overall outlook suggests AC should carefully consider the timing of its expansion plans and explore ways to reduce its cost base before committing to large-scale borrowing **[E]**

Evaluate the likely impact on UBH of the changes the government made to its economic policies in response to the recession.
parts.solutionMd:
The government's decision to delay payment of business and property taxes was likely the most important policy for UBH's immediate survival **[K] [E]**. In 2020, UBH had almost no working capital - its current ratio was approximately 0.18:1 (current assets of \$0.8m against current liabilities of \$4.5m) **[Ap]**, meaning it could barely cover its short-term debts. Deferring tax payments reduced UBH's immediate cash outflows, giving it the breathing space it needed to continue paying rent on its beehives and servicing its bank loans **[An]**. Without this relief, UBH would almost certainly have run out of cash and been forced to close **[E]**

The cut in income tax and reduction in interest rates helped UBH recover by stimulating demand in the wider economy **[K]**. Lower income tax increased households' disposable income and boosted business confidence, which supported the formation of new business start-ups **[An]**, UBH's core target market. This helped explain the recovery in revenue from \$6m in 2020 to \$14.4m in 2021 **[Ap]**. The reduction in interest rates also reduced the cost of servicing UBH's \$9m in non-current liabilities, limiting the size of its 2020 loss, and made it more affordable to fund the opening of three new beehives in 2021 **[Ap] [E]**. Infrastructure investment in roads and rail would also benefit UBH over time, as customer feedback identifies distance from transport hubs as one of the three most important factors when choosing a co-working centre **[An]**

Overall, the tax deferral was the most critical policy because it had an immediate impact on cash flow at a time when UBH was on the verge of insolvency **[Ap]** **[E]**. The other policies - income tax cuts, lower interest rates, and infrastructure spending - were important for the longer-term recovery, but their effects take time to feed through to business demand **[An]**. However, the tax deferral is not a permanent fix; UBH still owes the deferred taxes, which remain a future liability. Ultimately, UBH's survival depended on both government support and its own strategic decisions, particularly its choice to expand aggressively in 2021 to capitalise on improving conditions **[Ap]**. Without that combination, the government policies alone may not have been sufficient **[E]**

For the Hydrocamel, stronger CSR credentials could serve as a USP to differentiate it from the Hippo Barrel competitor launched in 2019 **[Ap]**, helping to win back charities and NGOs that may prefer buying from a more ethical supplier **[An]**. Higher sales volume would increase revenue and, if fixed costs are spread across more units, improve profitability **[An]**

Overall, a genuine focus on CSR is likely to have a positive impact on WTZ's long-term profitability, but the short-term effect will be higher costs **[E]**. This is a concern since WTZ's profit margin has already fallen from 12.8% in 2021 to 9.3% in 2022 **[Ap]**. The biggest gains are most likely to come from improved employee productivity and lower absenteeism, as these directly address existing operational problems that are already costing the business money **[E]**. The reputational benefits of CSR are real but harder to quantify and may take longer to feed through to higher sales. There is also a significant risk. If WTZ promotes CSR credentials while continuing to treat workers poorly, it could face a damaging backlash from the environmental pressure groups highlighted in the PEST analysis **[Ap]**. For CSR to benefit profitability, it must be genuine and applied consistently across the business rather than used selectively as a marketing tool **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **4** | - Shows understanding of two  impacts on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one  on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two  impacts on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one  impact on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two impacts on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one  impact on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two  impacts on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one  impact on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR) |
> 
> **Indicative content **
> 
> - CSR requires businesses to consider the impact of their decisions on society and the environment, including how they treat employees. WTZ currently pays many factory workers the minimum wage, operates long working hours, and provides poor facilities with limited ventilation and no break areas. The operations manager has reported rising absenteeism and a 5% quality rejection rate at the Hydrocamel factory. Improving working conditions and pay above the minimum wage could motivate employees, reduce absenteeism, and lower labour turnover - reducing recruitment and training costs. If quality standards also improve, the cost of rejected output falls, which could improve profit margins even after the additional wage expenditure
> - CSR can be used to build a positive brand image and attract customers who value ethical and sustainable business practices. WTZ already has strong environmental credentials - recycling plastic waste, manufacturing the Hydrocamel to help communities access clean water, and generating electricity from waste. Kofi recommends actively promoting these activities to strengthen brand identity. Given the PEST analysis shows growing environmental awareness and the threat of consumer boycotts against unsustainable businesses, this approach could differentiate the Hydrocamel from its competitor the Hippo Barrel - helping to win back charity customers and increase sales towards the target of 50,000 units, which would improve both revenue and profitability
> - Increased CSR focus is likely to raise costs in the short term, particularly if WTZ invests in better working conditions, higher wages, and employee training. WTZ's profit margin has already declined from 12.8% in 2021 to 9.3% in 2022, so any additional cost pressure could further reduce profitability in the near term. However, if improvements in employee motivation lead to higher productivity and lower absenteeism, these savings may eventually offset the additional costs - meaning the long-term impact on profitability could be positive
> - Greater focus on CSR could also protect WTZ from reputational and regulatory risk. The PEST analysis highlights proposed regulations in country R to reduce plastic use in food packaging, and global pressure groups are calling for boycotts of unsustainable businesses. If WTZ is seen as a leader in sustainable practices, rather than a business that exploits workers and harms the environment, it could avoid boycotts, attract government contracts, and appeal to environmentally conscious buyers in country R and country S, supporting long-term revenue growth.
> 
> Evaluation
> 
> - The most significant impact is likely to be improved employee productivity and lower absenteeism, since these directly address existing operational problems that are already reducing profitability; the marketing benefits are real but harder to quantify
> - CSR must be genuine - if WTZ promotes environmental credentials while continuing to pay minimum wage and refuse trade union recognition, it risks a damaging backlash from pressure groups, which could harm sales and profitability more than the cost savings gained
> - In the short term, CSR is likely to reduce profitability due to higher costs, but the long-term impact could be positive if it drives productivity gains, brand loyalty, and revenue growth
> - Do WTZ's customers in the recycled materials market care about CSR? Buyers may prioritise price over ethics, meaning the marketing benefits of CSR may be limited in that segment
> - WTZ may have more urgent priorities in the short term, such as addressing quality problems and the competitive threat from the Hippo Barrel, before investing heavily in broader CSR initiatives

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Child Play (CP) **
> 
> Su is a sole trader who started a business called CP which operates a play area for children. The play area is inside a building and includes toys and other play equipment. Customers book on CP’s website for each hour that they would like to use the play area. CP is two kilometres away from the nearest city which has a large population.
> 
> Su does not pay for any promotion and she relies on recommendations and reviews from previous customers. Su currently charges a price of \$10 an hour for a group of up to 5 children. Only one group can book CP for each hour. Demand is greater than supply so Su may increase the price to \$15 per hour. She has completed some market research to see if this is a good idea. Her findings are in Table 1.1.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Market research about prices for CP**
> 
> | **Price** | **Quantity (hours) demanded per day** |
> |---|---|
> | \$10 | 10 |
> | \$15 | 6 |
> 
> Su is also thinking about expanding the business by opening a café targeted at parents with children.
> 
> The café would be located at the entrance to CP’s play area. There are many other cafés in the city centre two kilometres away. Su believes that product differentiation is essential for the profitability of the café.
> 
> Su plans to use CP’s working capital as the source of finance to open the new café. The café will need to earn revenue quickly, so she plans to open it in four weeks. She will need quick and low‑cost promotion methods if the café is to succeed.

Explain **one **way in which the size of CP can be measured.
parts.solutionMd:
One way to measure the size of CP is by revenue - the total income earned from bookings **[1]**. At \$10 per hour with 10 hours of demand per day, CP currently earns \$100 per day **[1]**. This figure can be compared to other play area businesses to show how large CP is relative to its competitors **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Number of customers who book CP's services / use the café
> - Revenue from CP's services or café sales
> - Size of the building owned or rented
> - Capital invested / value of assets
> - Number of employees
> - Market share compared to competitors
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The more customers who book, the bigger the business is likely to be
> - The more revenue earned, the higher the value of goods and services sold and therefore the larger the business
> - The size of CP's building can be compared to similar businesses — a café with twice the floor space would be considered bigger
> - The value of CP's building reflects the assets of the business and therefore its size
> - Su appears to be the only employee, suggesting CP is a very small business
> - CP's market share is likely to be small as it operates from a single location and Su is a sole trader
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'organic growth'.
parts.solutionMd:
Organic growth is when a business expands by increasing its own output or opening new outlets **[1]**, using its own resources rather than by merging with or taking over another business **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Growth achieved by a business expanding its own operations, such as selling more products, opening new premises or entering new markets, funded from its own resources
> - An increase in the size of a business generated from within, without acquiring or merging with another firm
> - Expansion arising from the business's own activities - raising output, widening the product range or attracting more customers - rather than from external growth

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students define organic growth simply as 'the business getting bigger', which cannot earn both marks. The second mark lies in the contrast: make clear the expansion comes from the business's own activities and resources, not from merging with or buying another firm.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'horizontal integration'.
parts.solutionMd:
Horizontal integration is when a business merges with or takes over another business **[1]** that operates at the same stage of the same industry **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A merger with, or takeover of, a business at the same stage of production within the same industry
> - The combining of two firms that produce the same type of product or provide the same type of service
> - Integration between businesses that are direct competitors operating at the same level of the supply chain

> **[exam-tip]**
> Horizontal and vertical integration are easily confused. Ask yourself whether the two businesses sit at the same stage of the supply chain or at different stages - same stage is horizontal, different stages is vertical. Naming the stage in your definition makes the distinction unmistakable.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business might choose to remain small.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason a business might choose to remain small is to keep close personal contact with its customers **[1]**. In a small business the owner usually serves customers directly and can remember their individual preferences **[1]**. This kind of personal service becomes much harder to maintain as a business grows and employs more staff, so staying small allows the owner to keep the loyal customers who value being known and dealt with personally **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Reasons include keeping close contact with customers, retaining full control, avoiding diseconomies of scale, limited finance for expansion, serving a niche market, and the owner preferring a manageable workload
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Personal service is easier to provide when the owner deals with customers directly, and customers who value this are more likely to stay loyal and recommend the business
> - Remaining small allows the owner to keep full control of decisions rather than sharing it with investors or delegating to managers who may not share their priorities
> - Larger businesses can suffer diseconomies of scale such as poor communication and weaker motivation, which raise average costs - staying small avoids these
> - A business serving a niche market may find there are too few customers to justify growth, so expanding would raise costs without a proportionate rise in revenue
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is worth knowing where the three marks sit: one for naming a valid reason, and two for developing it. That means about a quarter of your answer identifies the reason and the rest explains it - so a single-sentence answer can never reach full marks, however accurate it is.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'hostile takeover'.
parts.solutionMd:
A hostile takeover is when one business buys another **[1]** against the wishes of the directors of the business being bought **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The purchase of one company by another where the directors of the target company oppose the sale
> - A takeover completed by appealing directly to shareholders because the board of the target business has rejected the offer
> - An acquisition that proceeds without the agreement of the management of the business being acquired

> **[exam-tip]**
> A one-mark answer says that one business buys another - but that is simply a takeover. The second mark comes from the word 'hostile', so you must show that the target company's directors do not want it to happen. Build the distinguishing word of the term into your definition every time.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'strategic alliance'.
parts.solutionMd:
A strategic alliance is an agreement between two or more businesses to work together on a particular project **[1]**, while each remains a separate and independent business **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An arrangement in which businesses co-operate to achieve a shared objective while remaining independent of one another
> - A partnership in which firms pool resources or expertise for a specific purpose without forming a new company
> - An agreement to work together, for example on research or distribution, which does not involve either business buying a share of the other

> **[exam-tip]**
> With two marks available, give two distinct pieces of information rather than one idea expressed twice. Here that means saying what the businesses do together and saying that they stay independent. Writing your definition as two clear clauses makes both marks easy to award.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Meridian (MR)**
> 
> Meridian (MR) is a coach travel company in country T. It runs scheduled services between towns and cities, and hires out coaches for school trips and private tours.
> 
> MR owns a fleet of 48 coaches, kept at two depots. It employs 90 people, most of whom are drivers. Because modern coaches are expensive to buy, MR has a large amount of money tied up in its fleet compared with many businesses employing a similar number of people.
> 
> **Table 1.1: MR selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 90 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 14 |
> | Capital employed (\$m) | 22 |
> | Coaches owned | 48 |
> | Share of the coach travel market in country T (%) | 11 |
> 
> MR's Managing Director has been asked to compare MR with a rival coach operator that employs 260 people but owns only 20 coaches, because it hires the rest.

Explain **one** method that could be used to measure the size of MR.
parts.solutionMd:
One method of measuring the size of MR is capital employed **[1]**. MR has \$22m of capital employed, which is high compared with its revenue of \$14m because coaches are expensive to buy **[1]**. This measure suits MR better than counting employees, because the rival operator employs 260 people but hires most of its coaches, so it would appear larger by headcount even though MR owns far more of the assets it uses **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Methods include number of employees, revenue, capital employed, market share, and the number of units of equipment or outlets owned
> 
> AO2
> 
> - MR's capital employed of \$22m reflects the money invested in its 48 coaches, making it the most informative measure for a business whose main asset is its fleet
> - Counting MR's 90 employees would understate its size against a rival employing 260 people, because that rival hires most of its coaches rather than owning them
> - MR's revenue of \$14m allows direct comparison of sales with competitors, though it reveals nothing about how much has been invested to generate them
> - MR's 11% market share shows its position relative to competitors in country T rather than its absolute size
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks about measuring business size, resist naming the first method that comes to mind. The development marks come from showing why that method suits this particular business - here, why capital employed tells you more about a coach operator than a headcount does.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Willow (WL)**
> 
> Willow (WL) owns six garden centres in country S. It sells plants, tools, compost and garden furniture, and each centre has a small cafe.
> 
> WL was started in 1971 by Grace Adeyemi, who opened a single plant nursery. It is now run by her daughter and two grandchildren, and the family still owns all of the shares. WL employs 210 people.
> 
> Several of WL's managers began as weekend staff and have worked for the business for more than twenty years. WL is well known in country S for the quality of its plants and for staff who can give expert gardening advice.
> 
> A national garden retailer has recently opened two large stores in the same region, selling similar products at lower prices.

Explain **one** strength of WL being a family business.
parts.solutionMd:
One strength of WL being a family business is that decisions can be made quickly **[1]**. WL is owned entirely by Grace Adeyemi's daughter and two grandchildren, so they can agree a change between themselves without consulting outside shareholders **[1]**. This speed matters now that a national garden retailer has opened two large stores in the same region, because WL can adjust its prices or its range of plants far sooner than a competitor whose managers must wait for approval from head office **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Strengths include quick decision-making, a long-term outlook, shared values and commitment, strong staff loyalty, and a reputation built on the family name
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Ownership rests with three family members, so decisions can be agreed without consulting outside shareholders - valuable now that a national retailer has opened nearby and WL must respond
> - The family is not under pressure to deliver short-term profit to investors, so it can keep investing in plant quality and staff expertise that take years to repay
> - Managers who started as weekend staff and stayed over twenty years show the loyalty family firms often build, and their expert advice is one of the few things the cheaper national retailer cannot match
> - WL's reputation in country S is tied to the Adeyemi family name, giving the owners a personal reason to protect standards rather than cut costs to compete on price
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The command asks you to explain **one** strength, so listing three or four will not score better than a single developed point - it usually scores worse. Pick the strength you can take furthest, then use your remaining two marks explaining what it actually lets the business do.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Orbit (OB)**
> 
> Orbit (OB) manufactures cases, chargers and headphones for mobile phones in country R. It was set up eight years ago and employs 45 people at a single factory.
> 
> OB sells mainly to independent phone shops across country R. Demand for its products has grown steadily, and OB's factory now runs at 96% of its capacity. In the past year OB has turned down two large orders because it could not produce enough units in time.
> 
> **Table 1.1: OB selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 45 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 3.8 |
> | Capacity utilisation (%) | 96 |
> | Average cost per unit (\$) | 4.20 |
> | Orders refused in 2025 (units) | 60,000 |
> 
> OB's owner is considering renting a second factory unit nearby.

Explain **one** reason why OB might want to grow.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason OB might want to grow is to meet demand that it currently has to turn away **[1]**. OB's factory already runs at 96% of capacity, and in the past year it refused orders totalling 60,000 units **[1]**. By renting a second factory unit, OB could accept these orders rather than losing them, raising its revenue and reducing the risk that the independent phone shops it supplies find another manufacturer and stay with them permanently **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Reasons for growth include meeting unmet demand, achieving economies of scale, increasing market share and profit, spreading risk, and improving the owner's security
> 
> AO2
> 
> - OB runs at 96% capacity and refused 60,000 units of orders in 2025, so demand already exists that the business cannot currently supply
> - Turning away orders risks losing customers for good, as the independent phone shops may switch to a manufacturer able to deliver in full and not return
> - Producing across a second factory would spread fixed costs over more units, which could bring OB's average cost below \$4.20 and widen its profit margin
> - Running so close to full capacity leaves no room for machine breakdowns or urgent orders, so extra capacity would make OB more reliable for its customers
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two of the three marks here are for development, and development means going somewhere new rather than restating the point in different words. Once you have given the reason, ask yourself "so what happens next for this business?" - the answer to that question is where the remaining marks are.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Harbour (HB)**
> 
> Harbour (HB) is a supermarket chain with 34 stores along the coast of country Q. It employs 1,400 people and is known for stocking fish and fresh produce from suppliers in the towns where its stores are located.
> 
> HB buys from around 200 small local suppliers. Many of these suppliers sell most of what they produce to HB.
> 
> A national supermarket group has offered to buy HB. The national group operates 600 stores across country Q, buys centrally from a small number of large suppliers, and sells at lower prices than HB.
> 
> HB's directors have recommended that shareholders accept the offer. Local newspapers have reported concern among shoppers and suppliers about what the sale would mean.

Explain **one** way the proposed takeover could affect HB's suppliers.
parts.solutionMd:
One way the takeover could affect HB's suppliers is that many of them could lose their main customer **[1]**. The national group buys centrally from a small number of large suppliers, so it is unlikely to keep contracts with around 200 small local producers **[1]**. Because many of these suppliers sell most of what they produce to HB, losing that contract would threaten their survival rather than simply reduce their sales, and some may have to cut output or close altogether **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A takeover can affect suppliers through cancelled contracts, changed payment terms, pressure to reduce prices, larger order volumes, or greater certainty of payment from a bigger buyer
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The national group buys centrally from a small number of large suppliers, so most of HB's 200 local producers are unlikely to be retained
> - Many of these suppliers sell most of their output to HB, so losing the contract puts their survival at risk rather than simply reducing their revenue
> - Suppliers who are kept on may have to accept lower prices or longer payment periods, as a group with 600 stores has far greater bargaining power than HB
> - A small number of suppliers could gain if the national group offers access to all 600 of its stores, producing far larger orders than HB could ever place
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read carefully which group the question names. This one asks about suppliers, so points about shoppers or staff earn nothing however well argued. Underlining the stakeholder named in the question before you begin is a quick way to avoid throwing marks away.

Lewis is a sole trader and he set up BR 25 years ago. > > BR is the smallest of all the hairdressers in city Y. Lewis works on his own. He has repeat customers who have been using BR for many years. One advantage of operating as a small business is that Lewis can offer highly personalised customer service **[K]**. This loyalty gives BR a competitive advantage that does not depend on price, helping Lewis retain customers despite cheaper competition > - As a small business, Lewis has the flexibility to respond quickly to changes in the market. If a franchise launches a promotion or cuts its prices, Lewis can adapt immediately - for example by adjusting his prices or offering new services - whereas a large franchise would need to gain approval through multiple layers of management, slowing its response > - BR is easier to organise and manage because Lewis is the only employee. There are no communication issues, no need to coordinate staff rotas, and Lewis has full oversight of bookings and finances. By operating across multiple locations and serving many more customers, they can buy supplies in bulk at lower cost and spread fixed costs more widely, allowing them to charge prices significantly lower than BR's \$8. parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Cedar (CD)**
> 
> Cedar (CD) is a building firm in country N. It employs nine people - two bricklayers, three carpenters, a plasterer and two apprentices - alongside its owner, Tomas.
>

> **[case-study]**
> **Super Heroes (SH) **
> 
> SH is a leisure (theme) park aimed at 10–18 year olds. It is owned by two companies, X and Y, which started SH as a joint venture. Company X owns many leisure centres and swimming pools. Company Y owns many brands based on superheroes.
> 
> SH employs 200 full-time workers and an extra 50 seasonal workers during the busiest times of the year. The park has 10 large rides which take up 2km<sup>2</sup> of land. There are also many smaller rides, restaurants, toilets and shops. The price of an entrance ticket is \$11 per customer. Table 1.1 shows the costs for SH in 2019.
> 
> **Table 1.1: SH costs for 2019**
> 
> | Total fixed costs (per year) | \$12m |
> |---|---|
> | Variable costs (per customer) | \$3 |
> | Total costs | \$42m |
> 
> One of the larger rides at SH is the Iron Blaster. The number of customers who use this ride has decreased each year for the last three years. This has led the management of SH to consider its options for internal growth.
> 
> *Option 1 – A new virtual reality (VR) ride *
> This option would involve developing the Iron Blaster into a VR ride. Most of the structure of the Iron Blaster could be used, but customers would be given a VR headset to wear during the ride. The cost of developing the VR ride would be \$2m. The Iron Blaster ride would be closed for a three-month period during the off-peak season for the development to be carried out. No employees would be made redundant or dismissed.
> 
> *Option 2 – A new hotel *
> SH does not currently have a hotel. It could demolish the Iron Blaster to provide the space to build one. Many of the competitors of SH have a hotel near or within their leisure parks. Hotel customers would pay a high price for a room but have free access to the leisure park’s facilities. Market research suggests that the average hotel customer would spend twice as long in the leisure park than a non-hotel customer. The cost of developing the hotel would be \$15m and take a year to build. All of the employees currently working on the Iron Blaster ride would face redundancy or dismissal.

Recommend which one of the two options SH should choose for internal growth. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
The VR ride costs \$2m compared to \$15m **[Ap]** for the hotel, making it significantly lower risk for SH **[K]**. If it fails to attract customers, the financial loss is much more manageable. VR technology is also likely to appeal strongly to SH's target market of 10–18-year-olds **[Ap]**, who tend to adopt new technology quickly. Development takes place during the off-peak season, minimising lost revenue, and no employees face redundancy, avoiding costly legal complications **[An]**

The hotel would create a valuable new revenue stream **[K]**. Because hotel guests spend twice as long in the park **[Ap]**, SH would earn more from its restaurants and shops. Many competitors already have hotels, so SH risks falling behind without one. However, the \$15m cost and one-year closure **[Ap]**represent a very large financial commitment, and all Iron Blaster employees would face redundancy, adding further costs and legal risk **[An]**

I recommend Option 1. The most important factor is financial risk **[E]**- at \$2m versus \$15m **[Ap]**, the VR ride is far more affordable and leaves SH better protected if visitor numbers do not increase as expected. Option 2's long-term potential is real, but only if demand for hotel rooms is strong, which the case study does not confirm **[Ap]**. Option 1 delivers a faster, lower-risk improvement that directly targets SH's existing customer base **[E]**

Recommend whether the directors of HD should accept MW’s joint venture offer. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason HD should accept the joint venture is that MW manufactures the board, placing no additional burden on HD's already over-stretched factory **[K] [Ap]**. HD contributes design expertise and marketing — its core competencies. Financially, the risk is low: HD's current ratio is a strong 5:1 (\$20m current assets ÷ \$4m current liabilities) **[Ap]** and gearing is just 16.7%, meaning internal finance is available without taking on new debt. The \$0.5m profit is modest but achievable with limited financial exposure **[An]**

However, there are serious concerns. HD's design engineers are already under pressure **[K]** - five left in just five months **[Ap]** and project deadlines are slipping. Adding more design work could worsen this significantly. The joint venture also offers a profit margin of only 10% (\$0.5m ÷ \$5m revenue), compared to HD's current operating margin of 20% **[Ap]**, making it far less profitable per dollar of revenue. With only one marketing employee, HD may also struggle to fulfil its agreed marketing role effectively **[An]**

Overall, I recommend HD accepts the joint venture, but only if it can resource the design work without further overloading its engineers **[E]**. Financial risk is low, MW bears the manufacturing costs, and the two-year product life limits long-term commitment **[Ap]**. However, the most important condition is that HD addresses its design capacity problem first **[E]** - if labour turnover continues to rise **[Ap]**, HD risks being unable to deliver the design work the joint venture depends on, undermining both the project and HD's wider reputation **[E]**

parts.solutionMd:
Between 2008 and 2015, RF's strategy of organic growth through profit reinvestment was effective **[E]**. Gearing remained just 5% in 2015 and ROCE was a reasonable 9% **[K] [Ap]**, suggesting the business was financially stable. Specialising entirely in sugarcane increased efficiency and benefited from large profit margins, though it also concentrated risk in a single product **[Ap] [An]** The 2016 takeover of BKL marked a turning point **[E]**. Financed by a bank loan and share issue, gearing rose to 30% and John ceded some control over RF **[Ap]**. More significantly, the cultural clash between RF's hard HRM and BKL's soft HRM caused half of BKL's employees to leave **[Ap]**. Recruitment difficulties and falling productivity contributed to ROCE declining from 9% to 5% by 2018 and profit falling from \$2.3m to \$0.6m **[Ap]**, suggesting the takeover was poorly managed **[An]** The 2018 building was strategically logical - greater inventory capacity allowed RF to hold sugarcane and benefit from price changes **[K] [Ap]**.
