Holding excessive stock ties up cash, restricts the ability to meet short-term obligations, and increases vulnerability to disruption - exactly the situation LH found itself in as problems mounted from 2022 onwards > - Trade receivables increased dramatically after the takeover as LH shifted to international corporate customers who demanded longer payment terms. This worsened cash flow and increased financial risk, contradicting the benefit of PS's short 15-day receivables period identified in the SWOT analysis > - PS was acquired partly for its established international brand awareness, yet LH abandoned the PS brand entirely by 2021. This raises serious questions about whether the expected synergies were ever realised, and suggests the integration of PS was poorly managed > - DPS fell from \$5 to \$0.5 between 2017 and 2021 - a 90% reduction. Declining shareholder returns alongside rising gearing would have increased pressure on Loretta, and may have contributed to shareholder dissatisfaction culminating in her replacement at the EGM > - The central question is whether revenue growth justified the dramatic deterioration in every other financial indicator. Loretta's stated objective was profit maximisation - yet OPM was cut by two-thirds, suggesting the takeover directly contradicted her own strategic aim > - The high gearing created a chain of consequences: debt servicing costs restricted investment, leading to outdated IT and quality control failures, which contributed to the cyber-attack that ultimately destroyed the business's data, reputation, and Loretta's position. This suggests the takeover created structural fragility that LH could not recover from > - Some deterioration in short-term profitability and liquidity is expected when funding rapid international expansion, and that the revenue growth achieved would eventually have restored margins. However, the online reviews in 2022 suggest quality and service were already failing before the cyber-attack, indicating deeper operational problems beyond timing > - On balance, the takeover was the wrong decision for LH. The synergies identified in the SWOT analysis - international brand awareness, strong supplier network, short receivables - were either not realised or cancelled out by PS's weaknesses. The most important outcome of the takeover was not growth, but the creation of financial vulnerability that LH was unable to withstand > > Accept all valid responses.

parts.problemMd:
‘Marketing is the most important factor for the success of small businesses.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Marketing involves identifying and satisfying customer needs profitably **[K]**. For a small business, it is undeniably important - without customers, there is no revenue. A new small business is largely unknown **[Ap]**, so marketing creates awareness and communicates its value proposition **[An]**. In a competitive market, effective marketing helps attract customers away from larger competitors, and digital and social media marketing makes this relatively affordable for businesses with limited budgets **[An]**

However, many small businesses fail not because of poor marketing but because of inadequate cash flow management **[K]**. A business can attract customers through effective marketing but still fail if it cannot pay suppliers, employees or rent on time. Sound financial management - monitoring cash flow and controlling costs **[K] **- is arguably more fundamental to short-term survival, particularly in the early stages when cash is scarce and margins are tight  **[Ap]** **[An]**

Product quality **[K] **is also critical. If a small business cannot consistently deliver what it promises, marketing can accelerate its failure by raising customer expectations it cannot meet **[Ap]**. Negative online reviews damage reputation quickly and are difficult to recover from. A business with a genuinely distinctive product may need very little formal marketing - satisfied customers generate recommendations that drive growth organically at no cost **[An]**

Overall, marketing is important but is unlikely to be the single most important factor for the success of small businesses **[E]**. Its significance depends on the stage of the business: in the short term, financial management and operational quality are more critical - a business must first stay solvent and deliver reliably before marketing can have any meaningful impact **[An]**. Marketing becomes the most important factor once these foundations are in place and the business needs to grow and compete in the market. For most small businesses, survival must come before growth **[Ap]** **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **5** | 17-20 | - Effective evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that marketing is the most important factor for the success of small businesses |
> | **4** | 15-16 | - Limited evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that marketing is the most important factor for the success of small businesses |
> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of the extent to which you agree with the view that marketing is the most important factor for the success of small businesses |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the view that marketing is important to the success of small businesses |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of marketing/small businesses |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> Arguments for marketing being the most important factor
> 
> - Marketing creates awareness of a small business and communicates its value proposition to potential customers. Without customers there is no revenue, so attracting and retaining them is fundamental to success. A new small business is largely unknown, making marketing essential for establishing itself in the market
> - Effective marketing helps a small business differentiate itself from larger, better-resourced competitors. If a small business cannot compete on price, it must compete on perceived value - communicating quality, uniqueness or personal service through targeted promotion
> - Digital and social media marketing is relatively low-cost and accessible, meaning small businesses can reach large audiences without the significant budgets required for traditional advertising. This partially levels the playing field with larger competitors
> - Marketing sustains customer relationships and encourages repeat business, which is often the primary revenue source for small businesses. Loyal customers also generate word-of-mouth referrals, which costs nothing but can be highly effective
> 
> Arguments against marketing being the most important factor
> 
> - Many small businesses fail due to poor cash flow management rather than poor marketing. A business can attract customers through effective marketing but still collapse if it cannot pay suppliers, employees or rent on time. Financial management is arguably more fundamental to survival, particularly in the early stages
> - The quality of the product or service is critical. If a business cannot consistently deliver what it promises, marketing raises customer expectations it cannot meet - accelerating its failure through negative reviews and damaged reputation. A distinctive, high-quality product may generate sufficient word-of-mouth with very little formal marketing
> - Skilled management and operational efficiency are also essential. Poor decision-making, weak record-keeping, or inability to scale operations will undermine any marketing success
> - The economic environment can outweigh the impact of marketing entirely. In a recession, reduced consumer spending may mean that even highly effective marketing cannot generate sufficient demand to keep a small business viable
> 
> Evaluation
> 
> - The relative importance of marketing depends on the stage of the business. In the short term, financial management and product quality are more critical to survival. Marketing becomes the most important factor once the business is financially stable and needs to grow its customer base
> - The degree of competition matters. In a crowded market, marketing may be the key differentiator; in a niche market with little competition, operational quality and financial management may matter more.
> - A balanced conclusion might argue that marketing is a necessary but not sufficient condition for success - it amplifies a well-run business but cannot compensate for poor financial management, weak products or operational failure.
> - The time horizon of "success" is also relevant: short-term survival depends most on cash flow; long-term growth depends more on marketing and brand building
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘stakeholder’.
parts.solutionMd:
A stakeholder is any person or group that is affected by the activities of a business **[1]** and therefore has an interest in how it operates **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - People/groups of people who can be affected by a business/organisation
> - AND therefore have an interest in the business/organisation
> 
> A clear, correct definition earns 2 marks. A partial, vague or unfocused definition earns 1 mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure your definition includes two key ideas: that stakeholders are affected by the business, and that they have an interest in it. Simply listing examples of stakeholders (e.g. employees, customers) without explaining what a stakeholder is will not earn marks.

**[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **reasons why conflict might arise between different stakeholders.
parts.solutionMd:
Stakeholders often have conflicting interests because what benefits one group may harm another **[1]**. For example, shareholders may want the business to cut labour costs to increase profit, while employees want higher wages - these two groups want opposite things **[1]**. Similarly, a business expanding its operations may benefit shareholders through higher profits, but the local community may be negatively affected by increased traffic, noise or environmental damage **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Different stakeholders have different and often conflicting interests, needs and expectations from a business
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Shareholders may want the business to cut costs by reducing wages, while employees want higher pay - directly opposing interests
> - A growing business may bring more local employment, but increased traffic, noise or pollution may conflict with the interests of the local community
> - The government may push for greater corporate social responsibility, while shareholders resist because it increases costs and reduces profits
> - A business may pressure suppliers to reduce their prices to cut its own costs, while suppliers need to maintain their prices to remain profitable
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure each reason clearly identifies which stakeholders are in conflict and what their competing interests are. A common mistake is to simply list stakeholders without explaining why their objectives clash. For full marks, develop each reason fully – state the stakeholder groups, explain what each group wants, and show why these wants are incompatible. Using real-world or realistic examples (e.g. shareholders wanting higher profits versus employees wanting higher wages) will strengthen your explanation.

**[3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'internal stakeholder'.
parts.solutionMd:
An internal stakeholder is a person or group who has an interest in a business **[1]** and is part of the organisation itself, such as an employee, a manager or an owner **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A person or group with an interest in a business who is part of the organisation, such as owners, managers and employees
> - A stakeholder who works within or owns the business, and is therefore directly affected by its day-to-day decisions
> - Someone inside the business whose job, income or investment is influenced by how the business performs

> **[exam-tip]**
> A two-mark definition should take one sentence, not a paragraph. Writing at length here costs time you will need for the longer questions later in the paper and earns nothing extra once both marking points are made. Be accurate, then move on.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'external stakeholder'.
parts.solutionMd:
An external stakeholder is a person or group who has an interest in a business **[1]** but is not part of the organisation, such as a customer, a supplier or a local resident **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A person or group affected by a business's activities who neither works for it nor owns it, such as customers, suppliers, the government or the local community
> - A stakeholder outside the organisation whose interests are influenced by what the business does, even though they take no part in running it
> - Someone with a stake in the business from outside it - because they buy from it, supply it, regulate it, or live near it

> **[exam-tip]**
> A definition that would work equally well for an internal stakeholder cannot earn both marks. Test your answer by asking whether it rules the other type out - if it does not, you have not yet said what makes this stakeholder external.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'stakeholder conflict'.
parts.solutionMd:
Stakeholder conflict is a disagreement that arises when two or more stakeholder groups want different things from a business **[1]**, so that meeting the aims of one group means the aims of another cannot be met **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A situation in which different stakeholder groups hold aims that cannot all be satisfied at the same time
> - Disagreement between stakeholders because a decision that benefits one group disadvantages another
> - Tension arising from stakeholders having incompatible objectives, so the business must decide whose interests to prioritise

> **[exam-tip]**
> Everyday words such as "argument" or "people falling out" will not reach full marks. Examiners look for the subject's own vocabulary - aims, objectives, groups, trade-off. Using business language signals that you understand the concept rather than just the ordinary meaning of the word.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'accountability'.
parts.solutionMd:
Accountability means a business being answerable for its decisions and actions **[1]** to the groups affected by them, who can require it to explain and justify what it has done **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The obligation of a business to explain and justify its decisions to those affected by them
> - Being answerable to stakeholders for the consequences of the business's actions, and accepting responsibility for them
> - The duty of managers to report on their decisions and performance to groups with a legitimate interest in the business

> **[exam-tip]**
> Abstract terms such as accountability are easier to define if you say who is accountable and to whom. A definition built around "a business being answerable to X for Y" will almost always reach both marks, whereas swapping in a one-word substitute like "responsibility" will not.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Reel (RL)**
> 
> Reel (RL) operates 22 cinemas in country F. Fourteen are large multi-screen cinemas in cities. The other eight are small single-screen cinemas in country towns.
> 
> Audiences at the eight town cinemas have fallen sharply since streaming services became popular.
> 
> **Table 1.1: RL selected data**
> 
> | Average seats sold per showing, city cinemas | 96 |
> |---|---|
> | Average seats sold per showing, town cinemas | 21 |
> | Cost of running one town cinema for a year (\$000) | 180 |
> 
> RL's directors have decided to close all eight town cinemas at the end of the year. In several of these towns, RL's cinema is the only one.

Explain **one** way RL's decision to close its town cinemas could affect its customers.
parts.solutionMd:
One way the decision could affect customers is that people in the country towns will lose access to a cinema altogether **[1]**. In several of these towns RL's cinema is the only one, so customers cannot simply switch to a competitor **[1]**. They would have to travel to a city cinema instead, which costs both time and money, so many are likely to stop going to the cinema at all and watch films on streaming services instead **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A business decision can affect customers through availability, price, choice, quality of service, or convenience
> 
> AO2
> 
> - RL's cinema is the only one in several towns, so closure removes the service entirely rather than reducing customers' choice of provider
> - Customers wanting to see a film must travel to a city cinema, adding cost and time that may outweigh the value of the trip
> - Some customers will move permanently to streaming services, which have already cut town audiences to 21 seats per showing
> - Customers at RL's 14 city cinemas may be unaffected, or may benefit if money saved from the closures is reinvested in the remaining sites
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a case study offers several possible effects, choose the one its material actually supports. Here the detail that RL's cinema is the only one in several towns is what turns a general point about inconvenience into a specific, creditworthy one. Look for the sentence in the case that you could not have guessed.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Cascade (CS)**
> 
> Cascade (CS) collects and processes household waste for recycling in country E. It holds contracts with fourteen local councils and employs 260 people across three processing sites.
> 
> Last year, residents living near one site complained about dust and noise. A local newspaper reported that CS had not replied to any of the complaints.
> 
> The council that awarded that contract has since asked CS to publish a monthly report on dust levels and to hold public meetings twice a year. The contract is worth \$2.9m a year and is due for renewal in eighteen months.

Explain **one** reason why CS needs to be accountable to its stakeholders.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that CS depends on stakeholders who are able to take its business away **[1]**. The council that awarded the contract for the site where residents complained pays CS \$2.9m a year, and that contract is due for renewal in eighteen months **[1]**. If CS continues to ignore complaints, the council may decide it is difficult to work with and award the contract to a competitor, so being accountable protects income that CS could not easily replace **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Accountability matters because stakeholders can influence a business through their spending, their contracts, their power to regulate it, or their willingness to work for it
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The council contract is worth \$2.9m a year and is up for renewal in eighteen months, so ignoring residents risks income CS cannot easily replace
> - Residents who feel ignored may campaign against CS or object to future planning applications, which could block expansion or continued use of the site
> - Publishing dust readings and holding public meetings lets CS demonstrate the problem is being managed, which is far more persuasive than private assurances
> - Newspaper coverage of unanswered complaints may damage CS's standing with the other thirteen councils, making future contracts harder to win
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Where a case study gives you a figure, build your reasoning around it. Saying CS could lose "some income" is much weaker than saying it could lose a contract worth \$2.9m a year. The number itself earns no mark, but using it shows the examiner you are answering about this business rather than any business.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Balm (BM)**
> 
> Balm (BM) owns 90 pharmacies in country D. Until this year its stated objective was "to give every customer expert personal advice about their medicines".
> 
> BM's profits have fallen for three years. Its new owners have set a different objective: to reduce operating costs by 15% within two years.
> 
> To achieve this, BM plans to reduce the number of qualified pharmacists in each branch from two to one, and to install machines that dispense common prescriptions automatically.
> 
> BM employs 180 pharmacists and 700 other staff.

Explain **one** way BM's change of objective could affect its employees.
parts.solutionMd:
One way the change could affect employees is that many pharmacists will lose their jobs **[1]**. BM plans to cut the number of qualified pharmacists in each of its 90 branches from two to one in order to reduce operating costs by 15% **[1]**. That puts around half of BM's 180 pharmacists at risk of redundancy, and those who remain are likely to feel less secure and more pressured, because each will be doing alone the work that two people previously shared **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A change of objectives can affect employees through job security, workload, training, motivation, pay, or the nature of the work itself
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Cutting from two pharmacists per branch to one across 90 branches puts roughly half of BM's 180 pharmacists at risk of redundancy
> - Pharmacists who keep their jobs will carry alone the workload two people previously shared, which may raise stress and increase the risk of dispensing errors
> - Staff who joined BM because of its objective of giving expert personal advice may feel the business no longer stands for what attracted them, weakening motivation
> - Automatic dispensing machines change the work of the 700 other staff, who may need retraining, though some could gain useful new skills as a result
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "affect" is neutral, so an effect that benefits employees scores just as well as one that harms them, provided it is properly developed. Choose whichever you can explain most convincingly from the case rather than assuming the examiner is looking for bad news.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ridge (RG)**
> 
> Ridge (RG) is a haulage company in country C. It runs 140 lorries delivering goods between ports and warehouses, and employs 310 people.
> 
> RG planned to build a new depot on land beside a village. The depot would have allowed RG to add 40 lorries and take on a large new contract.
> 
> Residents of the village formed a group to oppose the plan, collecting 1,200 signatures and arguing that lorry traffic would make the village road unsafe. The local council refused RG planning permission.
> 
> RG is now considering a site eleven kilometres further from the main road, which would add around \$340,000 a year to its fuel and driver costs.

Explain **one** way an external stakeholder has influenced RG's decisions.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is that the local community has prevented RG from building its depot where it wanted **[1]**. Village residents formed a group, collected 1,200 signatures and persuaded the local council to refuse planning permission **[1]**. RG must now consider a site eleven kilometres further away, which would add about \$340,000 a year to its fuel and driver costs, so a group with no ownership of RG has directly reduced the profit the new contract will earn **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - External stakeholders can influence decisions through their purchasing choices, campaigning, regulation, planning control, supply terms, or media attention
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Residents collected 1,200 signatures and organised opposition, giving the council both evidence and public support for refusing permission
> - The council holds legal authority over land use, so its refusal is binding on RG in a way that customer preferences would not be
> - The alternative site adds around \$340,000 a year in fuel and driver costs, so the community's influence has a measurable financial effect
> - RG may have to redesign its plans or negotiate with residents before applying again, delaying both the new contract and the 40 extra lorries
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every external stakeholder has an interest, but not all of them have influence. The marks here come from showing the mechanism - how the group actually changed what RG did. Name the steps: the signatures, the council, the refusal. Saying residents "were unhappy" describes a feeling, not an influence.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Charlie’s Chocolates (CC) **
> 
> CC is a large public limited company that manufactures a wide range of chocolate bars. Production takes place in low wage countries so that costs can be kept low. CC has suffered recently from poor publicity due to the high levels of sugar used in the production of its chocolate. A national newspaper has recently published an article about how CC exploits employees in low wage countries. The Marketing Director, Alan, is aware of recent trends showing that consumers are becoming more ethical in their buying decisions. He thinks this might explain why sales decreased by 10% last year.
> 
> He has asked to meet with the Managing Director, Ikram, to discuss a major change towards more ethical production methods. This could mean re-locating production back to the home country. This will increase costs and involve the recruitment of additional employees. In response to recent Government guidelines to improve health, Alan wants to decrease the amount of sugar used in the chocolate bars.
> 
> Alan is also thinking about the financial accounts for this year that he received this morning from Ikram (see Table 1 and Table 2).
> 
> **Table 1 – Extract from Income Statement**
> 
> |   | \$000s |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue | 7000 |
> | Cost of sales | 4150 |
> | Gross profit | 2850 |
> | Profit for the year | 1350 |
> | Retained earnings | 565 |
> 
> **Table 2 – Extract from Statement of Financial Position**
> 
> |   | \$000s |
> |---|---|
> | Non-current assets | 3000 |
> | Current assets | 900 |
> | Current liabilities | 400 |
> | Working capital | 500 |
> | Net assets | 3500 |
> 
> With sales declining from last year, Alan has to think carefully about the next steps for marketing. He knows that the product range is of good quality – the problem is the poor image of the company. For example, he is aware that a local consumer group is trying to organise a demonstration outside one of CC’s factories in the next few weeks.

Analyse the usefulness of the financial accounts to **two **of CC’s stakeholders.
parts.solutionMd:
Shareholders can use the income statement to assess the likelihood of receiving a dividend **[K]**. CC's profit for the year is \$1.35m, suggesting funds are available for distribution. However, sales fell 10% last year due to CC's poor ethical image, and retained earnings are only \$565,000 **[Ap]**, suggesting limited reinvestment **[An]**. The accounts are useful for assessing current profitability, but they only show historical data and cannot tell shareholders how much further the reputational damage from the newspaper article and consumer protests might reduce profits in future **[An]** Consumer groups can use the accounts to make a powerful argument against CC **[K]**. With a gross profit of \$2.85m on revenue of \$7m - a margin of 40.7% **[Ap] **- the accounts demonstrate clearly that CC is profitable and has the financial means to change its practices **[An]**. The consumer group planning to demonstrate outside CC's factories could use this data to argue that CC's decision to continue exploiting low-wage workers and using high sugar content is a deliberate choice, not a financial necessity. This makes the accounts genuinely useful for the campaign, though they do not capture the full extent of the reputational and ethical problems CC is now facing **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer shows knowledge of **two** relevant points that answer the question | **2 marks**

- The answer links **two** relevant points to the business in the case study | **4 marks**

- The answer clearly explains the causes, impacts or consequences of **two** points | > | **3 marks**

- The answer clearly explains the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > | **1** | **1 mark**

- The answer shows knowledge of **one** relevant point that answers the question | **1 mark**

- The answer links **one** relevant point to the business in the case study | **2 marks**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **two** points. | > | **1 mark**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > > **Indicative content** > > - Shareholders can use the income statement to assess their likely dividend payment - profit for the year is \$1.35m, suggesting funds are available for distribution. However, with sales already declining by 10% due to poor brand image, the accounts show only past performance and give no guarantee of future profits. Shareholders will be concerned that the ethical and reputational problems facing CC could further reduce profits in the coming year, making the accounts a useful but incomplete picture > - Consumer groups can use the accounts to strengthen their campaign. CC made over \$1.35m profit while being publicly accused of exploiting workers and using excessive sugar - the accounts demonstrate that CC has the financial means to make ethical changes but has chosen not to. A gross profit of \$2.85m on revenue of \$7m (a gross profit margin of 40.7%) makes it difficult for CC to argue it cannot afford to act. This makes the accounts a powerful campaigning tool > - Employees and trade unions can use the income statement to support wage demands, pointing to the \$2.85m gross profit as evidence that the business can afford to pay higher wages - particularly if production is relocated to the home country. However, the accounts are historical and may not reflect future performance if the reputational problems worsen > - The usefulness of the accounts to all stakeholders is limited by the fact that they are historical, may involve window dressing, and do not capture non-financial information such as the reputational damage CC is currently facing > > Accept any other appropriate response

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **responsibilities to a business of an employee as a stakeholder.
parts.solutionMd:
One responsibility of an employee is to work productively and meet the standards set out in their contract of employment **[K]**. This means completing tasks to a high standard, managing time well, and making effective use of working hours. When employees do this consistently, the business benefits from efficient use of its resources - unit costs are kept low relative to output, helping to improve profit margins **[An]**. If employees regularly underperform through absenteeism or poor quality work, the business faces higher costs, lower customer satisfaction, and reduced competitiveness, which could ultimately threaten jobs **[Ap] [An]** A second responsibility is to maintain the confidentiality of the business and not share sensitive information with competitors **[K]**. Employees often have access to information about pricing strategies, production methods, or new product development **[Ap]**. If this is leaked, the business loses its competitive advantage - competitors could use the information to undercut prices or copy products, leading to falling market share and reduced profitability **[An]**. A business that cannot trust its employees to protect confidential information is also likely to face higher monitoring and security costs, further reducing efficiency and performance **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to a relevant business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer shows knowledge of **two** relevant points that answer the question | **2 marks**

However, local residents are concerned about the pollution of water supplies that tin mining can cause. Clean water is essential for everyday life, and contamination would directly damage the community's health and quality of life. The government's economic priorities conflict directly with the community's need for a safe environment **[An]**

Since the remote area has high unemployment and low incomes **[Ap]**, TM may offer relatively low wages knowing workers have few alternatives, but this risks creating resentment and high labour turnover, which could increase costs and affect productivity over time **[An]**

The government has already prioritised economic development over environmental concerns **[Ap]**, but if water pollution occurs, local trust in both TM and the government will be seriously damaged. Accountability means a business being answerable to the groups affected by its decisions **[K]**. Publishing a supply chain report would let EM answer the campaign group's claims with evidence rather than denial, and 46% of the customers it surveyed said ethical sourcing affects where they buy coffee **[Ap]**. Those customers can switch to a competing cafe very easily, so a report showing that EM inspects its farms could protect a large share of its \$420m revenue **[An]**

However, the report would cost \$4.2m a year, which is more than an eighth of EM's \$31m profit **[Ap]**. It would also be difficult to produce accurately, because 62% of EM's beans are bought through intermediaries rather than directly from farms, so EM does not currently know conditions at every farm it depends on **[K]**. Publishing incomplete findings, or findings that confirm the campaign group's claims, could damage EM's reputation more than staying silent would **[An]**

Whether EM should publish depends largely on how quickly it can gain control of its supply chain **[E]**. Reporting while most beans still arrive through intermediaries risks publishing figures EM cannot stand behind, so a stronger approach would be to begin inspections now and publish only once EM buys directly from most of its farms **[E]**. The \$4.2m cost is significant but not decisive; it is around 1% of revenue, and losing even a small proportion of the 46% of customers who care about sourcing would cost EM more than that **[E]**. Overall EM should commit to publishing, because a public limited company of this size cannot leave campaign group claims unanswered without appearing to have something to hide **[E]**. The finance director is right about one thing though: the timing and scope of the first report matter as much as the decision to publish at all **[E]**

> **Indicative content**

> - EM could publish the report in full, naming every farm and the findings of independent inspections. This answers the campaign group with evidence rather than denial and protects the 46% of surveyed customers who say ethical sourcing affects where they buy, a live commercial risk for a business earning \$420m in a market customers can leave very easily. However, 62% of EM's beans arrive through intermediaries, so a report published now would be incomplete and could trigger a second and more damaging story about inaccurate reporting

> **[case-study]**
> **Snappy Box (SB) **
> 
> SB is owned by Ralph who is a sole trader. The business prints photographs. Ralph has one shop on the main street of city D. Customers bring their saved digital photographs into the shop and these are printed on high-quality paper.
> 
> SB uses a large printing machine that can print on almost any size of paper to produce different sized photograph prints. The process is very capital-intensive and most customers request a batch of photographs to be printed.
> 
> SB is the only shop in city D that prints photographs. However, recently a number of online competitors have started to offer low-priced photograph prints to customers. Ralph has noticed that his sales have decreased significantly because of this competition. Ralph estimates the demand for his photograph prints has a price elasticity of demand of –4.
>

He could stop printing photographs and instead focus on framing individual photographs for customers. These frames will be made for any sized photograph or picture and can be made from a variety of materials chosen by the customer.

>

>

Explain the term ‘profit margin'.
parts.solutionMd:
Profit margin is profit shown as a percentage of revenue** [1]**. SB already has a low profit margin, and this is getting worse because of competition from online photo printers offering lower prices. parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘gross profit margin’.
parts.solutionMd:
Gross profit margin is a profitability ratio **[1]** that shows gross profit as a percentage of revenue **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A profitability ratio that compares gross profit (profit before the deduction of overheads/expenses) with revenue, usually expressed as a percentage.
> - A measure showing how much gross profit a business makes for every dollar of revenue, calculated as gross profit divided by revenue.
> - The percentage of revenue remaining after cost of sales has been deducted, but before other expenses are taken away
> - $\mathrm{Gross} \mathrm{profit} \mathrm{margin}=\frac{\mathrm{Gross} \mathrm{Profit}}{\mathrm{Total} \mathrm{Revenue}(\mathrm{Sales})}\times100$

parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘liquidity ratio’.
parts.solutionMd:
A liquidity ratio is a financial ratio that measures whether a business has enough short-term assets **[1]** to pay off its short-term debts **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A financial ratio that assesses the short-term financial strength of a business, measuring its ability to pay its short-term debts.
> - A ratio, such as the current ratio or acid test ratio, that measures how easily a business's assets can be turned into cash to cover its short-term liabilities.
> - A measure of a business's ability to meet its short-term financial obligations using its current assets
> - $\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{ratio}=\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$
> 
> - $\mathrm{Acid} \mathrm{test}=\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets} \mathrm{inventory}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$

Rehana markets her products as ‘Lovely for the planet, lovely for you’. The business has a strong local brand image. Rehana has recently invested in marketing which focuses on her unique selling point of recycling waste.

parts.problemMd: Explain why financial efficiency is important to a business.
parts.solutionMd:
Financial efficiency measures how well a business manages the working capital tied up in its inventory, its customers and its suppliers **[1]**. It matters because a business can be profitable and still run out of cash: money sitting in unsold stock, or in invoices customers have not yet paid, cannot be used to pay wages or suppliers **[1]**. Improving these ratios releases cash the business already owns, which is cheaper than borrowing and avoids the interest costs that would otherwise reduce profit **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Financial efficiency measures how effectively a business manages inventory, trade receivables and trade payables
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Cash tied up in inventory or in unpaid invoices is not available for day-to-day payments
> - A profitable business can still fail if its working capital is managed badly
> - Releasing cash from working capital is cheaper than borrowing the same amount
> - Collecting from customers faster reduces the risk of bad debts
> - Efficient inventory management cuts storage, insurance and obsolescence costs
> - The ratios show whether a growing business can fund its growth from its own operations
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Efficiency ratios are about speed, not size. They measure how quickly money moves through the business, not how much of it there is. A business holding large inventories is not automatically inefficient; one that takes a long time to sell them is. Keeping that distinction clear stops the answer drifting into a general discussion of costs.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'trade receivables turnover'.
parts.solutionMd:
Trade receivables turnover measures the average number of days a business takes to collect the money owed to it by credit customers **[1]**, calculated by dividing trade receivables by revenue and multiplying by 365 **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The average number of days customers take to pay what they owe
> - Trade receivables divided by revenue, multiplied by 365
> - A measure of how quickly a business converts credit sales into cash
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Say whose money it is and which way it moves. Receivables are owed to the business by its customers; payables are owed by the business to its suppliers. These two ratios are easy to reverse under pressure, and a definition that swaps them describes the opposite side of the business entirely.

parts.problemMd: Explain why a business monitors its trade payables turnover.
parts.solutionMd:
Trade payables turnover measures the average number of days a business takes to pay its suppliers **[1]**. A business monitors it because taking longer to pay keeps cash inside the business for longer, which improves liquidity without any need to borrow **[1]**. However, if the figure rises too far, suppliers may withdraw credit terms, demand payment in advance or give priority to other customers, so the business watches the ratio in order to take the cash benefit without damaging the relationships it depends on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Trade payables turnover shows the average number of days taken to pay suppliers
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Paying more slowly retains cash in the business, improving liquidity at no interest cost
> - A rising figure may signal to suppliers that the business is struggling
> - Suppliers may withdraw credit, shorten terms or require payment in advance
> - Early payment discounts may be lost by paying too slowly
> - Comparing payables days with receivables days shows whether cash leaves before it arrives
> - A very low figure may mean cash is going out faster than it needs to
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most ratios have an optimum rather than a direction. Neither a rising nor a falling payables figure is automatically good, and answers that simply argue "higher is better" tend to stop at one mark. The marks come from showing what goes wrong if the figure moves too far either way, which is exactly why the business monitors it.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which a business could improve its rate of inventory turnover.
parts.solutionMd:
The rate of inventory turnover shows how many times a business sells and replaces its inventory in a year, so it improves when the same level of sales is achieved from a smaller average inventory **[1]**. One way is to identify slow-moving lines and discount them to clear the stock **[1]**. This reduces average inventory immediately, releases cash and storage space, and stops the business reordering items that were never selling, so the ratio improves for a genuine reason rather than as a one-off effect **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The rate of inventory turnover improves when average inventory falls relative to cost of sales
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Clearing slow-moving or obsolete lines through discounting reduces average inventory
> - Ordering smaller quantities more frequently, as under just in time, cuts the inventory held
> - Improving demand forecasting reduces over-ordering
> - Better warehouse systems identify stock that is not moving
> - More effective promotion raises sales without increasing inventory
> - Reducing the product range concentrates sales on fewer lines
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Know which half of the ratio you are changing. Cost of sales sits on top and average inventory underneath, so a business improves the figure either by selling more or by holding less, and a strong answer says which of the two it is doing. Naming the half you are moving keeps the chain of reasoning straight.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the view that profitability ratios are more important than liquidity ratios to a business that sells expensive jewellery.
parts.solutionMd:
Profitability ratios are likely to be very useful to a business selling expensive jewellery **[E]**, as it should have a high gross profit margin due to the large mark-up on luxury items **[Ap]**. This shows how well the business is turning its high-value sales into actual profit **[K]**, which is important for judging whether its business model is working **[An]**

However, liquidity ratios cannot be ignored **[E]**. A jewellery business is likely to hold expensive items in inventory for a long time before they sell, since jewellery is not an everyday purchase **[Ap]**. This can make liquidity ratios like the current ratio look artificially strong **[An]**, even though the business may struggle to access cash quickly if it needed to pay suppliers, since so much of its value is tied up in unsold stock **[Ap] [An]**

Overall, I think profitability ratios are particularly important for this type of business **[E]**, because its naturally slow inventory turnover means liquidity ratios can be misleading if looked at alone **[An]**. However, liquidity is still essential, as a business that cannot pay its short-term debts risks being forced to close, no matter how profitable it looks on paper **[An]**. A business would need to look at both types of ratio together, along with trends over time, rather than relying on just one **[E]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Liquidity ratios measure the ability of a business to meet its short-term liabilities. If the liquidity ratios are good then the business should not experience any problems with paying suppliers etc. and therefore should not cease to trade due to a cashflow problem.
> - Profitability ratios measure different types of profit relative to sales revenue. A business selling expensive jewellery is likely to have a high gross profit margin and a high value added.
> - A business selling expensive jewellery would be unlikely to expect a quick turnover of inventory. Expensive jewellery is not an everyday item.
> - It is likely that the business will be more interested in profitability ratios that demonstrate the ability of the business to generate profit and the quality of that profit. Profit can help to guarantee the future of the business; perhaps buying more outlets or more special jewellery items.
> - Ratios of any type have limitations: a liquidity ratio or a profitability ratio give a numerical value but they do not explain the underlying factors that result in that ratio.
> - For example, liquidity ratios might be good and profitability ratios weak due to the business holding high levels of inventory. This would give a higher result for the current ratio. The high levels of inventory would also generate associated costs such as security and insurance and the inventory held means that sales are not made which could reduce the Gross Profit and the Profit margin.
> - Any business needs more information that any ratio, liquidity or profitability.
> - The business would need to look at trends over time and also make comparisons with other businesses in the same type of market/industry.
> - Liquidity ratios might be thought to be less important than profitability ratios but if the business cannot meet short-term debts then the business will be declared bankrupt and therefore any hope of future profit is gone

parts.problemMd: Discuss whether the published accounts of a luxury hotel provide a good measure of the performance of the business.
parts.solutionMd:
Published accounts can show useful information about a luxury hotel's financial performance, such as its profit margin **[K]**, which could reveal whether rising costs, like providing high-quality food or facilities **[Ap]**, are affecting profitability even if revenue looks strong. This gives a clear, measurable view of how the business is doing financially **[An]**

However, published accounts are historical and only show past results, not the current guest experience **[K]**. A luxury hotel's success also depends heavily on qualitative factors like service quality and reputation **[Ap]**, which are not shown in the accounts at all. A hotel could have strong recent financial figures while customer reviews are actually declining, which the accounts would not reveal until it starts affecting bookings and profit much later **[An]**

Overall, I do not think published accounts alone provide a good measure of a luxury hotel's performance **[E]**. Since luxury hotels compete strongly on reputation and guest experience, measures like customer reviews and repeat bookings are likely to give a more complete and up-to-date picture **[Ap]**. Published accounts should be used alongside these other, more qualitative sources of information, rather than relied on by themselves **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **4** | - Shows understanding of two implications in context |
> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one implication in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two implications |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one implication |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two implications in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one implication in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two implications |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one implication |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Published accounts provide quantitative measures, such as revenue and profit margin, which could show a luxury hotel how efficiently it is turning bookings into profit - for example, comparing profit margin year on year could reveal whether rising costs (such as high-quality food or staffing for a luxury service) are eating into profitability, even if revenue looks healthy
> - However, published accounts are historical, reflecting past performance rather than current conditions - a luxury hotel's most recent published accounts might not reflect a sudden change, such as a recent drop in bookings due to new competition or a decline in service quality, meaning they may not give an accurate picture of how the business is performing right now.
> - A luxury hotel's performance depends heavily on qualitative factors, such as guest experience, the quality of facilities, and reputation
> 
>   - Published accounts do not capture this at all, so a hotel could show strong financial figures while customer satisfaction and reviews are declining, which could signal future problems not yet visible in the accounts.
> - Because luxury hotels compete partly on reputation and exclusivity rather than price alone, other measures like customer reviews, repeat booking rates, or guest satisfaction scores might give a more complete picture of performance than the published accounts alone, especially for judging whether the hotel is meeting the expectations of its high-paying target market.
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - Published accounts are likely to give a useful, but incomplete, measure of a luxury hotel's performance, as they show financial results but not the quality of the guest experience that underpins a luxury brand's reputation.
> - Different stakeholders may value published accounts differently - investors or banks may rely heavily on them, while a guest or manager may see the quality of service and reviews as far more revealing of true performance.
> - Given the level of competition in the luxury hotel market, non-financial measures like reviews and repeat customers may actually be more important leading indicators of future performance than the accounts, which only show what has already happened.
> - Overall, published accounts alone are unlikely to provide a complete measure of a luxury hotel's performance and should be used alongside qualitative measures to get a fuller picture.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘zero budgeting’.
parts.solutionMd:
Zero budgeting is when a business sets each budget back to zero every year **[1]**, meaning managers must justify their spending from scratch rather than basing it on the previous year's budget **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An approach to budgeting that sets budgets to zero each year, rather than basing them on the previous year's figures, requiring budget holders to justify their budget from scratch each time
> - A budgeting method where every cost must be justified for each new period, rather than simply adjusting the previous budget
> - A method where budget holders start at zero and must argue for the funding they need each year, rather than automatically carrying over previous allocations
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

parts.solutionMd:

This helps Dayo see where costs are going wrong, which is useful information when deciding whether DB can afford a bank loan or a partner like Kofi to fund the new bakery location **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **benefit to a business of using budgets.
parts.solutionMd:
A budget is a financial plan for the future that helps a business control its performance **[1]**. One benefit is that it allows managers to compare actual results against targets using variance analysis **[1]**. For example, a retail business could quickly spot that its labour costs are higher than budgeted and take action before this seriously affects its profit **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A budget is a detailed financial plan for the future, which can be used to help control and monitor a business's performance.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Budgets allow a business to compare actual results against targets, using variance analysis to identify areas that need management attention - for example, a retail business could spot that its labour costs have exceeded budget and investigate why.
> - This system of budgeting also increases accountability, as individual budget holders, such as department managers, become responsible for staying within their own budgets, which can motivate them to control spending more carefully.
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'incremental budget'.
parts.solutionMd:
An incremental budget takes the previous period's budget as its starting point **[1]** and adjusts it up or down by a set amount or percentage to give the figure for the new period **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A budget set by taking the previous period's figures and adding or subtracting a small amount, rather than starting again from zero
> - A method in which the existing budget forms the base, with changes made only at the margin
> - A budget built by adjusting the current allocation, often for inflation or expected growth
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every budgeting method is a financial plan for future spending, so writing that alone earns nothing here. The mark is for what separates this method from the others, and that is the starting point: last period's budget rather than zero. If your definition would read equally well for zero budgeting, it is not yet a definition of this one.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'flexible budget'.
parts.solutionMd:
A flexible budget is one that is adjusted to reflect the actual level of output or activity achieved **[1]**, so that budgeted costs and revenues rise or fall in line with how much the business has really produced or sold **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A budget that changes with the level of activity, so figures are restated at the output actually achieved
> - A budget in which variable costs are set per unit rather than as a fixed total, allowing the plan to move with volume
> - A budget designed so performance is compared at the same level of output, rather than against a plan built for a different volume
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any budget can be changed, so "a budget that can be changed" does not earn the marks. Say what the budget flexes with. The whole point of a flexible budget is that it moves with output, which is what makes a fair comparison possible when sales turn out higher or lower than planned.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'adverse variance'.
parts.solutionMd:
An adverse variance is the difference between a budgeted figure and an actual figure **[1]** where the actual outcome leaves the business worse off than planned, such as costs above budget or revenue below budget **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A variance where the actual result is worse for profit than the budgeted figure
> - Occurs when actual costs exceed budgeted costs, or actual revenue falls below budgeted revenue
> - The opposite of a favourable variance, which improves profit compared with the plan
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Adverse does not simply mean the number went up. A revenue figure below budget is adverse even though it is a smaller number, and a cost figure below budget is favourable. The word describes the effect on profit, not the direction of the figure, so decide first whether the item is a cost or a revenue.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** benefit to a business of using a flexible budget rather than a fixed budget.
parts.solutionMd:
A flexible budget is adjusted to the level of output the business actually achieved **[1]**. This means costs are compared at the same activity level, so a manager whose department produced more than planned is not judged against a spending limit set for lower output **[1]**. The variances that remain then show genuine differences in efficiency or price rather than differences in volume, so the business can investigate the right problems instead of chasing figures that were always going to move **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A flexible budget restates budgeted figures at the actual level of output achieved
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Variances are no longer distorted by output being higher or lower than planned, so they show real performance
> - Managers are judged on factors within their control, which is fairer and more motivating
> - Investigation time is spent on genuine problems rather than on differences caused by volume alone
> - The business gets a more accurate picture of costs where demand is seasonal or hard to predict
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a three-mark Explain the third mark is almost always the consequence. Many answers name the benefit, describe it, then stop, which is two marks. Finish by saying what the business can now do differently: make a better decision, avoid a cost, act sooner. That final step is what turns a description into an explanation.

parts.problemMd: Explain why a favourable variance is not always good news for a business.
parts.solutionMd:
A favourable variance means the actual result was better for profit than the budget planned **[1]**. However, the reason behind it may be damaging; raw material costs below budget could mean cheaper, lower-quality inputs have been bought **[1]**. The saving appears immediately in this period's figures, while the cost of returns, complaints and lost repeat custom appears later, so a favourable variance can hide a problem rather than signal success **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A favourable variance occurs where the actual result is better for profit than the budgeted figure
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Lower costs may result from cheaper, poorer-quality materials, damaging quality and reputation
> - Underspending on training, maintenance or marketing flatters this period's figures but weakens future performance
> - A large favourable variance may show the budget was set too easily, making it a poor target rather than good performance
> - Higher revenue than budgeted may come from unplanned discounting the business cannot repeat
> - A favourable variance in one department may have been achieved by shifting costs or work onto another
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question says "not always", it is asking you to argue against the obvious answer. There is no credit for explaining why a favourable variance is normally welcome, however well written. Go straight to the case where it is not, and give the reason behind the figure, because that reason is where the marks sit.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** drawback to a business of using budgets.
parts.solutionMd:
A budget sets an agreed spending limit for a manager over a fixed period **[1]**. One drawback is that this can encourage unhelpful behaviour, such as a manager spending what remains of an allocation near the year end simply to avoid a smaller budget next time **[1]**. Money then goes on things the business does not need in order to protect a department's position, so the budget drives decisions that reduce profit rather than controlling costs as intended **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A budget is a financial plan setting agreed targets for income and spending over a period
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Budget holders may spend up to their limit unnecessarily to protect next period's allocation
> - Managers may deliberately overstate their requirements when budgets are negotiated
> - Budgets set in advance become unrealistic if trading conditions change, making them a poor guide
> - Rigid budgets may block worthwhile spending that arises after the budget was agreed
> - Preparing and monitoring budgets takes management time and can create conflict between departments
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The strongest budget drawbacks are about people, so put a person in your answer. "Budgets are inflexible" is a statement; "a manager spends the rest of the allocation in March so the budget is not cut next year" is an explanation, because it names who acts and why. Behaviour is far easier to develop into a chain of reasoning than a general criticism.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which budgets can help a business to allocate its resources.
parts.solutionMd:
Allocating resources means deciding how limited finance is divided between the competing demands of different parts of the business **[1]**. Setting budgets forces those claims to be compared against one another before any money is committed, so a department expecting to grow can be given a larger share than one whose workload is falling **[1]**. Because every request is justified at the same time, spending is directed towards the areas that contribute most to the objectives rather than to whichever manager asks first **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Allocating resources means dividing limited finance between competing uses within the business
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Budgeting forces competing claims to be compared before money is committed
> - Departments can be funded in line with expected workload or contribution rather than by habit
> - Spending is directed to the areas that support the business objectives most closely
> - Zero budgeting strengthens this further by requiring each claim to be justified from scratch
> - Setting limits in advance stops one department consuming finance needed elsewhere
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Allocate" means choosing between competing claims, so your answer needs at least two claims in it. If what you have written would make just as much sense in a business with a single department, you have explained planning rather than allocation. Naming two parts of the business pulling on the same money is the quickest way to show you understand the term.

> **[case-study]**
> **Denby**
> 
> Denby makes cardboard boxes for food producers in country J. Its budget for the year was prepared on the assumption that it would produce 40 000 boxes.
> 
> Demand was stronger than expected and Denby actually produced 46 000 boxes.
>

>

> 
> |   | Budget | Actual |
> |---|---|---|
> | Output (boxes) | 40 000 | 46 000 |
> | Variable production costs (\$) | 128 000 | 151 800 |
> | Fixed costs (\$) | 50 000 | 50 000 |
> 
> The finance director wants the budget flexed to the actual level of output before any variance is reported.

Calculate Denby's flexed budget for variable production costs and the resulting variance.
parts.solutionMd:
**Variance = \$4,600 adverse ****[4]**

**Method**

Budgeted variable cost per box

$= \frac{\$ 128 , 000}{40 , 000} = \$ 3.20$ **[1]**

Flexed budget for variable production costs

$= 46 , 000 \\times \$ 3.20 = \$ 147 , 200$ **[1]**

Variance = Actual − Flexed budget

$= \$ 151 , 800 - \$ 147 , 200 = \$ 4 , 600 \text{adverse} ( \mathrm{A} )$ **[2]**

> - 4 marks for the correct answer of \$ 4,600 A
>

> Work out the cost per unit before you flex anything. Comparing the actual \$151,800 with the original budget of \$128,000 gives a variance of \$23,800 adverse, which looks alarming but is mostly just the cost of making 6,000 extra boxes the budget never allowed for. Flexing strips out the effect of volume, so what remains is the part management can actually do something about.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Draycott**
> 
> Draycott supplies and services commercial kitchen equipment for restaurants and hotels in country F. Nadia founded the business alone and it now employs 54 people across four departments.
> 
> Two years ago Draycott nearly closed. Spending on new vans went ahead without any check while a large customer delayed payment, and Nadia had to sell equipment to meet the wage bill. She introduced departmental budgets shortly afterwards.
> 
> Nadia is now unsure they are worth keeping. Each of the four managers spends around three days a quarter preparing budget submissions. Last year two departments underspent by \$22 000 and \$14 000, which Nadia believes shows they asked for more than they needed. Revenue is growing at about 30% a year, so figures agreed in January are often out of date by June.
> 
> Her accountant has suggested replacing budgets with a monthly review of management accounts.

Evaluate whether Draycott should stop using budgets.
parts.solutionMd:
A budget is a financial plan setting agreed targets for income and spending over a period **[K]**. Draycott's four managers each spend around three days a quarter preparing submissions **[Ap]**. That is roughly 48 management days a year in a business of 54 people, and in a firm growing at 30% a year those days have an obvious alternative use in winning and servicing customers **[An]**. The case is stronger still because figures agreed in January are out of date by June, so managers are held to targets the business has already outgrown **[An]**

The underspends point to a second problem **[K]**. Two departments came in \$22 000 and \$14 000 below budget **[Ap]**. Nadia reads this as managers overstating their needs, and if she is right the budgets are not controlling spending but recording inflated requests, which makes the process misleading as well as slow **[An]**. A budget nobody expects to be accurate stops being a control and becomes an administrative routine **[An]**

Against this, the reason budgets exist at Draycott has not gone away **[E]**. The business nearly closed because van spending went ahead unchecked while a customer delayed payment, and it was the absence of any approval process, not a faulty one, that caused it **[E]**. Monthly management accounts report what has already been spent, whereas a budget sets a limit before the money leaves; the two do different jobs, and the accountant's proposal replaces control with reporting **[E]**. Draycott should keep budgets but change them, moving to quarterly figures so they keep pace with 30% growth and cutting the submission process down so it costs days rather than weeks **[E]**. Abandoning them entirely would remove the one safeguard introduced precisely because its absence almost ended the business **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Brayford Events**
> 
> Brayford Events hires out marquees and staging for weddings and festivals in country T. Demand is highly seasonal, with 62% of annual revenue earned in four months.
> 
> Brayford sets one fixed budget each year. Last year's was built on 480 bookings; the business actually took 611. Every cost centre reported an adverse variance, and managers argued the figures told them nothing they could use.
> 
> Priya, the operations director, wants Brayford to move to flexible budgets so costs are compared at the level of bookings actually achieved.
> 
> Sam, the finance manager, is not convinced. Brayford's marquee crew of 26 are on annual salaries and are paid whether or not there is work, while transport and casual labour rise with each booking. Some costs, such as vehicle servicing, are partly fixed and partly variable. Brayford employs one part-time accountant, who already works two days a week.

Evaluate whether Brayford Events should replace its fixed budget with a flexible budget.
parts.solutionMd:
A flexible budget is restated at the level of activity actually achieved, so costs are compared on a like-for-like basis **[K]**. Brayford budgeted for 480 bookings and took 611 **[Ap]**. Under a fixed budget almost every variable cost was certain to exceed its target simply because 27% more work was done, which is why every cost centre showed an adverse variance and managers dismissed the figures **[An]**. Flexing removes that distortion, leaving variances that reflect price and efficiency, so Brayford could see whether casual labour actually cost more per booking rather than only that it cost more in total **[An]**

The gain is largest in a business this seasonal **[K]**. Brayford earns 62% of revenue in four months **[Ap]**. A single annual budget spread across twelve months bears little relation to what any individual month should cost, so a manager working through the peak is judged against an average that never described their workload **[An]**. Flexed monthly figures would give each period a target built on its own volume, making the comparison fair and the variance worth investigating **[An]**

The obstacles are real, however **[E]**. Flexing requires costs to be split reliably into fixed and variable, and Brayford's do not divide cleanly; 26 salaried crew are fixed whatever the volume, while vehicle servicing is partly both **[E]**. If those splits are estimated badly the flexed budget will be wrong, and a confidently wrong variance is more dangerous than an obviously useless one, because managers will act on it **[E]**. There is also the question of who does the work, since one accountant working two days a week must produce the restatements on top of existing duties **[E]**. On balance Brayford should still move to flexible budgets, but begin only with the costs that clearly vary, such as transport and casual labour, leaving salaried crew in a fixed block **[E]**. That captures most of the benefit at the volumes which caused the problem, without asking a part-time accountant to model costs nobody has yet separated accurately **[E]**
