parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Penhale**
> 
> Penhale operates 22 hardware stores in country B. Head office sets each store's quarterly budget by taking the previous year's figures and adding 4%. Store managers receive a bonus if they meet their budget.
> 
> Store 7 is in a town that lost its bus route in February, and footfall fell by 19%. Its manager, Ilene, kept all staff on so customers were still served quickly. Store 14's manager met the budget by cutting staff hours.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows results for the two stores last quarter.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Penhale results, quarter ended June 2026**
> 
> |   | Store 7 | Store 14 |
> |---|---|---|
> | Labour cost variance (\$) | 31 000 adverse | 12 000 favourable |
> | Customer complaints | 11 | 47 |
> | Employees leaving | 0 | 2 |
> 
> Complaints at Store 14 rose from 9 to 47 in one quarter, and the two employees who left had each worked there for over ten years.
> 
> Marek, the finance director, argues that variances are the only fair way to compare 22 managers, because every store is measured in the same way.

Evaluate the usefulness of budget variances to Penhale in measuring the performance of its store managers.
parts.solutionMd:
A variance is the difference between a budgeted figure and the actual result, and Penhale uses these differences to judge its store managers **[K]**. Store 7 reported a \$31 000 adverse labour variance while Store 14 reported \$12 000 favourable **[Ap]**. Taken alone the figures rank Ilene as the weaker manager, yet her town lost its bus route and footfall fell 19%, a change she could not influence and could not have foreseen when the budget was set **[An]**. Measuring her against a target built on last year plus 4% charges her with the consequences of an event outside her control, which tells Penhale nothing about how well she managed **[An]**

Store 14 shows the same weakness from the other direction **[K]**. Its manager met budget by cutting staff hours, and complaints rose from 9 to 47 while two employees of more than ten years' standing resigned **[Ap]**. The variance records the saving because it is a cost, but not the recruitment and training needed to replace experienced staff, nor the customers who may not return **[An]**. Penhale is therefore paying a bonus for a decision that has probably reduced the store's profit over a longer period than the quarter being measured **[An]**

Variances are not useless, however **[E]**. They are consistent across all 22 stores, cheap to produce and available quickly, and no realistic alternative measures 22 managers as promptly **[E]**. The problem is not the variance but that Penhale treats it as the whole answer, since a variance identifies where results differ from plan and was never designed to explain why **[E]**. Penhale should keep variances as the starting point and require each to be investigated before any bonus is decided, separating causes managers control from those they do not **[E]**. Adding a small number of non-financial measures, such as complaints and staff turnover, would also stop a manager improving one figure by damaging another, which is the precise failure Store 14 illustrates **[E]**

However, Store 7's \$31 000 adverse figure was caused by a bus route closing and footfall falling 19%, which its manager could not influence

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **reason why a business manager needs to understand the difference between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.
parts.solutionMd:
Capital expenditure is spending on long-term assets like machinery, while revenue expenditure is spending on everyday running costs like raw materials **[1]**. A manager needs to understand this difference because they are usually funded in different ways **[1]**, so using the wrong type of finance for the wrong type of spending could cause cash flow problems for the business **[1]**

> AO1
> 
> Capital expenditure is money spent on long-term fixed assets, such as premises or machinery, while revenue expenditure is money spent on the everyday running costs of a business, such as raw materials.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A manager needs to understand the difference because capital and revenue expenditure are normally funded differently, so confusing the two could lead to a business using the wrong source of finance, such as using short-term working capital to fund a long-term asset purchase.
> - Recording expenditure correctly matters because revenue expenditure is recorded in the income statement and capital expenditure in the statement of financial position
> - A manager who does not understand the difference could misread financial documents, leading to poor decisions about the business's true financial position.

> | Closing balance | 2 | -1 | **X** |
> 
> Priya’s grant application was successful and she opened PB well aware of the need for both cash and profit.
> 
> Priya now wants to raise awareness of PB in town R. Priya did some market research and decided to use market segmentation. This will help her to decide on the promotional methods she could use for her bookshop. See Table 1.2.
> 
> **Table 1.2: Age and gender of residents in town R**
> 
> | Age group (years) | Percentage of residents in age group | Percentage of age group who are female |

> | 0-15 | 19% | 50% |

Explain the difference between cash and profit.
parts.solutionMd:
Cash is the actual money PB has coming in and out, like the grant and owner's capital shown in the cash flow forecast **[1]**. Profit is different - it is PB's revenue minus its costs **[1]**. PB could have cash from the grant in Month 1 even if it is not yet making a profit, and it could also run low on cash, like in Month 2, even if it is generating a profit from sales **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Cash is the physical flow of money in and out of a business, used to pay day-to-day costs, while profit is the difference between revenue and total costs, calculated at the end of a trading period.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - PB's cash flow forecast shows cash coming in from sources like the owner's capital and the council grant, which are not revenue and so would not count towards PB's profit, even though they increase PB's cash balance.
> - PB's forecast shows a negative closing balance of -\$1,000 in Month 2, meaning PB could be short of cash that month even if its sales were covering its costs and it was making a profit overall.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a new business needs finance.
parts.solutionMd:
Businesses need finance to start up, to grow and to survive **[1]**. A new business must pay for premises, equipment and initial inventory before it has sold anything or received any money from customers **[1]**. Without finance to cover that period it could not begin trading at all, because those costs arise weeks or months before the first revenue arrives **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Businesses need finance at start-up, to fund growth, and to survive periods of difficulty
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Premises, equipment and opening inventory must be paid for before any sales are made
> - Wages and other running costs continue during the period before revenue arrives
> - A new business has no retained profits to draw on, so external finance is usually the only option
> - Growth also requires finance, since expansion is paid for before the extra sales it generates
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Businesses need finance for different reasons at different stages, so say which stage you mean. Starting up, growing and surviving a difficult period are three distinct needs, and an answer that names one and follows it through is far stronger than one describing finance in general.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business might need long-term rather than short-term finance.
parts.solutionMd:
Short-term finance is needed for periods of up to about a year, while long-term finance is repaid over several years **[1]**. A business buying machinery expected to last ten years is making a purchase that will only generate returns gradually over that period **[1]**. Funding it with short-term finance would mean repaying long before the machinery had earned enough to cover its cost, leaving the business facing repayments it could not meet from the asset it had bought **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Short-term finance covers periods up to around a year; long-term finance is repaid over several years
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Machinery and premises generate returns gradually, so repayment must be spread over a similar period
> - Repaying a long-life asset from short-term finance creates repayments the asset cannot yet fund
> - Long-term finance gives certainty over funding, so the business is not forced to renew arrangements annually
> - Short-term finance suits temporary needs such as a seasonal inventory build, where the cash returns quickly
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The useful principle here is to match the length of the finance to the life of whatever it buys. Long-term assets need long-term funding; a short-lived need such as a seasonal stock build does not. Framing your answer around that match gives the examiner a clear reason rather than a preference.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'liquidation'.
parts.solutionMd:
Liquidation is the process of closing a business by selling its assets **[1]** and using the money raised to pay what it owes to its creditors **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Liquidation is the winding up of a business, with its assets sold and the proceeds distributed to those it owes money to
> - Liquidation means a business ceases trading and its assets are converted into cash to settle its debts
> - Liquidation is the formal closure of a company, with any remaining funds after creditors are paid returned to shareholders

> **[exam-tip]**
> Liquidation and administration are not the same thing and are frequently swapped. Liquidation ends the business and sells off what it owns; administration is an attempt to rescue it while creditors are held back. Make clear in your definition that liquidation is the end, not a stage on the way back.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a lack of finance may cause a business to fail.
parts.solutionMd:
A business fails when it can no longer meet its financial obligations, which may lead to administration or liquidation **[1]**. Even a profitable business must pay wages, suppliers and rent on the dates they fall due **[1]**. If customers have not yet paid and no finance is available to bridge the gap, the business cannot settle those debts, and creditors may force it into liquidation despite it trading profitably **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Business failure occurs when a business cannot meet its financial obligations, leading to administration or liquidation
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Wages, rent and suppliers must be paid on fixed dates regardless of when customers pay
> - A profitable business can still run out of cash if receipts and payments do not align
> - Without access to finance there is no way to bridge the gap, and creditors can force closure
> - Rapid growth increases the problem, since expansion is paid for before it generates revenue
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Business failure is usually a cash event rather than a profit event. Firms go under owing money they cannot pay today, not because the year's figures were poor. Making that distinction is often what lifts an answer here, because it explains how a profitable business can still fail.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'working capital'.
parts.solutionMd:
Working capital is the finance available to a business for its day-to-day operations **[1]**, calculated as current assets minus current liabilities **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Working capital is the difference between a business's current assets and its current liabilities
> - Working capital is the finance a business has available to meet its short-term obligations and fund daily trading
> - Working capital measures whether a business's short-term assets are sufficient to cover its short-term debts

> **[exam-tip]**
> Working capital is what remains after short-term debts are taken off, not simply the money a business holds. A firm with plenty of cash and even larger bills due next month has weak working capital. Getting the subtraction into your definition is what secures the second mark.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why working capital is important to a business.
parts.solutionMd:
Working capital is the finance available for day-to-day operations, found by subtracting current liabilities from current assets **[1]**. A business needs it to pay wages, suppliers and other short-term bills as they fall due **[1]**. Without sufficient working capital it cannot buy the materials needed to keep producing or meet payments on time, so suppliers may withdraw credit and production may stop even though the business has profitable orders waiting **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, the finance available for daily operations
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Wages, suppliers and short-term bills must be paid as they fall due
> - Insufficient working capital means materials cannot be bought and production may halt
> - Suppliers may withdraw credit terms, worsening the shortage
> - Adequate working capital allows a business to accept profitable orders it would otherwise turn down
> - Too much working capital is also a problem, since cash and inventory sitting idle earn nothing
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> More working capital is not automatically better, which is worth knowing even when the question only asks why it matters. Cash sitting unused and inventory nobody has ordered are resources earning nothing. The strongest position is sufficient rather than maximum, and showing you know that marks out a careful answer.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business should manage its trade receivables carefully.
parts.solutionMd:
Trade receivables are amounts owed to a business by customers who have bought on credit **[1]**. Those sales have already been recorded as revenue, but no cash has yet been received **[1]**. If customers take longer to pay than agreed, the business must still meet its own bills from money it does not yet have, so poor management of receivables can create a cash shortage even while sales and profit appear healthy **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Trade receivables are amounts owed to a business by customers who have bought on credit
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Revenue is recorded at the point of sale, but the cash arrives later or not at all
> - Late payment forces the business to meet its own obligations from money it has not yet received
> - Some receivables become bad debts, so the sale generates no cash at all
> - Chasing overdue payments consumes administrative time and can damage customer relationships
> - Offering a discount for early payment costs margin but improves the timing of cash inflows
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A sale is not cash until it has been paid for. Trade receivables are sales already counted in profit but still sitting outside the bank account, which is exactly why a business can look successful on paper and still struggle to pay its bills. Keep that gap between profit and cash at the centre of your answer.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'capital expenditure'.
parts.solutionMd:
Capital expenditure is spending by a business on non-current assets, such as machinery or premises **[1]**, which will be used to generate income over more than one year rather than being consumed immediately **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Capital expenditure is spending on assets that will be used in the business over the long term
> - Capital expenditure is money spent acquiring or improving non-current assets such as buildings, vehicles or equipment
> - Capital expenditure is expenditure whose benefit extends beyond the current accounting period, unlike revenue expenditure

> **[exam-tip]**
> The test is how long the benefit lasts, not how much was spent. A delivery van costing thousands is capital expenditure; a year's fuel for it, which may cost as much, is revenue expenditure. Anchoring your definition in the life of the benefit avoids the common assumption that expensive means capital.

> 
> |   | **2023** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Revenue (\$000) | 2 100 | 1 780 |
> | Operating profit (\$000) | 210 | (60) |
> | Cash at bank (\$000) | 145 | 12 |
> | Proportion of overdraft limit used (%) | 30 | 98 |
> | Children enrolled | 310 | 244 |
> | Staff required by regulation | 42 | 52 |
> 
> Larchmere's bank has declined a further loan. Its landlord has offered to defer three months' rent, worth \$90 000, if Larchmere signs a five-year lease extension.
> 
> The Finance Director, Nia Roberts, argues the immediate problem is cash, and the deferral buys the time Larchmere needs.
> 
> The Operations Director, Sam Oduya, disagrees. Enrolments have fallen 21% while regulation forces staff numbers up, so in his view deferring rent only postpones the moment of failure.

Evaluate whether a lack of finance is the main reason Larchmere is at risk of business failure.
parts.solutionMd:
Business failure occurs when a business can no longer meet its financial obligations as they fall due **[K]**. Larchmere holds just \$12 000 in cash, has used 98% of its overdraft, and has been refused a further loan **[Ap]**. Staff must be paid monthly and rent quarterly regardless of enrolment levels, so with no headroom remaining a single large payment could leave Larchmere unable to settle its debts **[An]**. At that point creditors could force closure within weeks, whatever its longer-term prospects, so the shortage of finance is certainly what would end the business **[An]**

However, the figures suggest finance is the symptom rather than the cause **[K]**. Enrolments have fallen from 310 to 244, a drop of 21%, while regulation has raised required staff from 42 to 52 **[Ap]**. Revenue has fallen by \$320 000 while the largest cost has risen, turning an operating profit of \$210 000 into a loss of \$60 000 **[An]**. A business losing money on its ordinary operations will exhaust any finance it obtains, so lending Larchmere more would postpone failure rather than prevent it **[An]**

Overall, a lack of finance is the immediate danger but not the main reason **[E]**. The distinction matters because it determines what would actually help: more borrowing addresses the symptom, while the operating loss is what makes the business unsustainable **[E]**. The landlord's offer illustrates the trap, since it relieves three months of pressure in exchange for a five-year commitment, trading a short reprieve for a long obligation Larchmere may not be able to meet **[E]**. Larchmere should therefore treat the deferral as breathing space only if it uses those three months to close or consolidate a site and rebuild enrolments, since without that the finance question simply returns in a worse form **[E]**

> **[case-study]**
> **Orrell Signs**
> 
> Orrell Signs manufactures industrial signage in country F. A national logistics company has offered it a contract for 4 000 signs, the largest single order Orrell Signs has ever received.
> 
> **Table 1: Orrell Signs, current position and proposed contract**
> 
> |   | **Current annual position** | **Proposed contract** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Revenue (\$000) | 1 900 | 620 |
> | Profit margin (%) | 14 | 11 |
> | Customer payment terms | 30 days | 90 days |
> | Materials to be purchased before production (\$000) | - | 280 |
> | Cash at bank (\$000) | 95 | - |
> | Overdraft facility (\$000) | 150 | - |
> 
> Materials must be bought before production begins, and Orrell Signs would not be paid until around five months after that point.
> 
> The Sales Director, Ade Balogun, wants to accept. The contract would earn roughly \$68 000 of profit and establish Orrell Signs with a national customer likely to reorder.
> 
> The Finance Director, Ruth Lindqvist, points out that cash of \$95 000 plus a \$150 000 overdraft comes to \$245 000, against a materials bill of \$280 000.

Evaluate whether Orrell Signs should accept the contract.
parts.solutionMd:
Profit is the difference between revenue and costs, while cash is the money a business actually holds **[K]**. The contract is worth \$620 000 at an 11% margin, giving roughly \$68 000 of profit from a single order, against annual revenue of \$1.9m **[Ap]**. That is a substantial addition, and winning a national logistics customer could lead to repeat orders that would matter more than the first contract alone **[An]**. Turning down the largest order Orrell Signs has been offered would also mean a competitor takes it and gains that relationship instead **[An]**

However, a profitable contract is not the same as an affordable one **[K]**. Orrell Signs must buy \$280 000 of materials before production starts, while cash and overdraft together come to \$245 000 **[Ap]**. It is therefore \$35 000 short before paying any wages, and with 90-day terms no money would return for around five months **[An]**. Accepting on these terms would leave Orrell Signs unable to pay its existing suppliers and staff during that period, so a contract intended to strengthen the business could instead cause it to fail **[An]**

Overall, the question is not really whether to accept but whether the terms can be changed **[E]**. The contract is genuinely valuable, so rejecting it outright forfeits both the profit and the relationship for a problem of timing rather than of profitability **[E]**. Equally, accepting as it stands is not possible, since the arithmetic shows the materials cannot be bought **[E]**. Orrell Signs should therefore seek a deposit or staged payments, or additional finance secured against the order, and accept only if one is obtained. Committing without that risks failing to deliver, which would cost it the reputation the contract was meant to build **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'break-even point'.
parts.solutionMd:
The break-even point is the level of output where a business's total revenue equals its total costs **[1]**, so it makes neither a profit nor a loss **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The level of output/sales at which total revenue equals total costs, meaning the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
> - The point at which a business's income from sales is exactly equal to its total costs.
> - The output level a business must reach before it starts making a profit, where total costs and total revenue are the same

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose a mark by simply writing "the point where a business makes no profit or loss" without explaining why — i.e. that total revenue equals total costs. Make sure your definition includes both the cause (revenue equals costs) and the effect (no profit or loss) to secure full marks. Avoid vague language such as "the business breaks even" — this is circular and does not demonstrate understanding of the concept.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** limitation of contribution costing.
parts.solutionMd:
Contribution costing calculates the contribution a product makes by subtracting only its variable costs from its selling price **[1]**. Because fixed costs are not allocated to individual products, a product showing a positive contribution appears worthwhile even when it may not be **[1]**. If a business accepts too many orders priced only slightly above variable cost, total contribution may fail to cover its fixed costs, so it can make an overall loss while every individual product still appears to be contributing **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Contribution costing subtracts only variable costs from selling price, leaving fixed costs unallocated
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A positive contribution does not guarantee the product is profitable once fixed costs are considered
> - Accepting many low-contribution orders can leave total contribution below total fixed costs
> - Fixed costs still have to be recovered from somewhere, so ignoring them only defers the question
> - Contribution costing gives no guide to long-term pricing, since a price above variable cost may be unsustainable
> - Splitting costs into fixed and variable is not always straightforward, and some costs are partly both
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A limitation has to show where the method can mislead, not merely what it leaves out. "It ignores fixed costs" describes how contribution costing works; the limitation is that ignoring them can produce a decision that turns out to be wrong. Take the extra step to the bad decision and the mark follows.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of accurate cost information to managers of a small business.
parts.solutionMd:
Accurate cost information is important because it lets managers monitor changes in specific costs **[K]**. For example, a small furniture maker could notice that the price of wood has increased **[Ap]** and switch to a cheaper supplier before this seriously affects profit. Without this information, a small business might not notice rising costs until it is already losing money, which is especially risky for a small business with limited cash reserves **[An]**

It is also important for setting the right price **[K]**. A small café that miscalculates its costs might set prices too low **[Ap]**, eating into its profit, or too high, making it less competitive than bigger rivals. Since small businesses often cannot benefit from the same economies of scale as larger competitors, controlling and understanding costs is one of the few ways they can stay price competitive **[An]**

Overall, I think accurate cost information is very important for most small businesses **[E]**, as they usually have less financial cushion to survive mistakes than larger businesses **[Ap]**. However, its importance may be lower for a small business with a strong USP, where customers are willing to pay a premium regardless of price **[Ap]**, so cost control, while still useful, may matter slightly less than factors like quality or customer service **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Halcott Roasters**
> 
> Halcott Roasters buys green coffee beans, roasts them and sells ground coffee to independent cafés in country D. It can roast 80,000 kg a year and is currently roasting 62,000 kg.
> 
> Cafés pay \$11.00 per kg. The variable cost of each kg is \$6.40. Fixed costs are \$260,000 a year.
> 
> Verrow Hotels has offered Halcott a one-off order for 15,000 kg at \$8.20 per kg. The coffee would carry Verrow's own label, which would add \$0.90 to the variable cost of every kg in the order.
> 
> The finance director has calculated that the order would add \$13,500 to annual profit and points out that Halcott has the spare capacity to roast it.
> 
> The marketing director is less certain. Verrow runs 40 hotels in the region and has said it would expect the same price on any repeat order. Two of Halcott's café customers have recently asked for a discount. The sales manager also forecasts that café orders will grow by 12% next year.

Evaluate whether Halcott Roasters should accept the one-off order from Verrow Hotels.
parts.solutionMd:
Contribution costing compares the extra revenue an order brings in with the extra variable costs it causes **[K]**. Verrow would pay \$8.20 per kg against a variable cost of \$7.30 once own-label packaging is included **[Ap]**. Each kg therefore contributes \$0.90, and 15,000 kg would add \$13,500 **[An]**. Because Halcott has 18,000 kg of spare capacity, the \$260,000 of fixed costs is already being paid whether or not the order is taken, so the whole \$13,500 falls through to profit **[An]**. Set against a current profit of \$25,200, that is an increase of more than half for output the business would not otherwise be producing **[An]**

The difficulty is that the order is unlikely to remain one-off **[K]**. Verrow runs 40 hotels and has already said it would expect \$8.20 again **[Ap]**. At that price a kg earns \$0.90 rather than the \$4.60 a café pays, and once café orders grow by the forecast 12% to 69,440 kg, the 80,000 kg capacity could not hold both **[An]**. Halcott would then be choosing between them, and every kg switched from a café to Verrow would cost \$3.70 in lost contribution **[An]**

There is also a risk to existing prices **[K]**. Two cafés have already asked for a discount **[Ap]**. If they discover that a hotel chain buys the same coffee for \$8.20, holding the \$11.00 price becomes harder, and because contribution per kg is high a small general discount would wipe out the gain; a cut of just \$0.25 across 62,000 kg removes \$15,500, more than the order earns **[An]**

Halcott should accept, but only on terms that keep the order genuinely one-off **[E]**. The arithmetic holds while capacity is spare, and \$13,500 for coffee that would otherwise not be roasted is worth having **[E]**. What makes the decision risky is not the price but what the price implies about the future, since contribution costing answers only the question of this order and says nothing about the next one **[E]**. The order should be agreed in writing as a single delivery with no guarantee on repeat pricing, and own-label work used to fill capacity only while café demand sits below forecast **[E]**. If Verrow will not accept those terms the order should be declined, because a permanent \$0.90 customer displacing \$4.60 customers would leave Halcott busier and poorer **[E]**

> Accept any other valid response

Define the term ‘income statement’.
parts.solutionMd:
An income statement is a financial statement that shows a business's revenue, cost of sales and expenses **[1]**, to work out how much profit or loss it has made over a period **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A financial statement that reports a business's revenue, cost of sales and resulting profit over a given period
> - A document showing how much profit or loss a business has made, calculated by subtracting costs, such as cost of sales and expenses, from revenue

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a public limited company must publish its financial statements.
parts.solutionMd:
A public limited company has limited liability, which means its shareholders are not personally responsible for its debts **[1]**. Because those dealing with the company cannot pursue the owners' private assets if it fails, the law requires it to publish financial statements so anyone considering trading with it or investing in it can judge its financial position **[1]**. Publication is in effect the price of limited liability, giving suppliers, lenders and shareholders the information they need to decide whether to take that risk **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Public limited companies are legally required to publish their financial statements each year
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Limited liability protects shareholders' personal assets, so creditors need published information to assess the risk of dealing with the company
> - Shareholders who do not run the business need an account of how their money has been used
> - Potential investors require reliable information before buying shares
> - Lenders use the statements to judge whether the company can repay borrowing
> - Publication allows tax authorities to check the profit declared
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question asking why a company must do something is about the obligation, not the advantage. An answer explaining that publishing is useful can still miss marks if it never reaches the point that this is a legal requirement flowing from limited liability. Deal with the "must" first, then explain who benefits.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'statement of financial position'.
parts.solutionMd:
A statement of financial position is a financial document showing what a business owns and owes at a particular date **[1]**, setting out its assets, liabilities and equity so its overall financial position at that moment can be seen **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A statement listing a business's assets, liabilities and equity at one specific date
> - A summary of what a business owns and what it owes at a given point in time
> - A financial statement showing how a business's assets have been funded, by liabilities or by equity
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the moment. A statement of financial position describes a single date, while a statement of profit or loss covers a whole period, and that difference is often the second mark. Writing "over the year" instead of "at the year end" quietly turns a correct definition into the wrong statement.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'non-current asset'.
parts.solutionMd:
A non-current asset is an item owned by a business that it expects to keep and use for more than one year **[1]**, such as machinery, vehicles or premises, rather than something bought in order to be sold on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An asset the business intends to use for longer than one year rather than sell within it
> - A long-term resource such as property, machinery, equipment or vehicles
> - An item held for use in the business rather than as inventory for resale
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The time test does most of the work, but add the purpose test too. A delivery van is a non-current asset to a bakery and inventory to the dealership selling it; the same object is classified differently depending on why it is held. "Kept for more than a year and used in the business, not sold" covers both.

parts.problemMd: Explain how the statement of profit or loss is linked to the statement of financial position.
parts.solutionMd:
The statement of profit or loss shows the profit earned over a period, while the statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity at the end of that period **[1]**. The two are joined by retained earnings, because profit not paid out as dividends is added to the reserves shown within equity **[1]**. A profitable year therefore increases equity on the statement of financial position without any new investment by shareholders, which is why the two statements have to be read together rather than separately **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Retained earnings link the two statements, carrying profit from one into equity in the other
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Profit not distributed as dividends increases reserves within equity
> - A loss reduces retained earnings and therefore reduces equity
> - Depreciation charged in the statement of profit or loss reduces the carrying value of non-current assets
> - Inventory valued at the year end appears as a current asset and also determines cost of sales
> - Together they show both performance over the year and position at the end of it
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question about how two documents are linked wants the item that appears in both. Describing what each statement contains, however accurately, does not answer it. Name the connecting figure, usually retained earnings, then say which direction it travels.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'net realisable value'.
parts.solutionMd:
Net realisable value is the amount a business expects to receive from selling an item of inventory **[1]**, after deducting any costs still needed to complete it and sell it **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The expected selling price of inventory less the costs of completing and selling it
> - The amount a business would actually realise from disposing of inventory, net of the costs of doing so
> - An estimate of what inventory is genuinely worth if sold, rather than what it originally cost
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not define the term by the rule it appears in. "The lower of cost and net realisable value" describes how inventory is valued; it does not say what net realisable value means, and on its own it earns nothing. Give the meaning first: the expected proceeds, minus the costs of getting them.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** difficulty a business may face when valuing its inventory.
parts.solutionMd:
Inventory is normally valued at the lower of what it cost and what the business expects to receive for it **[1]**. A difficulty arises with items whose value falls sharply over time, such as fashion clothing at the end of a season **[1]**. The business must estimate what that stock will eventually sell for, and if it judges this too optimistically the inventory is overstated on the statement of financial position and profit is reported as higher than it really is **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, which requires an estimate
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Items that go out of fashion or perish may be worth far less than they cost, and the fall is a matter of judgement
> - Work in progress is difficult to value because it is unfinished and has no established selling price
> - Where identical items were bought at different prices, the business must choose which cost to apply
> - Damaged or obsolete stock may still be recorded at full cost if nobody identifies it
> - Estimating selling costs, such as the discounts needed to shift slow-moving lines, is uncertain
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the kind of stock. "Inventory can be hard to value" simply restates the question, whereas fashion clothing, fresh food or half-finished products each carry their own reason why the right figure is unclear. Choosing a specific type gives you something concrete to explain and makes the third mark far easier to reach.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which a supplier could use a business's statement of financial position.
parts.solutionMd:
A statement of financial position shows what a business owns and owes at a particular date **[1]**. A supplier deciding whether to offer trade credit would compare current assets with current liabilities, because that indicates whether the business can meet its short-term debts **[1]**. If current liabilities are close to or above current assets, the supplier risks not being paid and may insist on payment in advance or refuse credit altogether, which directly affects the terms the business is offered **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity at a specific date
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Comparing current assets with current liabilities indicates whether short-term debts can be met
> - A supplier can judge whether to offer trade credit, and on what terms
> - High non-current liabilities may show the business is already heavily committed to lenders
> - Comparing two years shows whether the position is improving or deteriorating
> - A weak position may lead a supplier to require payment in advance, cut credit limits or decline the order
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Match the user to the figure they would actually look at. A supplier's concern is whether it will be paid, so it goes straight to current assets and current liabilities, not to the equity section. Answers that describe the whole statement rather than the part that stakeholder cares about tend to stall at one mark.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business charges depreciation in its accounts.
parts.solutionMd:
Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset across the years in which the business uses it **[1]**. Without it, the full cost of a machine expected to last eight years would be charged to the year it was bought, making that year's profit look artificially low and the following seven look artificially high **[1]**. Charging depreciation each year matches the cost to the revenue the asset helps to earn, so profit gives a fairer picture of performance in every year rather than being distorted by when the purchase happened **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life
> 
> AO2
> 
> - It matches the cost of the asset to the periods in which it generates revenue
> - Without it, profit is badly distorted in the year of purchase and overstated afterwards
> - It reduces the carrying value of the asset so the statement of financial position is not overstated
> - It recognises that assets lose value through use, age and obsolescence
> - It allows fairer comparison of profit between years and between businesses
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Depreciation is not cash. No money leaves the business when it is charged, and nothing is being saved up to replace the asset; the cash went when the asset was bought. Answers claiming a business "sets money aside through depreciation" lose marks, so keep your explanation about spreading a cost that has already been paid.

> Ormesby manufactures workwear for construction and healthcare businesses in country K.

> Two years ago Ormesby moved to a cheaper fabric supplier and raised its prices by 6%. It also opened a showroom and increased its sales team from 4 people to 11.

parts.problemMd:
‘The published accounts of a public limited company are only useful to internal stakeholders.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Published accounts are useful to internal stakeholders in some ways. Shareholders can check the company's profit and dividend **[K]** to see the return on their investment, and employees might look at the accounts to judge whether a pay rise is likely **[An]**. Managers can also use trends in the published accounts, such as changing revenue or profit over time, to help with future financial planning **[An]** External stakeholders also rely on them heavily, often more than internal stakeholders do. A bank **[K] **deciding whether to lend money to a public limited company would use the published accounts to judge whether the company can afford to repay a loan **[Ap]** **[An]**. Potential investors use them to decide whether buying shares is a good investment, and the government uses them to work out how much tax the company owes. These external groups usually have no other way of finding out this information, so published accounts may actually matter more to them than to internal stakeholders **[E]** It is also worth noting that managers, as internal stakeholders, often have access to much more detailed financial information **[K]** than what is published, such as the profitability of individual departments. This means the published accounts themselves may be of limited extra use to managers specifically, even though they are internal stakeholders **[An]**. This weakens the idea that published accounts are especially useful to internal stakeholders as a group **[E]** Overall, I disagree with the statement **[E]**. Published accounts are clearly useful to a wide range of external stakeholders, such as banks, investors and government, who depend on them as one of their only sources of financial information about the company **[An]**. If anything, they may be more useful to certain external stakeholders than to internal ones like managers, who already have access to more detailed data than the published accounts provide **[E]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge and application, analysis and evaluation > - A full-mark answer will include > > - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout > - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning > - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning > - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed > > **Knowledge and application** > > | **Mark** | **Descriptor** | > |---|---| > | **5** | - Developed knowledge of relevant key term(s) and/or factor(s) is used to answer the question

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Talgarth Scaffolding**
> 
> Talgarth Scaffolding hires out scaffolding to builders in country V. It has asked its bank for a loan of \$600 000 to buy new equipment.
> 
> Talgarth's directors have given the bank its statement of profit or loss, pointing out that profit for the year has risen from \$210 000 to \$340 000.
> 
> Three further facts are not obvious from the statement:
> 
> - \$180 000 of the 2026 profit came from selling a depot that Talgarth no longer needed
> - Talgarth changed its depreciation policy in 2026, extending the assumed useful life of its scaffolding from five years to eight, which reduced the annual depreciation charge by \$70 000
> - Two large customers now take 90 days to pay rather than 30
> 
> Anya, the bank's lending manager, must decide whether the statement of profit or loss gives her enough information.

Evaluate the usefulness of Talgarth Scaffolding's statement of profit or loss to the bank in deciding whether to lend.
parts.solutionMd:
A statement of profit or loss shows revenue, costs and the profit earned over a period **[K]**. Talgarth's profit for the year rose from \$210 000 to \$340 000, and this is the figure the directors have put to the bank **[Ap]**. Taken at face value it describes a business whose earnings grew by 62% in a year, which would make this a straightforward lending decision **[An]**. The statement is useful to Anya precisely because it reduces a year of trading to a single comparable figure, and no other document does that job **[An]**

The difficulty is what that figure contains **[K]**. \$180 000 of the 2026 profit came from selling a depot, and a further \$70 000 from extending the assumed life of scaffolding from five years to eight **[Ap]**. Neither has anything to do with hiring scaffolding out: a depot can only be sold once, and the depreciation change is an accounting judgement rather than a change in performance **[An]**. Stripping both out leaves around \$90 000 of profit from trading, well below the \$210 000 earned in 2025, so the statement reports growth in a business that has actually declined **[An]**

The statement is therefore useful but not sufficient **[E]**. It gives Anya the right starting point, and read carefully it is what allows the one-off gain and the policy change to be identified at all, so the fault lies with the directors' presentation rather than the document **[E]**. What it cannot tell her is whether Talgarth will generate the cash to make repayments, and with two large customers now taking 90 days rather than 30, profit and cash are moving apart **[E]**. A lender is repaid out of cash, not profit, so a statement of profit or loss can never be the whole basis of the decision **[E]**. Anya should use it as evidence of trading performance across several years, adjusted for the one-off items, and require a cash flow forecast and the statement of financial position before committing \$600 000 **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ellersby**
> 
> Ellersby manufactures office furniture in country G. It currently makes its own metal frames and is considering buying them from an outside supplier instead.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows Ellersby's statement of profit or loss for 2026 and the directors' forecast for 2027 if frames are bought in.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Ellersby statement of profit or loss (\$000)**
> 
> |   | 2026 actual | 2027 forecast |
> |---|---|---|
> | Revenue | 9 400 | 9 400 |
> | Cost of sales | 6 110 | 5 640 |
> | **Gross profit** | **3 290** | **3 760** |
> | Expenses | 2 820 | 3 015 |
> | **Profit from operations** | **470** | **745** |
> 
> The 2027 forecast includes redundancy payments of \$390 000 to the 14 employees who make frames. Without those payments, expenses would fall to \$2 625 000.
> 
> The supplier is the only business in country G able to make the frames to Ellersby's specification. It quotes a seven-week lead time; Ellersby currently offers its corporate customers four weeks, which is its main selling point.

Evaluate whether Ellersby should buy in its metal frames rather than making them.
parts.solutionMd:
The statement of profit or loss shows the effect of the change on each line of trading **[K]**. Buying frames in would cut cost of sales from \$6 110 000 to \$5 640 000, raising gross profit from \$3 290 000 to \$3 760 000, while profit from operations would rise from \$470 000 to \$745 000 **[Ap]**. That is an increase of 59% in a single year, achieved even though the forecast carries \$390 000 of redundancy payments that will not recur **[An]**. Excluding those, expenses would be \$2 625 000 rather than \$3 015 000, so from 2028 profit from operations would be around \$1 135 000, more than double the current figure **[An]**

The forecast rests on an assumption the statement cannot test **[K]**. Revenue is held at \$9 400 000, yet the supplier quotes seven weeks against the four Ellersby currently offers, and that lead time is its main selling point with corporate customers **[Ap]**. If even a tenth of revenue were lost, \$940 000 of sales would disappear, and at the forecast gross margin of 40% that removes \$376 000 of gross profit, more than wiping out the year-one gain of \$275 000 **[An]**. Once frame-making has stopped and 14 employees have been paid off the decision cannot easily be reversed, so a fall in revenue would be discovered only after the capacity to correct it has gone **[An]**

On the figures alone Ellersby should buy in **[E]**. The saving is large, it recurs every year, and the redundancy cost is a one-off the forecast has already absorbed **[E]**. What makes the decision finely balanced is that the whole case depends on revenue holding at \$9 400 000, and the change most likely to break that assumption, a lead time rising from four weeks to seven, is precisely what Ellersby sells on **[E]**. There is also no second supplier in country G, so Ellersby would have no alternative if prices rose later and the savings shown here could be reclaimed by the supplier over time **[E]**. Ellersby should therefore not commit yet: it should establish with its largest corporate customers whether seven weeks is acceptable, and negotiate a fixed-price agreement of several years before closing frame production **[E]**. If lead times can be protected, perhaps by holding frame inventory, the change is clearly worth making; if they cannot, the profit gain is being bought with the business's main competitive advantage **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** impact on a business of having a negative cash flow.
parts.solutionMd:
Negative cash flow means more money is leaving a business than coming in** [1]**. This could mean a business is unable to pay its suppliers on time, for example a small manufacturer struggling to pay for raw materials** [1]**. This could damage its relationship with suppliers, who may then be less willing to offer credit in the future** [1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Negative cash flow means more money is leaving a business than coming in over a given period, leaving it short of cash to cover its immediate costs.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A business with negative cash flow may be unable to pay suppliers or employees on time — for example, a small manufacturer might struggle to pay for raw materials, which could disrupt production if suppliers stop delivering on credit.
> - This could force the business to seek additional short-term finance, such as a bank overdraft, to cover the shortfall, which could add extra interest costs on top of its existing financial pressure.
>

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'cash flow forecast'.
parts.solutionMd:
A cash flow forecast is a financial document predicting the money expected to flow into and out of a business over a future period **[1]**, usually month by month, showing the expected cash balance at the end of each period **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A cash flow forecast is a prediction of a business's future cash receipts and payments, normally set out month by month
> - A cash flow forecast estimates the timing and size of money entering and leaving a business over a coming period
> - A cash flow forecast projects expected inflows, outflows and the resulting closing balance for each future period

> **[exam-tip]**
> A cash flow forecast predicts money moving, not profit. It records when cash actually arrives and leaves, which is why a sale made in March but paid for in May appears in May. Keeping that timing idea in your definition separates it cleanly from a profit statement.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'net cash flow'.
parts.solutionMd:
Net cash flow is the difference between the total cash flowing into a business and the total cash flowing out over a period of time **[1]**. It is positive when inflows exceed outflows and negative when outflows are greater **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Net cash flow is total cash inflows minus total cash outflows for a given period
> - Net cash flow measures whether a business received more money than it paid out over a period
> - Net cash flow is the change in a business's cash position during a period, which may be positive or negative

> **[exam-tip]**
> Net cash flow can be negative, and a negative figure is not automatically a sign of trouble. A business investing heavily in one month will show negative net cash flow that month while remaining perfectly healthy. Defining it as "the money left over" misses that, so use the idea of inflows minus outflows instead.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'closing balance'.
parts.solutionMd:
The closing balance is the amount of cash a business is expected to hold at the end of a period **[1]**, calculated by adding that period's net cash flow to the opening balance **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The closing balance is the cash held at the end of a period, found by adding net cash flow to the opening balance
> - The closing balance is the forecast cash position at the close of a month, which becomes the opening balance of the next
> - The closing balance shows how much cash remains after all receipts and payments for the period have been taken into account

> **[exam-tip]**
> The closing balance of one month becomes the opening balance of the next, which is what links the months of a forecast into a chain. Mentioning that connection shows you understand how a forecast works rather than treating each month as a separate calculation.

parts.problemMd: Explain what a forecast negative closing balance tells a business.
parts.solutionMd:
A closing balance is the cash expected to be held at the end of a period, found by adding net cash flow to the opening balance **[1]**. A negative figure means the business is forecast to pay out more than it holds, so it could not meet its payments from its own funds that month **[1]**. It therefore needs to arrange finance such as an overdraft in advance, or change the timing of its receipts and payments, rather than discovering the shortfall only when it arrives **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A negative closing balance means forecast payments exceed the cash available in that period
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The business could not meet its obligations from its own funds in the month concerned
> - Finance such as an overdraft can be arranged in advance, on better terms than in an emergency
> - The timing of receipts or payments could be adjusted to remove the shortfall
> - Identifying the month in advance is the main value of producing the forecast at all
> - A single negative month is not the same as business failure, provided finance is available
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A forecast negative balance is a warning, not a verdict. It tells the business it will need funding in a particular month, which is useful precisely because there is still time to arrange it. Answers treating it as evidence the business is failing overstate what the figure actually shows.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a cash flow forecast may differ from the actual cash flow.
parts.solutionMd:
A cash flow forecast is a prediction built on assumptions about future receipts and payments **[1]**. One assumption is that customers will pay within the agreed credit period, yet some pay late and a few do not pay at all **[1]**. If receipts arrive a month later than forecast, the business holds less cash than predicted in that month, so a forecast showing a comfortable positive balance can turn out negative in practice **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A cash flow forecast is based on assumptions about the timing and size of future receipts and payments
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Customers may pay later than the agreed credit terms, delaying inflows into a later month
> - Sales may be lower than forecast if demand or the economy weakens
> - Costs such as materials or energy may rise unexpectedly, increasing outflows
> - Unplanned events such as equipment failure create outflows no forecast anticipated
> - The further ahead the forecast reaches, the less reliable its assumptions become
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the specific assumption that fails. Saying a forecast is "just a prediction" is true of every forecast and earns little. Identify what was assumed, whether that customers pay on time or that sales hold up, and then trace what happens to the balance when it does not.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which a business could improve its cash flow by reducing its cash outflows.
parts.solutionMd:
Cash flow can be improved by reducing the money leaving the business or delaying when it leaves **[1]**. A business could lease equipment rather than buying it outright, spreading the cost across monthly payments instead of paying a large sum at once **[1]**. This avoids a single large outflow that might push the closing balance negative, though the total paid across the lease is usually higher than the purchase price would have been **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Cash flow improves when outflows are reduced or their timing is delayed
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Leasing rather than buying spreads a large payment into smaller monthly amounts
> - Negotiating longer credit terms with suppliers delays outflows without reducing them
> - Reducing inventory levels releases cash currently tied up in unsold stock
> - Postponing non-essential spending moves outflows into a month with a healthier balance
> - Each of these has a cost, whether higher total payments, strained supplier relations or lost sales
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every method of improving cash flow has a price attached, and naming it is what earns the third mark. Leasing costs more overall, delaying supplier payments risks the relationship, and cutting inventory risks stockouts. An answer presenting a method as pure gain has not finished the reasoning.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which a business could improve its cash flow by increasing its cash inflows.
parts.solutionMd:
Cash flow can be improved by bringing money into the business sooner **[1]**. A business could offer customers a discount for paying within ten days rather than the usual thirty **[1]**. This brings cash in around three weeks earlier and can remove a forecast shortfall, but the discount reduces the amount finally received, so cash flow improves while profit falls **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Cash flow improves when inflows are increased or received sooner
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A discount for early payment brings receipts forward by several weeks
> - Debt factoring converts receivables into cash immediately, though at less than full value
> - Reducing the credit period offered speeds collection but may lose price-sensitive customers
> - Selling unused assets generates a one-off inflow without affecting trading
> - Improving cash flow this way often reduces profit, so the two do not move together
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Improving cash flow is not the same as improving profit, and this is the clearest case of the two pulling apart. A discount for early payment brings money in sooner and leaves less of it. Showing that you know cash and profit can move in opposite directions marks out a strong answer.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** drawback of relying on an overdraft to solve a cash flow problem.
parts.solutionMd:
An overdraft allows a business to withdraw more than it holds in its account, up to an agreed limit **[1]**. Overdrafts are normally repayable on demand, so the bank can reduce or withdraw the facility at short notice **[1]**. A bank is most likely to do that when it becomes concerned about the business's position, which is exactly when the business is depending on the overdraft most, so the finance disappears at the worst possible moment **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - An overdraft permits withdrawals beyond the account balance up to an agreed limit
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Overdrafts are repayable on demand, so the facility can be withdrawn without warning
> - Withdrawal is most likely when the business appears to be struggling, which is when it is needed most
> - Interest rates on overdrafts are typically much higher than on loans
> - An overdraft addresses the symptom while leaving the underlying cash flow problem unresolved
> - Persistent use of the full limit signals difficulty to the bank and may affect future lending
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The particular danger of an overdraft is its timing: it can be removed precisely when the business most needs it. That makes it different from a loan, which cannot simply be recalled. Building your answer around repayable on demand gives you a chain the examiner can follow rather than a general point about interest being high.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a bank would want to see a cash flow forecast before lending to a business.
parts.solutionMd:
A cash flow forecast predicts the money expected to flow into and out of a business over a future period **[1]**. A bank lends on the expectation of being repaid in instalments on fixed dates **[1]**. The forecast shows whether the business expects to hold enough cash in each of those particular months to make the repayments, which a profit forecast would not reveal, since a profitable business can still lack the cash to pay on a given date **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A cash flow forecast predicts the timing and size of a business's future receipts and payments
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Repayments fall due on fixed dates, so the bank needs to know the cash position in those specific months
> - Profit does not show whether cash will be available when a payment is due
> - The forecast reveals whether the business has understood its own cash position
> - Unrealistic assumptions in the forecast are themselves a warning sign to the lender
> - The forecast indicates how much needs to be borrowed and for how long
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Answer this from the bank's point of view rather than the business's. The bank is not asking whether the business will be successful; it is asking whether the money will be there on the dates repayments fall due. Keeping the lender's question in focus is what earns the application marks.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of cash flow forecasting to a new car hire business.
parts.solutionMd:
Cash flow forecasting is likely to be very important for a new car hire business. It can help the business spot in advance if there will be a shortfall in cash **[K]**, for example during quiet seasons when fewer people are hiring cars **[Ap]**. This gives the business time to arrange extra short-term finance, like an overdraft, rather than being caught out and unable to pay for things like vehicle maintenance or staff wages **[An]**

It can also help the business decide how to fund its vehicles **[K]**. A cash flow forecast might show that leasing cars, with smaller regular payments, is more manageable for a new business than buying vehicles outright **[Ap]**, which would be a large one-off cost **[An]**. This is especially useful for a new business that does not yet have a steady, predictable income **[E]**

Overall, I think cash flow forecasting is very important for a new car hire business **[E]**, mainly for helping it survive its first, most risky period, when running out of cash could mean the business fails before it gets established **[An]**. However, in the longer term, other factors like good marketing, competitive pricing and reliable vehicles **[Ap]** are likely to become just as important for the business's overall success **[E]**, so cash flow forecasting should be seen as essential early on, but not the only thing that determines whether the business does well overall **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation
> - A full-mark answer will include
> 
>   - Strong knowledge applied to the business context or question stem throughout
>   - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
>   - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
>   - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
