parts.problemMd: Define the term 'feedback'.
parts.solutionMd:
Feedback is the response a receiver gives to the sender of a message **[1]**, which shows whether the message has been received and understood as intended **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The reply or reaction from the receiver that tells the sender whether a message has been understood
> - Information returned to the sender showing how a message was interpreted, completing the communication process
> - The receiver's response, which allows the sender to check understanding and correct any misunderstanding

> **[exam-tip]**
> Feedback is a stage in a process, so say where it sits: it travels back from receiver to sender, and it completes the loop. A definition describing it only as "a response" could mean almost anything. Saying who responds to whom, and what that response shows, secures both marks.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'electronic communication'.
parts.solutionMd:
Electronic communication is the sending of messages using electronic devices or systems **[1]**, such as email, video calls and instant messaging, which allows information to travel almost instantly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Communication carried out through electronic media such as email, video conferencing, intranets and messaging applications
> - The transmission of information using digital technology rather than paper or face-to-face contact
> - Any exchange of messages that depends on electronic devices and networks to carry the information

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a category term, name the category and show its range. Listing only email suggests you know one example rather than the group. Say that messages travel by electronic device or system, then give two or three different examples to show the breadth of what the term covers.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'visual communication'.
parts.solutionMd:
Visual communication is the presentation of information in a form that is seen rather than read or heard **[1]**, such as charts, diagrams and photographs, which helps people take in information quickly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Conveying information through images, charts, diagrams, film or symbols rather than through words alone
> - The use of pictures, graphs and other visual material to present information so it can be understood at a glance
> - Communication relying on what the receiver sees, often used to make complex data easier to grasp

> **[exam-tip]**
> Where a term names the medium, say what form the message actually takes. Visual communication is information the receiver sees, such as a chart or diagram, as opposed to words they read or hear. Naming the form and contrasting it with the alternatives makes the definition precise.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'informal communication'.
parts.solutionMd:
Informal communication is the exchange of information between employees outside the official channels of the business **[1]**, such as conversations between colleagues, sometimes called the grapevine **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Communication taking place outside official reporting lines, often between colleagues on a personal basis
> - Unofficial exchanges of information within a business, commonly known as the grapevine
> - Messages passing between employees without following the formal structure or approved procedures

> **[exam-tip]**
> Some terms are defined by what they are not, and this is one. The mark comes from saying the communication happens outside the official channels of the business. An answer describing "chatting at work" captures the flavour but not the definition, so anchor it to the formal structure it bypasses.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'barrier to communication'.
parts.solutionMd:
A barrier to communication is anything that prevents a message reaching the receiver or being understood as the sender intended **[1]**, such as unclear language, too many layers of hierarchy, or a noisy workplace **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Any obstacle that stops a message being transmitted, received or understood correctly
> - A factor preventing effective communication, whether physical, technical, linguistic or organisational
> - Something that distorts or blocks a message so the receiver does not understand what the sender meant

> **[exam-tip]**
> An obstacle term needs you to say what is being obstructed. Here it is the message reaching the receiver, or being understood as intended. Calling it "a problem with communication" simply repeats the term back; naming what fails is what earns the second mark.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** purpose of communication within a business.
parts.solutionMd:
One purpose of communication is to give employees the instructions they need to do their work **[1]**. A manager must tell staff what needs doing, by when, and to what standard, because employees cannot be expected to guess **[1]**. Clear instructions mean work is done correctly the first time, so the business avoids the wasted materials and repeated effort that follow when someone has misunderstood what was wanted **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Communication is used to instruct, to inform, to consult, to motivate, to coordinate different parts of the business, and to obtain feedback
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Instructing tells employees what must be done and to what standard, so work is completed correctly without guesswork
> - Informing keeps staff aware of changes such as new procedures or targets, so they are not working to out-of-date expectations
> - Consulting gathers employees' views before a decision, producing better decisions and making staff more willing to accept them
> - Coordinating aligns departments whose work depends on each other, so production knows what sales has promised customers
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A purpose is best expressed as a verb: to instruct, to inform, to consult, to motivate. Starting your answer with one of those keeps you answering the question asked. Descriptions of how communication happens, such as by email or in meetings, answer a different question about methods.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Sentinel (SN)**
> 
> Sentinel (SN) provides security guards for offices, warehouses and building sites in country D. It employs 540 guards working across 90 sites.
> 
> Most guards work alone on night shifts and never meet head office staff. Instructions are sent by post to each site and pinned to a noticeboard.
> 
> Last month a change to fire evacuation procedure did not reach 31 sites before an inspection. SN was fined \$12,000.
> 
> SN's operations director is considering giving every guard a mobile application through which instructions would be sent directly.

Explain **one** way SN could overcome a barrier to communication.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is to give every guard the mobile application the operations director is considering **[1]**. At present instructions are posted to each site and pinned to a noticeboard, which is why a change to fire evacuation procedure never reached 31 of SN's 90 sites **[1]**. Sending instructions straight to a guard's phone removes both the postal delay and the risk that nobody reads the noticeboard, so a safety change would reach all 540 guards on the day it was made rather than whenever they next happened to look **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Barriers can be overcome by choosing a more suitable medium, shortening the chain of communication, confirming receipt, simplifying the message, or training staff
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A mobile application delivers instructions directly to each guard rather than relying on post and a noticeboard nobody may read
> - Requiring guards to confirm they have read a message would have shown SN that 31 sites had not received the fire procedure before the inspection
> - Guards work alone at night and never meet head office, so any method needing a meeting is impractical; the medium must reach people who are dispersed and on shift
> - Shorter, simpler instructions would help, since a long posted notice is less likely to be read in full by someone working a night shift alone
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The marks depend on matching the solution to the barrier. Identify what is actually blocking the message, then choose a remedy that removes that specific obstacle. A general answer such as "communicate better" or "hold more meetings" will not score if it would not have solved the problem described.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Millgate (MG)**
> 
> Millgate (MG) manufactures office furniture in country T and employs 210 people.
> 
> MG's sales team agrees delivery dates with customers by telephone and writes them on a paper order form. The form is passed to the factory the following morning.
> 
> Production staff say they often learn of urgent orders too late to fit them into the schedule. In the past year MG delivered 18% of orders after the promised date, and remade 340 items because the specification written on the form was unclear.
> 
> MG is considering a shared order system that sales and production could both see immediately.

Explain **one** way improved communication could increase MG's efficiency.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is that a shared order system would let production see orders as soon as they are taken **[1]**. At present sales write delivery dates on a paper form that only reaches the factory the next morning, which is why production staff learn of urgent orders too late to schedule them **[1]**. Seeing orders immediately would let production plan the day's work around what has actually been promised, cutting into the 18% of orders MG currently delivers late without needing any extra staff or machinery **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Efficiency means getting more output from the same resources; better communication raises it by reducing wasted time, wasted materials and duplicated work
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A shared system removes the overnight delay, so production can schedule urgent orders on the day they are taken rather than the morning after
> - Typed specifications visible to both teams would reduce the 340 items remade last year because a handwritten form was unclear, saving materials and machine time
> - Cutting late deliveries from 18% protects MG's reputation without spending anything on extra capacity, so output rises relative to cost
> - Production staff would spend less time chasing sales for clarification, freeing that time for actual manufacturing
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Efficiency compares output with the resources used, so a strong answer says which side of that comparison moves. Here MG produces more usable furniture from the same staff and machines. Saying communication would make the business "better" or "faster" without linking it to output or resources leaves marks on the table.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** drawback to a business of relying on electronic communication.
parts.solutionMd:
One drawback is that electronic communication provides no immediate feedback **[1]**. When a manager sends an email, the receiver may not read it for hours, and the sender cannot see whether it has been understood **[1]**. A face-to-face conversation would reveal confusion at once through the other person's questions or expression, so relying on email risks a misunderstanding continuing unnoticed until work has already been done incorrectly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Drawbacks of electronic communication include the absence of immediate feedback, information overload, loss of tone, security risks, and dependence on technology working
> 
> AO2
> 
> - An email gives no immediate response, so the sender cannot tell whether the message was understood until something goes wrong
> - Employees receiving a high volume of messages may miss important ones among routine ones, so a critical instruction goes unread
> - Tone is easily misread in writing, and a brief instruction meant to be efficient can be taken as abrupt, damaging working relationships
> - If systems fail or a message is intercepted, the business may lose access to information or have confidential material exposed
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A drawback is only meaningful against an alternative. The weakness of email is clearest set beside a conversation, where confusion shows immediately. Naming the comparison, even briefly, turns a vague criticism into a developed point, and is usually the difference between two marks and three.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Brookvale (BK)**
> 
> Brookvale (BK) runs eleven children's nurseries in country N and employs 260 staff.
> 
> BK's owner announced a change to staff rotas by email at 6pm on a Friday, to take effect the following Monday. Many staff did not see the email before the weekend.
> 
> On the Monday, four nurseries were short-staffed. Two parents complained that their child's usual key worker had been moved without warning.
> 
> Nine staff resigned over the following three months. Several said they felt decisions were made without any consultation.

Explain **one** reason why effective communication is important to BK.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason is that BK depends on its staff accepting changes to how they work **[1]**. The rota change was emailed at 6pm on a Friday to take effect on the Monday, and many staff did not see it before the weekend **[1]**. Announcing a change this way left employees feeling decisions were made without consultation, and nine resigned over the following three months, which for a business relying on familiar key workers means both a recruitment cost and unhappy parents **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Effective communication matters because it affects how well employees understand decisions, how motivated they feel, and whether the business runs as intended
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Emailing a rota change at 6pm on a Friday gave staff no chance to raise problems, so four nurseries were short-staffed on the Monday
> - Nine resignations in three months, with staff citing a lack of consultation, show the cost of poor communication in a business whose main resource is its people
> - Parents complained that their child's key worker had changed without warning, so poor internal communication became a customer problem as well
> - Consulting staff before changing rotas would have identified the four nurseries at risk in advance, avoiding the disruption entirely
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To show why something is important, show what happens without it. Here poor communication produced short-staffed nurseries, complaining parents and nine resignations. Building your answer around the consequence, rather than asserting that communication "is very important", is what makes the point convincing and earns the development marks.

Analyse **two** limitations to WP of its methods of internal communication.
parts.solutionMd:
One limitation is that Rona's weekly meeting with all 35 employees is one-way communication **[K]** - information flows from Rona to employees, but there is no structured opportunity for employees to respond or share ideas. Production workers are likely to have useful knowledge about manufacturing processes and product quality **[Ap]**, but with no way to feed this back to Rona, their ideas are ignored. Over time, employees who feel they have no voice in the business are likely to become demotivated, which could reduce their productivity and increase labour turnover **[An]**. This is particularly damaging for WP because it relies on skilled workers, and replacing them is both costly and time-consuming **[An]**

A second limitation is that the three functional managers - operations, marketing, and finance - only communicate with Rona individually rather than meeting as a group **[K]**. This means the managers have very little direct communication with each other, limiting coordination between departments. For example, the marketing manager's sales forecasts may not be shared promptly with the operations manager, making it difficult to plan production schedules around WP's highly seasonal demand **[Ap]** **[An]**. FF sells its plastic frames to wholesale businesses that market well-known brands of plastic frames which they sell globally. The wholesalers reject 7% of the frames supplied by FF because of substandard quality. The FF design team create dynamic styles based on the demands of the wholesalers. Meeting delivery times is very important. FF only delivers 85% of its sales on time. FF needs to improve this percentage. Improving quality Chang, the production manager, aims to reduce the high level of rejects by the wholesalers. He has identified a number of factors which make this difficult including: • employees know that rejected frames can be recycled • production targets are very difficult to meet • problems with suppliers of raw materials • breakdowns with machinery. Chang proposes introducing Total Quality Management (TQM). He thinks this will reduce the number of substandard frames and improve FF’s delivery times. Chang forecasts successful implementation of TQM will also increase output by 10% and average variable cost will fall by 5%. However, Chang is aware that there may be problems with TQM and forecasts can be inaccurate. Table 1 shows information on FF’s output, costs and prices, before TQM is implemented. Table 1: FF’s output, costs and prices Year ending September 2021 Maximum capacity 16 million frames Actual output 14 million frames Average variable cost \$20 Average selling price \$40 Communication challenges FF has a centralised organisational structure with a low degree of delegation. Directors make decisions, department managers plan how to implement these and supervisors give instructions. Employees have little responsibility or control. FF has provided good pay, good conditions of work and security of employment. However, employees are aware that the directors are considering significant changes to working conditions. All employees find it difficult to discuss this with their line managers. Many employees work alone so information is passed on informally and often inaccurately. This uncertainty has begun to lead to dissatisfaction, complaints, higher absence rates and lower productivity. Privatisation of electricity and water industries In country W, state-owned businesses supply all electricity and water. Prices of services in these industries have risen at above the rate of inflation for the last three years. Sometimes, electricity supply is interrupted and FF finds it difficult to obtain information about reconnection. Water quality is variable. The government has announced it intends to privatise these industries in the next three years, to improve these services.

Buying 3D printers 3D printers that make frames for glasses as part of a CAD/CAM process are becoming available. Chang is considering whether FF should invest in this rapidly developing technology. 3D printers have a guaranteed life span of four years but he believes they are probably usable for six years. There is no way of accurately estimating their value after four years. The directors have told Chang that an acceptable accounting rate of return (ARR) is 5%. Chang thinks new 3D printers will increase FF’s long-term profitability. The 3D printers will result in significant reductions in employee costs and waste and substandard reject costs. Maintenance and training costs will, however, increase. Table 2 and Table 3 show some of Chang’s research. He knows competitors are considering buying them. Product development and marketing The marketing manager is concerned that FF relies only on specific orders from wholesalers for plastic frames. He proposes that FF should use product development to design and manufacture metal glasses frames. These would be marketed to wholesalers and directly to businesses who sell glasses with globally recognised brands. FF would have to acquire new skills and equipment in order to design and manufacture metal frames. The marketing manager visited international trade fairs and found that several competitors have research and development (R&D) departments. Strategic choice: enter the Asia Pacific retail market The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) states: ‘My strategic analysis shows that FF must continue with the current business model but should take a new direction as well. My strategic choice is that FF should enter the retail glasses market in the Asia Pacific region. This will mean selling our own glasses in retail shops. We will need to work closely with lens manufacturers. Increased eye strain and higher disposable income are driving the increasing demand for higher value glasses. We could use the Ansoff Matrix to help analyse the link between this business strategy and risk. There are several approaches we could use to enter this new market.’

The CEO illustrates his proposal with Table 4 and Table 5. There are nine stages in the production process, including cutting out plastic sheets, smoothing component parts, attaching them, and final shaping and polishing. Employees only carry out the one task they have been trained for in the production process. The Directors are considering a proposal from Chang to move to team working. A team would be responsible for the whole production of a product and would take all necessary decisions. If successful, FF could possibly reduce the lead-time from order to completion by 60%, inventory levels by 27% and increase productivity by 20%. A change to team working means greater delegation and less centralisation. Control, authority and trust involving directors, managers, supervisors and production employees will have to change. This strategic change must be managed effectively and directors are confident that Chang has the necessary theoretical knowledge. The benefits he identified will only be achieved if he applies the correct techniques to manage the introduction of team working.

Evaluate the most effective way that FF’s directors could improve communication between line managers and employees.
parts.solutionMd:
Effective communication is the exchange of information between people with the opportunity for feedback **[K]**. FF currently has one-way, top-down communication - directors make decisions, managers plan how to carry them out, and supervisors give instructions to employees. There is no formal channel for employees to respond, and many work in isolation, which has led to information spreading informally and inaccurately **[Ap]**

The most effective short-term improvement **[E] **would be to introduce regular two-way meetings between line managers and employees **[K]**. Currently, employees cannot discuss proposed changes to working conditions with their managers **[Ap]**, creating uncertainty that is directly causing higher absence rates and lower productivity. Scheduled meetings where employees can ask questions and raise concerns would replace the inaccurate informal grapevine with reliable, consistent information **[An]**. This would reduce uncertainty and help employees feel more comfortable with the significant changes FF is planning, including TQM and team working **[An]**

Moving to team working, which is already being considered, would also bring lasting structural improvements to communication **[K]**. Production workers currently work alone on a single task, which makes communication difficult **[Ap]**. Organising employees into teams responsible for the whole production process would create natural channels for horizontal communication between workers and make it easier for line managers to communicate through a team leader rather than reaching each employee individually **[An]**

However, any improvement in communication will only work if line managers are trusted by employees **[E]**. FF's centralised culture means employees have little responsibility and may be sceptical that new communication channels are genuinely two-way. If managers simply pass on instructions in a different format, the underlying problem remains **[An]**

Overall, introducing structured two-way meetings is the most immediately effective approach, because it directly addresses the uncertainty and dissatisfaction that are already damaging FF's performance **[E]**. Team working would then provide a more sustainable, long-term improvement, but only if it is introduced carefully with genuine involvement of employees at every stage **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Clearvale (CV)**
> 
> Clearvale (CV) manufactures glass for windows and doors in country T. It employs 620 people across two factories working around the clock.
> 
> Communication problems are frequent. Production targets are posted on noticeboards, changes to specifications are passed on verbally between shift supervisors, and staff say they often learn about company decisions from colleagues rather than from managers.
> 
> **Table 1.1: CV selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 620 |
> |---|---|
> | Glass panels rejected for wrong specification last year | 2,900 |
> | Value of rejected panels (\$000) | 410 |
> | Staff saying in a survey that they are told about decisions in good time (%) | 22 |
> | Cost of proposed digital display system for both factories (\$000) | 260 |
> | Cost of proposed programme of weekly team briefings (\$000 per year) | 95 |
> 
> CV's directors must choose between installing digital display screens showing live targets and specification changes, or introducing weekly team briefings led by supervisors.

Evaluate whether CV should install digital display screens or introduce weekly team briefings to improve its communication.
parts.solutionMd:
Digital display screens would give every worker the same information at the same time **[K]**. CV currently posts targets on noticeboards and passes specification changes verbally between shift supervisors, which is why 2,900 panels were rejected last year for being made to the wrong specification **[Ap]**. Screens showing live specifications would remove the verbal handover where information is most easily lost, so fewer panels would be made incorrectly and CV would recover part of the \$410,000 those rejects cost **[An]**

Weekly briefings would address a different problem **[K]**. Only 22% of staff say they are told about company decisions in good time, and many learn of them from colleagues instead **[Ap]**. A briefing led by a supervisor lets employees ask questions and gives managers a sense of what workers are actually concerned about, which a screen cannot do **[An]**

Which option is better depends on which problem CV most needs to solve **[E]**. The rejected panels are the more measurable cost, at \$410,000 against a one-off \$260,000 for the screens, so on financial grounds the screens repay themselves within a year while briefings cost \$95,000 every year indefinitely **[E]**. However, screens only push information outwards, and would do nothing about the 78% of staff who feel uninformed; a workforce that hears company news through the grapevine tends to become harder to manage over time **[E]**. On balance CV should install the screens first, because they attack the largest measurable loss and the payback is quick **[E]**. Briefings should follow once those savings arrive, since the two options solve different problems and CV will eventually need both **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Marchmont Motors (MM)**
> 
> Marchmont Motors (MM) owns fourteen car dealerships in country K. Each dealership has a sales department and a separate service and repair workshop.
> 
> Sales staff sometimes promise customers a delivery or repair date without checking with the workshop. Workshop staff order parts only once a car arrives.
> 
> **Table 1.1: MM selected data**
> 
> | Dealerships | 14 |
> |---|---|
> | Employees | 900 |
> | Cars waiting for parts at any one time | 210 |
> | Average customer wait for a repair (days) | 9 |
> | Customer satisfaction score (out of 10) | 5.8 |
> | Cost of a shared booking and parts system (\$000) | 480 |
> | Cost of employing four extra mechanics per dealership (\$000 per year) | 2,300 |
> 
> MM's directors are considering whether to invest in a shared system linking sales and the workshop, or simply to employ more mechanics.

Evaluate whether MM should invest in a shared booking and parts system rather than employing more mechanics.
parts.solutionMd:
A shared system would let sales see what the workshop can actually do **[K]**. At present sales staff promise dates without checking, and the workshop orders parts only once a car arrives, which is why 210 cars are waiting for parts at any one time **[Ap]**. If a booking triggered a parts order immediately, most of those cars would have their parts waiting when they arrived, cutting the nine-day average wait without any extra labour at all **[An]**

Employing more mechanics would raise capacity directly **[K]**. Four extra mechanics at each of 14 dealerships would add considerable labour, but at \$2.3m every year against a one-off \$480,000 for the system **[Ap]**. More mechanics would also do nothing for a car waiting on a part rather than on a person, so much of that expensive extra labour could stand idle while the underlying problem continued **[An]**

The system looks the stronger option because it addresses the actual cause of delay **[E]**. Cars are waiting for parts, not for mechanics, so adding labour treats a symptom while leaving the coordination failure untouched **[E]**. The cost comparison reinforces this: \$480,000 once against \$2.3m a year that MM would go on paying indefinitely **[E]**. However, a system only works if staff use it properly, and sales staff who currently promise dates without checking may carry on doing so unless MM also changes how they are managed and rewarded **[E]**. MM should therefore invest in the system, but treat it as a change in working practice rather than simply a purchase, because the technology alone will not fix a habit **[E]**

The delay is caused by parts rather than people, since 210 cars wait for components because the workshop orders only once a car arrives, so linking the booking to the parts order removes the wait rather than working around it, and the same 900 employees would complete more repairs at no extra wage cost. However, a system only delivers if staff use it, and sales staff who currently promise dates without checking may continue to do so unless MM also changes how they are supervised and rewarded

This adds capacity that is certain rather than dependent on software working as intended, and would help wherever cars are genuinely waiting for labour. > - Efficiency means obtaining more output from the same resources, which is exactly what the system delivers by stopping cars sitting idle. However, the underlying failure is one of communication between two departments, and technology does not by itself change a habit of promising dates without checking

The swimming pool will cost \$400 000 and George has yet to decide on the best source of finance. He has \$50 000 in savings that he could use and he does not have any mortgage or loans. Explain the term ‘contract of employment’.
parts.solutionMd:
A contract of employment is a legal document drawn up by an employer and issued to an employee **[1]**. parts.problemMd: Explain **one **type of training that a business may use.
parts.solutionMd:
On-the-job training involves employees learning new skills while carrying out their normal work duties, usually by watching or working alongside an experienced colleague **[1]**. For example, a new employee at a restaurant might be shown by a senior member of staff how to prepare food correctly and follow hygiene procedures **[1]**. This approach is cost-effective for the business because no specialist venue is needed, and the training is directly relevant to the tasks the employee will carry out every day **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Induction training
> - On-the-job training
> - Off-the-job training
> - On-line training
> - Video training
> - Shadowing/mentoring training.
> 
> **AO2 Application **
> 
> - Induction training - given to new employees to introduce them to the business; covers health and safety procedures, the layout of the premises, key colleagues, and business rules and expectations, helping new recruits settle in quickly and make an effective start
> - On-the-job training - employees learn by watching or working alongside experienced colleagues in the workplace; it is cost-effective as no external venue is needed, and the skills learned are directly relevant to the employee's role
> - Off-the-job training - employees attend a course or training programme away from the workplace, delivered by a specialist provider; this can introduce new skills and ideas that employees bring back to the business, though it can be more expensive and takes staff away from their duties
> - Online training - employees complete training using computer software at a time and place that suits them; this is flexible and relatively low-cost, making it useful for delivering induction or skills updates to large numbers of staff
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why businesses invest in the training and development of employees.
parts.solutionMd:
Businesses invest in training and development to increase employee productivity **[1]**. When employees are given the skills and knowledge to carry out their jobs more effectively, they are likely to work faster and to a higher standard, reducing errors and wasted time **[1]**. This allows the business to produce more output with the same number of staff, lowering the cost per unit and improving profit margins **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Training and development is investment in improving employees' skills and abilities so they can perform their roles more effectively.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Increased productivity - well-trained employees can carry out tasks more quickly and accurately, reducing errors and wasted resources, which lowers costs and increases the output the business can deliver with the same workforce
> - Higher motivation and lower labour turnover - employees who receive training feel valued by the business and are more likely to stay, reducing the cost of recruiting and inducting replacement staff
> - Better customer service - in service businesses, trained employees are more confident and capable in dealing with customers, leading to higher satisfaction, repeat business, and a stronger competitive advantage
> - Employer of choice - a reputation for investing in staff development helps the business attract high-quality job applicants, as candidates are more likely to apply to businesses that support career progression
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you identify a clear reason and then develop it fully. A common mistake is to simply state that training improves skills without explaining the wider impact on the business, such as increased productivity, reduced staff turnover or improved competitiveness. To access the higher marks, link your reason to a tangible business outcome. For example, rather than writing "training makes employees better", explain that training equips employees with up-to-date skills, which can increase efficiency and output, ultimately improving the firm's profitability.

**[3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why it is important for a business to have effective human resource management (HRM).
parts.solutionMd:
Effective HRM ensures that a business recruits and selects the right employees for each role **[1]**. If the right people are hired, they are more likely to perform well, require less corrective training, and stay with the business longer **[1]**. This reduces the costs associated with poor performance and frequent staff replacement, and helps the business achieve its objectives more efficiently **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - HRM is responsible for managing the workforce, including recruitment and selection, training and development, and maintaining employee motivation and morale
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Recruitment and selection — effective HRM ensures the business hires employees with the right skills and attitude for each role; this reduces the likelihood of poor performance, lowers staff turnover, and avoids the cost of repeatedly recruiting replacements
> - Training and development — effective HRM ensures employees have the skills needed to carry out their roles well, increasing productivity and quality of output, which directly benefits the business's performance and reputation
> - Employee motivation and morale — effective HRM keeps employees motivated and satisfied at work, reducing absenteeism and labour turnover and helping the business maintain consistent levels of output and customer service
> - Impact on other departments — because every department depends on having capable, motivated staff, effective HRM supports the performance of the whole business; poor HRM in one area can cause problems across all functions
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Super Heroes (SH) **
> 
> SH is a leisure (theme) park aimed at 10–18 year olds. It is owned by two companies, X and Y, which started SH as a joint venture. Company X owns many leisure centres and swimming pools. Company Y owns many brands based on superheroes.
> 
> SH employs 200 full-time workers and an extra 50 seasonal workers during the busiest times of the year. The park has 10 large rides which take up 2km<sup>2</sup> of land. There are also many smaller rides, restaurants, toilets and shops. The price of an entrance ticket is \$11 per customer. Table 1.1 shows the costs for SH in 2019.
> 
> **Table 1.1: SH costs for 2019**
> 
> | Total fixed costs (per year) | \$12m |
> |---|---|
> | Variable costs (per customer) | \$3 |
> | Total costs | \$42m |
> 
> One of the larger rides at SH is the Iron Blaster. The number of customers who use this ride has decreased each year for the last three years. This has led the management of SH to consider its options for internal growth.
> 
> *Option 1 – A new virtual reality (VR) ride *
> This option would involve developing the Iron Blaster into a VR ride. Most of the structure of the Iron Blaster could be used but customers would be given a VR headset to wear during the ride. The cost of developing the VR ride would be \$2m. The Iron Blaster ride would be closed for a three month period during the off-peak season for the development to be carried out. No employees would be made redundant or dismissed.
> 
> *Option 2 – A new hotel *
> SH does not currently have a hotel. It could demolish the Iron Blaster to provide the space to build one. Many of the competitors of SH have a hotel near or within their leisure parks. Hotel customers would pay a high price for a room but have free access to the leisure park’s facilities. Market research suggests that the average hotel customer would spend twice as long in the leisure park than a non-hotel customer. The cost of developing the hotel would be \$15m and take a year to build. All of the employees currently working on the Iron Blaster ride would face redundancy or dismissal.

Explain the difference between ‘redundancy’ and ‘dismissal’.
parts.solutionMd:
Redundancy occurs when an employee loses their job because the role itself is no longer needed by the business **[1]** - for example, if SH demolishes the Iron Blaster, the jobs associated with operating that ride no longer exist. Dismissal, by contrast, is when an employer ends an individual employee's contract because of something related to that specific person, such as poor performance or misconduct **[1]**. The key difference is that redundancy is about the job disappearing, not the person, whereas dismissal is a decision made about the individual employee **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Redundancy is where an employee is made to leave an organisation because their job role is no longer required
> - Dismissal is where an employer ends a worker’s employment
> - The difference is that redundancy is about the job role not being required any more, whereas dismissal is when the employee is no longer required
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** effect on a business of a high rate of labour turnover.
parts.solutionMd:
A high rate of labour turnover means the business must frequently recruit and train replacement staff, which is expensive and time-consuming **[1]**. While new employees are being inducted and learning their roles, they are unlikely to work as efficiently as the experienced staff they replaced, which can reduce productivity and lower the quality of output or customer service **[1]**. Over time, these additional costs and disruptions can significantly reduce the business's profit margins **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> A high rate of labour turnover means employees leave the business frequently and must be replaced, increasing recruitment, selection, and training costs
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Higher costs - the business must repeatedly spend money on advertising vacancies, interviewing candidates, and training new recruits; while replacements are being inducted, productivity is likely to fall, adding further to costs and potentially reducing output or customer satisfaction
> - Loss of skills and experience - when experienced employees leave they take their knowledge with them, which can reduce the quality of work and place extra pressure on remaining staff who may need to cover additional responsibilities until a replacement is found
> - Impact on morale - remaining employees may feel unsettled or overburdened if colleagues frequently leave, leading to lower motivation and potentially causing further staff to leave, making the problem worse over time
> - Disruption to operations - constant changes in staffing make it difficult to maintain consistent standards, which can damage customer relationships and harm the business's reputation
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you do more than simply state an effect - the command word "explain" means you need to develop your point. For example, do not just write "higher costs"; instead, explain why costs increase and what impact this has on the business. A good approach is to identify the effect, then link it to a consequence such as reduced productivity, lower quality of output or decreased employee morale. Many students lose marks by listing multiple effects rather than fully developing one - focus on depth, not breadth.

**[3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **advantages to a business of using induction training.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of induction training is that new employees quickly learn what is expected of them **[1]**, including the business's rules, procedures, and health and safety requirements. This means they can make an effective start to their role and are less likely to make costly mistakes in the early stages of employment **[1]**

A second advantage is that induction training helps new employees feel welcomed and confident in their new workplace **[1]**. When employees feel settled and supported from the start, they are more likely to be motivated and to stay with the business **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)

> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
>

> 
> AO1
>

> - It helps new employees understand the structure of the business and their role within it.
> 
> AO2
>

> - Feeling welcomed and settled increases new employees' motivation and sense of belonging, making them more likely to remain with the business and reducing the costs associated with high labour turnover
> - Understanding future promotion routes can motivate employees to work hard and develop their skills, benefiting the business through a more capable and committed workforce over time
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **advantage to an employer of using a person specification.
parts.solutionMd:
A person specification lists the skills, qualifications and personal qualities needed for a job, showing which are essential and which are just desirable **[1]**. This gives an employer a clear, consistent set of criteria to compare every candidate against, which makes it easier to spot the most suitable person for the role **[1]**. It also means the employer is less likely to rely on personal opinion or guesswork when choosing between applicants, reducing the risk of hiring the wrong person **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded up to 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A person specification sets out the skills, qualifications, experience, and personal qualities required for a role, distinguishing between essential and desirable attributes
> - It informs potential applicants about the type of person the business is looking for, helping them to self-select before applying.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - By making the requirements of the role clear, unsuitable candidates are less likely to apply, reducing the volume of applications the employer must review and shortening the recruitment process — saving both time and money
> - Having a clear list of essential and desirable criteria allows the employer to assess all candidates consistently and objectively, making it easier to identify the most suitable person for the role and reducing the risk of a poor hiring decision
> - A well-written person specification can also attract higher-quality applicants, as candidates who closely match the criteria are more likely to apply, improving the overall standard of the candidate pool
>

parts.solutionMd:
**23.23%** **[3]**

Remember that labour turnover is expressed as a percentage, so do not forget to multiply by 100. A common mistake is simply subtracting the number of leavers (e.g. 5 − 1 = 4) rather than calculating the turnover rate for each division first and then finding the difference - this approach will only earn 1 mark at most.

MS employs specialist marketing workers as well as administrative support workers. > > **Table 2.1 shows some data about employees of MS.** > > | | **Specialist marketing workers** | **Administrative support workers** | > |---|---|---| > | Average number of workers in 2019 | 40 | 88 | > | Payment method | Salary plus bonus | Performance related pay plus bonus | > | Number of workers who left in 2019 | 2 | 11 | > | Average pay (compared to national average) | High | Low | > | Main need of the workers | Achievement | Affiliation | > | Main hygiene factors | - Pay
- Flexible hours of work | - Staff restaurant
- Holidays | > | Is a bonus expected in 2020? | Yes | No | > > MS has recently employed Hetti as the new Human Resources Manager. Hetti thinks that the ideas of the motivational theorists are important when managing employees. She is particularly worried about the labour turnover of the administrative support workers. > > MS has recently taken on a new customer, named Books Outlet (BO). BO has an objective to increase its revenue by targeting a younger market segment. BO has provided MS with the following information about its current marketing mix (see Table 2.2). > > **Table 2.2: Current marketing mix for BO** > > | **Product **

- Books aimed at customers who are 30 years and older
- Specialist books on many topics – BO is often the only seller in the area | **Price **

- Price skimming | > |---|---| > | **Promotion **

- Window display
- Local newspaper advertising | **Place **

- A retail shop on the main street
- Postal sales from a brochure | Calculate the **difference **between the labour turnover of the specialist marketing workers and the labour turnover of the administrative support workers.
parts.solutionMd:
**7.5% ****[4]**

Labour turnover formula:

$\frac{\text{Number of workers who left}}{\text{Average number of workers}} \times 100$  **[1]**

Specialist marketing workers:

`\frac{2}{40} \times 100 = 5\%`   **[1]**

Administrative support workers:

`\frac{11}{88} \times 100 = 12.5\%`   **[1]**

Difference:

12.5% - 5% = 7.5%** **  **[1]**

Cash4Trash (C4T) C4T is located in the capital city of country A in Africa. This private limited company was started six years ago by Andy and Kris, who both had experience working for a large international charity. C4T is a social enterprise, initially financed by international charities and a grant from the government of country A. The government also provided land to C4T for its factory. C4T’s corporate objectives include two social objectives which are to: • improve the environment of the city • provide jobs for the unemployed. C4T collects and cleans all types of recyclable materials that have been discarded as trash (rubbish). The clean materials are then used to create products for sale, such as bags made from woven plastic. A local artist volunteers her services to help with product designs. C4T has grown and now manufactures a range of products from recycled materials, including bags and jewellery. Cases for laptops and smartphones are currently its most popular products. Products are sold to local people and tourists in its shop next to the factory. C4T also sells via its website. C4T employs 90 people in its factory, who were previously unemployed. It runs training courses for 16 to 18 year olds to teach them basic skills. All profit is re-invested to expand and improve the business. C4T has won awards for being a sustainable social enterprise. Operations problems Factory employees work in teams and are rewarded with bonus payments if they exceed targets. Each team collects materials and other resources needed for production from a central store. However, sometimes this store runs out of resources, halting production. Products are checked for quality at the end of the production process and many are rejected and faults have to be corrected. Employees have been trained to specialise in one task within one team. Andy and Kris feel that time and resources are being wasted and would like to reorganise the factory and improve employee flexibility. Marketing Marketing products made from recycled materials can be a major challenge in country A. Many consumers think these products are of inferior quality. However, C4T’s brand image is strong. Its products have featured in premium magazines and on websites aimed at consumers who are ‘socially responsible’. Kris works hard to keep the C4T website up-to-date and maintain its social media presence, as part of the company’s attempt to establish good customer relationships. An ambitious new idea Plastic water bottles have become a real environmental problem over recent years as more are bought and thrown away when empty. Kris is planning to introduce a new type of product. He thinks there is a market for durable, reusable plastic drinking bottles. These will be made from recycled plastic and marketed as souvenirs for tourists. Demand will be highest during holiday periods. They will be produced in a range of colours, with country A’s name and flag on them. A new C4T slogan ‘Protecting the environment’ will be printed on each bottle. A factory extension will be required to recycle the plastic materials to be used and to manufacture the bottles. Kris is planning to recruit the new employees required on part-time flexible contracts. C4T’s objective for the bottles would be to make a profit, so labour costs will need to be kept low. The recruitment of skilled employees able to achieve high productivity levels will be important.

Finance The factory extension will cost \$1.5m to build and equip with machinery. The government of country A will provide a grant of \$1m. Andy and Kris are hoping to raise the remaining \$0.5m from a bank loan. However, a local venture capitalist has offered to invest \$0.5m in return for 30% of the profit from the new product and substantial involvement in future decision making. It is one of the fastest growing economies in Africa. The government is stable and incomes are rising, especially in the cities. Unemployment is falling which has led to some worries about increasing inflation which means the central bank may raise interest rates.

Further options for growth In addition to the reusable bottles, Andy and Kris are looking for other growth opportunities for C4T. Evaluate the importance of workforce planning to C4T’s future success.
parts.solutionMd:
Workforce planning involves identifying the number of employees needed, the skills required, and the most appropriate contract types **[K]**. For C4T, this is important given current operational problems - employees specialise in one task and lack flexibility **[Ap]**, meaning production cannot easily be reorganised when needed, as the special order for 5,000 laptop cases demonstrates **[Ap] [An]**. The new factory extension for reusable bottles will need employees capable of high productivity on part-time flexible contracts to manage seasonal demand peaks **[An]**. Without careful planning to determine the right staffing mix, C4T risks being over- or under-staffed at different times of year, increasing costs or leading to unmet orders and undermining the profitability objective for the new product **[An]**

Workforce planning is also essential for C4T's longer-term growth. Option 1 requires experience of high-volume mass production; Option 2 demands specialist design and quality skills for luxury goods **[K]**. Both require recruiting and training the right employees well in advance. Since C4T reinvests all profit rather than holding large cash reserves **[Ap]**, unplanned recruitment or training costs could strain its finances and delay implementation at a critical point in the business's growth **[An]**

Overall, workforce planning is essential, but must be designed around C4T's dual objectives **[E]**. A purely productivity-focused plan could conflict with the social mission to employ as many previously unemployed people as possible **[Ap]**. The most effective plan balances commercial efficiency with C4T's social commitments. Without any workforce planning, C4T is unlikely to manage its growing complexity across multiple new products and potential overseas expansion, making it a critical priority for Andy and Kris **[E]**

parts.solutionMd:
A person specification sets out the skills, qualifications, and personal qualities required for a role, helping the employer attract suitable candidates and assess applicants consistently **[K]**. Some elements of Lewis's specification are appropriate. Requiring a hairdressing qualification is sensible, as the new employee must work independently and deliver a professional service to BR's loyal long-term customers **[Ap]**. Including good communication skills is also reasonable, since the role involves taking bookings, dealing with customers, and handling financial transactions without Lewis being present **[An]**

The misclassification of criteria is also a significant problem - listing "no experience required" as essential and customer service experience as merely desirable is contradictory **[Ap]**. Since Lewis needs someone who can work completely alone from day one, prior customer-facing experience should be essential. Listing "ability to work in a team" as an essential quality makes no sense when the employee will be working independently, and this could confuse or deter suitable applicants **[An]**

The discriminatory criteria could expose him to legal action, and the misaligned essential and desirable criteria mean he is likely to attract unsuitable applicants while missing the experienced, self-sufficient candidate the role actually requires **[Ap] [An]**.Since BR is a small business that relies heavily on loyal repeat customers, hiring the wrong person could cause serious damage. ‘Limited investment in employee training and development in a primary sector business will lead to poor business performance.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Employee training and development refers to activities that improve workers' skills and knowledge so they can carry out their roles more effectively. A primary sector business extracts or harvests natural resources, including farming, mining, forestry, fishing, and quarrying **[K]**. The question is whether limited training investment in these businesses will necessarily lead to poor performance There is a strong case for agreeing with this view. Primary sector businesses are increasingly dependent on specialist skills and technology **[K]**. Modern farming uses GPS-guided machinery and precision agriculture techniques; mining requires the operation of complex automated equipment and strict adherence to safety and environmental regulations **[Ap]**. Workers who are not trained to use this equipment effectively will be less efficient, make more errors, and waste resources, directly reducing productivity and increasing costs **[An]**. There is also a well-established link between training investment and employee motivation **[K]**. Workers who receive little development are more likely to feel undervalued, increasing labour turnover. Since the cost of recruiting and retraining replacements is generally higher than retaining and developing existing staff, limited training investment can create a damaging cycle of higher costs and declining performance **[An]** However, the impact depends on the nature of the business **[K]**. Some primary sector operations - particularly labour-intensive, lower-technology activities - may not require formal training programmes for most workers. A small-scale farm may perform adequately because the skills needed are traditional and passed on informally through experience **[Ap]**. In such cases, external factors like weather, commodity prices, and access to equipment are likely to have a far greater impact on performance than training investment **[E]**. Businesses can also recruit already-skilled workers from the labour market, reducing the need to fund training internally while still maintaining output quality **[An]** Overall, the statement is broadly correct **[E]**. In modern, technology-dependent primary sector businesses, such as large-scale commercial mining or precision agriculture, limited training is very likely to lead to poor performance, as skilled, adaptable workers are essential for efficiency, safety, and quality **[An]**. However, in simpler, lower-technology operations, the link is weaker and other factors matter more **[E]**. parts.problemMd:
‘Human Resource Management is the most important department in any large manufacturing business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Human Resource Management (HRM) is the department responsible for planning, recruiting, developing, and retaining a business's workforce **[K]**. In a large manufacturing business, the quality and efficiency of output depends heavily on having skilled, motivated employees in every area **[K]**, giving HRM a strong claim to being the most important department **[E]** The case for HRM being most important rests on its unique cross-departmental role **[K]**. Unlike other departments that focus on a specific function, HRM supports every other department by ensuring each has the right people with the right skills. In a large manufacturer, this includes production line workers, quality control engineers, procurement specialists, and senior managers **[Ap]**. If any of these roles are filled poorly, the consequences spread across the whole business. Poorly recruited or undertrained production workers will make more errors, waste more materials, and work more slowly, reducing output and damaging the business's reputation for quality **[An]** HRM also manages ongoing training **[K]** to ensure employees keep pace with evolving manufacturing technology, maintaining productivity over time **[Ap]**. High labour turnover is particularly costly in manufacturing, where technical experience matters greatly; effective HRM reduces turnover and preserves the operational knowledge that keeps production running efficiently **[An]** However, other departments make an equally strong case. The Operations department carries out the core purpose of the business - producing goods - and without efficient production processes, skilled recruitment alone will not generate revenue **[Ap] [An]**. Finance ensures the business has working capital to pay wages, buy raw materials, and invest in equipment; without it, the business may fail regardless of the quality of its workforce **[An]**. Marketing identifies customer needs and drives sales, generating the revenue that funds everything else. In practice, all departments depend on each other: HRM cannot recruit without Finance's budget; Production cannot operate without the workers HRM provides; and Marketing cannot sell goods that Production has not made **[An]** Overall, while HRM is undeniably important, it is an overstatement to call it the most important department in all large manufacturers **[E]**. Its unique value lies in underpinning every other department - no function can operate well without the right people - but this influence is indirect. HRM does not produce goods, generate sales, or manage cash flow **[Ap]**. Its relative importance also depends on the context: in a highly labour-intensive manufacturer where skilled workers are scarce, HRM may be the critical limiting factor **[E]**; in a heavily automated factory, production technology and engineering may matter more **[Ap] [E]**. > **[case-study]**
> **Quality Furniture (QF) **
> 
> QF is a public limited company in country S. It manufactures furniture for cafés. The number of cafés in country S has increased by more than 50% over the last 5 years. This has meant that QF has been able to expand and achieve internal economies of scale. However, the growth of the café market has attracted new firms supplying café furniture and increased competition for QF.
> 
> An extract from QF’s income statement is shown in Table 1.1.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Extract from QF’s income statement for 2020**
> 
> |   | \$m |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue | 300 |
> | Cost of sales | 120 |
> | Gross profit | 180 |
> | Expenses | 150 |
> 
> Although QF has been successful so far, Javid, the Managing Director, has identified two problem areas: inventory and human resources.
> 
> **Inventory **
> 
> QF’s inventory includes raw materials, work in progress and finished tables and chairs. QF buys 80% of its materials from country T and there is a long delivery lead time. This means that QF holds a high level of buffer inventory which has a high value.
> 
> **Human resources **
> 
> QF’s production employees are unhappy that they have not received any benefit from the company’s expansion. Profit has doubled over the past three years but employees have not received any pay increases or bonuses. The employees have all been trained by QF and have specialist skills which had ensured that customer expectations were met. However, customers are starting to complain about a fall in the quality of the furniture, which could be the result of the low morale of the employees. Some highly trained employees have left QF to work for competitor firms.

Recommend how QF’s management could improve the morale of its production employees. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
The most effective way to improve morale at QF is to introduce financial rewards that reflect the company's success **[K]**. Employees have received no pay increases or bonuses despite profits doubling over three years **[Ap]** - this is the root cause of the morale problem and must be addressed directly. A profit-sharing scheme or annual bonus linked to company performance would signal that employees share in QF's success, reducing the sense of unfairness that is driving low morale and the departure of skilled staff to competitors **[An]**. Since QF is a public limited company, it could also offer employees shares in the business, giving them a direct stake in its profitability. Employees who own shares are more motivated to maintain quality and keep customers satisfied, because poor performance would affect the value of their own investment. This could help reverse the fall in furniture quality that is currently generating customer complaints **[Ap] [An]**

QF could also support this with non-financial measures, particularly greater employee involvement in decision-making **[K]**. QF's production workers are highly trained and experienced **[Ap]**, so involving them in discussions about quality standards or production improvements would make them feel valued and respected **[An]**. However, since the core grievance is clearly financial - employees have seen no benefit from doubled profits - non-financial methods alone are unlikely to be sufficient **[E]**

Overall, QF should prioritise financial rewards, specifically a profit-sharing bonus or share ownership scheme **[E]**. These directly address the cause of low morale rather than working around it. The cost is likely to be justified by the benefits: retaining skilled workers whose departure is expensive to replace, improving product quality, and recovering customer satisfaction **[An]**. Competitors are already attracting QF's trained staff **[Ap]**, so acting quickly is important - a pay increase or bonus alone may be the fastest and simplest first step, with share ownership considered as a longer-term motivational strategy **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
‘The most important role of human resource management (HRM) in a fast food restaurant is to maintain a high level of employee morale and welfare.’

Evaluate this view.
parts.solutionMd:
HRM covers activities including recruitment, training, workforce planning, and managing employee morale and welfare **[K]**. In a fast food restaurant, morale is particularly important because employees interact directly with customers **[Ap] **- staff who are disengaged or unhappy will deliver poor service, reducing repeat business. The fast food industry also has traditionally high labour turnover **[Ap]**, so if HRM successfully improves morale and welfare, employees are more likely to stay, reducing the cost of constant recruitment and retraining **[An]**

However, other HRM responsibilities may be more fundamental. Without effective recruitment **[K]**, employees may not be suited to the fast-paced, process-driven demands of fast food work. Training **[K]** is equally critical - staff must follow strict hygiene and food safety procedures **[Ap]**, and poor training can result in safety risks and reputational damage regardless of how high morale might be **[An]**. Workforce planning is also essential: too few staff at peak times leads to slow service and complaints, while overstaffing during quiet periods inflates costs in a business where profit margins are already tight **[An]**

Overall, morale and welfare are important but not the single most important HRM role in a fast food restaurant **[E]**. Good recruitment, training, and workforce planning must be in place first - without them, morale efforts cannot deliver results. However, given the fast-food industry's reputation for high turnover and low job satisfaction, investing in employee wellbeing can provide a meaningful advantage by retaining experienced staff and cutting recruitment costs **[An]** **[E]**. The relative importance of morale will also depend on the stage of the business - a newly opened restaurant may need to prioritise recruitment and training, while an established one may find that morale is the most effective lever for further improving performance **[Ap]** **[E]**

The fast food industry has traditionally high labour turnover, so improving morale and welfare can help retain staff, reducing the significant cost of continually recruiting and training new employees
> - Training is a core HRM responsibility and is especially important in a fast food restaurant where employees must follow strict hygiene, food safety, and operational procedures. Without effective training, staff are more likely to make mistakes that risk customer safety, damage the restaurant's reputation, or result in regulatory penalties. Even highly motivated employees cannot perform well without the skills and knowledge to do their jobs correctly, meaning training may be a more fundamental HRM priority than morale and welfare alone
> - Recruitment and selection are critical HRM functions because hiring employees who are well-suited to the work reduces the likelihood of poor performance and high turnover. In a fast food environment, employees need to work efficiently under pressure, follow consistent processes, and communicate well with customers. > - Workforce planning - ensuring the right number of employees are available at the right times - is essential in a fast food restaurant where demand fluctuates significantly across the day and week. Too few staff at peak times leads to slow service and dissatisfied customers; too many staff during quiet periods inflates labour costs in a low-margin business. Pop Cool (PC) PC is a public limited company. Its head office is in Europe and it operates with centralised decision making. The company owns the Pop Cool brand name, logo and the distinctive bottle shape that is still used in some markets. PC operates its own bottling and canning factories in some countries. However, it also has joint venture agreements with packaging businesses in other countries. Much of the fruit and sugar used in producing the soft drinks is imported from African and Asian countries. 75% of PC’s sales and 90% of its profits are earned in the USA and Europe. The directors of PC are keen to develop other markets and other products so that the company becomes less dependent on a few key markets and products. Economic changes The economies of the USA and Europe have experienced very slow economic growth since 2008 – and some have even been hit by recession. Interest rates are very low as the monetary policy of these countries is aiming to boost demand. However, this has contributed to exchange rate depreciations of the US dollar and the European euro. Consumer spending has fallen due to declining real incomes. There are ageing populations in most of the countries where PC sells its products. A loss of competitiveness in many industrial sectors has resulted in rising unemployment. Statement of financial position valuations Since 2008 PC’s share price has fallen. This has been the trend for many public limited companies. PC’s Finance Director has been considering three changes that will affect PC’s accounts. He could make all three changes or just one or two of them. • When calculating depreciation of new production equipment bought last year for \$25m, use an estimated life of 8 years not 5 years. The equipment would still have an estimated residual value of \$3m. • Sell \$10m of property assets and lease them back at an annual leasing cost of \$1.5m. • Revalue the company’s intangible assets by 50%. He used an extract of PC’s most recent accounts to calculate what the impact of these changes might be on profit and gearing (see Appendix 1). Entering new markets – Africa and Asia Paul, PC’s Chief Executive Officer (CEO), has been discussing with the Marketing Director, Suzy, alternative marketing strategies the company could use to enter the rapidly expanding markets of Asia and Africa. They have different views. Paul stated that: ‘I think we should take over an existing soft drinks manufacturer in, for example, India or China. We would then have all of the production facilities and distribution channels through large supermarkets that we will need. The existing brand names could then be replaced with the Pop Cool brand which we would advertise very heavily for a short period. Consumers will be attracted to this because it is so popular elsewhere in the world.’ Suzy replied: ‘There could be local opposition to this globalised approach – although the marketing economies of scale will be substantial. The Human Resources department is under pressure from PC’s Head Office to reduce labour costs in country X by 15%. The Human Resources manager in country X, Bill, thinks that cutting labour costs might be risky. He told other senior managers: ‘We must maintain consistent and adequate production levels so that consumers can always buy the quantity they want. Production workers are sometimes reluctant to learn new skills and they are resistant to job flexibility. Should we cut back on sales and marketing staff? Perhaps we should employ more production workers on flexible contracts. Another option is to introduce even more automation at our main packaging plant.’ The other managers agreed with him that meeting this new company objective of reducing labour costs was going to need careful workforce planning. Future options for PC’s growth PC’s Board of Directors has been criticised by the newspapers and by major shareholders for the company’s slow rate of growth in sales and profits since 2008. Evaluate the factors that the Human Resources manager should consider before completing the workforce plan for PC’s operations in country X.
parts.solutionMd:
Workforce planning means ensuring PC has the right number of workers with the right skills to meet its business objectives **[K]**. Bill, the HR manager in country X, must consider several important factors before finalising the plan

One key factor is the 15% labour cost reduction set by Head Office. PC employs 468 people in country X and labour is its biggest expense there **[Ap]**, so this target represents a large cut. Bill could achieve it by reducing headcount, moving more workers onto flexible contracts, or introducing multi-skilling so fewer specialist staff are needed **[K] [An]**. However, production workers have already shown resistance to learning new skills and to flexible working **[Ap]**. If Bill forces these changes, workers may take industrial action or leave the company, which could increase costs rather than reduce them. This means the workforce plan must carefully assess which approach is most likely to achieve the target without causing disruption **[An]**

A second important factor is the need to maintain consistent production **[K]**. PC already produces 45 million cans per year in country X, which is close to its 50 million capacity limit **[Ap]**. Cutting production staff to save costs could cause output to fall short of demand, leading to stock shortages and damaging PC's reputation in one of its most important markets **[An]**. Any reduction in staffing must therefore be planned so that enough workers remain to meet consumer demand reliably **[E]**

Overall, automation is likely the most important factor in the workforce plan **[E]**. It permanently reduces the need for production workers - lowering labour costs without depending on reluctant workers to multi-skill - while also maintaining output levels **[E]**. Although the upfront investment is high, it offers a long-term solution that protects both the cost target and production capacity **[Ap]**. Bill should recommend phasing in automation gradually while using natural wastage and flexible contracts for new hires, rather than making immediate large-scale redundancies that could harm morale and disrupt production in the short term **[An] [E]**

> 
> Ravi founded RS in country J eight years ago. The business designs and sells sportswear and running shoes. RS employs 25 full-time staff and sells its products through its own website and a small number of selected sports retailers across country J.
> 
> Ravi has recently launched a new range of women's sportswear, targeting the growing women's fitness market in country J. He has invested heavily in digital promotion and influencer partnerships to promote the new range, which has led to high marketing expenditure in the first quarter of 2024.
> 
> RS currently uses on-the-job training to develop all new employees. Ravi is considering whether to switch to off-the-job training, which would be more expensive in the short term but would develop employees' skills more systematically.
>
