Evaluate whether RS should introduce off-the-job training rather than continuing to use on-the-job training for new employees.
parts.solutionMd:
On-the-job training means employees learn while doing their normal work, supervised by an experienced colleague. Off-the-job training means employees attend external courses or workshops away from the workplace **[K]**

One reason RS should switch to off-the-job training is that it develops skills to a higher standard **[K]**. RS operates in specialist areas such as digital marketing and product design, where external trainers have more current knowledge than internal supervisors **[Ap]**. RS has recently invested heavily in influencer partnerships and digital promotion for its women's range **[Ap]**, so employees with formally trained digital marketing skills could manage these campaigns more effectively, potentially increasing sales revenue **[An]**. Off-the-job training also reduces the risk of employees learning bad habits from colleagues, helping to maintain consistent standards across the team **[An]**

However, RS is already under significant cash flow pressure. In January 2024, net cash flow is −\$4,000 and in February it is −\$7,000, mainly due to the \$15,000 marketing spend on the new range **[Ap]**. Paying external training fees and losing the productivity of employees **[K]** while they are away from their roles would make this pressure worse. With only 25 staff, RS cannot easily cover the absence of employees during training without affecting day-to-day service and operations at an already demanding time **[An]**

Overall, a full switch to off-the-job training is not the right decision for RS right now **[E]**. While the long-term benefits are clear, especially for specialist roles in digital marketing and product design **[Ap]**, the short-term cost is too high given the current negative cash flow. Ravi should continue with on-the-job training for most roles in the short term, but introduce targeted off-the-job training for key specialist employees from March 2024 onwards, when net cash flow turns positive at +\$10,000 **[Ap]** and the business is in a stronger financial position to absorb the cost **[E]**

> 
> - On-the-job training: employees learn skills while doing their normal work, supervised by an experienced colleague; e.g. coaching, mentoring, job shadowing
> - Off-the-job training: employees receive training away from the workplace through external providers; e.g. formal courses, workshops, professional qualifications

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'hard HRM'.
parts.solutionMd:
Hard HRM is an approach that treats employees as a resource to be used as efficiently as possible **[1]**, hiring, deploying and releasing them according to what the business needs at the time **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An approach viewing employees as a cost to be controlled and a resource to be deployed wherever the business needs them
> - HRM focused on efficiency, with staffing levels adjusted to demand and decisions taken with little consultation
> - Managing people primarily to meet the organisation's needs, using short-term contracts and close control rather than long-term development

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "hard" describes how employees are viewed, not how the manager behaves. A hard HRM approach treats staff as a resource to be used efficiently. Answers describing a manager who is strict or unkind miss the point, because the term is about the underlying view of labour, not about personality.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'zero hours contract'.
parts.solutionMd:
A zero hours contract is an employment contract that does not guarantee the employee any set number of hours **[1]**, so the business offers work only when it is needed and the employee is paid only for hours actually worked **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A contract under which an employer is not obliged to provide any minimum hours of work
> - An arrangement where hours vary according to demand and the employee is paid only for the hours worked
> - A flexible contract giving the business the right to call on an employee as required, without committing to regular hours

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a contract term, say what is guaranteed and what is not. Here nothing is guaranteed: no minimum hours, and pay only for hours actually worked. Definitions describing the contract as "flexible" capture the effect but not the substance, so state the absence of guaranteed hours explicitly.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'Management by Objectives'.
parts.solutionMd:
Management by Objectives is a system in which managers and employees agree individual objectives that support the objectives of the business **[1]**, and performance is then reviewed against those agreed objectives **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A process in which each employee's targets are agreed with their manager and aligned with the organisation's overall objectives
> - A system of setting individual objectives derived from company objectives, with progress reviewed at regular intervals
> - An approach where employees are managed and appraised according to whether they achieve objectives agreed in advance

> **[exam-tip]**
> Named systems have a defining mechanism, and for MBO it is that objectives are agreed between manager and employee rather than simply imposed, then used to review performance. Naming who sets the objectives and what happens afterwards is what distinguishes MBO from ordinary target setting.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'labour productivity'.
parts.solutionMd:
Labour productivity is a measure of output per worker over a period of time **[1]**, calculated by dividing total output by the number of employees **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Output per employee in a given period, found by dividing total output by the number of workers
> - A measure of how much each worker produces, used to compare performance over time or between businesses
> - The quantity of goods or services produced per unit of labour employed

> **[exam-tip]**
> Where a term is a ratio, say what is divided by what. Labour productivity is output divided by the number of workers. Giving the formula as well as the meaning is the surest way to earn both marks, and it takes only a few extra words.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'flexi-time'.
parts.solutionMd:
Flexi-time is an arrangement allowing employees to choose when they start and finish work **[1]**, provided they work an agreed total number of hours and are present during any core hours the business sets **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A working arrangement letting employees vary their start and finish times within limits set by the employer
> - A system where the total hours worked are fixed but the timing is partly chosen by the employee
> - An arrangement combining employee choice over hours with a requirement to be present at agreed core times

> **[exam-tip]**
> With arrangement terms, say what varies and what stays fixed. Under flexi-time the timing varies but the total hours do not. Answers stating only that employees "choose their hours" suggest they can also choose how many, which is a different arrangement altogether.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Eastvale (EV)**
> 
> Eastvale (EV) operates a warehouse in country S, packing and dispatching online orders. It employs 480 staff, of whom 310 are on temporary contracts.
> 
> Staff are set an individual target of 140 items packed per hour. A screen above each packing station shows how each worker is performing against that target.
> 
> **Table 1.1: EV selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 480 |
> |---|---|
> | Staff on temporary contracts | 310 |
> | Target items packed per hour | 140 |
> | Average items packed per hour | 112 |
> | Orders returned because of packing errors (%) | 6 |
> | Staff leaving within their first three months (%) | 41 |
> 
> Temporary staff receive one morning of training before starting work.

Explain **one** cause of poor employee performance at EV.
parts.solutionMd:
One cause is that EV's staff receive very little training **[1]**. Temporary workers, who make up 310 of EV's 480 employees, are given only one morning of training before they begin packing **[1]**. Someone who has not been properly shown how to pack different items will be both slower and more likely to make mistakes, which helps explain why average output is 112 items an hour against a target of 140, and why 6% of orders come back because of packing errors **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Poor performance can be caused by inadequate training, unclear or unrealistic targets, weak motivation, poor working conditions, unsuitable equipment, or ineffective management
> 
> AO2
> 
> - One morning of training for temporary staff who make up nearly two thirds of the workforce leaves most employees learning the job while doing it
> - A target of 140 items an hour against an average of 112 may be unrealistic, and a target nobody reaches tends to discourage rather than motivate
> - Displaying each worker's performance on a screen above their station may raise pressure and errors rather than output, which fits the 6% return rate
> - With 41% of staff leaving within three months, EV constantly has inexperienced people packing, so average performance stays low however many are recruited
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Take care to name the cause rather than the symptom. Low output and packing errors are what poor performance looks like; the cause is what produced them, such as inadequate training. Examiners want the step behind the problem, so ask yourself why the figures are as they are before you start writing.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Larkspur (LS)**
> 
> Larkspur (LS) operates 46 travel agency branches in country W, employing 390 consultants who sell holidays to walk-in customers.
> 
> Consultants are paid a fixed salary. Their performance is reviewed once a year in a meeting with a branch manager, and no targets are set between reviews.
> 
> **Table 1.1: LS selected data**
> 
> | Branches | 46 |
> |---|---|
> | Consultants | 390 |
> | Average sales per consultant per week (\$) | 4,100 |
> | Sales per consultant in the best-performing branch (\$) | 7,300 |
> | Consultants saying their annual review was useful (%) | 19 |
> 
> LS's HR director has proposed introducing quarterly objectives agreed between each consultant and their manager.

Explain **one** way LS's proposal could improve employee performance.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is that quarterly objectives would give consultants something specific to work towards **[1]**. At present LS sets no targets between annual reviews, and only 19% of consultants find those reviews useful **[1]**. Agreeing objectives every three months means a consultant knows what is expected while there is still time to act on it, so someone selling well below the \$7,300 a week achieved in the best branch could be helped to improve during the year rather than being told about it twelve months later **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Performance can be improved through target setting, training, financial and non-financial incentives, better management, job redesign, or more frequent feedback
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Quarterly objectives replace a single annual conversation, so problems are identified while there is still time to address them
> - Only 19% of consultants find the annual review useful, so more frequent and specific discussion is likely to be taken more seriously
> - The gap between \$4,100 average weekly sales and \$7,300 in the best branch suggests substantial room to improve, and objectives make that gap visible to each consultant
> - Objectives agreed rather than imposed tend to gain more commitment, since a consultant who has helped set a target is more likely to accept it as fair
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A strategy earns marks when you show how it changes what people actually do. Setting objectives works because employees then know what to aim at and get feedback in time to act. Answers that name a strategy and assert it will "motivate staff" stop short of the mechanism, and usually stop short of the third mark too.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way information technology is used in human resource management.
parts.solutionMd:
One way IT is used in HRM is to manage recruitment **[1]**. Software can advertise a vacancy on several websites at once, collect applications in one place, and filter out candidates who do not meet the essential requirements **[1]**. This saves the HR department a great deal of time on early sorting, so staff can spend it interviewing the strongest applicants and the business fills the vacancy more quickly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - IT is used in HRM for recruitment, record keeping, payroll, monitoring performance, delivering training, and planning future workforce needs
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Recruitment software advertises vacancies widely, gathers applications centrally and filters unsuitable candidates, saving HR staff time on early sorting
> - Digital personnel records let managers find information on qualifications, absence and training instantly rather than searching paper files
> - Online training modules can be completed at a time that suits each employee, so training does not require everyone to leave work at once
> - Workforce planning software can identify how many employees will retire in coming years, letting HR recruit and train replacements in advance
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Questions about technology in a business function reward naming the task, not the technology. Saying a business "uses computers" explains nothing; saying it uses software to filter job applications identifies the work being done. Start with the HR task, then say what the technology does to it.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** benefit to a business of using artificial intelligence in human resource management.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit is that AI can sort large numbers of job applications quickly **[1]**. A business advertising a popular vacancy may receive hundreds of applications, and AI can rank them against the requirements far faster than a person could read them **[1]**. This shortens the time between advertising and interviewing, which matters because strong candidates often accept another offer while a slower employer is still reading applications **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - AI can be used in HRM to screen applications, analyse patterns in absence or turnover, personalise training, schedule shifts, and answer routine employee queries
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Screening large volumes of applications quickly shortens the gap between advertising and interviewing, helping a business secure candidates before competitors do
> - Analysing absence and turnover data can reveal patterns a manager would not notice, such as one shift or department losing staff faster than others
> - Automated systems can answer routine questions about holiday entitlement or pay, freeing HR staff for work needing judgement
> - AI-based scheduling can match staffing to expected demand more precisely, reducing both overstaffing and gaps in cover
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Be careful not to overclaim for new technology. AI is good at handling volume and spotting patterns; it does not replace judgement, and screening tools can repeat bias present in past decisions. An answer showing awareness of what the technology actually does, rather than treating it as a solution to everything, reads as far more credible.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Fernbank (FB)**
> 
> Fernbank (FB) provides IT support to small businesses in country C. It employs 85 technicians who visit customers or resolve problems by telephone.
> 
> FB currently judges technician performance by the number of jobs each one closes per week.
> 
> **Table 1.1: FB selected data**
> 
> | Technicians | 85 |
> |---|---|
> | Average jobs closed per technician per week | 24 |
> | Jobs where the customer contacted FB again about the same problem within a week (%) | 19 |
> | Customer satisfaction score (out of 10) | 6.1 |
> 
> FB's operations manager thinks the current measure may be encouraging technicians to close jobs before problems are properly fixed.

Explain **one** other way FB could measure the performance of its technicians.
parts.solutionMd:
One way would be to measure how many problems are solved at the first visit **[1]**. FB currently counts jobs closed per week, but 19% of jobs bring the customer back within a week about the same problem, so a closed job does not necessarily mean a solved one **[1]**. Counting only jobs that stay solved would reward technicians for fixing a fault properly rather than quickly, which should also lift a customer satisfaction score currently standing at 6.1 out of 10 **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Employee performance can be measured through output, quality, error or rework rates, customer feedback, absence, punctuality, or achievement of agreed objectives
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Measuring first-time fixes rather than jobs closed captures whether a problem was actually solved, addressing the 19% of jobs that recur within a week
> - Customer satisfaction ratings for individual technicians would show which staff customers are happiest with, which a count of jobs cannot reveal
> - Time taken per job could be combined with the repeat rate, so speed is judged alongside whether the work lasted
> - Any single measure can be gamed, so FB would do better to combine two or three rather than replace one narrow measure with another
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When suggesting a measure, say what it would show and be alert to what it would miss. Counting jobs closed rewards speed; counting first-time fixes rewards doing the job properly. Recognising that a measure changes behaviour, not just records it, is what lifts an answer to the top of the mark range.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ashford (AF)**
> 
> Ashford (AF) assembles electronic control units for washing machines and ovens in country D. It employs 520 people and supplies four large appliance manufacturers.
> 
> AF's largest customer has warned that it will review the contract unless quality improves.
> 
> **Table 1.1: AF selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 520 |
> |---|---|
> | Units assembled per day | 9,400 |
> | Units failing final inspection (%) | 8 |
> | Units returned by customers after delivery (%) | 2.1 |
> | Cost of rework and replacement last year (\$000) | 780 |
> | Share of revenue from the largest customer (%) | 39 |
> 
> AF's production manager says the failures are concentrated among a group of assemblers who have not met the required standard for several months.

Analyse **two** consequences for AF of poor employee performance.
parts.solutionMd:

> **[case-study]**
> **Vinehall (VH)**
> 
> Vinehall (VH) provides catering for weddings, conferences and corporate events in country R. Demand is highly seasonal, with around 60% of its work falling between May and September.
> 
> VH employs 90 permanent staff and takes on up to 400 casual workers during the busy season. Casual staff are recruited afresh each year, given a two-hour briefing, and paid by the shift.
> 
> **Table 1.1: VH selected data**
> 
> | Permanent staff | 90 |
> |---|---|
> | Casual staff at peak | 400 |
> | Share of annual revenue earned May to September (%) | 60 |
> | Casual staff returning from the previous season (%) | 18 |
> | Events receiving a complaint about service (%) | 14 |
> | Cost of proposed training and guaranteed return contracts (\$000 per year) | 620 |
> 
> VH's operations director argues that better-trained returning staff would reduce complaints. VH's finance director argues that casual labour must stay cheap and flexible because demand collapses in winter.

Evaluate whether VH should adopt a softer approach to human resource management.
parts.solutionMd:
Soft HRM treats employees as an asset to be developed rather than a cost to be minimised **[K]**. Only 18% of VH's casual staff return from the previous season, so almost every one of the 400 peak workers is new each year and receives just a two-hour briefing **[Ap]**. Guaranteed return contracts and proper training would build a pool of staff who already know how VH runs an event, which should reduce the 14% of events attracting a complaint about service **[An]**

However, VH's demand is genuinely seasonal **[K]**. Sixty per cent of revenue is earned between May and September, so VH has little work for 400 people during the winter **[Ap]**. Committing \$620,000 a year to training and guaranteed contracts creates a fixed cost in a business whose income is anything but fixed, and in a poor season that commitment would have to be met from much reduced revenue **[An]**

Whether VH should soften its approach depends on how much the complaints are actually costing it **[E]**. Corporate and wedding customers choose caterers largely on reputation, so 14% of events producing a complaint is very likely losing VH future bookings, and that loss may well exceed \$620,000 even though it never appears as a line in the accounts **[E]**. The finance director is right that VH cannot carry 400 people through the winter, but a softer approach need not mean employing everyone permanently **[E]**. VH could offer guaranteed return contracts to a core of perhaps 100 experienced casuals while keeping the rest flexible, lifting the return rate well above 18% at a fraction of the full cost **[E]**. On balance VH should move some way towards soft HRM, but selectively rather than across the whole casual workforce **[E]**

> **[case-study]**
> **Kingsmere (KM)**
> 
> Kingsmere (KM) is an estate agency with 31 branches in country B, employing 280 negotiators who value homes and sell them.
> 
> Negotiators are currently judged only on the number of properties they sell each month, and a monthly bonus is paid to the top ten performers.
> 
> **Table 1.1: KM selected data**
> 
> | Branches | 31 |
> |---|---|
> | Negotiators | 280 |
> | Average properties sold per negotiator per month | 3.4 |
> | Properties valued above the eventual selling price (%) | 44 |
> | Sales that fell through before completion (%) | 27 |
> | Customer satisfaction score (out of 10) | 6.4 |
> 
> KM's HR director proposes judging negotiators on a combination of sales completed, valuation accuracy and customer satisfaction.

Evaluate whether KM should change how it measures the performance of its negotiators.
parts.solutionMd:
A single measure encourages employees to maximise that measure whatever else happens **[K]**. KM judges negotiators only on properties sold, and 44% of properties are valued above what they eventually sell for, while 27% of sales collapse before completion **[Ap]**. Over-valuing a house wins the instruction from the seller, which counts towards the sales figure, but it also makes the sale far harder to complete, so the present measure is rewarding behaviour that damages KM **[An]**

However, a combined measure is harder to operate **[K]**. Sales completed can be counted exactly, whereas valuation accuracy and a satisfaction score of 6.4 out of 10 depend on judgement and on customers choosing to respond **[Ap]**. Negotiators may distrust a bonus resting partly on measures they feel they cannot control, and a measure staff do not accept as fair tends to demotivate rather than direct **[An]**

KM should change the measure, because the present one is actively causing the problem it needs to solve **[E]**. A negotiator behaving exactly as KM rewards them to behave produces inflated valuations and collapsed sales, so the fault lies in the measure rather than in the staff **[E]**. The concern about fairness is real, but it argues for designing the new measure carefully rather than for keeping a broken one **[E]**. Weighting completed sales most heavily, with valuation accuracy and satisfaction as smaller components, would keep the measure understandable while removing the incentive to over-value **[E]**. KM should also expect the change to take time, since negotiators who have built their habits around a single target will not adjust the week the rules change **[E]**

> Thornbury (TB) supplies gas and electricity to homes in country W. It employs 4,000 people across a head office, three regional centres and a field engineering team.
> 
> TB's HR department keeps personnel records on paper at each location. Holiday requests, training records and absence data are held separately and are not shared between sites.

parts.solutionMd:
An integrated system would hold every employee record in one place **[K]**. TB currently keeps paper records separately at a head office, three regional centres and among a field team, and last year it could not locate the training records of 310 employees **[Ap]**. Missing training records matter enormously in an energy business, because TB may be unable to prove that an engineer working on gas equipment holds the qualifications the law requires, which exposes it to both danger and prosecution **[An]**

However, the system costs \$1.4m against an estimated saving of \$290,000 a year **[K]**. On those figures TB waits almost five years before the investment repays itself, and that assumes the saving is achieved in full **[Ap]**. Large system projects frequently overrun, and 34 HR staff across four locations would need training and time to change how they work, during which the saving would be smaller than forecast **[An]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why emotional intelligence is an important quality of an effective business leader.
parts.solutionMd:
Emotional intelligence is the ability to understand and manage your own emotions and to recognise and respond appropriately to the emotions of others **[1]**. This is an important quality for a business leader because a leader who understands how employees are feeling is better placed to motivate them effectively **[1]**. For example, a leader with high emotional intelligence will notice when a team member is struggling and offer support, rather than simply applying pressure, making it more likely that employees remain engaged and productive, which helps the business to achieve its objectives **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise and manage your own emotions, and to understand and respond appropriately to the emotions of others
> - EI involves competencies identified by Goleman, including self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and social skills
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A leader with high EI is better able to understand how employees are feeling and respond in a way that motivates them, making it more likely that employees will work productively towards the business's goals
> - Leaders who rely on intellectual ability (IQ) alone, without emotional intelligence, may struggle to inspire or connect with their teams; EI allows a leader to build trust and empower employees, which is essential for long-term business effectiveness
> - A leader with strong social awareness can manage conflicts within a team more effectively, reducing disruption and helping the business to maintain focus on its objectives
> - Self-management - a key component of EI - allows a leader to remain calm and make clear decisions under pressure, rather than reacting emotionally in ways that could damage team morale
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'trait theory'.
parts.solutionMd:
Trait theory is the idea that leaders possess particular personal characteristics that others do not **[1]**, so leadership depends on the qualities a person is born with rather than on what they learn **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The view that effective leaders share identifiable personal qualities, such as confidence, intelligence or determination
> - A theory holding that leadership ability comes from inherent characteristics rather than from training or circumstance
> - The belief that leaders are born rather than made, and can be identified by the traits they possess

> **[exam-tip]**
> A theory definition should say what the theory claims, not simply what it is about. Trait theory claims that leaders have particular inborn qualities. An answer stating only that the theory "is about the qualities of leaders" describes the subject matter without committing to the argument, and the second mark rests on that argument.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Wrenfield (WF)**
> 
> Wrenfield (WF) publishes school textbooks in country M and employs 140 people.
> 
> WF's editorial team of 45 works on long projects, often taking two years to develop a textbook. Editors are highly qualified and expect to make their own decisions about content.
> 
> WF's production department of 30 works to fixed printing dates. If a file misses its slot at the printer, the whole print run is delayed by up to six weeks.
> 
> WF's new managing director previously ran a factory and intends to apply the same close, directive management style to both departments.

Explain **one** implication of contingency theory for WF's new managing director.
parts.solutionMd:
One implication is that the same leadership style is unlikely to suit both of WF's departments **[1]**. Contingency theory holds that the most effective style depends on the situation, and WF's 45 editors are highly qualified people working on two-year projects who expect to decide content themselves **[1]**. A close, directive style borrowed from a factory would probably frustrate them and could drive experienced editors away, whereas that same style may work well in production, where fixed printing dates leave little room for discussion **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Contingency theory holds that no single leadership style is best, and that the most effective approach depends on the task, the people and the circumstances
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Editors are highly qualified, work on long projects and expect autonomy, so a directive style is likely to demotivate them and may prompt resignations
> - Production works to fixed printer slots where a missed deadline delays a whole run by six weeks, so clear direction and close control suit that situation far better
> - The managing director's factory experience is not irrelevant, but it fits one of WF's two departments rather than both
> - Contingency theory suggests he should vary his approach between departments rather than applying a single style across all 140 employees
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Contingency theory is the theory that says "it depends", so an answer scoring well must say what it depends on. Here it depends on the qualifications of the staff and the nature of the deadline. Naming the factors is what turns a general statement about flexibility into a developed point.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'behavioural theory' of leadership.
parts.solutionMd:
Behavioural theory is the idea that effective leadership comes from how a leader acts rather than from who they are **[1]**, which means leadership can be learned through training **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The view that leadership is determined by what leaders do, so the behaviours of effective leaders can be identified and taught
> - A theory holding that leaders are made rather than born, since leadership consists of learnable actions
> - An approach focusing on a leader's observable conduct towards their team rather than on their personal characteristics

> **[exam-tip]**
> Trait theory and behavioural theory disagree about where leadership comes from: inborn qualities in one, learned actions in the other. Making that location explicit, and drawing the consequence that behaviour can be trained, is what separates a definition from a vague gesture at the topic.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'transformational leadership'.
parts.solutionMd:
Transformational leadership is an approach in which a leader inspires employees to commit to a shared vision of change **[1]**, encouraging them to perform beyond what their job normally requires **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Leadership that motivates employees to embrace change by setting out a compelling vision of what the business could become
> - An approach in which the leader raises the commitment and capability of followers rather than simply directing their work
> - Leadership aimed at changing how employees think about their work, so they contribute more than their role strictly demands

> **[exam-tip]**
> The prefix tells you what to include: transformational leadership is about transforming something. Say what is transformed, which is the commitment and outlook of employees, and what it is transformed towards, which is a shared vision. A definition mentioning only that the leader is inspiring leaves the second mark unearned.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ashwell (AW)**
> 
> Ashwell (AW) runs nine leisure centres in country J, employing 620 staff including swimming instructors, lifeguards, fitness coaches and reception teams.
> 
> Priya manages AW's largest centre. In a normal week she agrees the coming month's class timetable with her team, represents AW at a meeting of the local council's sports committee, and speaks to staff individually about their training and development.
> 
> Attendance at Priya's centre has risen 12% in a year, while attendance across AW's other eight centres has fallen slightly.

Explain **one** leadership role carried out by Priya.
parts.solutionMd:
One leadership role Priya carries out is developing her people **[1]**. She speaks to staff individually about their training and development, which a manager concerned only with running the timetable would not do **[1]**. Instructors and coaches who feel their development matters are more likely to stay and to put effort into their classes, which helps explain why attendance at Priya's centre has risen 12% while it has fallen slightly across AW's other eight centres **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Leadership roles include setting direction, motivating and developing people, representing the organisation externally, allocating resources, and deciding on behalf of the team
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Speaking to staff individually about training and development shows Priya investing in her team's capability, not simply supervising their work
> - Agreeing the class timetable with her team rather than imposing it involves staff in a decision that affects them, which supports their commitment
> - Representing AW at the council's sports committee is an external role, protecting AW's standing with a body that influences local facilities
> - The 12% attendance rise at her centre against a fall elsewhere suggests these roles are producing measurable results
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A role is something a person does for or on behalf of others, so express it as an activity: developing staff, representing the business, setting direction. Answers describing personal qualities such as "she is approachable" name a trait rather than a role, and the question asked for the latter.

parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘emotional intelligence’.
parts.solutionMd:
The capacity to understand and control your own feelings **[1]**, and to recognise how the feelings of other people may affect their behaviour and performance at work **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The extent to which employees/managers are aware of and understand their own emotions/feelings and the feelings and emotions of others
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure your definition addresses both dimensions of emotional intelligence - awareness of your own emotions and awareness of others' emotions. A common mistake is to mention only one side, which limits you to 1 mark. If you can reference Goleman's competencies (e.g. self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management), this can also earn credit.

**[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** difference between trait theory and behavioural theory of leadership.
parts.solutionMd:
Trait theory holds that leaders possess particular personal qualities that other people lack, so leaders are essentially born **[1]**. Behavioural theory holds instead that leadership consists of things a leader does, which means it can be learned **[1]**. The difference matters to a business because it changes what the business should do: if trait theory is right it should concentrate on selecting the right people, whereas if behavioural theory is right it can develop leaders through training **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Trait theory locates leadership in a person's inherent characteristics; behavioural theory locates it in what leaders actually do
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Under trait theory a business should invest in identifying and selecting people with the right characteristics, since training cannot supply what is not there
> - Under behavioural theory a business can develop leaders internally, so leadership training becomes a worthwhile investment
> - Trait theory struggles to explain why someone who leads well in one situation fails in another, since their traits have not changed
> - The two are not wholly incompatible, since certain characteristics may make particular behaviours easier to adopt
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When two theories are compared, the clearest way to show you understand both is to say what each would have the business actually do. Trait theory points to selection; behavioural theory points to training. Tying a theory to a decision proves understanding far more convincingly than restating the definition.

>

The plant manager, Dulce, told every affected worker personally before the announcement was made public, explained why the line was closing, and arranged for a local college to run free retraining courses on site.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of emotional intelligence to a manager of a luxury holiday resort.
parts.solutionMd:
Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to understand and manage your own emotions and to recognise and respond appropriately to the emotions of others **[K]**. Goleman identified four key competencies: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and social skills **[K]**. All four are relevant to managing a luxury holiday resort

Self-management is particularly important **[E]**. At a luxury resort, problems, such as staff shortages, equipment failures or difficult guests **[Ap]**, can arise at short notice. A manager who reacts visibly with stress or frustration is likely to unsettle employees, who take their lead from the behaviour of those above them **[An]**. A manager who stays calm and composed under pressure helps the team maintain their focus, which is essential when guests are paying a premium price and expecting an exceptional experience **[Ap]** **[An]**

Social awareness - the ability to understand the needs and feelings of others  **[K]**- is equally valuable when managing a diverse workforce. Employees at a luxury resort will have different motivations: some may be driven by financial rewards, others by recognition or career development. A manager who recognises these individual differences can adapt their leadership approach accordingly, making each employee feel valued **[An]**. Employees who feel understood and appreciated are more likely to be motivated, and motivated employees deliver a better quality of service to guests **[An]**

Strong social skills also enable the manager to build positive relationships with guests directly. When a guest raises a concern, a manager with high EI can listen carefully, acknowledge how the guest feels, and resolve the issue in a way that turns a negative experience into a positive one, protecting the resort's reputation and encouraging repeat visits **[Ap]** **[An]**

However, emotional intelligence alone is not enough to manage a luxury resort effectively **[E]**. Financial planning, resource management and operational efficiency are also essential. A manager who is empathetic but fails to control costs or plan staffing levels correctly may create a pleasant working environment but an unprofitable business **[An]**

Overall, EI is especially important in this context because luxury hospitality depends on personal, high-quality interactions at every level **[Ap]** **[E]**. The higher the expectations of guests, the more a manager needs to understand and inspire the people who serve them, making emotional intelligence one of the most commercially valuable qualities a luxury resort manager can have **[An]**  **[E]**

> 
> - Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise and manage your own emotions, and to understand and respond appropriately to the emotions of others. Goleman identified four key competencies: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skills
> - Self-management requires a manager to control their own emotional responses, particularly in difficult situations - at a luxury resort, where unexpected problems such as complaints or staff shortages can arise at any time, a manager who reacts with visible frustration or anxiety creates a negative atmosphere
> - Employees take their cues from the manager's behaviour, so a calm and composed response helps the team to remain focused and continue delivering the high standard of service that luxury guests expect
> - Social awareness - the ability to understand the emotions and needs of individuals - is particularly valuable in a luxury resort where employees have very different backgrounds, levels of experience, and personal motivations
> - A manager who recognises that one employee is motivated by recognition while another values flexible working can tailor their approach to get the best performance from each person; higher employee motivation leads to a more positive attitude towards guests, which directly improves the quality of the guest experience
> - Social skills allow a manager to build strong relationships with both employees and guests - when guests at a luxury resort feel genuinely listened to and valued by management, they are more likely to be satisfied with their stay, leave positive reviews, and return in future; the reputation of a luxury resort depends heavily on these personal interactions, making strong social skills a commercially important quality in a manager
> - Empathy - a component of social awareness - enables a manager to recognise dissatisfaction among guests or employees before it escalates; at a luxury resort where standards are exceptionally high, a guest who feels ignored or dismissed may leave a damaging review that harms future bookings
> - A manager with high EI can identify and resolve issues early, protecting both the guest's experience and the resort's reputation
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - EI is arguably more important at a luxury resort than in other hospitality settings because guests pay a premium price and have extremely high expectations - every interaction with staff must feel personal, attentive, and exceptional, which is only achievable if employees are led by a manager who understands and manages people effectively
> - However, emotional intelligence alone is not sufficient - a manager also needs strong technical and operational skills, including financial planning, inventory management, and strategic decision-making; a manager who is highly empathetic but unable to control costs or manage resources efficiently could put the resort's financial sustainability at risk
> - The value of EI also depends on the manager's ability to apply it consistently under pressure; some managers may be emotionally intelligent in calm situations but struggle when they are stressed, which is precisely when these skills are most needed in a luxury hospitality environment
>

parts.problemMd:
‘The business leaders and managers of a school must have a high level of emotional intelligence if they are to be successful.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Emotional intelligence is the ability to understand and manage your own emotions, and to recognise and respond appropriately to the emotions of others **[K]**. Goleman identified four key competencies: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship management **[K]**. School leaders include the headteacher, senior managers, and department heads, all of whom are responsible for both staff and student outcomes **[Ap]**

There is a strong case that EI is essential for school leaders. Social awareness - the ability to understand the emotions and needs of individuals - is particularly important when managing teaching staff **[K]**. Teachers are motivated by different things: some value professional development, others value recognition or autonomy. A department head who recognises these differences and adapts their management approach accordingly is more likely to create a motivated and effective team, which directly improves the quality of teaching and student outcomes **[Ap]** **[An]**

EI is also important in managing relationships with parents and the wider community **[Ap]**. School leaders regularly deal with parents who are anxious or dissatisfied about their child's progress. A leader with strong relationship management can listen carefully, acknowledge concerns, and respond in a way that builds trust, which is essential for the school's reputation and for maintaining a positive relationship between families and the school **[An]**

However, EI alone is not sufficient for a school leader to be successful **[E]**. Headteachers must also analyse student performance data, manage significant budgets, make strategic decisions about curriculum and staffing, and respond to government policy and inspection frameworks **[Ap]**. A leader who is empathetic but lacks these analytical and strategic skills may fail to identify or address the root causes of underperformance **[An]**

Overall, I partially agree with the statement. A school is a people-centred environment where staff wellbeing and relationships directly affect student outcomes, making EI more important here than in many other organisations **[Ap] [E]**. However, "must have a high level" is too absolute. Effective school leadership requires EI alongside intellectual ability, strategic thinking and operational skills. The most successful school leaders combine all of these qualities rather than relying on any single one **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
‘Good leaders are more important for business success than good managers.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
A leader inspires and motivates people to work towards a shared goal or vision. A manager plans, organises, and controls day-to-day activities to achieve the business's objectives **[K]**. Both roles are important, but they serve different purposes within a business

There is a strong argument that good leaders are essential for long-term business success. Without a clear and inspiring vision, a business may operate efficiently but in the wrong direction **[K]**. Leaders identify new opportunities, encourage innovation, and give employees a sense of purpose that motivates them to perform at a higher level. In fast-moving industries such as technology or fashion **[Ap]**, the ability to anticipate change and set a new direction is often what separates successful businesses from those that fall behind. No amount of good management can compensate for the absence of strategic vision **[An]**

However, leadership alone is not sufficient **[E]**. Even the most brilliant strategic idea will fail if managers cannot implement it effectively. Managers are responsible for planning resources, coordinating teams, monitoring progress, and maintaining quality **[K] **- without these capabilities, a leader's ideas remain plans on paper. Many businesses have failed not because of weak leadership but because poor operational management allowed costs to rise, deadlines to be missed, or quality to fall. Good management is the mechanism that turns leadership decisions into real results **[An]**

The relative importance of the two also depends on context. In stable, well-established industries where the business model is unlikely to change rapidly - such as food manufacturing or logistics **[Ap]** - strong management may contribute more to daily profitability than visionary leadership. In more innovative or entrepreneurial contexts, strong leadership may be the greater driver of competitive advantage  **[E]**

Overall, I disagree with the view that good leaders are more important than good managers **[E]**. Both are essential, and neither can fully compensate for the absence of the other. The most successful businesses develop strong leadership to set the direction and strong management to deliver it. Treating the two as competing priorities misunderstands how they work together to create sustainable business success **[E]**

> - A business with strong management but weak leadership may run its existing operations efficiently, but without a clear and inspiring sense of direction it is unlikely to grow, innovate or adapt when the market changes; managers focus on implementing what already exists, whereas leaders identify what the business should be doing next; in competitive markets where businesses must continually evolve, the absence of strong leadership leaves the organisation without a strategy for long-term success

parts.problemMd: ‘Effective business leaders need to be more emotionally intelligent than intellectually brilliant.’ Discuss this statement.
parts.solutionMd:
Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to understand and manage your own emotions, and to respond appropriately to the emotions of others. Intellectual intelligence refers to the analytical ability to understand complex situations, evaluate information, and make sound decisions **[K]**. Both are qualities that business leaders can possess

There is a strong argument in favour of EI being crucial for leadership effectiveness. Leadership is fundamentally about people - inspiring employees, building trust, and creating a culture where people are motivated to perform at their best **[K]**. A leader who is intellectually brilliant but unable to manage their own emotions, or who fails to understand how employees feel, may create a culture of fear or disengagement **[An]**. Employees who do not feel valued or understood are less likely to be committed, creative or willing to go beyond the minimum, which limits the organisation's performance regardless of how smart the leader is **[K]**

However, intellectual ability is also essential **[E]**. Leaders must analyse financial data, assess market trends, evaluate risks, and make strategic decisions that shape the long-term direction of the business **[K]**. A leader who is empathetic but lacks the analytical capability to distinguish between a good and a bad strategic decision may steer the business confidently in entirely the wrong direction. Good intentions and strong interpersonal skills cannot compensate for consistently poor judgement **[An]**

The relative importance of EI and intellectual intelligence also depends on context. In a technical or data-driven industry such as pharmaceuticals or finance **[Ap]**, intellectual credibility is essential for a leader to be taken seriously by employees and stakeholders. In a customer-facing service business **[Ap]**, where employee motivation and relationships directly affect performance, EI may be the greater determinant of success **[E]**

Overall, I disagree with the statement. The most effective business leaders do not need to be more emotionally intelligent than intellectually brilliant - they need to be both **[E]**. EI and intellectual intelligence are not in competition; they serve different purposes. EI enables leaders to motivate and inspire, while intellectual ability enables them to make sound strategic decisions. A leader who develops both qualities is more likely to achieve sustained business success than one who excels in only one area **[E]**

Goleman identified four key competencies: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skills. Intellectual intelligence refers to the analytical and cognitive ability to understand complex information, evaluate options, and make sound strategic decisions
> - A leader with high intellectual ability but low EI may be capable of identifying the right strategy but unable to persuade, inspire, or motivate the people needed to implement it; employees who do not feel valued or understood by their leader are less likely to be committed to the business's goals, and high-achieving individuals may leave for organisations where they feel more respected; this means that intellectual brilliance without EI can actually undermine the very performance the leader is trying to drive
> - Intellectual ability is essential for effective leadership because leaders must understand complex market data, evaluate financial performance, assess risk, and identify strategic opportunities; a leader who cannot distinguish between a short-term tactical decision and a long-term strategic one may make choices that feel good in the moment but damage the business's competitive position over time; without analytical intelligence, even the most emotionally connected leader may take the business in entirely the wrong direction

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'paternalistic management'.
parts.solutionMd:
Paternalistic management is a style in which the manager makes decisions on behalf of employees **[1]**, consulting them and considering their welfare but keeping the final decision to themselves **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A style in which the manager decides what is best for employees, taking their wellbeing into account but retaining control of decisions
> - An approach in which the manager acts rather like a parent, explaining decisions and caring for staff without allowing them to decide
> - Management that consults employees and considers their interests, but where authority to decide remains with the manager

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word paternalistic invites answers about a manager being kind or caring, but the marks are for how decisions get made. Say that the manager consults and considers welfare yet still decides alone. Style definitions should describe the decision-making, not the manager's personality.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way Fayol's view of the manager's role differs from Mintzberg's.
parts.solutionMd:
Fayol described management as a set of functions, such as planning, organising and controlling, which set out what a manager ought to do **[1]**. Mintzberg instead observed what managers actually did, and grouped this into roles such as figurehead, negotiator and disturbance handler **[1]**. The difference matters because Fayol presents management as orderly and planned, whereas Mintzberg found it fragmented and reactive, with managers spending much of their time responding to people and problems rather than working steadily through functions **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Fayol identified functions describing what managers should do; Mintzberg identified roles describing what managers were observed actually doing
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Fayol's functions are prescriptive, setting out an ideal of orderly planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling
> - Mintzberg's roles are descriptive, drawn from observing managers and finding their work fragmented and frequently interrupted
> - Fayol implies management can largely be planned in advance, while Mintzberg suggests much of it is reactive, dealing with people and unexpected problems
> - The two are complementary rather than contradictory, since Fayol describes the purpose of management while Mintzberg describes how that purpose is pursued in practice
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Fayol and Mintzberg both answer the question of what managers do, which makes them easy to confuse. Fayol gives functions; Mintzberg gives roles. Naming which writer you are drawing on, and using their own vocabulary, is the quickest way to show the examiner you can tell them apart.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'laissez-faire management'.
parts.solutionMd:
Laissez-faire management is a style in which the manager gives employees a great deal of freedom to decide how work is done **[1]**, becoming involved very little once objectives have been set **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A style in which employees are left largely to organise their own work, with minimal direction from the manager
> - An approach where the manager sets broad aims and then allows staff to decide how to achieve them
> - Management characterised by very limited intervention, with decisions delegated almost entirely to employees

> **[exam-tip]**
> Laissez-faire is a French phrase, and repeating it back is not a definition. Translate the idea into what actually happens: the manager sets the aim, then leaves employees to decide how to reach it. If your answer would not make sense to someone who had never heard the phrase, it needs more work.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Clearwater (CW)**
> 
> Clearwater (CW) is a commercial laundry in country K. It washes bed linen and towels for hotels, and employs 180 people.
> 
> Two years ago CW was losing customers because deliveries were often late. A new operations manager, Tomas, reorganised the work into three shifts, introduced a system for tracking each hotel's order, and began holding a short meeting with drivers every morning.
> 
> **Table 1.1: CW selected data**
> 
> | Deliveries arriving on time, before the changes (%) | 71 |
> |---|---|
> | Deliveries arriving on time, now (%) | 96 |
> | Hotels supplied, before the changes | 74 |
> | Hotels supplied, now | 90 |

Explain **one** way Tomas has contributed to CW's business performance.
parts.solutionMd:
One way Tomas has contributed is by improving the reliability of CW's deliveries **[1]**. By reorganising the work into three shifts and introducing a tracking system, he lifted the proportion of deliveries arriving on time from 71% to 96% **[1]**. Hotels depend on clean linen being there when they need it, so a laundry that delivers late risks losing contracts; more reliable delivery is why CW now supplies 90 hotels rather than the 74 it had before the changes **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Managers contribute to performance by organising resources, setting standards, motivating staff, monitoring results and correcting problems
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Reorganising into three shifts and tracking orders lifted on-time delivery from 71% to 96%, addressing the exact reason customers had been leaving
> - Reliability is the main requirement for hotels buying laundry services, so improving it explains the rise from 74 to 90 hotels supplied
> - Daily meetings with drivers give Tomas early warning of problems, letting him correct issues before customers notice them
> - The changes also make CW easier to manage as it grows, since a tracking system and shift structure can handle more hotels without proportionately more supervision
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question about a manager's contribution needs you to connect what the person did to something the business can actually measure. Here that runs from the shift reorganisation, to the rise in on-time deliveries, to the increase in hotels supplied. Describing the actions alone leaves the last two marks unclaimed.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'management style'.
parts.solutionMd:
Management style is the way in which a manager makes decisions and works with employees **[1]**, including how much authority they keep and how far staff are involved **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The general approach a manager takes to making decisions and to dealing with the people they manage
> - The way authority is used and employees are involved in decisions, ranging from autocratic through to laissez-faire
> - A manager's characteristic pattern of behaviour towards staff, particularly in how decisions are reached and communicated

> **[exam-tip]**
> This asks for the umbrella term, not one example of it. Describing autocratic management answers a different question. Define the category itself, then, if you have room, note that styles range from autocratic to laissez-faire to show you know what the category contains.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'Theory X'.
parts.solutionMd:
Theory X is McGregor's description of managers who assume employees dislike work and avoid responsibility **[1]**, and who therefore rely on close supervision and control to get results **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - McGregor's view of managers who believe workers are naturally unwilling to work and must be directed and closely controlled
> - A set of assumptions that employees lack ambition, dislike responsibility, and need supervision or the threat of punishment to perform
> - The belief that workers are motivated mainly by money and security, which leads managers to use tight control and detailed instruction

> **[exam-tip]**
> Theory X and Theory Y are sets of assumptions a manager holds about employees, not styles of behaviour in themselves. Start your definition with what the manager believes about workers, then say what that belief leads them to do. Getting the assumption in first is what secures the mark.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** traditional function of management.
parts.solutionMd:
One traditional function of management is planning **[1]**. Planning means deciding what the business is trying to achieve and working out the steps and resources needed to get there **[1]**. Without it, departments may pull in different directions or duplicate each other's work, so setting clear objectives and a route towards them lets a manager coordinate effort and judge later whether the business is on track **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The traditional functions of management are usually given as planning, organising, commanding or directing, coordinating, and controlling
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Planning sets objectives and decides how resources will be used to reach them, giving employees a common direction and a standard to be measured against
> - Organising arranges people, equipment and money so that the plan can be carried out, putting the right resources in the right place at the right time
> - Commanding or directing means instructing and motivating employees so the work is actually done, turning a plan into activity
> - Controlling compares actual performance against the plan and corrects differences, without which a business would not know whether its objectives were being met
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Naming a function earns the first mark only. The other two come from saying what it involves and why the business needs it. A one-word answer such as "planning", or a list of all five functions, will not reach three marks. Take one and develop it.

parts.problemMd: Analyse the potential benefits for a business of a laissez-faire leadership style.
parts.solutionMd:
Laissez-faire leadership is a style in which employees are given significant freedom to make their own decisions and manage their work with minimal interference from management **[K]**. One potential benefit is that it encourages creativity and innovation. In businesses with highly skilled employees - such as a design agency or research and development team **[Ap] **- workers often have greater specialist knowledge than their managers. Allowing these employees to direct their own work enables them to apply their expertise freely, leading to more original and higher-quality outcomes **[An]**. This can help the business develop better products or services, giving it a competitive advantage in its market **[An]** A second benefit is that laissez-faire leadership can improve the motivation and retention of skilled employees **[K]**. Highly skilled workers, such as software developers or creative professionals, often place a high value on autonomy and independence **[Ap]**. A business that gives these employees the freedom to manage their own work demonstrates trust in their abilities, increasing job satisfaction and commitment. Employees who feel trusted and valued are less likely to leave for alternative employers, reducing the significant cost of recruiting and training replacements **[An]**. This is particularly important in industries where specialist talent is in high demand and staff turnover is costly, as retaining experienced employees helps the business maintain consistent quality and productivity over time **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to a relevant business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problemMd:

> **Harvest Lane (HL)**
> 
> Harvest Lane (HL) freezes and packs vegetables in country R. It employs 420 people, many of whom live in the small town where the factory is located.
> 
> HL is run by Anneke, whose grandfather founded the business. She provides a subsidised canteen, free transport to the factory, and paid training. Anneke decides shift patterns, holiday periods and pay rates herself, explaining her decisions to workers at a meeting each quarter but never asking them to vote.
> 
> Labour turnover at HL is 4%, against a national average of 17% in food processing.
> 
> HL has recently won a large supermarket contract requiring weekend production. Anneke has announced a new Saturday shift without consulting staff. Several younger employees have said they would have preferred a choice of shift.

Analyse **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage to HL of Anneke's paternalistic management style.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage is that HL keeps hold of its workers **[K]**. Anneke provides a subsidised canteen, free transport and paid training, and explains her decisions to staff each quarter, so employees feel the business looks after them **[Ap]**. Labour turnover at HL is only 4% against a national average of 17% in food processing, which means HL spends far less than its competitors on recruiting and training replacements **[An]**. Retaining experienced staff matters particularly in food processing, where workers who know the machinery and the hygiene rules make fewer costly mistakes than a constantly changing workforce would **[An]** One disadvantage is that employees have no say in decisions that affect them **[K]**. Anneke announced the new Saturday shift required by the supermarket contract without consulting anyone, and several younger employees have said they would have preferred a choice of shift **[Ap]**. Workers who feel decisions are simply imposed may become less willing to cooperate, and in a business that has just committed to weekend production, reluctance to work Saturdays could make the new contract difficult to fulfil **[An]**. parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Northgate (NG)**
> 
> Northgate (NG) runs a customer service centre in country V for a telecoms company. It employs 600 people who answer calls from mobile phone customers.
> 
> Eighteen months ago NG was struggling. Staff were leaving quickly, callers waited a long time, and the telecoms company threatened to move the contract elsewhere.
> 
> A new centre manager, Priya, made three changes. She introduced a training programme so that staff could answer billing and technical questions rather than transferring calls. She gave team leaders authority to resolve complaints up to \$200 without approval. She also replaced a system that ranked staff publicly by the number of calls taken with one that measured how many problems were solved first time.
> 
> **Table 1.1: NG selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 600 |
> |---|---|
> | Annual labour turnover, before the changes (%) | 52 |
> | Annual labour turnover, now (%) | 23 |
> | Calls resolved at first contact, before (%) | 58 |
> | Calls resolved at first contact, now (%) | 84 |

Analyse **two** ways in which Priya has contributed to NG's business performance.
parts.solutionMd:
One way is that Priya has raised the proportion of problems solved at the first attempt **[K]**. Her training programme means staff can now answer billing and technical questions themselves instead of transferring callers, and first-contact resolution has risen from 58% to 84% **[Ap]**. Every call that no longer needs a transfer takes less of NG's time, so the same 600 staff can deal with more customers without NG employing anyone else **[An]**. It also removes the main reason callers were waiting a long time, which was the complaint that had put the telecoms contract at risk **[An]** A second way is that Priya has cut the rate at which staff leave **[K]**. She replaced a system that ranked employees publicly by call numbers with one measuring problems solved first time, and gave team leaders authority to settle complaints up to \$200 themselves **[Ap]**. Staff judged on solving problems rather than on speed are less likely to feel pushed into rushing callers, and turnover has fallen from 52% to 23% **[An]**. Lower turnover means NG keeps trained staff for far longer, so the money spent on the training programme goes on benefiting the business rather than walking out of the door with each person who leaves **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problemMd:
‘In a hospital, managers using a democratic style are more likely to be successful than managers using an autocratic style.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Democratic leadership involves consulting employees and encouraging participation in decision-making, with two-way communication between managers and staff. Autocratic leadership involves the manager making decisions independently and issuing clear instructions with little or no employee input **[K]**

There is a strong case for democratic leadership being more successful in a hospital. Patient care requires collaboration between doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and other specialists who must share information and coordinate decisions about diagnosis and treatment **[Ap]**. A democratic manager who encourages open communication facilitates this teamwork **[K]**, reducing the risk of errors and improving patient outcomes **[An]**. Furthermore, hospitals employ highly qualified professionals with specialist knowledge that managers may not possess; consulting these staff leads to better-informed decisions and demonstrates respect for their expertise, increasing motivation and making it less likely that talented clinicians will leave **[An]**

However, autocratic leadership is likely to be more effective in emergency situations **[K]**. In a cardiac arrest, a surgical crisis, or a major trauma case **[Ap]**, there is no time for consultation - immediate, unambiguous decisions must be made and followed without delay **[An]**. A manager who pauses to seek consensus in these moments could put patients at risk. Autocratic leadership is also more appropriate for enforcing non-negotiable safety protocols and clinical governance requirements, where consistency and compliance matter more than participation **[An]**

The type of employee also matters. Hospitals employ a broad range of workers beyond clinical staff - including porters, cleaners, and kitchen workers **[Ap]** - who may respond better to clear direction than to participative decision-making **[An]**

Overall, the statement is over-simplistic **[E]**. Neither style is universally more successful in a hospital - the most effective managers adapt their approach to the situation, using democratic methods when working with skilled clinical teams on complex decisions and autocratic methods in emergencies or when enforcing mandatory standards **[Ap]**. A manager who is inflexibly democratic in all situations is no more likely to succeed than one who is inflexibly autocratic **[E]**
