> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of the extent to which you agree with the view that, in a hospital, managers using a democratic style are more likely to be successful than managers using an autocratic style |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the view that, in a hospital, managers using a democratic style are more likely to be successful than managers using an autocratic style |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of democratic leadership and/or autocratice leadership style |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Democratic leadership: a participative style in which employees are consulted and involved in decision-making, with two-way communication between managers and staff
> - Autocratic leadership: a directive style in which the manager makes decisions independently and issues clear instructions, with little or no employee consultation
> 
> **For democratic leadership in a hospital**
> 
> - Hospital care involves multidisciplinary teamwork between doctors, nurses, specialists, and pharmacists who must share information and coordinate treatment decisions; democratic leadership that encourages participation and open communication facilitates this collaboration, reducing the risk of errors and improving patient outcomes - making it central to managerial success in a clinical environment
> - Hospitals employ many highly qualified professionals who have specialist expertise that their managers may not possess; a democratic approach that invites their input leads to better-informed decisions and signals respect for professional knowledge, increasing motivation and reducing the risk of talented clinicians leaving for other employers
> - Staff retention and morale are significant challenges in hospital environments; managers who consult employees and take their concerns seriously are more likely to build trust and job satisfaction among their teams, reducing absenteeism and turnover in a setting where losing experienced staff has serious consequences for patient care
> 
> **Against - autocratic leadership may be more appropriate in some situations**
> 
> - Emergency and crisis situations in hospitals, such as cardiac arrests, major trauma cases, or surgical complications, require immediate, unambiguous decisions with no time for consultation; in these life-or-death moments, autocratic leadership that issues clear and rapid instructions is essential, and a manager who pauses to seek consensus could put patients at risk
> - Hospitals employ a wide range of workers beyond clinical staff, including porters, cleaners, kitchen workers, and administrative staff; these employees may respond better to clear, direct management than to participative decision-making, and democratic consultation may be unnecessary or impractical in roles that involve following set procedures
> - Hospitals must adhere to strict clinical protocols, safety regulations, and governance requirements; some decisions are non-negotiable and must be enforced consistently; autocratic enforcement of these standards ensures compliance and protects patient safety in ways that democratic discussion could undermine
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - Neither style is universally "more likely to be successful" - the most effective hospital managers adapt their style to the situation, using democratic approaches for routine decisions involving skilled clinical teams and autocratic approaches in emergencies or when enforcing mandatory safety protocols
> - The type of employee matters significantly: highly skilled clinicians expect to be consulted and respond poorly to autocratic management, while support staff in more routine roles may need clearer direction
> - The statement is arguably over-simplistic - success in hospital management depends not on choosing one style, but on the ability to move between styles as circumstances demand; a manager who is inflexibly democratic in all situations is no more effective than one who is inflexibly autocratic
> - Some theorists would argue that a situational or contingency approach - selecting the most appropriate style for each context - is the only meaningful framework for evaluating leadership success in a complex organisation like a hospital
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Discuss the significance of McGregor’s leadership styles for managers in a hospital.
parts.solutionMd:
McGregor's Theory X assumes workers are lazy and need close supervision, leading to an autocratic management style. Theory Y assumes workers are self-motivated and seek responsibility, leading to a more democratic approach **[K]**. Theory Y is most significant for managing highly skilled clinical staff such as doctors, nurses, and surgeons **[Ap]**, who are deeply committed to patient care and intrinsically motivated by their work. A manager who assumes these professionals need constant direction risks damaging their motivation and professional autonomy **[An]**. Treating them as Theory Y workers by trusting them to take responsibility and contribute to clinical decisions is more likely to produce effective performance and reduce turnover among the hospital's most valuable employees **[An]**

However, Theory X has significant relevance in emergency situations. In a cardiac arrest or surgical crisis  **[Ap]**, managers must issue clear and immediate instructions without time for discussion. In these contexts, autocratic direction is essential for patient safety **[An]**. Theory X may also be more appropriate for managing support staff, such as porters and cleaners **[Ap]**, who carry out routine, structured tasks and may benefit from clearer direction than clinical professionals **[An**

Overall, McGregor's theory is significant for hospital managers because it highlights how their underlying assumptions about workers directly shape their management style and that the wrong assumptions can seriously damage performance **[E]**. A manager who applies Theory X to motivated, skilled doctors risks demotivating them, while a manager who is too democratic in an emergency situation could put patients at risk **[Ap]**. McGregor's framework is, however,  over-simplistic for a hospital environment: no single set of assumptions fits all staff or all situations **[E]**. The most significant lesson for hospital managers is not to choose between Theory X and Theory Y, but to reflect on whether their assumptions match the reality of the people and situations they face, and adapt accordingly **[E]**

> | **3** | 7-8 | - Limited evaluation of the significance of McGregor’s leadership styles for managers in a hospital |
> | **2** | 3-6 | - Analysis and application of the significance of McGregor’s leadership styles for managers in a hospital |
> | **1** | 1-2 | - Knowledge and understanding of McGregor’s leadership styles and/or management |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Theory X: managers assume workers are lazy, dislike work, and need close supervision and direction to perform; leads to an autocratic management style
> - Theory Y: managers assume workers are self-motivated, enjoy work, and seek responsibility; leads to a democratic and participative management style
> - Theory Y is likely most significant for managing highly skilled clinical staff such as doctors, surgeons, and specialist nurses, who are intrinsically motivated by their work and deeply committed to patient care; a manager who assumes these professionals need constant supervision and direction (Theory X) risks damaging their motivation, undermining their professional autonomy, and increasing turnover among the most valuable members of the hospital workforce
> - Treating them as Theory Y workers - trusting them to take responsibility and contribute to decisions - is more likely to produce effective performance and job satisfaction
> - Theory X assumptions may be more appropriate in emergency situations, where there is no time for consultation or participation; in a cardiac arrest or surgical crisis, managers must issue clear, unambiguous instructions that are followed immediately
> - In these life-or-death contexts, autocratic direction based on Theory X thinking is not merely appropriate but essential for patient safety
> - Hospitals employ a wide range of workers beyond clinical staff, including porters, cleaners, kitchen workers, and administrative employees; these workers carry out more routine, structured tasks and may require clearer direction and closer supervision; Theory X management may be more relevant for this group than for clinical professionals
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - McGregor's most significant contribution for hospital managers is the recognition that their underlying assumptions about workers directly shape how they manage - and that mismatched assumptions can seriously damage performance; a manager who applies Theory X assumptions to highly motivated doctors risks demotivating skilled professionals and undermining patient care
> - However, McGregor's framework is binary, and its significance is limited by the complexity of a hospital environment where different staff, roles, and situations demand different approaches; no single set of assumptions is appropriate across an entire hospital
> - The most significant insight for hospital managers may be that they need to reflect on whether their assumptions match the reality of each group they manage, adapting their style accordingly rather than applying Theory X or Theory Y universally
> - In a public sector hospital, where managers face significant accountability, regulatory oversight, and complex demands, the ability to flex between Theory X and Theory Y approaches may be more important than committing to either one
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Discuss the view that a democratic leadership style could cause some businesses to underperform.
parts.solutionMd:
Democratic leadership involves consulting employees and seeking their input before decisions are made **[K]**. While this can strengthen engagement, it significantly slows down decision-making. In fast-moving or competitive markets, the time spent seeking consensus can cause businesses to miss opportunities or respond too slowly to change. Competitors using more decisive leadership styles may act faster and gain market share while a democratically managed business is still consulting its workforce. This is particularly damaging in industries where speed of response is critical to performance **[Ap]** **[An]**

A second reason is that not all employees have the knowledge or experience to contribute meaningfully to strategic decisions **[K]**. In organisations with largely low-skilled or inexperienced workforces **[Ap]**, involving employees in complex choices may produce poor outcomes, as workers lack the business understanding needed to evaluate options effectively. A manager who feels obliged to incorporate a wide range of views may end up with watered-down decisions that reflect a desire for consensus rather than the most effective course of action **[An]**

However, democratic leadership does not automatically cause underperformance. In knowledge-based or creative businesses - such as design agencies or technology firms **[Ap]** - employees often have specialist expertise that their manager lacks **[K]**. Here, democratic leadership produces better decisions and higher motivation, both of which improve performance. Skilled workers who are not consulted may become demotivated and leave, which can be far more damaging than slower decision-making **[An]**

Overall, whether democratic leadership causes underperformance depends on the type of business and the situations it faces **[E]**. It is most likely to harm performance in fast-moving markets or businesses with largely unskilled workforces. It is least likely to cause underperformance in professional or creative organisations where employee expertise is valuable **[An]**. The view is therefore partially correct but over-generalises - democratic leadership is neither universally effective nor universally harmful to business performance **[E]**

> | **2** | 3-6 | - Analysis and application of the view that a democratic leadership style could cause some businesses to underperform |
> | **1** | 1-2 | - Knowledge and understanding of democratic leadership and/or business performance |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Democratic leadership is a participative style in which employees are consulted and involved in decision-making, with two-way communication between managers and staff.
> 
> **For - democratic leadership can cause underperformance**
> 
> - Democratic leadership significantly slows down decision-making because managers must consult employees and seek consensus before acting; in fast-moving or highly competitive markets, this delay can cause the business to miss opportunities or respond too slowly to problems, while competitors using more decisive leadership styles act faster and gain advantage, directly reducing the business's market share and performance
> - Not all employees have the knowledge or experience to contribute meaningfully to business decisions; in organisations with largely low-skilled or inexperienced workforces, involving employees in strategic choices may produce poor or watered-down decisions that reflect a desire for consensus rather than the most effective course of action, ultimately harming business performance
> - Opening decisions up to employee input can generate disagreement and conflict, consuming management time and energy in internal debate rather than productive activity; if consensus proves difficult to reach, morale and efficiency may both suffer
> 
> **Against - democratic leadership does not always cause underperformance**
> 
> - In knowledge-based, creative, or professional organisations, such as design agencies, consultancies, or technology firms, employees often have specialist expertise that exceeds their manager's; democratic leadership that draws on this collective knowledge leads to better-informed decisions and higher motivation, improving rather than damaging performance
> - Employees who feel consulted and valued are more motivated, more committed, and less likely to leave; reduced absenteeism and staff turnover can improve productivity and lower costs, more than offsetting any loss of speed in decision-making
> - The impact on performance depends heavily on the business context: in a routine, stable environment with clear procedures, the slowness of democratic leadership may matter little; in a crisis or fast-moving market, it may matter greatly
> 
> **Evaluation**
> 
> - Democratic leadership is most likely to cause underperformance in businesses facing rapid change, strong competition, or crisis situations where speed of decision-making is critical
> - It is least likely to cause underperformance in professional or creative organisations where employee expertise is valuable, motivation is central to output quality, and staff retention is a key driver of business success
> - The statement is qualified with "some businesses" - this is appropriate; the view is partially correct but over-generalises; no single leadership style universally improves or damages performance, and the most effective managers adapt their approach to the needs of the business and the situation
>

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **disadvantage of a piece rate payment method.
parts.solutionMd:
One disadvantage of piece rate is that workers may rush to complete as many units as possible in order to earn more money **[1]**. This can cause quality standards to fall because workers are focused on speed rather than care **[1]**, which could lead to an increase in defective products and customer complaints **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Workers may rush to complete as many units as possible in order to maximise their earnings
> - If the production line breaks down or materials are unavailable, workers cannot produce units and therefore earn nothing
> - Workers may resist changes to working methods or machinery
> - A competitive atmosphere can develop between workers chasing higher piece rates
> - Piece rate can only be used where output is easily measured and standardised
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Rushing production can cause quality standards to fall or create safety risks, as workers prioritise speed over care
> - The inability to earn during stoppages creates income insecurity and anxiety, which can reduce motivation and morale
> - Workers fear that changes will slow their output and cut their pay, making them unwilling to accept new processes even when these would benefit the business
> - Competition over pay can lead to jealousy, poor teamwork, or higher staff turnover
> - This limits the method's applicability and means it cannot be used for service, knowledge-based, or creative roles
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Even though the question asks for one disadvantage. Make sure you develop your point fully - state the disadvantage clearly and then explain the impact or consequence it has on the business or workers. For example, do not just write "quality may fall"; go on to explain that workers rushing to maximise output may cut corners, leading to defective products and potential loss of customers. Avoid simply listing disadvantages without explanation, as this will limit you to only 1 mark.

**[3 marks]**

> AO1
> 
> - Team working involves employees working together towards a shared goal, rather than each worker completing a single task in isolation
> - Team working creates opportunities for social interaction, mutual support, and shared responsibility among employees
> - Team working can provide greater variety, empowerment, and participation in decision-making
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Working alongside colleagues allows employees to build relationships and fulfil their social and esteem needs, making work more enjoyable and increasing their engagement and commitment
> - A supportive team environment reduces workplace conflict and provides emotional support, helping employees feel more comfortable and valued in their roles
> - Greater empowerment and involvement in team decisions gives employees a sense of ownership and responsibility, fulfilling higher-order needs and increasing intrinsic motivation
> - Working on a more complete and meaningful unit of work - rather than one repetitive task - gives employees a greater sense of achievement and satisfaction, which encourages them to work harder

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** effect on a business of low employee motivation.
parts.solutionMd:
One effect of low employee motivation is higher staff turnover **[1]**. When employees feel undervalued or disengaged, they are more likely to look for work elsewhere and leave the business **[1]**. This forces the business to spend time and money recruiting and training replacements, which increases costs **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Lower productivity / output per worker
> - Higher rates of absenteeism
> - Higher staff turnover, leading to increased recruitment and training costs
> - Poor quality of work or customer service
> - Reduced creativity and innovation among staff
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If employees lack motivation, they are less likely to work efficiently or take pride in the quality of their output; this can result in higher defect rates, more customer complaints, and potential damage to the business's reputation - particularly in a service business where customer interactions are central to the brand
> - Low motivation often leads to higher absenteeism, which disrupts production schedules or service delivery; if remaining staff must cover for absent colleagues, this adds pressure and may further reduce morale, creating a cycle of declining performance
> - Unmotivated employees are more likely to leave the business in search of more fulfilling or better-paid work; this increases recruitment and training costs, and the business may lose experienced workers whose skills and knowledge are difficult to replace quickly
> - Poor quality of work resulting from low motivation can lead to increased waste, reworking of faulty products, or dissatisfied customers; over time this can harm sales and damage the business's reputation for quality
> - Low motivation reduces employees' willingness to suggest new ideas or find better ways of working; this limits the business's ability to innovate or improve its products and processes, putting it at a competitive disadvantage
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks by simply listing several effects rather than developing one in depth. Focus on a single effect and build a chain of analysis - show how the effect leads to a consequence for the business, and ideally extend this to a further impact (e.g. low motivation → higher absenteeism → disrupted operations → increased costs or lost revenue). Using connective phrases such as "this means that…" or "as a result…" helps demonstrate the analytical thinking examiners are looking for. Avoid vague statements like "the business will do badly" - be specific about the business impact.

**[3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **advantage to a business of using a time based payment method.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of time-based pay is that it helps the business maintain consistent quality standards **[1]**. Workers are paid for the hours they work rather than the number of units they produce, so they have no financial incentive to rush **[1]**. This reduces the risk of defective products or careless work that can occur with piece rate **[1]**

>

> - Time-based pay helps the business maintain consistent quality standards
> - Time-based pay allows the business to plan and control its labour costs effectively
> - Time-based pay gives the business flexibility to increase output through overtime when needed
>

> - Because wages are calculated simply by multiplying hours worked by the hourly rate, the business spends less time on payroll administration, reducing overhead costs and the risk of errors in pay calculations

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **advantage to employees of performance-related pay.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of PRP to employees is that it rewards hard work and strong performance with higher pay **[1]**. Employees who meet or exceed their targets receive a bonus on top of their basic salary, meaning their earnings directly reflect the effort and quality they put into their work **[1]**. Many employees see this as fairer than a fixed pay system where everyone earns the same regardless of performance, and this sense of being fairly rewarded increases job satisfaction and motivates them to continue working to a high standard **[1]**

> AO1
> 
> - PRP directly rewards employees who work hard and exceed their targets with higher pay
> - PRP is seen by many employees as a fairer system, since pay reflects individual effort and contribution rather than simply time worked
> - PRP gives employees a clear incentive to develop their skills and demonstrate their capabilities
> - PRP allows employees in roles where output cannot be counted in units, such as management,to be financially rewarded for the quality of their work
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Earning more through strong performance allows employees to better meet their financial needs and improve their standard of living, increasing their overall satisfaction with the job
> - Employees who feel their pay reflects their individual contribution are more likely to feel valued and fairly treated compared to a fixed pay system where all workers earn the same regardless of effort or results
> - High performance recognised through PRP can increase an employee's chances of promotion, providing career development opportunities beyond the immediate financial reward

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **benefit to a business of having motivated employees.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit to a business of having motivated employees is lower staff turnover **[1]**. Employees who feel engaged, valued, and satisfied in their work are less likely to leave and look for jobs elsewhere **[1]**. parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **possible disadvantages to a business of using performance-related pay to motivate its employees.
parts.solutionMd:
Performance-related pay links employees' pay to an assessment of their performance against pre-agreed targets **[K]**. One disadvantage is that it is difficult for a business to measure performance fairly, particularly in roles such as management or customer service **[K] **where output cannot easily be counted. If managers assess employees subjectively, some workers may feel their evaluation was biased or inconsistent **[An]**. This causes employees to lose trust in the system and feel resentful, meaning PRP reduces motivation rather than improving it, working against the very objective the business was trying to achieve **[An]**

A second disadvantage is that PRP can cause conflict between employees **[K]**. Because individuals are rewarded based on their own performance, some workers will earn significantly more than colleagues doing similar work. Those who narrowly miss their targets and receive no bonus may feel undervalued compared to those who do, even if the difference in performance was small **[An]**. This creates jealousy and resentment within teams, damaging cooperation. In a business that depends on employees working together effectively, this breakdown in teamwork could reduce overall productivity **[An] **and actually harm business performance, offsetting any benefits from the individual incentives PRP provides **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the disadvantages to a business of using performance-related pay to motivate its employees |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the disadvantages to a business of using performance-related pay to motivate its employees |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the disadvantages to a business of using performance-related pay to motivate its employees |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of performance-related pay and/or motivation |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Performance-related pay (PRP) links an employee's salary or bonus to an assessment of their performance against pre-agreed targets or criteria
> - PRP requires managers to assess whether each employee has met their targets, but in many roles - particularly management and supervisory positions - performance is difficult to measure objectively; if employees feel their assessment was unfair, inconsistent, or influenced by favouritism, they will lose trust in the system and feel demotivated, meaning PRP achieves the opposite of its intended effect and may increase staff grievances or turnover
> - Because PRP rewards individuals based on their own performance, some employees will earn significantly more than colleagues doing similar work; employees who narrowly miss their targets and receive no bonus may feel undervalued compared to those who do, creating resentment and jealousy that damages teamwork and cooperation - in a business that relies on collaborative working, this breakdown in team relations could reduce overall productivity and offset any individual performance gains
> - For employees already working at full capacity, the pressure to meet or exceed targets in order to protect their income can lead to stress, burnout, and higher rates of absenteeism; the business may find that health-related absences increase costs and disrupt output, negating the productivity improvements PRP was designed to create
> - Setting PRP targets that employees consider achievable but stretching is difficult; if targets are set too high, employees may give up trying to reach them, reducing motivation rather than increasing it, while targets that are too easy fail to drive the improvements in performance the business is looking for
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Analyse how a business might satisfy the self-actualisation needs of its employees.
parts.solutionMd:
Self-actualisation is the highest level of Maslow's hierarchy of needs - the desire to fulfil one's full potential through creative, meaningful, and challenging work **[K]**. One way a business might satisfy these needs is through job enrichment, which involves adding greater responsibility, variety, and challenge to employees' existing roles **[K] [An]**. When employees are given complex or creative tasks that require them to use their full range of skills, they feel they are growing and developing as individuals **[An]**. This increases intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction, making employees more engaged and productive, and reducing the likelihood that they will leave the business to seek more fulfilling work elsewhere **[An]**

A second way is to empower employees by giving them greater autonomy over how they carry out their work **[K]**. For example, allowing creative or specialist teams to make their own decisions - rather than following instructions from managers - satisfies the need for self-expression and personal achievement **[An]**. Employees who feel trusted to direct their own work are more likely to take ownership of outcomes and develop innovative ideas **[An]**. This benefits the business by encouraging creativity and new approaches, which can lead to improved products or processes, while also keeping highly skilled employees motivated and committed to the organisation **[An]**

> 
> - Self-actualisation is the highest level of Maslow's hierarchy of needs - the desire to fulfil one's full potential, achieve personal growth, and engage in creative, meaningful work that makes use of one's abilities
> - A business can satisfy self-actualisation needs through job enrichment - adding greater responsibility, variety, and challenge to employees' roles; when employees are given the opportunity to take on complex or creative work, they feel they are using and developing their full capabilities; this increases intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction, leading to higher levels of engagement, productivity, and commitment to the business
> - Empowering employees by giving them greater autonomy over how they carry out their work - for example, allowing creative or specialist teams to make their own decisions - satisfies the self-actualisation need for self-expression and personal achievement; employees who feel trusted to direct their own work are more likely to produce innovative solutions and new ideas, which can benefit the business through improved products, processes, or customer experiences

parts.problemMd:
‘Non-financial motivators are the most effective way of improving employee motivation in a house building business’.

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Non-financial motivators are approaches that do not involve direct pay increases, such as job rotation, team working, and empowerment. Financial motivators use money to incentivise employees, for example through higher wages, deadline bonuses, or performance-related pay **[K]**

One reason non-financial motivators can be effective in a house building business is that many construction tasks, such as bricklaying, plastering, and roofing, are physically repetitive **[Ap]**. Job rotation could reduce the boredom this creates, helping to maintain employee engagement and productivity across the site **[An]**

>

parts.solutionMd:
One way CTV employees could participate in the management and control of the business is through a works council **[K]**. This would make employees feel more valued and listened to, reducing anxiety and rebuilding trust in management, which could improve motivation and productivity in the factories that remain open **[An]**

A second method is profit sharing or share ownership **[K]**. CTV is a public limited company, so it could offer employees shares in the business. If automation in the STV factory **[Ap]** increases efficiency and profits, employees with a financial stake would benefit directly from this success. This aligns employee interests with those of the business, making them more likely to support decisions like automation rather than resist them – and helps CTV manage a period of significant change more smoothly **[Ap] [An]**

parts.problemMd:
*‘The economic man* theory used by Taylor is the best way to motivate the employees of a customer service call centre business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Taylor's economic man theory argues that workers are motivated primarily by financial reward, and that management should monitor performance closely and link pay directly to output **[K]**

In a customer service call centre, performance can be measured objectively - through call handling times, resolution rates, and sales conversions **[Ap]** - making Taylor's approach feasible **[E]**. Agents could be paid bonuses for hitting measurable targets, and call centres already use technology to monitor activity and record calls **[Ap]**, which is consistent with Taylor's principles of close observation and standardised working methods. For agents motivated primarily by earnings, financial incentives linked to clear targets can be a powerful motivator **[An]**

However, Herzberg's two-factor theory challenges this view. Herzberg argued that pay is a hygiene factor - it prevents dissatisfaction but does not create genuine motivation **[K]**. In a repetitive and emotionally demanding environment like a call centre, bonuses may reduce dissatisfaction without inspiring agents to deliver empathetic, high-quality service **[Ap] [An]**. True motivators, such as recognition, achievement, and development opportunities, are not addressed by Taylor's approach alone **[E]**

Maslow's hierarchy further suggests that once basic financial needs are met, higher-order needs such as belonging, esteem, and self-actualisation become more important **[K]**. High staff turnover, which is a widespread problem in call centres **[Ap]**, suggests that financial incentives alone are insufficient to retain experienced agents and that non-financial factors play a significant role in long-term motivation **[An]**

Overall, Taylor's theory is only partially correct **[E]**. Financial incentives linked to measurable targets can improve productivity and sales performance, and call centres are well-suited to performance monitoring **[E]**. However, delivering quality customer service requires emotional engagement that financial reward alone cannot fully motivate **[An]**. A combination of Taylor's financial incentives with non-financial motivators, such as recognition, team working, and career development, is likely to produce better results for both employee motivation and the quality of service delivered **[E]**

> **Indicative content **
>

> - Employee motivation is the internal and external factors that drive employees to remain committed to and engaged in their work
> 
> **For Taylor's theory in a call centre context**
> 
> - In a customer service call centre, employee performance can be measured objectively - for example, through the number of calls handled, call resolution rates, sales conversions, and average handling times; this makes Taylor's approach feasible, as agents can be paid bonuses for hitting measurable targets, directly linking financial reward to output and encouraging higher productivity
> - Call centres already use technology to record calls, track agent activity, and monitor performance in real time, which is consistent with Taylor's scientific management principles of close observation and standardised working methods; this oversight allows managers to identify the most efficient practices and ensure agents follow them, improving consistency of customer interactions
> - For agents motivated primarily by earnings - particularly in lower-paid roles - the prospect of bonuses for sales conversions or performance targets may be a powerful and direct incentive
> 
> **Against - alternative theories suggest Taylor's approach is insufficient**
> 
> - Herzberg's two-factor theory argues that pay is a hygiene factor rather than a true motivator - adequate pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not create genuine engagement; in a call centre where work is repetitive and emotionally demanding, financial incentives may reduce dissatisfaction without inspiring agents to deliver high-quality customer service; true motivators (recognition, achievement, development) are not addressed by Taylor's approach

> - Mayo's human relations theory highlights the importance of social factors and management attention; call centre work can be isolating and stressful, and teams that feel valued and well-supported by management often outperform those motivated by pay alone
> - High staff turnover is a well-known problem in call centres, suggesting that financial incentives alone are insufficient to retain experienced agents; non-financial factors such as a positive working environment, flexible working, and career development may be more effective in improving long-term retention and motivation
>

> 
> - Taylor's theory has some relevance in a call centre where performance is measurable and financial incentives can drive improvements in call volume, sales, and efficiency
> - However, call centre work requires emotional engagement and empathy to deliver quality customer service - qualities that financial incentives alone cannot fully motivate
> - The extent to which Taylor's theory is the "best" approach depends on business priorities: if raw productivity is the primary goal, financial incentives linked to measurable targets have merit; if quality of customer interactions and staff retention are priorities, non-financial approaches become more important
> - A combination of Taylor's financial incentives for measurable performance targets alongside non-financial motivators - recognition, team working, and development opportunities - is likely to produce better overall results than relying on Taylor's theory alone; if quality of customer interactions and staff retention are priorities, non-financial approaches become more important

> **[case-study]**
> **Auto Bike (AB) **
> 
> AB is a private limited company that repairs and maintains motorbikes. AB has nine garages in country J and employs eight highly qualified mechanics in each garage.
> 
> Two of the most popular motorbike services that AB sells are the standard service and the advanced service. Table 2.1 contains price and cost information for these services.
> 
> **Table 2.1: Price and cost information**
> 
> |   | **Price** | **Direct costs per service** | **Allocated indirect costs per service** |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Standard service | \$250 | \$50 | \$60 |
> | Advanced service | \$400 | \$60 | \$100 |
> 
> In April, AB sold 1000 standard services and 200 advanced services. The profit margin for an advanced service is higher than the standard service. The directors have decided to promote the advanced service to try and increase sales. Each garage has been given a budget to use for below the line promotion methods with an objective of increasing sales of advanced services in the next six months.
> 
> The level of motivation of the mechanics is low. Many mechanics believe that they are not paid well and the conditions of work are dirty and noisy. AB uses a time-based payment method which rewards each mechanic at the same hourly rate. In a recent survey, many mechanics complained that the payment method was unfair. They believe it rewards ‘lazy workers’ as much as those who work hard. It also does not take into account the difficulties involved in some jobs and the simplicity of others. The Human Resources Director has been asked to investigate a new payment method.

Recommend a new payment method for the mechanics at AB. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
One new payment method AB could introduce is performance-related pay (PRP) **[K]**. This links each mechanic's earnings to an individual assessment of their performance, rather than simply the hours they work. AB's mechanics have complained that the current time-based system rewards those who take on easy jobs or work slowly just as much as those who work hard on complex repairs **[Ap]**. PRP would address this directly - mechanics who complete more difficult jobs to a higher standard would earn more, making the system fairer. This could increase motivation significantly, as employees would feel that their effort and skill are properly recognised and rewarded **[An]**

A second option is to introduce bonuses **[K]** for mechanics who upsell customers from a standard to an advanced service. AB's directors have identified increasing advanced service sales as a key objective **[Ap]**, and bonuses linked to this outcome would directly incentivise mechanics to recommend the more expensive service where appropriate. Since the advanced service has a higher profit margin **[Ap]**, each additional sale also improves AB's overall profitability, meaning the bonus cost could be offset by the additional revenue generated **[An]**

PRP is the stronger recommendation for AB **[E]**. While bonuses can drive short-term sales of advanced services, they do not fully address the mechanics' core complaint  that the current system fails to account for the complexity and difficulty of different jobs **[Ap]**. PRP tackles this more directly by linking pay to the quality and nature of the work completed, not just the number of upsells achieved. This is particularly important for a business employing highly qualified mechanics, whose skills and expertise vary significantly between standard and advanced repairs **[Ap]**. Introducing PRP is therefore more likely to improve long-term motivation and reduce the risk of experienced mechanics leaving AB for better-paid work elsewhere **[E]**

parts.solutionMd:
One strategy NH could introduce is Management by Objectives (MBO). This involves managers and employees agreeing on individual targets together, with regular reviews and appraisal **[K]**. NH currently operates with detailed worksheets that tell employees exactly what to do, with no time allowed for consultation, and letters from employees suggesting improvements have not been acted on by Head Office **[Ap]**. MBO would give employees a say in setting their own targets and a clearer sense of purpose, addressing their need for recognition and involvement in the business **[An]**. The HR Director has already attended an MBO conference, suggesting this is a realistic option **[Ap]**. However, MBO requires a major cultural shift for an organisation as autocratic and centralised as NH - if targets are set too strictly, or if managers resist sharing authority, the system could increase frustration rather than motivation **[An]**

A second strategy is multi-skilling - training employees to perform more than one role **[K]**. Currently, all employees are trained for a single role, creating repetitive work that contributes to declining job satisfaction scores and sharply rising labour turnover (up from 14% to 26% for non-management employees) **[Ap]**. Training employees in a wider range of tasks would make their work more varied and challenging, addressing Herzberg's motivators of the work itself and personal development, which the current system ignores completely **[An]**

MBO is the stronger recommendation at this point **[E]**. It addresses multiple causes of low motivation simultaneously - lack of involvement, poor communication, and no recognition for performance - and fits with the HR Director's recent research **[Ap]** **[E]**. Multi-skilling would also help, but it alone does not tackle the fundamental problem that employees have no voice in how NH is run. Introducing MBO for assistant managers first would be a practical starting point, as their satisfaction has also declined and they are better placed to understand and implement the system before it is rolled out more widely **[E]**

Discuss strategies for reducing human resource problems in GR’s restaurants without increasing unit costs.
parts.solutionMd:
One effective strategy would be to move to a more consultative leadership style **[K]** across GR's restaurants. Currently, managers impose rigid work practices with no employee input, and the survey identifies lack of empowerment and limited consultation as the two main negative factors about working at GR **[Ap]**. Dissatisfaction with task allocation is the most commonly cited reason for leaving. If managers involved employees in decisions about their work, employees would feel more valued and engaged, consistent with Mayo's human relations theory, which emphasises the importance of communication and involvement **[An]**. This costs GR nothing, making it the most viable solution given the unit cost constraint **[E]** A second strategy is to pool tips across all restaurant staff rather than allowing only waiters to keep them **[K] [Ap]**. Kitchen employees earn only the legal minimum wage with no access to tips, while waiters supplement their income significantly. This inequality contributes to dissatisfaction and turnover among kitchen staff. Redistributing tips equally would improve kitchen employees' effective pay at zero additional cost to GR, directly addressing a key reason for leaving without raising unit labour costs **[An]** A third approach is to recruit restaurant managers internally rather than always appointing externally **[K] [Ap]**. parts.problemMd:
'Financial incentives are the most effective way to motivate employees in a retail business.'

Evaluate this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Financial incentives include commission, bonuses, profit sharing, and performance-related pay. In retail, individual performance can often be measured through sales figures, making commission straightforward to implement — staff who sell more earn more, directly linking effort to reward. This is consistent with Taylor's economic man theory, which argues workers are primarily motivated by financial gain. For full-time sales staff in higher-value retail environments such as electronics or furniture stores, the prospect of a meaningful bonus can be a powerful driver of performance and focus.

However, Herzberg's two-factor theory challenges this view. Herzberg argued that pay is a hygiene factor — sufficient pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not create genuine motivation. Once retail employees earn enough to meet their basic needs, additional bonuses are unlikely to make them significantly more engaged. True motivators are intrinsic to the job: recognition, responsibility, achievement, and development opportunities. A retail employee given responsibility for training new staff or managing a product range is more likely to feel genuinely motivated than one who receives a modest monthly bonus.

Commission can also undermine teamwork and service quality in retail by encouraging staff to prioritise their own individual sales over helping colleagues or building customer relationships. Many retail workers are part-time, and for them flexible hours and a positive team environment may be more motivating than financial incentives — a point supported by Mayo's human relations theory.

Overall, financial incentives are most effective for sales-focused roles where individual performance is measurable and employees are primarily income-driven. For the broader retail workforce — particularly part-time and customer service staff — non-financial motivators are likely to be equally or more effective. The most successful approach combines fair base pay to prevent dissatisfaction with non-financial motivators that address higher-order needs, creating genuine long-term engagement rather than short-term performance gains alone

> **Indicative content **
> 
> - Financial incentives are rewards that motivate employees through money, e.g. commission, bonuses, profit sharing, performance-related pay, piece rate
> - Non-financial motivators are approaches that improve motivation without direct pay increases, e.g. recognition, job enrichment, responsibility, promotion opportunities, a positive working environment
> 
> **For financial incentives in retail**
> 
> - In retail, individual performance can often be measured through sales figures, conversion rates, or customer satisfaction scores, making commission and performance-related pay straightforward to implement; staff who sell more earn more, directly linking effort to reward and encouraging higher productivity - consistent with Taylor's economic man theory, which argues workers are primarily motivated by financial gain
> - Bonuses for hitting weekly or monthly targets give retail employees a clear, tangible goal to work towards; for full-time sales staff in higher-value retail environments (e.g. electronics, car sales), the prospect of a significant bonus may be a powerful driver of performance and focus
> - Profit sharing gives all retail employees a financial stake in the store's success, aligning their interests with those of the business and encouraging a collective effort to improve sales and reduce waste
> 
> **Against — non-financial motivators may be more effective**
> 
> - Herzberg's two-factor theory argues that pay is a hygiene factor rather than a true motivator - sufficient pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not create genuine engagement; once retail employees earn enough to meet their basic needs, additional financial incentives are unlikely to make them significantly more motivated; true motivators, such as recognition, responsibility, achievement and personal development - are intrinsic to the job itself, not financial

>

> - Financial incentives are most effective in retail roles where individual performance is measurable and employees are primarily income-driven - such as full-time sales staff in high-value environments; they are less effective in roles requiring teamwork, empathy, and consistent customer care
> - Herzberg's research suggests that pay alone will not create lasting motivation - it removes dissatisfaction but does not engage employees with their work in a meaningful way
> - The type of retail employee matters significantly: a commission-driven full-time sales assistant and a part-time student working weekend shifts are unlikely to respond to the same motivational approach
> - The most effective strategy combines fair base pay - meeting hygiene needs and preventing dissatisfaction - with non-financial motivators such as recognition, development opportunities, and a positive team culture that address higher-order needs

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'span of control'.
parts.solutionMd:
Span of control is the number of employees who report directly to one manager **[1]**, and it determines how many people that manager is responsible for supervising **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The number of subordinates directly answerable to a single manager
> - A measure of how many employees one manager supervises directly, which affects how closely each can be monitored
> - The count of people immediately below a manager in the chain of command, described as wide when large and narrow when small

> **[exam-tip]**
> Span of control is a number, so your definition should make clear what is being counted: the employees reporting directly to one manager. The word "directly" matters, because people further down the chain are not part of that manager's span even though they sit below them.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Rosemont (RM)**
> 
> Rosemont (RM) manufactures skincare products in country H. It employs 260 people and sells to pharmacies and department stores.
> 
> RM is organised into four departments: production, marketing, finance, and human resources. Each is led by a director who reports to the managing director.
> 
> Staff in each department work only within their own specialism. RM's chemists all sit within production, and its designers all sit within marketing.
> 
> RM's managing director says the arrangement means she always knows who is responsible for what.

Explain **one** benefit to RM of a functional structure.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit is that RM's specialists work alongside others doing the same kind of work **[1]**. All of RM's chemists sit within production and all of its designers within marketing, so each group can share knowledge and solve problems together **[1]**. In a business making skincare products, where formulation expertise takes years to build, keeping chemists together means less experienced staff learn from more experienced colleagues, which raises the standard of RM's products over time **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A functional structure groups employees by the type of work they do, such as production, marketing, finance and human resources, each headed by a specialist director
> 
> AO2
> 
> - All RM's chemists sit within production, so expertise is concentrated and less experienced staff learn from colleagues doing the same work
> - Each of the four departments has a director accountable for it, which is why RM's managing director always knows who is responsible for what
> - Grouping by function avoids duplicating roles, since RM needs only one finance team rather than a separate one for each product line
> - Clear departmental boundaries give employees an obvious career path within their specialism, helping RM retain skilled chemists and designers
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A benefit of a structure is really a statement about how work gets done. Rather than calling a functional structure "organised" or "efficient", say what it lets people actually do: share expertise, avoid duplication, know who decides. Naming the mechanism is where the development marks are.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'delegation'.
parts.solutionMd:
Delegation is when a manager passes authority to carry out a task to a subordinate **[1]**, while remaining accountable for whether the task is completed properly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Passing authority for a task down to a more junior employee, with the manager still answerable for the outcome
> - Giving a subordinate the power to make decisions about a piece of work, without transferring ultimate responsibility for it
> - Entrusting work to someone lower in the hierarchy, together with the authority needed to complete it

> **[exam-tip]**
> The examiner is looking for what does and does not transfer. Authority passes to the subordinate; accountability stays with the manager. Getting that asymmetry into your definition secures the second mark, and it is the point students most often get wrong on this topic.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Fairstone (FS)**
> 
> Fairstone (FS) is an insurance company in country Y employing 2,400 people. It has nine levels of hierarchy between the chief executive and the staff who deal with customers.
> 
> A customer wanting to claim more than \$5,000 must have the claim approved at four separate levels.
> 
> FS's average time to settle a claim is 34 days. Two newer insurance companies in country Y settle claims in under a week, and have taken 6% of FS's market share in three years.

Explain **one** drawback to FS of its hierarchical structure.
parts.solutionMd:
One drawback is that decisions take a long time to reach **[1]**. FS has nine levels between the chief executive and customer-facing staff, and a claim above \$5,000 must be approved at four separate levels **[1]**. Every approval adds waiting time, which is why FS takes 34 days to settle a claim while two newer insurers manage it in under a week; those competitors have already taken 6% of FS's market share, so the delay built into the structure is costing FS customers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A tall hierarchical structure has many levels of management, long chains of command and narrow spans of control
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Four approval levels for claims above \$5,000 lengthen the time before a customer is paid, producing an average of 34 days against under a week at newer rivals
> - Nine levels between chief executive and front-line staff mean information travels slowly in both directions, so senior managers may learn of problems only after customers have left
> - Employees dealing with customers have little authority, which may reduce their motivation and their willingness to resolve problems themselves
> - Many management levels are expensive, as each carries salaries and overheads the flatter newer competitors do not have to cover
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A drawback question needs you to say who or what suffers as a result. Here it is not simply that decisions are slow; it is that customers wait 34 days, rivals settle in under a week, and FS has lost 6% of the market. Following the drawback through to its victim is what earns the third mark.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'authority'.
parts.solutionMd:
Authority is the power a person holds within a business to make decisions and instruct others **[1]**, given to them by the position they occupy in the organisational structure **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The right to make decisions, allocate resources and give instructions, arising from a person's position in the hierarchy
> - Legitimate power held by a post holder to direct the work of others and to commit the business's resources
> - The formal ability to require action from subordinates, granted by the organisation rather than earned personally

> **[exam-tip]**
> Authority and responsibility are usually taught together, so it is tempting to define both. This question asks for one. Define authority, the right to decide and instruct, and leave responsibility alone. Answering more than was asked costs time without adding marks.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Greenway (GW)**
> 
> Greenway (GW) maintains parks and business grounds in country F. It employs 140 people working in 18 teams across the country.
> 
> GW's owner, Marcus, requires every team leader to send him photographs of completed work and to telephone him before buying materials costing more than \$50.
> 
> Team leaders say the calls waste time, particularly when a job needs a part urgently. Three team leaders have left in the past year, two of them saying they were not trusted to do their jobs.
> 
> Marcus says he has seen work done badly in the past and cannot risk GW's reputation.

Explain **one** conflict between control and trust in the way Marcus delegates.
parts.solutionMd:
One conflict is that the checks Marcus uses to protect quality also signal that he does not trust his team leaders **[1]**. Requiring a telephone call before any purchase over \$50, and photographs of every completed job, means team leaders cannot act without approval even when a job needs a part urgently **[1]**. Two of the three team leaders who left last year said they were not trusted, so the controls Marcus uses to protect GW's reputation are costing him the experienced staff who protect that reputation day to day **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Delegation requires a manager to give subordinates authority while retaining accountability, which creates tension between controlling the work and trusting those who do it
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Requiring approval for purchases over \$50 keeps Marcus in control of spending but stops team leaders acting quickly when a job needs a part urgently
> - Photographing every completed job reassures Marcus about quality, yet signals to team leaders that their own judgement is not accepted
> - Two of the three team leaders who left cited a lack of trust, so the controls are driving out exactly the experienced staff Marcus depends on
> - Marcus's concern is not unreasonable, since poor work has damaged GW before, and with 18 teams spread across the country he cannot supervise directly
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A question about conflict needs both sides in your answer. Explaining only that the controls annoy staff, or only that Marcus has good reason for them, gives half the picture. Name what the control achieves and what it costs, then show why the two cannot both be fully satisfied.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'matrix structure'.
parts.solutionMd:
A matrix structure is an organisational structure in which employees are grouped into project teams **[1]** while also belonging to their usual department, so they report to two managers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A structure in which staff work in cross-functional project teams while retaining a place in their own department
> - An arrangement where an employee answers both to a departmental head and to a project leader
> - A structure combining functional and project reporting lines, so authority runs in two directions at once

> **[exam-tip]**
> Structure questions reward a description of the shape. For a matrix, the defining feature is two reporting lines: a department and a project. Saying employees "work together in teams" describes almost any structure, so name the dual reporting to make clear which one you mean.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'decentralisation'.
parts.solutionMd:
Decentralisation is when decision-making authority is passed from senior managers at the centre of a business **[1]** to managers in its divisions, branches or regions **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The transfer of decision-making authority away from head office to lower levels or local units
> - An arrangement where branches, divisions or regions decide matters themselves rather than referring them upwards
> - Spreading authority through the organisation so decisions are taken closer to where their effects are felt

> **[exam-tip]**
> A term beginning with "de-" tempts students to answer "the opposite of centralisation", which earns nothing. Define it in its own right: authority for decisions moves from the centre out to divisions or branches. Examiners want the idea itself, not a cross-reference to another term.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** difference between a line function and a staff function.
parts.solutionMd:
A line function is one that contributes directly to producing and selling the business's output, such as production or sales **[1]**. A staff function supports the line functions with specialist advice or services, such as human resources or legal **[1]**. The difference matters because line managers hold authority over the people below them in their own chain of command, whereas staff specialists usually advise rather than instruct, which can cause friction if their advice is ignored **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Line functions contribute directly to producing and selling the product; staff functions provide specialist support and advice to those line functions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A production manager holds line authority over production employees, and can instruct them directly as part of the chain of command
> - A human resources specialist advises on recruitment or discipline but does not usually have authority to direct production staff
> - Staff functions let expertise be shared across the whole business rather than duplicated within every department
> - Tension can arise where line managers treat staff advice as interference, particularly when the specialist has no authority to insist
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A difference question needs a point of contrast, not two separate descriptions. Say what line functions do, say what staff functions do, then state what actually separates them, which here is authority. Answers describing each in turn without naming the difference tend to stop at two marks.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business might change its organisational structure.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason a business might change its structure is that it has grown **[1]**. A structure that worked when the owner supervised everyone directly becomes unworkable once there are too many employees for one person to manage **[1]**. Adding layers of management, or grouping staff into departments, shares supervision out, so decisions are made by people close enough to the work to understand it rather than being delayed while everyone waits for one overloaded manager **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Structures change in response to growth, changes in objectives, new technology, competitive pressure, cost-cutting, or a merger or takeover
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Growth eventually makes a single manager's span of control unworkable, so extra levels or departments are needed to share supervision
> - A business seeking faster decisions may remove management levels, shortening the chain of command so front-line staff can act without waiting for approval
> - New technology can make layers of middle management unnecessary, since information now passes directly between senior managers and front-line staff
> - A merger creates duplicate departments, so the combined business must reorganise to avoid paying twice for the same function
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question asks why a structure changes, so name the trigger rather than describing the new structure. Growth, a merger, new technology and cost pressure are triggers; becoming flatter or adding departments is the response. Starting with the cause keeps your answer pointed at the question asked.

Devonice Ltd (DL) Gabriel Romana founded DL in 2012 in country Y. He used his savings to develop Devonice, a luxury ice cream brand made from natural ingredients. DL started manufacturing ice cream in a small factory in 2013. Organisation and growth DL has grown rapidly. Gabriel has increased the product range with new flavours of ice cream. In 2016, DL opened its second factory and its first Devonice ice cream shop in country Y. At present, most sales are made to supermarkets in country Y. However, Gabriel has plans to open more ice cream shops. He is also considering selling DL franchise agreements to increase export sales. Gabriel enjoys being in control of the business and intends to maintain a centralised structure. Managers of the functional departments report directly to Gabriel and he makes all major decisions. The production line project DL has two factories, operating 24 hours a day. In total, there are 5 production lines and 200 workers able to produce 30 million litres of ice cream per year. Capacity utilisation is currently 90%. To increase capacity and flexibility, Gabriel is considering investing in computerised production lines. Gabriel wants this project completed within 20 weeks in time for the summer season. The operations manager has prepared a critical path analysis (CPA) for the project (see Appendix 1 and Appendix 2). Table 1: Estimated net cash flows for the new production line project Year Net cash flow (\$m) Discount factor (8%) 0 (2.5) 1 1 0.5 0.93 2 0.8 0.86 3 1.2 0.79 4 1.5 0.74 5 1.5 0.68 A competitive market Devonice is now the market-leading brand in country Y and is exported to 10 other countries. DL’s innovative marketing and high quality product have contributed to sales growth. DL targets young adults and has developed a premium brand image. Promotion includes the use of social media, school sponsorship and celebrity endorsement. DL also donates a share of its profits to environmental charities.

Market conditions in country Y are challenging. A multi-million dollar advertising campaign by a global ice cream brand has increased competition. DL sales have remained stable but market share has fallen. In response, Gabriel is considering reducing the price of Devonice or increasing promotional spending. The marketing department has estimated the promotional elasticity of demand and price elasticity of demand for Devonice. Details are in Table 2. However, Gabriel believes this could damage the brand image. In his opinion, increasing promotional spending is the better decision. Corporate social responsibility (CSR) Despite rising incomes in country Y, there is concern about health related problems due to poor diet. In 2020, a pressure group started a campaign to persuade food manufacturers to take greater responsibility for the impact of their products. The group demanded government action to reduce sales of food products high in sugar and fat by: • regulating product labelling • restricting advertising • introducing a tax on these products. DL could change ingredients to reduce sugar content. However, Gabriel is worried about consumer reaction. There are alternatives DL could use, but these are more expensive. Appendix 1: Critical path analysis (CPA) for the production line project Activity Description A Run existing production lines at full capacity to increase inventory for changeover B Order and delivery of ice cream equipment C Order and delivery of packaging equipment D Removal of existing production equipment E Installation of new production equipment F Training of production line workers G Testing of production lines

Analyse **two **possible advantages to DL of centralisation as the business continues to expand.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of centralisation for DL is that it ensures consistency **[K]** in how the Devonice brand is presented as the business expands. Gabriel makes all major decisions from the centre, meaning that the brand's premium image is protected across every shop, factory, and export market **[Ap]**. As DL opens more ice cream shops and sells franchise agreements abroad, consistent decisions about pricing, promotion, and product quality will ensure that consumers in all markets experience the same premium brand **[An]**. If individual managers or franchisees were free to make their own decisions, they might reduce prices or change the product in ways that damage Devonice's premium positioning and reduce consumers' willingness to pay a higher price, harming DL's revenue **[An]**

A second advantage is faster decision-making **[K]**. In a centralised structure, Gabriel can make and implement decisions quickly without requiring lengthy consultation across multiple levels of management. DL is currently facing increased competition from a global ice cream brand backed by a multi-million dollar advertising campaign **[Ap]**, and needs to respond decisively - for example, by choosing between reducing prices or increasing promotional spending. Centralisation means Gabriel can act immediately, giving DL a competitive advantage over rivals whose decision-making processes may be slower **[An]**. As DL continues to expand, the ability to make fast, unified decisions will become increasingly important in maintaining its position as the market-leading brand in country Y **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Centralisation means keeping all key decision-making authority within head office, rather than delegating it to individual departments, factories, or branches
> - Centralisation allows DL to use central buying for key ingredients such as milk, cream, and natural flavourings across all five production lines; by purchasing inputs in large volumes on behalf of the entire business, Gabriel can negotiate significant bulk discounts from suppliers, reducing the cost per litre of ice cream produced
> - As DL continues to expand with new shops and potential franchises, the volume of purchasing will increase further, amplifying these savings and helping DL compete on cost against the global brand that has entered country Y's market
> - Centralisation means strategic decisions are made by Gabriel, who has led DL since founding it in 2012 and has deep knowledge of the ice cream market in country Y and internationally; this experience reduces the risk of poor decisions being made by less qualified managers at individual factories or shops
> - As DL expands into new markets through franchising, having experienced senior managers control key decisions ensures that the business's strategic goals - such as protecting the premium brand and achieving profitable growth - are consistently pursued
> 
> Accept any other valid response

AerCore (AC) Omar is the founder and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of AC, a private limited company. AC was founded in 2000 and manufactures fitness equipment in country K. Membership of fitness centres is increasing in country K as a result of rising incomes and greater awareness of the benefits of exercise. AC sells and leases fitness equipment such as treadmills and rowing machines to fitness centres, hotels and large corporations. AC does not currently sell directly to consumers. One benefit of decentralisation for AC is that it would give the operations manager greater authority to make decisions about production **[K]** without referring everything back to Omar. The operations manager has already reported that he has insufficient authority to manage operations effectively. Some pressure groups claim that metals used in micro circuit boards are obtained from mines which employ child labour. HD’s accountant also believes that some manufacturers make payments to foreign governments which do not appear in their company accounts. Two pressure groups and country Q’s government have asked HD for a detailed social audit. Organisational structure The Design Division is organised in a matrix structure. Design engineers work on their own and also in small teams, each on a specific project such as a customer’s special order. These temporary teams exist for the life of each custom made circuit board project. Each team has designers with the particular skills required. The Design Director delegates responsibility to each team for the completion of each project. The teams choose their own leaders and a team member to communicate with the customer. Evaluate the extent to which the organisational structure of the Design Division contributes to the success of HD.
parts.solutionMd:
A matrix structure organises employees into temporary project teams that cut across functional divisions, with team members reporting to both a functional manager and a project leader **[K]**. HD's Design Division uses this structure, assembling teams of engineers with the specific skills needed for each custom-made circuit board project **[Ap]**

The matrix structure has clearly contributed to HD's success. By drawing together engineers with different areas of expertise for each project, HD can deliver highly tailored solutions to customer specifications, a key requirement in a market where quality is the most important factor **[Ap] [An]**. Teams also choose their own leaders and customer liaison, which delegates responsibility and increases the sense of ownership among engineers. This autonomy suits a workforce of self-directed graduates and has contributed to HD's excellent reputation for problem-free circuit boards and strong customer loyalty, a USP that has sustained 20 years of growth **[Ap] [An]**

However, the structure is also creating problems that threaten HD's continued success. Having two managers to report to causes confusion about priorities and authority **[K]**. Combined with the instability of constantly changing teams, this is damaging morale - a point directly raised by one of HD's engineers **[Ap]**. The consequence is clear from the data: 5 out of 18 design engineers left in just five months, compared with 1 out of 22 in the Manufacturing Division **[Ap]**. High labour turnover increases recruitment and training costs, and the loss of experienced engineers threatens the design quality that HD's reputation depends on. Missed project deadlines add to this risk **[An]**

Overall, the matrix structure has been central to HD's success, but it is now also contributing to its most serious problems **[E]**. The structure remains appropriate for design work requiring specialist teams, but without clearer accountability for project deadlines and better management of the dual-reporting arrangement, the problems of low morale and high turnover **[Ap]** are likely to worsen. The structure needs refinement rather than replacement **[E]**
