Recommend appropriate changes to WTZ’s organisational structure to ‘support growth and drive innovation’. Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
A business's organisational structure shows how it is divided into departments and who makes decisions **[K]**. WTZ currently uses a hierarchical functional structure, where employees are grouped by function - such as operations, marketing and finance **[Ap]**. Amandi believes this structure is holding WTZ back as the business grows

I recommend that WTZ move to a product divisional structure **[E]**. This means organising the business around its different products, such as the Hydrocamel, recycled plastic bricks, metal recycling, and electricity generation **[K]** **[Ap]**. Each division would have its own management team responsible for that product. This would be beneficial for WTZ because the business has grown through diversification - each product serves a different market with different customers and competitors. Having managers who focus on one product line means decisions can be made faster and more appropriately for each market **[An]**. It would also reduce the pressure on Amandi, who currently struggles to maintain effective control as the business grows into new areas. Divisional managers would be empowered to lead their own teams, which could increase motivation and improve performance **[An]**

In addition, WTZ should consider introducing a matrix structure within its product development teams. This brings together employees from different departments, such as operations and marketing, to work together on new products **[K]**. WTZ's two most successful innovations, the Hydrocamel and the recycled plastic bricks **[Ap]**, required expertise from across the business. A matrix structure would make this kind of cross-functional teamwork easier and more regular, helping WTZ to continue innovating **[An]**

Overall, a product divisional structure is the best recommendation for WTZ **[E]**. The main benefit is that it directly addresses the problem Amandi has identified - the difficulty of managing a growing, diversified business through a single centralised structure **[Ap]**. However, there is a risk that Amandi may be reluctant to give up control to divisional managers, which could limit the effectiveness of the change **[E]**. If Amandi genuinely delegates authority, the new structure will give each product area the focus it needs to support growth and drive innovation across the business **[E]**

Jan Guiding Service (JGS) Jan loves being in the countryside. Many years ago, he visited country P, where mountains take up 80% of the land area. Country P is one of the poorest countries in the world, with very low income per head. Jan made his home there and took a job assisting with walking groups. JGS offers mountain walking tours. JGS organises and promotes these tours. Originally, Jan and Gorl guided most of the walking tours themselves. JGS has always outsourced all its travel and accommodation. Jan and Gorl are spending more time on managing the business and less time guiding as the demand for JGS tours increases. JGS now outsources most of its mountain guiding. Customers stay with host families in mountain villages, most of which cannot be reached by road. Host families are paid by JGS to provide food and accommodation for its customers. Many families compete to provide these services to JGS. Using outsourcing in this way gives JGS many benefits. JGS employs an administrator to organise outsourcing. JGS is one of the few businesses operating in this market. However, Jan knows that other businesses are becoming interested in offering mountain walking tours. Demand for JGS services JGS has not increased its prices for three years. Over 95% of JGS customers are visitors from country K. Demand for JGS tours is increasing and Jan thinks that income levels in country K are an important factor. Average income in country K rose by 5% in 2019. Demand for JGS tours from residents of country K increased by 20% in the same period. An organisational structure shows how a business is organised and who makes decisions **[K]**. I recommend that JGS uses a hierarchical functional structure, where Jan and Gorl remain in overall control but delegate some operational authority to the three new regional managers **[E]**

In this structure, JGS employees would be grouped into clear functions - such as administration, marketing, guiding, and accommodation - with Jan and Gorl at the top of the hierarchy, regional managers in the middle, and operational staff below **[Ap]**. This is appropriate for JGS because the business is taking on directly employed workers for the first time**[Ap]**, replacing its outsourced guides and hosts. Having a clear structure means every employee knows exactly who they report to and what they are responsible for **[An]**. This also makes it easier for JGS to show that it is meeting the new country P employment regulations, since Jan and Gorl can see clearly which regional manager is responsible for which employees and whether legal standards are being followed **[An]**

Jan and Gorl should keep control of the most important strategic decisions, such as pricing, CSR standards, and marketing **[Ap] [E]**. This is important because JGS has built a reputation for responsible and high-quality tours, which is a key reason customers choose JGS over other businesses **[Ap]**. As more competitors enter the market, maintaining consistent standards is essential. A centralised approach to strategy means Jan and Gorl can ensure that JGS's values and policies are applied in the same way across all tours **[An]**

However, regional managers must be given some delegated authority **[K] **to make operational decisions on the ground. Guides and host families work in mountain villages that are not accessible by road **[Ap]**, so Jan and Gorl cannot always be reached quickly when problems arise. Giving regional managers the authority to respond to situations - for example, replacing a guide who is unable to lead a walk - means customers are not affected by delays **[An]**

Overall, a hierarchical functional structure with some delegation to regional managers is the best recommendation for JGS **[K]**. It allows Jan to maintain the strategic control he wants, while ensuring that operational problems in remote locations can be resolved quickly **[Ap]**. Historic Buildings and Gardens (HBG) HBG was started in 1965 as a social enterprise in country R. HBG’s main objective is to protect the country’s heritage through conserving buildings and gardens of historic interest. HBG now owns over 200 historic buildings and gardens throughout country R. These are open to the public and HBG receives most of its income from the two million members who pay an annual subscription to visit the historic buildings and gardens. HBG charges admission fees to non-members. Gift shops and cafés also provide a source of income. HBG needs sufficient income to cover costs and finance expansion in new conservation projects. However, it is also aware of a responsibility to provide social benefits to local communities such as employment and education. HBG appointed Eusebio Alves as Managing Director in October 2018 with the objective of increasing membership, admissions and income as they had been falling in recent years. Strategic Review Eusebio started by conducting a strategic analysis of HBG. He completed a SWOT analysis. Table 1 is an extract from the results of the analysis. Table 1: SWOT Analysis 2018 Strengths • High brand awareness • Highest membership of any organisation in country R • High levels of customer satisfaction among the over 50 age group Opportunities • Increasing levels of international tourism to country R • Rising gross domestic product (GDP) per head • New technologies to improve the customer experience and marketing • Falling cost of renewable energy sources such as wind power Weaknesses • Average annual labour turnover of 11% in the last 5 years • 10% reduction in membership since 2015 • Limited access for disabled people at 40% of properties • 70% of members are over 50 • Narrow hierarchical organisational structure • Corporate culture unwilling to accept change Threats • Minimum wage legislation proposed for 2021 • Laws to protect the rights of disabled people being considered by the government • Increasing consumer awareness of social responsibility

Eusebio noted the following observations made by employees, managers and customers: • local managers were frustrated by the time taken for senior managers to respond to ideas for innovation and change • other employees feel they have little responsibility and are just given orders without explanation • customers complain that they are not valued and there is little opportunity for giving feedback to HBG. Eusebio used this analysis to identify four strategic changes required in order to achieve the objectives he had been set: • making the business more responsive to market changes • improving social responsibility • targeting younger customers • improving financial control by establishing profit centres. Eusebio recognised that these four strategic changes would need to be supported by developing a change culture within HBG to be successful. Centralised control At the end of 2018, Eusebio told his Board of Directors that: ‘HBG is bureaucratic with a centralised organisational structure. It is essential to change the way the business is organised and make it more responsive.’ He proposed the following changes. • remove three layers of middle management • delegate greater authority to managers of buildings and gardens to make decisions about local marketing and operations • operate buildings and gardens as individual profit centres • encourage two way communication with employees. However, the Board of Directors would retain control of national marketing, purchase of new buildings, IT infrastructure and strategic decision making. The Human Resources Director expressed concerns about the implications of decentralisation and the need for training. However, in early 2019 HBG began to implement the organisational changes proposed by Eusebio. This followed a two-month employee consultation. Social responsibility Eusebio thinks that HBG should focus more on its corporate social responsibilities. He told the Board of Directors that: ‘we can gain a competitive advantage over other businesses in the leisure industry if we focus on increasing our positive social and environmental impact. However, we must ensure that HBG makes a genuine change to its culture and uses independent social auditors to report on our progress.’

Target market Country R has an ageing population. HBG has used a consistent marketing strategy for targeting its core customers. National advertisements are placed in newspapers and magazines aimed at older readers. Every year HBG has a themed television campaign; in 2019 the theme was titled ‘Connecting with the past’. HBG cafés sell traditional style food and drinks. HBG recruited Nelinha Torres from a social media company to be the new Marketing Director. Her aim is to create a more dynamic marketing strategy that targets a younger audience without losing older members. She commissioned market research and found the following information. • 15% of visitors bring children to HBG buildings and of these 20% were grandparents bringing grandchildren • families with children (‘young families’) value their leisure time but have limited income • price elasticity of demand for young family membership is estimated to be −1.5 • most customers under 50 use the internet to plan and book their leisure activities in advance • although there is good brand awareness, 60% of respondents were not aware of the variety of facilities and events at HBG buildings and gardens. Nelinha and her team are due to present their marketing strategy proposals to the Board of Directors next week. Oldbury Castle Oldbury Castle is a building of historic interest owned by HBG. It attracts 105000 visitors per year. Following the creation of Oldbury Castle as a profit centre, visitor numbers have increased by 10%. However, the manager is concerned about the profitability of the café. He has monitored its financial performance and has noted that it does not cover its full costs. The café is similar to those at other HBG properties and sells a range of traditional meals and refreshments. A recent customer survey suggested that many visitors do not consider the café offers value for money. Feedback also indicates that the menu is considered old fashioned. The manager is considering whether to keep the café open or to use the space to expand the gift shop, which is highly profitable. Table 2 contains data regarding revenue and costs. Table 2: Revenue and cost data Café Year ending 15 May 2020 (\$000) Gift shop Year ending 15 May 2020 (\$000) Revenue 300 200 Direct costs of food/sales 50 80 Direct labour 120 40 Allocated fixed costs from Oldbury Castle 105 30 Allocated fixed costs from HBG 35 10 Project Alderly HBG’s mission is to conserve historic buildings and gardens in country R. It keeps a sizeable fund to enable it to purchase appropriate buildings and gardens. HBG is about to purchase Alderly Gardens. These gardens are of national significance. Although the gardens are well maintained, HBG will not open them to the public until facilities such as toilets for customersare improved. Discuss whether introducing a decentralised organisational structure will benefit HBG.
parts.solutionMd:
A decentralised structure passes decision-making authority from senior managers to lower levels of the hierarchy **[K]**. For HBG, this means removing three layers of middle management and giving local property managers more authority over marketing and operations **[Ap]**

The main benefit is that HBG will be able to respond more quickly to new ideas and opportunities **[K]**. Under the current structure, local managers reported frustration at how long it took to get decisions approved by HQ **[Ap]**. Giving property managers the authority to act locally - for example, creating events to attract international tourists, identified as a key opportunity in the SWOT analysis - means HBG can respond to market changes without waiting for head office approval **[An]**

Decentralisation is also likely to reduce HBG's labour turnover **[K]**, which has averaged 11% per year **[Ap]**. Employees currently feel they are given orders without explanation and have little real responsibility. Giving staff more authority should make them feel more trusted and valued, improving motivation and reducing the number who leave **[An]**

However, removing three layers of management will result in redundancies **[K]**, which conflicts directly with HBG's new commitment to improving its corporate social responsibility **[Ap]**. Simultaneously making employees redundant and emphasising CSR could damage HBG's reputation and reduce trust among remaining staff **[An]**

There is also a risk that local managers make decisions that harm HBG's brand **[K]** - with over 200 properties **[Ap]**, inconsistent standards could confuse customers and undermine the high brand awareness that is one of HBG's key strengths **[An]**

On balance, decentralisation is likely to benefit HBG, since the current centralised structure is clearly not working **[E]** - membership is falling and both employees and customers are dissatisfied **[Ap]**. However, the HR Director's concerns about training are valid **[E]**. If local managers are not properly prepared for their new responsibilities, decision-making quality could actually fall, making the change counterproductive **[E]**

Evaluate whether successful implementation of a new strategy requires NH to change its organisational structure.
parts.solutionMd:
Organisational structure describes how authority, responsibility, and communication are organised within a business. Chandler argued that strategy and structure are closely linked. A business's structure should be designed to support its chosen strategy, not the other way around **[K]** NH currently uses a centralised functional structure. This was appropriate when NH operated one hotel, but with 32 hotels across three very different market segments - luxury, family and basic **[Ap]** - it is creating serious problems. Hotel managers have very little authority to respond to local customer needs, which is contributing to rising complaint levels across all hotel types and occupancy rates falling below budget **[Ap]**. If Jolin's strategy includes improving customer service, one of NH's three stated core competencies, the structure must change to give local managers more decision-making authority, or the strategy simply cannot succeed in practice **[An]** If NH also pursues growth through Country Q and the EatBest acquisition **[Ap]**, a single functional structure will become even less suitable **[E]**. Managing three hotel types, an overseas operation, and a restaurant chain through one set of Head Office departments would be extremely complex. A divisional structure - organised by hotel type, geography, or product - would allow each area of the business to focus on its own customers and markets **[An]** Delayering would also support any new strategy. Currently, employees with improvement ideas are writing to Head Office with no response. A flatter structure would speed up communication and help NH implement changes such as lean production and MBO **[Ap]** more effectively **[An]** However, structural change alone will not be sufficient **[E]**. Labour turnover rising from 14% to 26% for non-management staff and falling job satisfaction scores **[Ap]** are rooted in management culture, not just structure. Reorganising departments without changing how people are led is unlikely to solve these problems **[An]** Overall, structural change is likely to be necessary, particularly if NH pursues international growth and diversification **[Ap] [E]**. Chandler's argument supports this, but it also implies that NH should clarify its strategic direction first, then design a structure to support it. > **Indicative content**
> 
> **AO1**
> 
> - Primary market research is the collection of new, original data gathered directly by the business itself, for the first time, for a specific purpose
> - It involves the business going out to collect data that does not already exist, for example through questionnaires, surveys, interviews or observation
> 
> **AO2**
> 
> - Thomas conducted primary market research by collecting new data about the needs of people in city X, for example through surveys or questionnaires
> - Because the research was carried out specifically for Thomas's purpose, the data directly relates to his decision about which type of shop to open in city X
> - Primary market research gives Thomas information that is up to date and specific to his needs
> - For example, Fig. 1.1 shows the findings of his research into what types of shops people in city X want, which helped him identify the coffee shop and sandwich shop as the two most promising options
> - Unlike secondary research, primary research can be expensive and time-consuming to collect
> - However, for Thomas, who is about to invest significant personal funds in a new business, having accurate, specific data about demand in city X is important to reduce the risk of the business failing

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **advantage to a business of using primary market research data.
parts.solutionMd:
When a business carries out primary research, it decides exactly what questions to ask and which customers to target **[1]**. This means the information collected directly answers the business's questions - for example, whether customers would buy a new product or what price they would be willing to pay **[1]**. Because primary data is tailored to the business's specific situation, it is more likely to lead to better-informed decisions **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> **AO1**
> 
> - Primary market research produces data that is up to date
> - Primary market research gives a business direct control over what information is collected and how
> - Primary market research data is confidential - competitors do not have access to it
> - Primary market research allows a business to target specific customer groups and collect precise information
> 
> **AO2**
> 
> - The data is up-to-date, meaning it reflects the current behaviour and preferences of customers - this is more useful than secondary data, which may have been collected months or years ago and may no longer be accurate, particularly in fast-changing markets where trends and customer preferences shift quickly
> - The business has direct control over what questions are asked and which customers are surveyed - this means the data collected directly answers the business's specific questions, rather than providing general information that may not be relevant to its particular situation
> - Primary research data is confidential and is not available to competitors  - this means a business can gain insights into customer needs or market trends that its rivals do not have, giving it a competitive advantage when making decisions about new products, pricing, or marketing
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** disadvantage to a business of using sampling in primary market research.
parts.solutionMd:
One disadvantage is that the sample may not accurately represent the whole target market **[1]**. When a business selects a sample, it is only collecting data from a small group of people rather than the entire population of potential customers. If this group is not chosen carefully - for example, if it only includes people of a similar age or from the same area - the results will be biased and will not reflect the views of all customers **[1]**. A business that bases its decisions on unrepresentative data may develop products or set prices that do not meet the needs of its wider customer base, which could lead to poor sales and wasted resources  **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> **AO1**
> 
> - The sample may be too small to produce reliable results
> - The sample may not represent the views of the whole target market
> - The wrong sampling method may be chosen, leading to biased results
> - Some people selected for the sample may refuse to take part, reducing its size and reliability
> 
> **AO2**
> 
> - If the sample size is too small, the results may not reflect the views of the wider market - for example, if a business surveys only 20 people out of a potential customer base of 10,000, the findings may not be accurate enough to base important business decisions on, such as whether to launch a new product
> - If the wrong sampling method is used - for example, only surveying customers in one location at one time of day - the sample is likely to include a narrow group of people who do not represent the full range of potential customers; the data collected will be biased, and decisions based on it may not meet the needs of the broader market, potentially leading to lost sales or wasted investment
> - If a large proportion of people selected for the sample refuse to respond, the final sample becomes smaller and less representative - those who do respond may share similar characteristics or views, which means the data collected does not accurately reflect the wider population and could lead the business to draw incorrect conclusions
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks by simply stating a benefit without developing it. To gain full marks, you need to clearly show *why* or *how* the benefit matters to the business. A useful approach is to use connective phrases such as "this means that…" or "as a result…" to extend your point into a chain of reasoning. Avoid listing multiple benefits — the question asks for **one**, so focus on depth rather than breadth.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** benefit of using secondary market research for a business.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit of using secondary market research is that it allows a business to understand competitor behaviour and the wider market without having to collect the data itself** [1]**. For example, a business can use published industry reports, competitor annual reports, or trade publications to find out information such as competitors' prices, product ranges, or market share** [1]**. This information would be very difficult and expensive to gather through primary research alone** [1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> **AO1**
> 
> - Secondary research is cheaper and quicker to obtain than primary research, as the data has already been collected
> - Secondary research provides access to large volumes of data, such as government statistics or industry reports
> - Secondary research is useful as background research before a business commits to more expensive primary research
> - Secondary research allows a business to analyse long-term trends in the market
> 
> **AO2**
> 
> - Because secondary data already exists, a business can access it quickly and at little or no cost**, **which frees up the business's budget for other activities, and is particularly useful for small businesses or start-ups that cannot afford to commission expensive primary research such as focus groups or large-scale surveys
> - Secondary research gives a business access to large amounts of data - for example, government statistics covering millions of households - that would be extremely costly and time-consuming to replicate through primary research -  this makes it possible for even a small business to gain a broad understanding of the market quickly, helping it to identify potential customer groups or spot opportunities for growth
> - Reviewing several years of industry sales data allows a business to identify long-term trends in the market -  understanding whether a market is growing or declining can help a business make better decisions about whether to launch a new product, enter a new market, or adjust its marketing strategy - decisions that are based on evidence rather than guesswork
> 
> Accept any other valid response

To access full marks, make sure you identify the benefit clearly and then explain *how* or *why* it helps the business — try to build a logical chain of reasoning. For example, don't just say "it is cheaper"; go on to explain what this means for the business, such as freeing up budget for other activities. Using a connective such as "this means that…" or "as a result…" can help you structure your development effectively.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'sampling'.
parts.solutionMd:
Sampling is the process of selecting a small group of people from a larger target population **[1]**, so that their responses can be used to draw conclusions about that whole population **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Marigold**
> 
> Marigold makes natural skincare products in country J. Before launching a new face cream, it surveyed 40 shoppers as they left its own city-centre store. The survey asked: "Would you buy our excellent new face cream?" 92% answered yes. Marigold then produced 20 000 units. Six months later, more than half remained unsold.

Explain **one** reason why the market research data collected by Marigold may not be reliable.
parts.solutionMd:
Reliable data is information that can be trusted to give a true picture of the market **[1]**. Marigold surveyed only shoppers who were leaving its own store, so it questioned people who already buy its products and are likely to view the brand positively **[1]**. This means the 92% figure reflects the views of existing loyal customers rather than the wider market Marigold hoped to reach, which helps explain why more than half of the 20 000 units remained unsold **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Reliable data is data that can be depended on to represent the target market accurately
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The sample of 40 is very small compared with the size of the market, so a few unusual opinions could distort the result
> - The survey took place at a single city-centre location, so rural and online customers were excluded
> - The wording "our excellent new face cream" is leading and encourages a positive answer
> - Respondents were asked about intention rather than actual purchase, and stated intention often overstates real buying behaviour
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks why data may not be reliable, look at how the research was carried out, not at whether you believe the finding. Saying "92% seems too high" is an opinion, not a reason. Point instead at who was asked, how many were asked, where they were asked, or how the question was worded; those are the things that make a figure untrustworthy.

Qualitative data records customers' opinions and reasons rather than numbers **[1]**. Knowing the cause allows Pinehurst to change that specific weakness rather than guessing, so any relaunch of the vegetarian range is more likely to recover the lost sales **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Sandpiper**
> 
> Sandpiper sells camping equipment in country H. It commissioned research into the camping equipment market in country H.
> 
> **Table 1: Camping equipment market in country H**
> 
> |   | **2023** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Number of customers | 240 000 | 288 000 |
> | Average annual spend per customer (\$) | 85 | 95 |

Using Table 1, calculate the percentage growth in the size of the camping equipment market in country H between 2023 and 2025.
parts.solutionMd:
**34.1% ****[4]**

Market size = number of customers x average annual spend

2023

$240 , 000 \\times \$ 85 = \$ 20 , 400 , 000$ **[1]**

2025

$288 , 000 \\times \$ 95 = \$ 27 , 360 , 000$ **[1]**

Percentage growth = (change in market size / original market size) x 100 **[1]**

$= \frac{\$ 27 , 360 , 000 - \$ 20 , 400 , 000}{\$ 20 , 400 , 000} \\times 100$

= ( $6 , 960 , \frac{000}{denominator}$ 20 , 400 , 000 ) x 100

$= 34.1 \%$**[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Award 1 mark for each correct stage of working and 1 mark for the final answer
> - Accept 34% or 34.12%; accept answers correctly rounded
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - 2023 market size: 240 000 x 85 = \$20 400 000
> - 2025 market size: 288 000 x 95 = \$27 360 000
> - Change in market size: \$6 960 000
> - Percentage growth: 6 960 000 / 20 400 000 x 100 = 34.1%

> **[exam-tip]**
> Market size by value has two ingredients, and the question is only answered when both are used. Here customer numbers rose 20% and average spend rose about 11.8%, so quoting either figure alone understates the real growth badly. Multiply first, then compare; work out each year's total value, and only then calculate the change between them.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the usefulness of secondary market research to a business planning to launch a new luxury perfume.
parts.solutionMd:
Secondary market research can be useful to a business launching a new luxury perfume because it allows the business to quickly build an understanding of the market at low cost **[K]**. For example, the business could use industry reports to identify the size of the luxury perfume market, the main competitors, and the typical price range for premium scents **[Ap]**. This background information helps the business make initial decisions, such as what price bracket to target and which customer groups to focus on, without spending money on expensive primary research. For a new business with limited funds, this ability to gather large amounts of information cheaply is a significant advantage **[An]**

However, secondary research has clear limitations in this context. The data was not collected specifically for this business or this product **[K]**, so it may not tell the business how customers will react to its particular perfume. Luxury goods are heavily influenced by image, trends, and consumer emotions **[Ap]**, which change quickly  research from even a year or two ago may no longer reflect what premium customers currently value. If the business is entering a specific niche, such as sustainable or gender-neutral luxury perfumes, there may be very little relevant secondary data available at all **[An]**

Overall, secondary market research is useful as a starting point but is unlikely to be sufficient on its own for a luxury perfume launch **[E]**. Its value depends largely on the budget available - a business with limited funds may have to rely on it more heavily, while a well-funded business may quickly move to primary research such as focus groups or trials with target customers **[Ap]**. In most cases, the most effective approach would be to use secondary research to understand the broader market, and then use primary research to test customer reactions to the specific product before committing to a full launch **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Discuss the usefulness to a furniture retailer of using secondary market research when planning to enter a new market.
parts.solutionMd:
Secondary market research can be very useful to a furniture retailer in the early stages of planning to enter a new market. By accessing competitor data through published accounts and industry reports, the retailer can quickly identify the main players, their products, and their prices **[K]**. This helps assess whether there is a gap it could fill - for example, if no competitor currently offers affordable flat-pack furniture in the new area  **[Ap]**. Gathering this through secondary sources is fast and cheap, which is valuable before the retailer has committed to entering the new market **[An]**

However, secondary market research has important limitations in this context. The data was collected for a different purpose and may not reflect the specific preferences of customers in the new market **[K]**. Furniture styles and designs vary considerably between geographic regions and demographic groups **[Ap]**- a retailer entering a new country may find that data from its home market tells it little about local tastes. If the retailer is also targeting a new demographic, such as young professionals rather than families, existing industry data may not capture their specific needs or price sensitivity **[An]**

Overall, secondary market research is a useful starting point for a furniture retailer planning to enter a new market, but its value depends on how different the new market is from the retailer's existing one **[E]**. If the markets are similar - for example, a retailer expanding to a neighbouring region - secondary data may be largely adequate **[E]**. If the new market is significantly different in culture, income level, or customer demographics, secondary research alone is unlikely to be sufficient, and the retailer would need to invest in primary research to understand local customer preferences for furniture before making a final decision **[Ap]** **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Discuss whether a successful soft drinks business needs to continue to carry out market research.
parts.solutionMd:
Even a successful soft drinks business should continue to carry out market research, because consumer tastes in the soft drinks market are changing rapidly **[K]**. In recent years there has been a significant trend towards healthier drinks, with many consumers reducing their intake of sugar and artificial ingredients **[Ap]**. A business that stops researching risks missing these shifts and continuing to produce products that no longer match what customers want. For example, if a rival launches a popular low-sugar version of a similar drink and the business has no market research to alert it to this trend, it may lose loyal customers before it has time to respond **[An]**

However, there is an argument that a truly successful business - one with a strong brand, a loyal customer base, and consistent profits - may not need to carry out the same volume of market research as a new or struggling business **[K]**. Market research is expensive, and if the product range is well-established and sales are stable, the cost of regular large-scale primary research may not be justified by the insights it provides **[An]**

Overall, a successful soft drinks business should continue to carry out market research, but it may not need to do so at the same intensity as when it was first starting out **[E]**. The soft drinks market is too competitive and too fast-changing for any business to become complacent - a trend that is missed, such as the shift towards functional or health-focused drinks **[Ap]**, could significantly damage a business that was previously successful. That said, it could reduce the cost of its research by relying more on secondary sources **[E]**, such as industry reports and competitor analysis, and reserving expensive primary research for key decisions such as new product launches **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Saffron Kitchen**
> 
> Saffron Kitchen operates 12 restaurants in country D. It is considering adding a vegetarian menu across all sites. To test the idea, the marketing team surveyed 50 diners at one restaurant on a Friday evening; 68% said they would order from a vegetarian menu at least once a month.
> 
> Repeating the survey at all 12 restaurants across different days would cost \$9 000 and delay the launch by three months. The finance director argues the existing result is clear enough and that competitors are already adding vegetarian dishes. The marketing director argues that 50 diners at one site on one evening cannot represent all of Saffron Kitchen's customers.

Evaluate whether Saffron Kitchen should increase the size of its sample before launching the new vegetarian menu.
parts.solutionMd:
A sample is a small group selected from a larger population whose responses are used to represent that population **[K]**. Saffron Kitchen surveyed only 50 diners at one restaurant on a single Friday evening **[Ap]**. Friday evening diners may be a particular group, such as younger customers or those eating socially, whose tastes differ from weekday lunchtime customers **[An]**. If the 68% figure is not typical, Saffron Kitchen could redesign menus, retrain kitchen staff and buy new ingredients across every restaurant, only to find demand is far lower, wasting money at all 12 sites **[An]**

However, widening the sample would cost \$9 000 and delay the launch by three months **[Ap]**. Competitors are already adding vegetarian dishes, so a delay risks losing customers who switch to rivals and then stay with them **[An]**. A 68% response is also a strong result; even if the true figure were considerably lower, demand might still justify the menu, meaning the extra research would only confirm what Saffron Kitchen already believes **[An]**

Overall, whether Saffron Kitchen should increase its sample depends chiefly on the size of the commitment involved **[E]**. If the launch requires significant spending on equipment and training that cannot be recovered, \$9 000 is small by comparison and worth paying to avoid a costly mistake repeated across 12 restaurants **[E]**. If the menu can be introduced cheaply, a better approach would be to trial it in two or three restaurants first, which produces real sales data rather than stated intentions and avoids most of the three-month delay **[E]**. On balance Saffron Kitchen should not simply repeat the same survey; a small live trial answers the question more reliably and more quickly **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Copperleaf**
> 
> Copperleaf manufactures wooden furniture in country M and sells through independent retailers. It is considering selling directly to customers online.
> 
> Free government trade reports show that online furniture sales in country M grew by 22% last year. Copperleaf's marketing manager wants to commission primary research: a survey of 800 households and six focus groups, costing \$40 000 and taking four months. The managing director points out that the secondary data is free, already available and shows clear growth. Copperleaf's profit last year was \$310 000.

Evaluate whether Copperleaf should commission primary market research before deciding to sell directly to customers online.
parts.solutionMd:
Primary research is data collected first-hand by a business for its own specific purpose **[K]**. The government reports tell Copperleaf that online furniture sales grew by 22%, but not whether Copperleaf's own customers would buy directly from it rather than from a retailer **[Ap]**. That growth is industry-wide and may have been driven largely by big national brands with established delivery networks, so it could overstate the opportunity for a smaller manufacturer **[An]**. Primary research would also reveal what customers will pay online and whether they expect free delivery, which affects whether direct selling is profitable at all **[An]**

On the other hand, \$40 000 is around 13% of last year's profit of \$310 000, a substantial sum for Copperleaf **[Ap]**. The four-month delay may allow competitors to establish their own online stores first **[An]**. The secondary data is free and already points clearly in one direction, so Copperleaf might reasonably act on it and use the \$40 000 towards building the website instead **[An]**

Overall, the decision depends on how much of the uncertainty the secondary data actually removes **[E]**. It answers whether the market is growing, but not the two questions that determine profitability for Copperleaf specifically: whether its own customers will switch channel, and at what price **[E]**. Selling direct also risks damaging relationships with the independent retailers Copperleaf currently depends on, a risk no trade report can quantify **[E]**. Copperleaf should therefore commission primary research, but on a smaller scale than proposed; the six focus groups alone would surface the retailer relationship risk and likely price expectations at a fraction of \$40 000, keeping the delay short **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Redwing**
> 
> Redwing manufactures sports footwear in country F. It commissioned an agency to research a new running shoe. The agency surveyed 1 200 people at three city sports events. 74% rated the shoe 'good' or 'excellent' and 61% said they would pay \$85 for it. Redwing is considering investing \$600 000 in production.
> 
> The operations director has noted two concerns: everyone surveyed was already attending a sports event, and the shoe was shown only as a prototype in a single colour. Two weeks after the research finished, a rival launched a similar running shoe priced at \$70.

Evaluate the extent to which Redwing should rely on its market research findings when deciding whether to invest \$600 000 in the new running shoe.
parts.solutionMd:
Reliable data is information that can be trusted to represent the target market accurately **[K]**. Redwing's sample of 1 200 is reasonably large, but everyone questioned was attending a sports event **[Ap]**. These people are likely to be committed runners who buy specialist footwear often and will pay more for it, so the 61% who accepted \$85 may not reflect casual buyers **[An]**. Respondents also saw only a prototype in one colour, so their ratings may change once the finished range appears, meaning the 74% approval could fall **[An]**

More seriously, a rival launched a comparable shoe at \$70 two weeks after the research ended **[Ap]**. The willingness to pay \$85 was measured in a market where that cheaper alternative did not yet exist, so the finding is already out of date **[An]**. Customers who would pay \$85 with no comparison may not do so when a similar shoe sits alongside it \$15 cheaper, which directly threatens the revenue Redwing has assumed **[An]**

Overall, Redwing should treat the findings as useful but no longer sufficient **[E]**. The sample size is a genuine strength and the enthusiasm is real, so the research is not worthless; it establishes that a market exists **[E]**. However, the \$85 price is the single figure the \$600 000 investment depends on, and it is precisely the figure the rival's launch has undermined **[E]**. Redwing should therefore not rely on the research as it stands. A short follow-up study testing the shoe against the \$70 rival, and among general shoppers rather than event attendees, would cost a small fraction of \$600 000 and would test the one assumption that matters most **[E]**

> Tansy Foods produces pet food in country K. Its best-selling range competes mainly on low price. The marketing team surveyed 500 pet owners and asked which feature they considered most important when choosing pet food.
> 
> **Table 1: Feature ranked most important by pet owners in country K**

> | Natural ingredients | 22 | 35 |

Using Table 1, evaluate whether Tansy Foods should reformulate its pet food range to emphasise natural ingredients.
parts.solutionMd:
Table 1 shows how the features pet owners value have shifted between 2023 and 2025 **[K]**. Natural ingredients rose from 22% to 35%, overtaking price, which fell from 41% to 33% **[Ap]**. This suggests the basis of competition in Tansy Foods' market is changing, and a range built on low price is aligned with a feature that is becoming less decisive **[An]**. If the trend continues, the best-selling range could steadily lose appeal to competitors offering natural recipes, reducing sales volumes **[An]**

Costs per bag would rise by 18%, and the table gives no indication of how much extra owners would actually pay for natural ingredients; ranking a feature as important is not the same as paying more for it **[An]**

Overall, the table justifies taking the trend seriously but does not by itself justify reformulating the whole range **[E]**. Tansy Foods should therefore introduce a natural-ingredient product alongside the existing range rather than replacing it. This captures the growing 35% without abandoning the 33% who still put price first, and real sales would then reveal whether the trend translates into buying behaviour **[E]**

> Stonebridge Fitness operates fitness studios in country B and is considering entering a new region. Research shows the fitness market in that region grew by 14% last year and is forecast to grow by 9% next year.

Evaluate whether market growth is the most important feature Stonebridge Fitness should research before entering the new region.
parts.solutionMd:
Market growth measures the change in the total size of a market over a period of time **[K]**. The region's 14% growth suggests rising demand, which matters to Stonebridge Fitness because a growing market can absorb a new entrant without existing firms losing customers, making retaliation less likely **[Ap][An]**. Growth of 9% forecast for next year indicates the expansion is expected to continue rather than being a one-off, so studios opened now could fill over time **[An]**

However, growth alone does not show whether there is room for Stonebridge Fitness **[K]**. Three national chains already hold 71% of the market, leaving only 29% shared among everyone else **[Ap]**. These chains can use their scale to advertise heavily or cut membership prices, and two are already opening new sites, so much of the forecast growth may be captured before Stonebridge Fitness arrives **[An]**. The region also has one gym per 2 400 residents against one per 4 100 in the current region, suggesting provision is already far denser and the market may be closer to saturation than the growth figure implies **[An]**

Growth describes the size of the opportunity, whereas competitor strength and market saturation determine how much of it Stonebridge Fitness could realistically win **[E]**. A market can grow quickly while remaining unattractive to enter if established firms are expanding into that growth themselves, which is precisely what the two chains appear to be doing **[E]**. Stonebridge Fitness should therefore treat the density figure and the 71% concentration as the decisive evidence, and research how the existing chains would respond to a new entrant before committing to the region **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **way price elasticity of demand influences the pricing decisions of a business.
parts.solutionMd:
Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how sensitive the quantity demanded of a product is to a change in its price **[1]**. If a business knows that demand for its product is price elastic, it can use this information to decide to lower its price, knowing that the percentage increase in the quantity demanded will be greater than the percentage fall in price  **[1]**. This means that total revenue will rise as a result of the price reduction  **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how much the quantity demanded of a product changes in response to a change in price
> - If demand is price elastic (PED > 1), a given percentage change in price leads to a larger percentage change in quantity demanded; if demand is price inelastic (PED < 1), the change in quantity demanded is smaller than the change in price
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If a business knows its product has price inelastic demand - for example, because it is unique or has few close substitutes - it can raise the price knowing that the percentage fall in demand will be smaller than the percentage increase in price. As a result, total revenue will increase, which suits a business whose objective is to maximise profit; this approach is commonly used by luxury goods brands or businesses with a strong USP that customers are reluctant to give up
> - A business can use PED to determine whether reducing prices is likely to increase total revenue; if a business knows demand for its product is price elastic, it can reduce the price and expect demand to rise by a greater percentage, increasing total revenue and potentially gaining market share from competitors. However, if the business misjudges PED and demand is actually inelastic, the price reduction will lead to lower total revenue, meaning the pricing decision backfires
> - The way in which PED influences pricing also depends on the business's objectives; a business that wants to maximise revenue will make different pricing decisions from one that wants to maximise market share - PED helps the business predict the likely outcome of each approach and choose the price that best meets its goals
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'income elasticity of demand'.
parts.solutionMd:
Income elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded of a product is to a change in consumer income **[1]**. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Income elasticity of demand is the responsiveness of demand for a product to a change in consumers' incomes, found by dividing the percentage change in quantity demanded by the percentage change in income
> - Income elasticity of demand shows the extent to which the quantity of a product bought rises or falls when income changes, expressed as a numerical value
> - Income elasticity of demand is a measure of how sensitive demand for a product is to changes in consumer income, used to classify products as normal, luxury or inferior

> **[exam-tip]**
> With income elasticity, a negative answer is a finding, not a mistake. A negative value tells you the product is an inferior good, one that people buy less of as they get richer, such as a supermarket's cheapest own-brand range. Students often assume they have made an arithmetic error and quietly drop the minus sign, losing the very piece of information the calculation exists to give.

parts.solutionMd:
Income elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded of a product is to a change in consumer income **[1]**. Portland Appliances' premium range has an income elasticity of +2.4, which means it is a luxury good whose demand changes proportionally more than income does **[1]**. With incomes forecast to fall by 3%, demand for the premium range would be expected to fall by around 7.2%, so Portland Appliances should cut planned production of that range to avoid building up unsold stock and tying up cash in finished goods **[1]**

> 
> AO2

> - A 3% fall in income implies roughly a 7.2% fall in demand, allowing Portland Appliances to plan a specific reduction in output rather than guessing
> - Overproducing a luxury range in a downturn would leave unsold stock, tying up cash and storage space
> - Portland Appliances could shift capacity towards products with lower income elasticity, which would hold up better as incomes fall

> **[exam-tip]**
> When you are given an elasticity value, direction and size are two separate pieces of information and the marks usually sit in the size. Saying demand will fall uses only the plus sign. Multiplying the elasticity by the income change, here 2.4 by 3%, turns a vague statement into a usable figure of about 7.2%, which is what lets you say something concrete about production.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'promotional elasticity of demand'.
parts.solutionMd:
Promotional elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded of a product is to a change in spending on promotion **[1]**. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in promotional spending **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Promotional elasticity of demand is the responsiveness of demand for a product to a change in the amount spent promoting it, found by dividing the percentage change in quantity demanded by the percentage change in promotional spending
> - Promotional elasticity of demand shows by how much sales change when a business increases or reduces its promotional budget, expressed as a numerical value
> - Promotional elasticity of demand is a measure of how effective promotional spending is at generating additional sales of a product

> **[exam-tip]**
> Define the measure, not what its answer means. "Promotional elasticity tells you whether advertising is working" describes an interpretation and earns little; the definition needs to say what is being compared with what. Get the two percentage changes into your sentence first, and save the interpretation for questions that actually ask for it.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Juniper Air**
> 
> Juniper Air is a budget airline operating in country V. It must decide six months in advance how many aircraft to lease for the summer season, and once signed, the leases cannot be cancelled.

Explain **one** reason why sales forecasting is important for Juniper Air.
parts.solutionMd:
Sales forecasting is the process of estimating future sales, usually based on past data and expected market conditions **[1]**. Juniper Air must commit to leasing aircraft six months ahead of the summer season, and those leases cannot be cancelled once signed **[1]**. An accurate forecast allows it to lease the right number of aircraft, because leasing too many would mean paying fixed lease costs on planes flying with empty seats, while leasing too few would mean turning away passengers and losing revenue it could not recover later in the season **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Sales forecasting is the process of predicting future sales levels using past data and expected market conditions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Aircraft leases must be signed six months ahead and cannot be cancelled, so the decision is irreversible and must be right first time
> - Leasing too many aircraft means paying fixed costs on planes carrying empty seats, reducing profit
> - Leasing too few means turning away passengers, and a summer season cannot be repeated once missed
> - Forecasts also allow Juniper Air to plan crew recruitment and training in line with the number of aircraft it will operate
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks why forecasting matters to a particular business, look for what that business cannot undo. Forecasting is far more valuable where a commitment is fixed and expensive than where a decision can be reversed cheaply. Here it is the uncancellable six-month lease that makes the forecast matter, so build your answer around that detail rather than around forecasting in general.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Loxley**
> 
> Loxley manufactures gardening tools in country E. Its sales have been flat for three years. The marketing director has suggested collecting ideas for new products from Loxley's own repair department, which sees which tools are returned as broken and how they have failed.

Explain **one** benefit to Loxley of using its repair department as a source of ideas for product development.
parts.solutionMd:
Sources of ideas for product development include customers, employees, competitors and a business's own internal records **[1]**. Loxley's repair department sees at first hand which of its tools are returned as broken and the way in which they fail **[1]**. This gives Loxley evidence of specific design weaknesses that its own customers have actually experienced, so it can develop a more durable tool that solves a known problem rather than one based on guesswork, improving the chance that the new product sells and helping to lift sales that have been flat for three years **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Ideas for product development can come from customers, employees, competitors, research and development, or a business's own internal records
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The repair department sees which tools fail and how, giving evidence of real design weaknesses rather than assumptions
> - The information is already held inside Loxley, so it costs nothing extra to collect
> - Fixing a known fault addresses a problem customers have already met, making the improved product easier to market
> - Reducing the failure rate would also cut Loxley's repair and warranty costs, so the benefit is not limited to new sales
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Naming a source of ideas is the easy half; the marks come from saying what that source knows which others do not. A repair department is useful precisely because it sees failures that customers never bother to report and that sales figures cannot reveal. Whenever a question names a specific source, ask yourself what unique information sits there, and make that the centre of your answer.

MT sources many of its components from suppliers based in country L, where labour costs are significantly lower than in country K. A pressure group called EthicsWatch has recently published a report claiming that some of MT's suppliers in country L use poor working conditions and pay employees below the minimum wage. The report has received widespread media coverage in country K and has been shared extensively on social media.

Calculate the **price elasticity of demand (PED)** for the smart thermostat
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **PED = -1.5 (price elastic)**

`\% \text{ change in price} = \frac{72 - 80}{80} \times 100 = -10\%`

`\% \text{ change in quantity demanded} = \frac{57{,}500 - 50{,}000}{50{,}000} \times 100 = +15\%`

`\text{PED} = \frac{+15\%}{-10\%} = -1.5`

Evaluate the importance to FF of following the product development process before adding metal glasses frames to its product range.
parts.solutionMd:
Following the product development process is important for FF because launching metal frames represents a major step beyond its current capabilities **[K]**. FF has no experience making metal frames and lacks an R&D department,  both of which make the risk of failure significantly higher than for a business that already works with metal **[Ap] [An]**. The market research stage would help FF understand exactly what wholesalers and branded companies want from metal frames, including preferred designs, price points and quality standards, before FF invests in new equipment or staff. Without this information, FF risks designing and producing frames that do not match what its target customers actually need, leading to the same rejection problems it currently experiences with plastic frames **[An]**

Prototype development and product testing are also important for FF in this context. Manufacturing metal frames requires different machinery, cutting techniques, and finishing processes to plastic **[K] [Ap]**. If FF attempts to move straight to full production without testing a prototype, it may discover serious manufacturing problems only after significant capital has been spent **[An]**. Given that FF is already considering other major investments, including 3D printers and entry into the retail market **[Ap]**, wasting resources on a poorly planned metal frame launch could seriously harm the business's financial position **[An]**

Overall, following the product development process is very important for FF, precisely because metal frames are so different from its current products **[Ap]** **[E]**. The process provides a structured way of managing the risk of entering unfamiliar territory. However, its value depends on FF's directors making a genuine commitment to fund the process properly - particularly market research and testing - and accepting that the process takes time before revenue is generated **[E]**. If the budget is inadequate or directors push for a faster launch, the process will be incomplete, and the risk of failure remains high regardless of whether the steps are followed **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Brackenfield**
> 
> Brackenfield produces bottled fruit drinks in country P. Research carried out two years ago estimated the price elasticity of demand for its main product at -1.8. The marketing director wants to cut the price by 10%, expecting sales volume to rise by 18%.
> 
> Since that research was completed, two new competitors have entered the market with similar drinks, a government health campaign has discouraged consumption of sugary drinks, and Brackenfield has launched a reformulated low-sugar version of the product. Its factory is currently operating at 88% capacity.

Evaluate whether Brackenfield should rely on its price elasticity of demand estimate of -1.8 when deciding to cut its price by 10%.
parts.solutionMd:
Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price **[K]**. Brackenfield's estimate of -1.8 was produced two years ago **[Ap]**. Since then two competitors have entered, a health campaign has discouraged sugary drinks, and the product itself has been reformulated, so the conditions under which -1.8 was measured no longer exist **[An]**. If the true elasticity is now weaker than 1, a 10% price cut would raise volume by less than 10% and total revenue would fall rather than rise, which is the opposite of what the marketing director expects **[An]**

A second problem is capacity **[K]**. The factory is already running at 88% **[Ap]**. Even if the estimate proves accurate and volume rises by 18%, Brackenfield could not produce the extra output without investment, so it would have surrendered margin on every unit sold while still failing to supply retailers who expected more stock **[An]**. Losing shelf space to the two new entrants at that point would be difficult to reverse, because retailers rarely restore listings quickly **[An]**

Overall, Brackenfield should not rely on the estimate as it stands **[E]**. The figure is not worthless; a bottled drink facing several substitutes is plausibly price elastic, so the direction is probably right, and that alone is useful **[E]**. What cannot be trusted is the precise value, and it is the precise value the 10% decision depends on, since the difference between an elasticity of 1.8 and one of 0.8 decides whether revenue rises or falls **[E]**. Brackenfield should re-estimate elasticity using current data, or trial the cut in one region first, and settle the capacity question before any national price change, because a correct forecast it cannot supply would still damage the business **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ashcroft Solar**
> 
> Ashcroft Solar installs solar panels on homes in country Y. It forecasts sales using four-period centred moving averages drawn from five years of quarterly data. These show steady underlying growth and a strong seasonal pattern, with installations peaking in spring and summer.
> 
> The government has just announced that the subsidy paid to homeowners for solar installation will end in 18 months. The sales director argues the existing forecasting method is reliable because it is built on real data. The operations director argues that past data cannot capture the effect of the subsidy ending, and that the judgement of experienced installers should be used instead.

Evaluate whether Ashcroft Solar should continue to rely on time series analysis rather than qualitative forecasting when planning for the next two years.
parts.solutionMd:
Time series analysis uses past sales data to identify an underlying trend and seasonal variations in order to forecast future sales **[K]**. Ashcroft Solar has five years of quarterly data and uses four-period centred moving averages **[Ap]**. This smooths out the strong spring and summer peak and isolates the trend, letting Ashcroft Solar plan how many installers to employ in each quarter and how much stock to hold **[An]**. Because it rests on recorded installations rather than opinion, it is also free from the optimism or pessimism of individual managers, which makes it a defensible basis for committing to staffing levels **[An]**

However, time series analysis extrapolates from the past and assumes the future resembles it **[K]**. The ending of the subsidy in 18 months has no precedent within the five years of data **[Ap]**. It is likely to produce a surge of installations as homeowners rush to claim the subsidy before the deadline, followed by a sharp fall once it is withdrawn, and a moving average will predict neither **[An]**. Recruiting installers on the strength of the trend would leave Ashcroft Solar heavily overstaffed within two years, carrying wage costs against far lower demand **[An]**

Overall, the answer depends on the time horizon rather than on which method is better **[E]**. For the next twelve months the subsidy remains in place and the seasonal pattern still holds, so time series analysis stays the more reliable guide for quarter-by-quarter operational planning **[E]**. Beyond the deadline it becomes actively misleading, because it would project growth into a period when the main driver of demand has been removed **[E]**. The choice presented is therefore a false one; Ashcroft Solar should keep time series analysis for short-term planning and use qualitative judgement to estimate the size and timing of the surge and the drop, since the two methods answer different questions **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'marketing plan'.
parts.solutionMd:
A marketing plan is a document that sets out a business's marketing objectives and the actions it will take to achieve them **[1]**. It usually covers the resources available, the findings of market research and the marketing mix to be used **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A marketing plan is a written statement of a business's marketing objectives together with the resources, research and marketing mix it will use to meet them
> - A marketing plan sets out what a business intends to achieve through marketing over a period of time and how it will do so
> - A marketing plan is a document combining marketing objectives, an assessment of resources, market research findings and decisions on the marketing mix

> **[exam-tip]**
> Give the purpose, not just the format. Saying a marketing plan "is a document" tells the examiner what category it belongs to, not what makes it a marketing plan. parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Wensley**
> 
> Wensley produces handmade artisan cheese in country D. It sells through delicatessens at premium prices, and its brand is built on traditional methods. Wensley has been offered shelf space by a discount supermarket chain, which would require it to cut its price by 40% and use plain packaging.

Explain **one** reason why Wensley's marketing strategy should be consistent with its product and its market.
parts.solutionMd:
A marketing strategy is consistent when the product, price, promotion and place all match one another and suit the customers being targeted **[1]**. Wensley sells handmade cheese at premium prices through delicatessens, and its brand rests on traditional methods **[1]**. Selling the same cheese at a 40% lower price in plain packaging through a discount chain would contradict that positioning, and customers currently paying a premium may conclude the product was never worth it, damaging the delicatessen sales Wensley depends on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A consistent marketing strategy is one in which the elements of the mix match the nature of the product and the market it is aimed at
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A 40% price cut contradicts a premium positioning built on handmade, traditional production
> - Plain packaging removes the visual signals customers use to justify paying more
> - Existing delicatessen customers may switch to the cheaper outlet or lose confidence in the brand entirely
> - Delicatessens may drop Wensley if the same cheese appears at a much lower price elsewhere, costing it its established route to market
>

> "Consistent" is a relationship, so it always needs a second half. An answer saying Wensley's strategy "should be consistent" without naming what it must be consistent with has not yet said anything. Artificial intelligence is the use of computer systems to carry out tasks that would normally require human judgement, such as recognising patterns or making predictions **[1]**. In marketing it is used to analyse customer data and decide what each customer is shown **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'pan-global marketing'.
