parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Hartley Instruments**
> 
> Hartley Instruments makes guitars and violins in country R. It has never written a marketing plan, and decisions about promotion are taken by the owner month by month. Sales have grown, but the marketing budget was overspent by 30% last year.

Explain **one** benefit to Hartley Instruments of producing a marketing plan.
parts.solutionMd:
A marketing plan sets out a business's marketing objectives and the actions needed to achieve them **[1]**. Hartley Instruments currently makes promotional decisions month by month and overspent its marketing budget by 30% last year **[1]**. A plan would set out spending for the whole year in advance and link it to agreed objectives, so the owner could see when spending was running ahead of target and correct it during the year rather than discovering the overspend once it had already happened **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A marketing plan sets out marketing objectives and the actions, resources and marketing mix needed to achieve them
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Planned annual spending would allow the 30% overspend to be spotted and corrected during the year rather than after it
> - Month-by-month decisions leave no way of judging whether promotion is working; a plan gives objectives to measure against
> - A plan would coordinate promotion across guitars and violins rather than treating each decision separately
> - Written objectives make it easier to justify marketing spending as the business grows and more people become involved in decisions
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Where a spec point covers two halves, benefits and limitations, check which half the question wants before you write. A well-argued limitation earns nothing on a question asking for a benefit. Underline the key word in the stem, then make sure every sentence you write serves that word.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Vanta Telecom**
> 
> Vanta Telecom provides mobile phone services in country F. It holds records of how much data each of its 2 million customers uses, when they contact customer service, and which tariffs they have changed. Until now it has sent the same promotional offer to every customer.

Explain **one** way in which information technology could improve Vanta Telecom's marketing.
parts.solutionMd:
Information technology allows a business to collect, store and analyse large amounts of customer data **[1]**. Vanta Telecom already holds records of data use, service contacts and tariff changes for 2 million customers **[1]**. Analysing these records would let it identify which customers show signs of leaving, such as repeated service complaints, and send those customers a targeted offer rather than the same offer to everyone, retaining more customers for the same promotional spending **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Information technology enables a business to collect, store and analyse customer data to inform marketing decisions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Records of data use and tariff changes allow Vanta Telecom to group customers and target offers rather than promoting to all 2 million identically
> - Patterns in customer service contacts could identify customers at risk of leaving, so retention offers can be directed where they matter
> - Targeted promotion reduces waste, so the same marketing budget generates more response
> - Usage data could reveal demand for tariffs Vanta Telecom does not yet offer, informing product decisions as well as promotion
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Marks for technology questions sit in what the technology changes, not in what it is. Describing the systems a business owns is background; the examiner wants the decision it can now make that it could not make before. Move quickly from "it holds data" to "so it can do this specific thing differently".

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ivybridge Cards**
> 
> Ivybridge Cards designs and prints greeting cards in country M. Its home market is small and sales have been flat for two years. Around 70% of its cards carry no written message, only images.

Explain **one** reason why international marketing may be important for Ivybridge Cards.
parts.solutionMd:
International marketing means promoting and selling a product in markets outside a business's home country **[1]**. Ivybridge Cards operates in a small home market where sales have been flat for two years **[1]**. Because 70% of its cards carry images rather than written messages, they would need little adaptation to sell abroad, so overseas markets offer Ivybridge Cards a route to the growth its home market can no longer provide, and without the cost of redesigning most of its range **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - International marketing is the promotion and sale of products in markets outside the business's home country
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The home market is small and sales have been flat for two years, so growth must come from elsewhere
> - Cards carrying images rather than text need little translation or redesign, lowering the cost of entering new markets
> - Selling in several countries would reduce dependence on one small market and the risk that comes with it
> - Higher volumes across more markets could reduce printing costs per card through economies of scale
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Importance" questions are always importance to the named business, never importance in general. Anyone can write that international marketing increases sales. The marks come from why it matters to this firm in this situation, so anchor your answer in the flat home sales and the fact that most of the cards carry no words.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Redmoor**
> 
> Redmoor is a parcel delivery business in country T, considering expansion into one of two neighbouring countries.
> 
> Country J has a large population and fast-growing online shopping, but poor roads and no address system in rural areas. Country K is smaller and growing slowly, but has reliable roads and an established postal address system.

Explain **one** factor Redmoor should consider when selecting which international market to enter.
parts.solutionMd:
Selecting an international market involves comparing possible countries against criteria such as market size, growth and how easily the business can operate there **[1]**. Country J has a large population and fast-growing online shopping, but poor roads and no address system in rural areas **[1]**. For a parcel delivery business, being able to locate an address and reach it is essential, so the country offering the larger opportunity may be the one Redmoor is least able to serve, and failed deliveries would raise its costs and damage its reputation with retailers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Selecting an international market means assessing possible countries against criteria such as size, growth, competition and ease of operating there
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Country J's poor roads and missing rural addresses directly obstruct the service Redmoor sells, whatever the size of the market
> - Country K's reliable roads and address system would allow Redmoor to operate its existing model with little change
> - Fast-growing online shopping in country J represents genuine long-term potential if the delivery obstacles could be overcome
> - Failed deliveries damage relationships with the retailers who provide the parcels, not only with the end customer
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Selecting a market means rejecting one, so a strong answer says what would rule a country out, not only what makes one attractive. Here the larger, faster-growing market is also the harder one to serve. Showing that the two criteria point in opposite directions is what lifts an answer above simply listing what a business "should think about".

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Thornbury Paints**
> 
> Thornbury Paints manufactures paint in country W and wants to sell in country B. Paint is heavy and expensive to transport, and country B applies a 25% import tariff on manufactured goods. Thornbury Paints has limited capital and no knowledge of country B's regulations on chemical products.

Explain **one** factor that may influence the method Thornbury Paints uses to enter country B.
parts.solutionMd:
Methods of entering an international market include exporting, licensing, joint ventures and setting up production overseas **[1]**. Paint is heavy to transport and country B charges a 25% import tariff on manufactured goods **[1]**. Both raise the delivered cost of exporting from country W, so Thornbury Paints may find a joint venture or licensing arrangement with a producer inside country B more viable, since producing locally avoids both the tariff and the freight cost, and a local partner would already understand country B's chemical regulations **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Methods of entry include exporting, licensing, franchising, joint ventures and direct investment in overseas production
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The 25% tariff makes exporting expensive, favouring a method that involves producing inside country B
> - Paint is heavy relative to its value, so transport costs reinforce the case against exporting
> - Limited capital makes licensing or a joint venture more realistic than building a factory
> - No knowledge of country B's chemical regulations makes a local partner valuable, since compliance failures could stop sales entirely
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read carefully whether the question asks whether to enter a market or how to enter it. This one asks about the method, so arguments about whether country B is worth entering at all score nothing, however well made. Once you have spotted that, use the case details to push towards one method rather than another.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Everdon Games**
> 
> Everdon Games publishes board games in country S. In January it produced a detailed marketing plan for the year, setting out promotional spending quarter by quarter and a launch date of October for its main new game.
> 
> In March, a competitor announced a very similar game for release in June, and the cost of printed cardboard rose by 20%.

Explain **one** limitation of marketing planning for Everdon Games.
parts.solutionMd:
Marketing planning involves setting out marketing objectives and the actions needed to achieve them in advance **[1]**. Everdon Games wrote its plan in January, but by March a competitor had announced a similar game for June release and cardboard costs had risen by 20% **[1]**. A plan can only reflect the conditions expected when it was written, so keeping to the original October launch would let the competitor reach the market four months earlier, while the promotional budget set in January would no longer cover Everdon Games' higher costs **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Marketing planning sets out objectives and the actions, resources and marketing mix needed to achieve them, decided in advance
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The plan was written in January and could not anticipate the competitor's June release announced in March
> - A fixed October launch date would leave Everdon Games four months behind a very similar rival product
> - Promotional spending set quarter by quarter no longer reflects costs after a 20% rise in cardboard prices
> - Following a plan too rigidly can prevent a business responding to change, while abandoning it removes the benefit of having planned at all
> - Preparing a detailed annual plan takes management time, which is wasted if conditions change soon after it is written
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A limitation is not an argument against doing the thing at all. The examiner wants to see where marketing planning falls short, not a claim that Everdon Games should stop planning. Show the specific point at which the plan stops helping, here the moment its assumptions were overtaken, and you have identified a limitation rather than simply objecting to planning.

> **Brightside Tyres**
> 
> Brightside Tyres operates 40 tyre-fitting centres in country Q and wants to expand into country M. It is considering franchising: local businesspeople would run centres under the Brightside Tyres name, paying an initial fee and a share of revenue, and buying tyres from Brightside Tyres.

parts.solutionMd:
Franchising allows a business to expand by letting others trade under its name in return for a fee and a share of revenue **[K]**. The franchisees, not Brightside Tyres, fund the cost of opening and equipping each centre **[Ap]**. Because Brightside Tyres has limited capital, this lets it enter country M without borrowing heavily or diverting funds from its 40 existing centres **[An]**. parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ledbury Print**
> 
> Ledbury Print provides commercial printing in country F. It has repositioned itself as a fast-turnaround service, promising delivery within 48 hours, and its advertising emphasises speed.
> 
> However, its website quotes a standard lead time of seven days, its sales team offers discounts to customers who place orders four weeks in advance, and its two largest presses are 15 years old and break down roughly twice a month.

Analyse **two** problems that a lack of consistency in Ledbury Print's marketing strategy may cause.
parts.solutionMd:
A marketing strategy is consistent when the promise made to customers matches what the business actually delivers **[K]**. Ledbury Print advertises 48-hour delivery, yet its website quotes seven days and its main presses break down about twice a month **[Ap]**. Customers attracted by the speed claim will therefore find it is not met, and in commercial printing, where work is usually placed under deadline, a missed delivery causes the customer real disruption **[An]**. Because printing is bought through repeat contracts rather than one-off purchases, a single failure risks losing all that customer's future orders, not just the one job **[An]** A second problem is that Ledbury Print's own activities contradict one another **[K]**. Its sales team discounts orders placed four weeks ahead, which rewards precisely the long lead times the advertising is designed to move customers away from **[Ap]**. The advertising therefore pulls customers towards urgent work while the pricing pulls them towards planning ahead, so the two cancel out **[An]**. Ledbury Print ends up paying for advertising that attracts urgent orders and then discounting away the premium that fast turnaround should earn, leaving it with the cost of the repositioning but not the benefit **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

**Extract:**

**Pop Cool (PC)**

PC is a public limited company. Its head office is in Europe and it operates with centralised decision making. The company owns the Pop Cool brand name, logo and the distinctive bottle shape that is still used in some markets. PC operates its own bottling and canning factories in some countries. However, it also has joint venture agreements with packaging businesses in other countries. Much of the fruit and sugar used in producing the soft drinks is imported from African and Asian countries. 75% of PC’s sales and 90% of its profits are earned in the USA and Europe. The directors of PC are keen to develop other markets and other products so that the company becomes less dependent on a few key markets and products. Economic changes The economies of the USA and Europe have experienced very slow economic growth since 2008 – and some have even been hit by recession. Interest rates are very low as the monetary policy of these countries is aiming to boost demand. However, this has contributed to exchange rate depreciations of the US dollar and the European euro. Consumer spending has fallen due to declining real incomes. There are ageing populations in most of the countries where PC sells its products. A loss of competitiveness in many industrial sectors has resulted in rising unemployment. Statement of financial position valuations Since 2008 PC’s share price has fallen. This has been the trend for many public limited companies. PC’s Finance Director has been considering three changes that will affect PC’s accounts. He could make all three changes or just one or two of them. • When calculating depreciation of new production equipment bought last year for \$25m, use an estimated life of 8 years not 5 years. The equipment would still have an estimated residual value of \$3m. • Sell \$10m of property assets and lease them back at an annual leasing cost of \$1.5m. • Revalue the company’s intangible assets by 50%. He used an extract of PC’s most recent accounts to calculate what the impact of these changes might be on profit and gearing (see Appendix 1). Entering new markets – Africa and Asia Paul, PC’s Chief Executive Officer (CEO), has been discussing with the Marketing Director, Suzy, alternative marketing strategies the company could use to enter the rapidly expanding markets of Asia and Africa. They have different views. Paul stated that: ‘I think we should take over an existing soft drinks manufacturer in, for example, India or China. We would then have all of the production facilities and distribution channels through large supermarkets that we will need. The existing brand names could then be replaced with the Pop Cool brand which we would advertise very heavily for a short period. Consumers will be attracted to this because it is so popular elsewhere in the world.’ Suzy replied: ‘There could be local opposition to this globalised approach – although the marketing economies of scale will be substantial. I think we should develop a range of soft drinks to suit local tastes with brand names that reflect local language and culture. We could distribute these new drinks through small retail stores and street markets. This way we will slowly but steadily build up consumer awareness and loyalty.’

Workforce planning in country X Country X is one of PC’s biggest markets. The company fully owns all of the production facilities in this country and it has a large sales and marketing team too. PC employs 468 people in country X and labour costs are the company’s biggest expense in this country. The Human Resources department is under pressure from PC’s Head Office to reduce labour costs in country X by 15%. The business specialised in designing workplace environments that aim to improve productivity. Whilst working in the US, Amit observed the growth of co-working. Co-working provides office space and support services for businesses. It offers a flexible solution for businesses which need an alternative to traditional long-term leasing or ownership of office space. In 2018, using his knowledge and experience, Amit founded UBH, a private limited company. It is based in country W, where co-working is still a relatively new idea. UBH focuses on providing office space to entrepreneurs and small businesses as and when they demand it. UBH calls its co-working centres ‘beehives’. There are three shareholders in UBH, all of whom are directors. Amit owns 50% of the shares while the other two shareholders own 25% each. A difficult economic climate Until 2020, UBH’s expansion was rapid. This internal growth was mainly financed by bank loans. However, in 2020 UBH came close to failing. There was a recession in country W when economic output fell by 10%. Many of UBH’s small business customers became insolvent during the recession. UBH was left with significant unused capacity and almost no working capital. The government responded quickly to the recession and made the following changes to its economic policies: • increased investment in infrastructure including road and rail transport • reduced income tax • reduced central bank interest rates • delayed payment of business and property taxes. Amit believes that without these changes to economic policies UBH would have failed. Marketing strategy UBH’s marketing strategy has targeted entrepreneurs starting new businesses and small, established businesses. Each UBH co-working centre (beehive) provides customers with shared kitchen facilities and snack vending machines. Customers are offered flexible contracts from 1 day to 1 year. They can either lease a hot desk (any desk available that day), a dedicated desk (the same desk for the duration of the contract) or a private office. Customers can also rent meeting rooms of various sizes by the hour. All customers benefit from unlimited internet access and printing facilities.

Evaluate **two **changes that UBH could make to its current marketing strategy to increase sales and reach its target capacity utilisation.
parts.solutionMd:
One change UBH could make is to increase its use of informative social media promotion **[K]** specifically targeting business start-ups. Market research shows that most new start-ups are unaware of the benefits of co-working, yet this group is exactly the type of customer UBH has always targeted  **[Ap]**. Social media advertising is already UBH's most cost-effective marketing method, meaning that increasing the budget for targeted campaigns is likely to produce a strong return **[An]**. These campaigns should focus on educating potential customers about what co-working offers - flexible contracts, internet access, printing, and meeting rooms - rather than simply promoting UBH's brand. Raising awareness among this previously unreached segment could increase demand significantly and help UBH move from 80% to its target of 100% capacity utilisation **[Ap]** **[An]**

A second change is to develop premium facilities in selected beehives **[K]** to attract large businesses and multinationals. Market research shows that some larger businesses use co-working centres but demand higher specification facilities **[Ap]**. These customers would generate significantly higher revenue per booking than small businesses or start-ups **[An]**. However, this change carries risks - premium facilities require more space per desk, which would reduce the total number of desks available and potentially lower overall capacity utilisation in those beehives unless the higher revenue compensates **[An]**

Overall, the most effective change is the social media promotion strategy **[E]**, because it directly addresses an identified gap - start-up unawareness - at relatively low cost and builds on a method already proven to work for UBH **[Ap]**. The premium facilities option could complement this in the longer term, but needs significant capital investment at a time when UBH is already planning major expansion **[Ap]**. UBH should prioritise promotion first, and consider targeted premium development once its expansion plans are more established and cash flow is stronger **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘cost-based pricing’.
parts.solutionMd:
Cost-based pricing is a method of setting the selling price of a product by first calculating the total cost of producing or supplying it **[1]** and then adding a fixed amount or percentage on top to ensure the business makes a profit **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Cost-based pricing is a method of setting prices where a business calculates its total costs of production and then adds a fixed amount or percentage on top in order to make a profit
> - Cost-based pricing involves working out the cost of producing or supplying a product and then adding a mark-up to arrive at the selling price
> - A pricing method in which the selling price is determined by adding a profit margin to the cost of producing or providing a good or service

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Child Play (CP) **
> 
> Su is a sole trader who started a business called CP which operates a play area for children. The play area is inside a building and includes toys and other play equipment. Customers book on CP’s website for each hour that they would like to use the play area. CP is two kilometres away from the nearest city which has a large population. Su does not pay for any promotion and she relies on recommendations and reviews from previous customers.
> 
> Su currently charges a price of \$10 an hour for a group of up to 5 children. Only one group can book CP for each hour. Demand is greater than supply so Su may increase the price to \$15 per hour. She has completed some market research to see if this is a good idea. Her findings are in Table 1.1.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Market research about prices for CP**
> 
> | **Price** | **Quantity (hours) demanded per day** |
> |---|---|
> | \$10 | 10 |
> | \$15 | 6 |
> 
> Su is also thinking about expanding the business by opening a café targeted at parents with children.
> 
> The café would be located at the entrance to CP’s play area. There are many other cafés in the city centre two kilometres away. Su believes that product differentiation is essential for the profitability of the café.
> 
> Su plans to use CP’s working capital as the source of finance to open the new café. The café will need to earn revenue quickly, so she plans to open it in four weeks. She will need quick and low‑cost promotion methods if the café is to succeed.

Explain the term ‘product differentiation’.
parts.solutionMd:
Product differentiation is the process of making a product or service appear different from those offered by competitors, in order to make it more attractive to a specific group of customers **[1]**. For Su's café, the most significant differentiating factor is its location at the entrance to CP's play area - parents can sit in the café and remain close to their children while they play, which no city centre café two kilometres away can offer **[1]**. This unique feature gives parents a strong reason to choose CP's café over other options, which could justify a higher price and help Su achieve the profitability she believes is essential for the café to succeed **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Product differentiation is the process of making a product or service stand out from competitors by giving it distinctive or unique features that appeal to a target market
> - It involves highlighting what makes a product different from both competitors' products and a business's own existing products
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Su could differentiate the café by offering a child-themed menu - for example, fun-shaped food or drinks named after toys and games - which would make it more appealing to parents with young children than a standard city centre café, giving parents a specific reason to choose CP's café over the many other cafés two kilometres away in the city centre, and helping Su to build a loyal customer base and improve the profitability of the new café
> - Su could differentiate the café by creating a safe, child-friendly environment - for example, with low seating, soft furnishings, and a calm atmosphere - that city centre cafés cannot easily replicate; parents who visit CP's play area are likely to value the convenience of a café designed specifically for them, making them more willing to spend money there rather than travelling further to a city centre café (2 marks)
> - Su could use product differentiation to charge a higher price for the café than competitors in the city centre, if customers feel the experience is unique and worth paying more for - this would increase CP's revenue per customer and contribute to the profitability of the café, which Su believes is essential for the new venture to succeed

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **disadvantage to a business of using price discrimination.
parts.solutionMd:
Customers who are charged a higher price may discover that others are paying less for the same product **[1]**. For example, if two customers compare what they paid and find they were charged different amounts, the customer who paid more is likely to feel that they have been treated unfairly. This can seriously damage the business's reputation  **[1]**- customers who feel cheated are unlikely to return, and may share their negative experience with others through reviews or word of mouth **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - If any two sets of customers have contact, there is a possibility that they will discover that they are being charged different prices and therefore their custom might be lost.
> - It might result in a loss of trust in the business if customers feel that they have been misled.
> - The administration might be complex in order to ensure that the price charged is the price agreed.
> - There is a possible loss of profit if the business agrees to sell to one set of customers cheaper than to others.

As demand grew for the bags, Hannah took on a partner, her brother Kwom. They both agreed to keep the name ‘Hannah’s Handbags’ as it is an established, reputable and widely recognised brand.
> 
> HH operates from a small workshop and showroom. Customers are encouraged to visit the showroom to discuss design and materials with either Hannah or Kwom.

The new market has many more competitors, with 15 large businesses and many small ones. The bags would have to be priced competitively. Kwom estimates that this new venture would require additional finance of \$350000. Explain the term ‘viral marketing’.
parts.solutionMd:
Viral marketing is a method of promotion where a business creates content, such as a video, image, or post, that people share with others through social media and online networks **[1]**. This approach is well-suited to HH launching its new batch-produced bags online, as the new market has many competitors and bags will need to be priced competitively, leaving limited funds for expensive advertising **[1]**. parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Super Heroes (SH) **
> 
> SH is a leisure (theme) park aimed at 10–18 year olds. It is owned by two companies, X and Y, which started SH as a joint venture. Company X owns many leisure centres and swimming pools. Company Y owns many brands based on superheroes.
> 
> SH employs 200 full-time workers and an extra 50 seasonal workers during the busiest times of the year. The park has 10 large rides which take up 2km<sup>2</sup> of land. There are also many smaller rides, restaurants, toilets and shops. The price of an entrance ticket is \$11 per customer. Table 1.1 shows the costs for SH in 2019.
> 
> **Table 1.1: SH costs for 2019**
> 
> | Total fixed costs (per year) | \$12m |
> |---|---|
> | Variable costs (per customer) | \$3 |
> | Total costs | \$42m |
> 
> One of the larger rides at SH is the Iron Blaster. The number of customers who use this ride has decreased each year for the last three years. This has led the management of SH to consider its options for internal growth.
> 
> *Option 1 – A new virtual reality (VR) ride* 
> This option would involve developing the Iron Blaster into a VR ride. Most of the structure of the Iron Blaster could be used but customers would be given a VR headset to wear during the ride. The cost of developing the VR ride would be \$2m. The Iron Blaster ride would be closed for a three month period during the off-peak season for the development to be carried out. No employees would be made redundant or dismissed.
> 
> *Option 2 – A new hotel *
> SH does not currently have a hotel. It could demolish the Iron Blaster to provide the space to build one. Many of the competitors of SH have a hotel near or within their leisure parks. Hotel customers would pay a high price for a room but have free access to the leisure park’s facilities. Market research suggests that the average hotel customer would spend twice as long in the leisure park than a non-hotel customer. The cost of developing the hotel would be \$15m and take a year to build. All of the employees currently working on the Iron Blaster ride would face redundancy or dismissal.

Explain **one **way in which SH could increase the sales of entrance tickets.
parts.solutionMd:
SH could run a targeted promotional campaign on social media platforms popular with 10–18 year olds, such as Instagram or TikTok **[1]**. SH's target market spends a significant amount of time on these platforms, so a well-designed campaign - for example, featuring video content of the rides or behind-the-scenes footage - could reach a large number of potential visitors at relatively low cost **[1]**. Increased awareness of SH among its core age group would be likely to drive more visits and increase the number of entrance tickets sold, particularly if the campaign highlights new attractions such as the proposed VR ride **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
>

> 
> AO1
> 
> - SH could reduce the price of entrance tickets
> - SH could develop new or improved rides to attract more visitors
> - SH could sell tickets through additional distribution channels
> - SH could invest in promotion to raise awareness and attract more customers
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Reducing the price of entrance tickets from \$11 could attract more price-sensitive customers, particularly given competition from other leisure parks; if demand is price elastic, the increase in the number of customers would more than offset the lower price per ticket, increasing SH's total revenue
> - Developing the Iron Blaster into a VR ride would give SH a new attraction that could generate significant interest among its target market of 10–18 year olds; the novelty of a VR experience is likely to attract new visitors and encourage previous customers to return, increasing ticket sales without the need to reduce prices
> - Selling tickets online or as advance-purchase packages - for example, discounted family or group deals - would make it easier for customers to buy tickets and could attract new types of visitor; this would increase accessibility to SH's target market and could boost ticket sales, particularly during off-peak periods when the park has spare capacity
>

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Electric Cars (EC) **
> 
> EC is a public limited company producing electric cars. Market research suggests that electric cars are in the early stage of the product life cycle. The demand for electric cars is likely to increase substantially in the next 10 years. EC is based in country X, where it is one of three electric car manufacturers. However, other manufacturers could start to produce electric cars if the forecast market growth is correct.
> 
> EC’s promotion has only been aimed at high income groups. The government of country X recently announced that it will support the use of electric cars. This will help EC to achieve its objective to increase sales volume by 50% over the next two years.
> 
> One year ago, EC invested \$10m in new production facilities. The investment was funded by a long-term bank loan. Interest payments on the bank loan have reduced EC’s profit margin from 9% to 4%. EC will need to cut unit costs through increased efficiency.
> 
> EC initially launched its cars using a price skimming strategy but sales growth has been slow. If EC can achieve a 50% growth in sales over the next two years, it will be in a strong financial position. This means it will be able to spend more on the development of a larger product portfolio of electric cars.
> 
> Jancie, the Finance Director, has produced forecasts for EC’s financial data over the next two years, as shown in Table 2.1.
> 
> **Table 2.1: Extract from EC’s forecast financial data**
> 
> |   | **2020 (\$m)** | **2021 (\$m)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Inventories | 30 | 50 |
> | Cash | 10 | 20 |
> | Trade receivables | 10 | 20 |
> | Trade payables | 25 | 30 |
> | Current ratio | 2 | **X** |

Explain the term ‘product life cycle’.
parts.solutionMd:
The product life cycle describes the stages a product goes through from the time it is first launched until it is eventually taken off the market- introduction, growth, maturity and decline **[1]**. EC's electric cars are currently in the introduction stage - sales growth has been slow, which is common at this point as customer awareness is still building **[1]**. As the market grows over the next 10 years, EC expects to move into the growth stage, where sales are expected to rise substantially **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The product life cycle describes the stages a product passes through from when it is first launched onto the market until it is eventually withdrawn
> - The typical stages are introduction, growth, maturity and decline - at each stage, sales, profits, and appropriate marketing strategies are different
> 
> AO2
> 
> - EC's electric cars are currently in the introduction stage of the product life cycle, as market research confirms they are at an early stage; at this point, sales are typically slow and costs are high as the business works to build awareness among customers; EC's slow sales growth reflects this - demand has not yet reached the levels needed to fully cover the \$10m investment in new production facilities, which is why EC's profit margin has fallen from 9% to 4%
> - As electric cars are expected to move into the growth stage over the next 10 years, EC anticipates a substantial increase in demand; understanding where the product sits in its life cycle helps EC plan ahead - for example, by investing in new facilities now and planning to expand its product portfolio, so it is well-positioned to benefit from the rapid sales growth expected during the growth stage
> - During the introduction stage, it is common for businesses to target early adopters with higher prices; EC's use of price skimming aimed at high-income groups is consistent with this stage of the product life cycle - as the product moves into growth and maturity, EC may need to lower prices or change its promotional strategy to attract a wider range of customers and achieve its target of 50% sales growth
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **reasons why a business might use a price skimming strategy.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason a business might use price skimming is to take advantage of its first-mover position in the market before competitors arrive **[K]**. When a business launches a genuinely new product, it may be the only seller of that product for a period of time - there are no close substitutes available **[Ap]**, so customers who want the product must pay whatever price the business sets. By charging a high price during this window, the business maximises its profit per unit sold **[An]**. Once competitors begin to enter the market with similar products, the business can gradually lower its price to remain competitive, but by then it will have already generated significant revenue from early sales at the premium price **[An]** A second reason is to capture the consumer surplus from early adopters - customers who are particularly enthusiastic about a new product and are willing to pay a much higher price than average consumers **[K]**. For example, technology enthusiasts often pay a premium to be among the first to own a new smartphone or games console **[Ap]**. These customers have a low price elasticity of demand; they will buy the product at a high price because they place a high value on being first **[An]**. A business that sets a lower launch price misses the opportunity to capture this extra willingness to pay, leaving money on the table. By starting high and reducing the price over time, the business earns more total revenue across all stages of the product's life cycle than it would by charging a single lower price from the start **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

by setting a high price at launch, the business generates a large contribution per unit sold, allowing it to pay back its investment before the product reaches the later stages of its life cycle; this is particularly important if the R&D costs were very high - for example, in the pharmaceutical or technology industries - where recouping investment quickly is essential to fund the development of future products > - If the demand for a product is price inelastic among its target customers, meaning customers are not very sensitive to price - a high price will not significantly reduce the number of units sold; a business can therefore charge a premium and still achieve strong sales, maximising revenue per unit; this is typical of products with unique features or limited availability, where customers feel they have no close alternative and are willing to pay more to get the product they want > - A high launch price positions the product as premium and exclusive in the minds of consumers; parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Great Resources (GR) **
> 
> GR is a business partnership that creates educational resources. It sells direct to schools and teachers via its own website.
> 
> Sanjay, Rukmal and Boris are entrepreneurial teachers who formed the GR partnership. One year ago, they identified a gap in the market to supply interactive, digital resources. GR’s website is subscription only. An online marketing campaign, which used penetration pricing, attracted 250 subscribers in the first six months of operation. The start-up costs were financed with a \$5000 bank overdraft, which is GR’s only debt.
> 
> Reviews for GR’s products in teaching journals are positive but cash flow is poor. Many customers have taken advantage of a recent sales promotion for one month’s free membership and posted positive reviews. Unfortunately, few have then taken out a regular subscription.
> 
> As revenue has not increased as much as the entrepreneurs had hoped, they must now consider alternative promotion methods. They have researched possible promotion methods and decided to advertise in an educational newspaper. The newspaper has a readership of half a million people.
> 
> Expert Materials (EM) is a large national company that also advertises in the newspaper. EM is GR’s closest competitor. The EM brand is well-known and trusted in the educational resources market. Table 1.1 shows some marketing data.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Marketing data**
> 
> |   | **GR** | **EM** | **Total market** |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Revenue (\$000) | 15 | 300 | 500 |
> | Number of customers | 300 | 5000 | 7000 |
> | Annual advertising spend (\$000) | 7.5 | 45 | 60 |

Evaluate whether price or promotion is the most important element of GR’s marketing mix.
parts.solutionMd:
GR's use of penetration pricing attracted 250 subscribers in six months, which suggests price does influence customers in the educational resources market **[Ap] [E]**. However, the recent sales promotion offering one month's free membership generated positive reviews but very few regular subscriptions. This indicates that while a low price can attract trial users **[K]**, it is not enough on its own to convert them into paying long-term customers. The fact that GR holds only 300 of the 7,000 customers in the total market - compared to EM's 5,000 **[Ap] **- suggests that price alone is not solving GR's fundamental challenge of winning and keeping customers **[E]**

Promotion is likely to be more important than price for GR at this stage **[E]**. EM has a well-known and trusted brand, and many schools and teachers will default to buying from an established supplier rather than searching for alternatives **[An]**. GR's reviews in teaching journals are positive, which shows the product quality is good - the problem is that most potential customers do not know GR exists. Advertising in an educational newspaper with a readership of 500,000 **[Ap] **could dramatically increase GR's brand awareness and bring it to the attention of decision-makers in schools who have never considered it as an option **[An]**

Overall, promotion is currently the more important factor **[E]**, because the evidence suggests GR's product is well-regarded - the barrier is awareness, not price **[Ap]**. Once more schools and teachers know about GR, the competitive price of its subscription is likely to be a strong selling point compared to EM. However, GR must also ensure its promotional spending is sustainable; it currently spends 50% of its revenue on advertising **[Ap]**, which contributes directly to its poor cash flow. GR needs promotion that builds awareness cost-effectively, such as targeted advertising in teaching journals, rather than broad campaigns that may not reach its specific audience **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
‘The most effective way for a loss-making retail clothing business to survive is to change the price element of its marketing mix.’

Discuss whether you agree with this statement.
parts.solutionMd:
Reducing prices could help a loss-making retail clothing business attract more customers **[K]**, particularly if it is losing sales to cheaper competitors. The retail clothing market is highly competitive - businesses such as H&M, Zara, and ASOS **[Ap] **compete aggressively on price, and customers who are price-sensitive may have switched to a cheaper rival. If demand is price elastic, a price reduction would increase sales volume by more than enough to compensate for the lower margin per item, raising total revenue and helping the business cover its costs **[An]**. In the short term, a price reduction is also one of the quickest changes a business can make, which matters for a business that needs to survive **[An]** However, changing the price alone is unlikely to be sufficient if the clothing range itself is unfashionable or fails to meet what customers want. Fashion trends change quickly, and customers in the retail clothing market have many alternatives **[Ap]**. A business selling outdated styles at a lower price will still struggle to attract customers **[K] **who can buy on-trend clothing from larger, well-resourced retailers. In this case, changing the product range - introducing new styles, better quality materials, or a more focused niche - would be a more effective strategy than cutting prices, because it addresses the root cause of why customers are not buying **[An]** Changing the place element of the marketing mix may also be more effective than changing price for a loss-making business. Many physical retail clothing stores carry very high fixed costs **[K] **- rent, rates, and shop floor staffing make up a significant proportion of total costs. Moving to an online-only model, or significantly reducing the number of physical stores, could lower these fixed costs substantially **[An]**. This directly improves the profit picture without requiring any change to prices, and also extends the business's reach to customers who do not live nearby **[An]** Overall, while changing price may help a loss-making retail clothing business in certain circumstances - particularly where price competition is the main problem - it is not the most effective strategy in all situations **[E]**. For many loss-making clothing retailers, the problem is high costs rather than low revenue **[Ap]**, in which case changing the place strategy (moving online) would deliver faster results **[E]**. parts.problemMd: Explain the link between corporate objectives and marketing objectives of a business.
parts.solutionMd:
Marketing objectives are set to help a business achieve its corporate objectives **[1]**. Corporate objectives are broad, business-wide goals that cannot be achieved by one department alone - they must be broken down into smaller, specific targets for each department **[1]**. The marketing department's targets are designed to contribute directly to the overall goal **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Corporate objectives are the overall goals of the whole business, such as survival, profit maximisation, or revenue growth — they set the direction for every department
> - Marketing objectives are the specific targets set for the marketing department, such as increasing market share, building brand awareness, boosting sales, or developing customer loyalty
> - Both types of objective are usually expressed in measurable, time-bound terms (e.g. increase market share by 5% within two years)
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Marketing objectives are derived from corporate objectives — they break the overall business goal down into specific targets that the marketing function is responsible for delivering
> - Corporate and marketing objectives must be aligned; if they point in different directions, the marketing department's activities will not help the business achieve its overall goals
> - Without marketing objectives that support the corporate objectives, the marketing budget may be spent on activities that do not contribute to what the business is ultimately trying to achieve
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

>   - Risk spreading
>   - Exposure to new ideas
>   - Avoiding a saturated domestic market

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **possible benefits to a business of increasing its market share.

One benefit of increasing market share is that it allows a business to benefit from economies of scale **[K]**. This spreads fixed costs, such as factory rent and management salaries, across more units, reducing the cost of producing each one **[An]**. A well-known brand builds trust with customers, making them more likely to choose it over less familiar competitors without needing to be convinced by large amounts of advertising **[An]**. This customer loyalty means the business can rely on repeat purchases, which makes its revenue more stable and reduces the cost of constantly finding new customers **[An]**. For example, if the objective is to attract families, the team can focus on affordable pricing and child-friendly events at the ground **[An]** However, other factors may be more important. Having enough financial resources is critical to any launch **[K]**. Starting a new women's football team requires significant investment - player wages, a ground, kit and marketing costs all need to be paid for **[Ap]**. Without sufficient funding, even well-written marketing objectives cannot be acted upon. Financial backing from investors, sponsors, or local authorities is therefore an essential foundation before any launch strategy can be put into practice **[An]** The quality of the team itself **[K] **also matters greatly. Marketing can attract first-time fans to a match, but if the standard of football is poor, those fans will not return **[Ap]**. parts.problemMd: Evaluate the importance of market share to a business operating in a competitive retail market.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason market share is important in a competitive retail market is that a higher share often allows the business to benefit from economies of scale **[K]**. As a business sells more units, it can buy in larger quantities and negotiate lower prices from suppliers than smaller competitors can. Lower costs allow the business to either reduce its prices to attract more customers, or maintain prices and earn higher profit margins **[An]**. In a competitive retail market where customers are sensitive to price **[Ap]**, this cost advantage can be decisive - a business with a large market share is better placed to undercut rivals and win sales **[An]**

Market share also reflects the relative strength of a business against its competitors **[K]**. A large market share usually means the business is well-known to customers, making it the first choice when they decide where to shop **[Ap]**. This brand recognition makes it easier to retain loyal customers without spending heavily on marketing **[An]**. However, the importance of market share is not the same for every retail business. A niche retailer - for example, one selling premium organic food **[Ap]** - may have a small market share but still be highly profitable, because its customers are willing to pay higher prices and are less likely to switch to cheaper alternatives **[An]**

Overall, market share is an important measure for most businesses in a competitive retail market **[E]**, but its significance depends on the business's objectives and the nature of the market. For a large retailer competing on price - such as a supermarket **[Ap]** - a high market share is crucial because it underpins the cost advantages that allow the business to stay competitive. For a smaller niche retailer, profitability and customer loyalty may matter more **[E]**. In highly competitive retail markets, gaining market share is likely to be closely linked to long-term success, but it should be seen as a means to an end rather than an objective in itself **[E]**

> **[case-study]** > **Benjamin’s Beds (BB) ** > > Benjamin’s Beds (BB) is a large manufacturer of beds and has a strong brand image for quality. Its main channel of distribution is through the producer market (B2B) to national hotel chains. Recently, BB has also entered the consumer market (B2C) by selling online direct to customers. > > BB uses flow production. BB’s existing machinery is old and cannot satisfy the increased demand. The directors of BB have decided its existing machinery needs replacing. Table 2.1 shows data for existing and proposed new machinery. > > **Table 2.1 Data for existing and proposed new machinery** > > | | Variable cost per unit
(\$) | Output per year | > |---|---|---| > | Existing machinery | 50 | 5000 | > | New machinery | 40 | 7500 | > > Fixed costs are \$500 000 per year. Using new machinery would reduce this by 10%. > > BB sales data suggests that its market share is growing rapidly. The consumer market (B2C) is becoming more important to BB because online orders are increasing. However, online demand is for a wide range of bed styles. The consumer market requires a substantial marketing budget and some retraining of employees. > > Orders from national hotel chains in the producer market (B2B) are for a more limited range of bed styles. These orders remain constant with low marketing costs. However, BB is increasingly under pressure to reduce prices to hotels. > > BB uses non-financial motivators and until recently had a motivated workforce. Efficiency is falling due to employees having to work longer hours because of increased demand. This is decreasing staff morale and welfare. Recommend whether BB should focus on the producer market (B2B) or the consumer market (B2C). Justify your recommendation.
parts.solutionMd:
BB could focus on the consumer market **[K]**. Online orders are increasing and BB's market share is growing rapidly **[Ap]**, and its strong brand image for quality matters far more to individual consumers than to hotel buyers, who are pressing BB to reduce its prices **[An]**. Selling direct also removes the bargaining power of the national chains, so BB would keep more of the value it adds instead of surrendering it in price negotiations **[An]**. However, consumer demand is for a wide range of bed styles, which sits badly with flow production, and BB would need a substantial marketing budget and staff retraining at a time when efficiency and morale are already falling **[E]**

BB could instead focus on the producer market **[K]**. Orders from hotel chains are for a limited range of styles and remain constant, which is exactly what flow production needs **[Ap]**. Running the new machinery at its full 7500 beds would cut total cost per bed from \$150 to \$100, because the same \$750 000 of total cost is spread across 50% more output **[An]**. That \$50 saving on every bed is what would allow BB to absorb the hotels' pressure on price and still widen its margin **[An]**. However, constant orders mean no growth, and depending on a few national chains that are already pushing prices down leaves BB badly exposed if one of them goes elsewhere **[E]**

I recommend that BB focus on the producer market **[E]**. The decisive point is that BB has just committed to new flow production machinery, and flow production delivers its cost advantage only when it runs long, uninterrupted batches of a limited range **[E]**. Chasing the variety the online market wants would mean frequent changeovers, so BB would never reach the 7500 beds on which the fall to \$100 depends, and would have paid for capacity it could not use **[Ap]**. The workforce position points the same way, since efficiency and morale are already falling and the consumer market would add retraining and marketing demands on top **[E]**. BB should not abandon B2C, which is growing and suits its brand, but should keep it as a secondary channel offering a deliberately narrow range of styles until the new machinery is running efficiently and the pressure on staff has eased **[E]**

parts.solutionMd:
One advantage to GT of renting the theatre to visiting groups, other than increased revenue, is that it can help improve GT's cash flow **[1]**. The case states that GT already experiences cash flow problems even though each performance makes a profit. Visiting groups pay GT 50% of their ticket revenue, and this income is likely to be received at a different time to GT's own performances **[1]**. This means GT has an additional, potentially more regular, source of cash coming into the business throughout the month, which could help GT manage its cash flow problems more effectively **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** impact on employees of a business operating under maximum capacity.
parts.solutionMd:
Operating under maximum capacity means a business is producing below the level its resources allow **[1]**. If this continues, the business may not need all of its workforce, so employees may face reduced hours or redundancy **[1]**. The resulting uncertainty can lower motivation and prompt the most employable staff to leave for more secure work, so the business loses experienced workers it will need again once demand recovers **[1]**

> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks

> 
> AO1
> 
> - Operating under maximum capacity means output is below what the business's resources could produce
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Reduced hours or redundancies become likely if under-utilisation persists
> - Job insecurity lowers motivation and productivity among remaining staff
> - The most employable workers leave first, so the business loses its strongest people
> - Recruiting and retraining when demand recovers is costly and slow
> - Quieter periods do allow time for training or maintenance that a busy business cannot fit in
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** implication for a business of operating at full capacity.
parts.solutionMd:
One implication for a business of operating at full capacity is that it is unable to increase output to meet any extra demand **[1]**. Since the business is already producing the maximum amount possible with its current resources, it cannot fulfil unexpected orders or a sudden rise in customer demand. This could mean the business has to turn potential customers away, resulting in lost sales that it cannot recover **[1]**. If this happens regularly, customers may become frustrated and take their business to a competitor instead, which could damage the business's reputation and reduce its future sales **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Unable to increase output to meet additional demand.
> - Risk of overstretching resources, leading to quality problems.
> - Opportunity to maximise revenue and spread fixed costs over maximum output.
> - May need to consider expanding capacity.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Unable to meet additional demand because the business is producing at its maximum, it cannot fulfil unexpected orders or increases in demand without turning customers away, which may result in lost sales and could damage relationships with customers who take their custom elsewhere.
> - Risk of overstretching resources - pushing machinery and staff to their limit for a sustained period increases the risk of breakdowns, staff fatigue or errors, which could lead to a fall in the quality of output and increased costs from reworking or rejected items.
> - Maximises revenue/spreads fixed costs because fixed costs are spread across the maximum possible number of units produced, operating at full capacity lowers the average fixed cost per unit, which can increase profitability; however, this leaves no spare capacity if demand rises further.
> - May need to expand capacity - consistently operating at full capacity may signal that current demand exceeds what the business can supply, so it may need to invest in additional capacity, such as new machinery or premises, to avoid permanently losing sales to competitors.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks by listing several implications rather than fully developing one. The command word "explain" means you need to go beyond identification - show the chain of reasoning by linking the implication to its effect on the business. A useful structure is: state the implication, then use connective phrases such as "this means that..." or "as a result..." to build your explanation. Make sure your explanation clearly relates back to the concept of full capacity, not just general business issues.

> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mechanism here is that fixed costs do not shrink when output does. Answers saying costs "go up" without explaining why rarely reach the third mark. Name the fixed costs, point out that they continue regardless, and the rise in cost per unit follows logically.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** problem for a business of operating over maximum capacity.
parts.solutionMd:
Operating over maximum capacity means a business is producing beyond the level its resources are designed to sustain **[1]**. Machinery is run for longer without maintenance and staff work extended hours, which increases the risk of breakdowns, fatigue and mistakes **[1]**. Defective output must then be scrapped or reworked, which adds cost and can mean orders are delivered late, damaging the business's reputation with the very customers whose extra demand caused the pressure **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Operating over maximum capacity means producing beyond the level resources can sustain
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Machinery run without maintenance breaks down more often, halting production entirely
> - Staff working extended hours become fatigued, so error rates and accidents rise
> - Reworking or scrapping defective output adds cost and consumes further capacity
> - Late delivery damages relationships with customers gained during a period of high demand
> - Overtime payments raise labour costs per unit even though output has increased
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Operating at full capacity and operating over it are different situations, and only one of them is a problem. At full capacity a business is efficient but inflexible; beyond it, resources are being pushed past what they can sustain. Make clear in your first sentence which of the two you are writing about.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** method a business could use to improve its capacity utilisation.
parts.solutionMd:
Capacity utilisation can be improved either by raising output or by reducing the maximum capacity available **[1]**. One method is to rent out unused premises or equipment to another business **[1]**. This generates income from resources that would otherwise sit idle and reduces the effective capacity the business is measured against, so utilisation rises without the business needing to find extra demand of its own **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Capacity utilisation improves when output rises relative to maximum capacity, or when maximum capacity falls
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Renting out spare premises or equipment earns income from idle assets and reduces effective capacity
> - Promotional activity or price reductions can raise demand and therefore output
> - Producing under another firm's brand name fills spare capacity without competing with existing sales
> - Rationalisation, such as closing one site, cuts maximum capacity so the remaining sites run fuller
> - Subcontracting work in from other businesses uses spare capacity during quiet periods
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are two routes to better capacity utilisation and most answers only ever use one. Raising output is the obvious one; reducing capacity is the other, and it is often the realistic choice when demand simply is not there. Showing you know both directions exist is a quick way to stand out.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** impact of outsourcing on a business.
parts.solutionMd:
Outsourcing is when a business pays another business to carry out an activity it would otherwise perform itself **[1]**. The specialist provider often produces at lower cost because it operates on a larger scale across many clients, so the business's own costs fall **[1]**. However, the business no longer controls that activity directly, so if the provider's quality slips or it delivers late, the business must answer to its own customers for a failure it did not cause and cannot immediately fix **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Outsourcing means paying an external business to carry out an activity previously done in-house
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Specialist providers operating at scale can perform the activity more cheaply than the business itself
> - Outsourcing frees management time and capital to focus on the core activity
> - Direct control over quality and timing is lost, and problems take longer to correct
> - The business remains accountable to its own customers for work it no longer performs
> - Redundancies among staff who previously did the work can damage morale among those remaining
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The saving and the loss of control are two sides of the same decision: the work is cheaper precisely because someone else is now doing it. Strong answers make that connection explicit rather than treating cost and control as unrelated points. Follow the consequence through to the customer, who still holds the business responsible.

**Fashion Frames plc (FF) **

FF makes plastic frames for glasses (spectacles) in a factory in country W, in South East Asia. FF sells its plastic frames to wholesale businesses that market well-known brands of plastic frames which they sell globally. The wholesalers reject 7% of the frames supplied by FF because of substandard quality. The FF design team create dynamic styles based on the demands of the wholesalers. Meeting delivery times is very important. FF only delivers 85% of its sales on time. FF needs to improve this percentage. Improving quality Chang, the production manager, aims to reduce the high level of rejects by the wholesalers. He has identified a number of factors which make this difficult including: • employees know that rejected frames can be recycled • production targets are very difficult to meet • problems with suppliers of raw materials • breakdowns with machinery. Chang proposes introducing Total Quality Management (TQM). He thinks this will reduce the number of substandard frames and improve FF’s delivery times. Chang forecasts successful implementation of TQM will also increase output by 10% and average variable cost will fall by 5%. However, Chang is aware that there may be problems with TQM and forecasts can be inaccurate. Table 1 shows information on FF’s output, costs and prices, before TQM is implemented. Table 1: FF’s output, costs and prices Year ending September 2021 Maximum capacity 16 million frames Actual output 14 million frames Average variable cost \$20 Average selling price \$40 Communication challenges FF has a centralised organisational structure with a low degree of delegation. Directors make decisions, department managers plan how to implement these and supervisors give instructions. Employees have little responsibility or control. FF has provided good pay, good conditions of work and security of employment. However, employees are aware that the directors are considering significant changes to working conditions. All employees find it difficult to discuss this with their line managers. Many employees work alone so information is passed on informally and often inaccurately. This uncertainty has begun to lead to dissatisfaction, complaints, higher absence rates and lower productivity. Privatisation of electricity and water industries In country W, state-owned businesses supply all electricity and water. Prices of services in these industries have risen at above the rate of inflation for the last three years. Buying 3D printers 3D printers that make frames for glasses as part of a CAD/CAM process are becoming available. There is no way of accurately estimating their value after four years. The directors have told Chang that an acceptable accounting rate of return (ARR) is 5%. Chang thinks new 3D printers will increase FF’s long-term profitability. The 3D printers will result in significant reductions in employee costs and waste and substandard reject costs. Maintenance and training costs will, however, increase. Table 2 and Table 3 show some of Chang’s research. He knows competitors are considering buying them. Product development and marketing The marketing manager is concerned that FF relies only on specific orders from wholesalers for plastic frames. He proposes that FF should use product development to design and manufacture metal glasses frames. These would be marketed to wholesalers and directly to businesses who sell glasses with globally recognised brands. FF would have to acquire new skills and equipment in order to design and manufacture metal frames. The marketing manager visited international trade fairs and found that several competitors have research and development (R&D) departments. Strategic choice: enter the Asia Pacific retail market The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) states: ‘My strategic analysis shows that FF must continue with the current business model but should take a new direction as well. My strategic choice is that FF should enter the retail glasses market in the Asia Pacific region. This will mean selling our own glasses in retail shops. We will need to work closely with lens manufacturers. Increased eye strain and higher disposable income are driving the increasing demand for higher value glasses.
