**Jan Guiding Service (JGS) **

Jan loves being in the countryside. Many years ago, he visited country P, where mountains take up 80% of the land area. Country P is one of the poorest countries in the world, with very low income per head. Jan made his home there and took a job assisting with walking groups. He gained a certificate as a professional mountain walking guide. The start of JGS Five years ago Jan set up JGS, in partnership with Gorl, another professional mountain walking guide. JGS offers mountain walking tours. JGS organises and promotes these tours. Originally, Jan and Gorl guided most of the walking tours themselves. JGS has always outsourced all its travel and accommodation. Jan and Gorl are spending more time on managing the business and less time guiding as the demand for JGS tours increases. JGS now outsources most of its mountain guiding. Customers stay with host families in mountain villages, most of which cannot be reached by road. Host families are paid by JGS to provide food and accommodation for its customers. Many families compete to provide these services to JGS. Using outsourcing in this way gives JGS many benefits. JGS employs an administrator to organise outsourcing. JGS is one of the few businesses operating in this market. However, Jan knows that other businesses are becoming interested in offering mountain walking tours. Demand for JGS services JGS has not increased its prices for three years. Over 95% of JGS customers are visitors from country K. Demand for JGS tours is increasing and Jan thinks that income levels in country K are an important factor. Average income in country K rose by 5% in 2019. Demand for JGS tours from residents of country K increased by 20% in the same period. Jan currently believes that there is still time to get more bookings for quarters 3 and 4 in 2020. He also knows that increasing the effectiveness of the JGS Internet presence is important. Gorl has analysed sales figures for the last three years. Table 1 shows his results. He has used the moving average method and has forecast the centred moving average (trend) sales figure for Quarter 3 2021 of \$86560.

Table 1: Sales figures for JGS Year Quarter Sales (\$000) Centred moving average (Trend) (\$000) Seasonal variation (\$000) 2017 3 34 4 78 2018 1 40 41.5 –1.5 2 10 45.0 –35.0 3 42 48.0 –6.0 4 98 50.0 48.0 2019 1 44 52.25 –8.25 2 22 56.75 –34.75 3 48 62.0 –14.0 4 128 64.25 63.75 2020 1 56 2 28 Increasing the number of employees – need for clearer organisational structure? Jan and Gorl are planning to increase the number of employees for two main reasons: • The rapid growth of JGS means that three regional managers and additional administrative employees will be needed. • The government of country P has introduced new, stricter employment regulations. It has stated these will apply to all businesses. This now means that businesses using outsourcing must insist that outsource providers keep to these stricter employment regulations. Jan and Gorl think that providing guiding and accommodation services through direct employment of workers is the best way of meeting these requirements. They are unsure whether to offer flexible temporary contracts or part time permanent positions. Jan suggested to Gorl that: ‘Our rapidly expanding business and external environment changes mean that a clear effective organisational structure will be very important.’ Jan wishes to keep control and is reluctant to give responsibility to employees who might not be reliable. He added: ‘Centralising decision making enables rapid decisions and is key to success. We must have authority and make employees accountable to us.’ Gorl replied: ‘Employees can be trusted to take decisions. They are closer to the problems and find solutions faster. Delegation is essential for success.’ They think JGS might need a marketing department. This would be responsible for the planned increase in marketing activities necessary to maintain expansion.

Costing each tour Gorl and Jan have different views on the minimum number of customers needed before each tour can take place. This is because they have different views about how to deal with the fixed and variable costs. JGS policy is to provisionally confirm that a tour will take place once customer numbers reach six. The business then hopes to get at least two more customers before the tour starts. However, Jan now thinks that a tour should go ahead with just two customers. Gorl is not happy about this. They discuss the financial information in Table 2. Table 2: Cost and price information (\$) Fixed costs per tour: administration, marketing, guide, transport 550 Variable costs per customer: accommodation, food 370 Price per customer 480 Corporate social responsibility issues JGS has a business model based on attracting customers who wish to experience the culture of people who live in country P’s high mountains. Jan and Gorl are aware that this culture is under threat from too many tourists, cheap souvenir production, corruption and increasing environmental damage. JGS tries to operate to the highest standards, which can result in high costs. However, other businesses do not. Consequently, there is irresponsible forestry, litter, inappropriate payments by tourists, bribes for local authorities and businesses not paying villagers a fair price for services. Pressure groups in country K and country P are increasing their demands that tourist businesses provide for the needs of the various communities in country P. Some customers might be willing to pay higher prices to ethical and responsible travel businesses. The government in country P has set up an official enquiry into the corporate social responsibility of the tourism industry. Additional opportunities for growth Jan and Gorl are always aiming to expand JGS. They are enthusiastic about the future and are considering two growth options. They know it is very important to make an assessment of the risk involved in each option.

Option 1: a partnership with KrazyTours Jan has held initial talks with KrazyTours; a large multinational tourist operator that is considering expanding into country P. KrazyTours is only interested in a partnership with a business already operating. In effect this would be a franchise agreement. > **[case-study]**
> **Ashmore Glass**
> 
> Ashmore Glass manufactures glass bottles and jars in country R, supplying drinks producers and food manufacturers. It operates its own fleet of 22 lorries and employs 34 drivers.
> 
> **Table 1: Ashmore Glass distribution data**
> 
> |   | **2023** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Distribution cost as % of revenue | 8.1 | 11.4 |
> | Average lorry utilisation per journey (%) | 71 | 58 |
> | Deliveries made on the agreed date (%) | 96 | 94 |
> | Number of drivers | 30 | 34 |
> 
> A national logistics company has offered to take over all of Ashmore Glass's distribution for a fixed fee equivalent to 8.5% of revenue. It would guarantee delivery within two days, but not on a specified date. Ashmore Glass would sell its lorries, and the 34 drivers would be made redundant.
> 
> The Finance Director, Priya Nadar, argues the offer would cut distribution costs immediately and release the capital tied up in an increasingly underused fleet.
> 
> The Sales Director, Tom Ackley, disagrees. Several of Ashmore Glass's largest customers run just-in-time production and specify exact delivery dates, and he believes recent contracts were won partly on the company's on-time record. He also questions whether an outside provider would handle fragile glass as carefully.
> 
> Ashmore Glass must respond within a month.

Evaluate whether Ashmore Glass should outsource its distribution to the national logistics company.
parts.solutionMd:
Outsourcing means paying another business to carry out an activity previously done in-house **[K]**. Ashmore Glass's distribution costs have risen from 8.1% to 11.4% of revenue, while the logistics company would charge 8.5% **[Ap]**. That is an immediate saving of almost three percentage points of revenue, and it removes a cost that has been rising steeply **[An]**. Lorry utilisation has also fallen to 58%, so Ashmore Glass is running half-empty vehicles; a national operator combining loads across many clients would not, which is precisely why it can charge less **[An]**

However, the provider guarantees delivery only within two days, not on a specified date **[Ap]**. Customers running just-in-time production hold almost no inventory, so a delivery arriving a day early or late is a serious problem for them rather than a minor inconvenience **[An]**. If those customers are among the largest, losing even one could cost more revenue than the 2.9 percentage points saved on distribution **[An]**

Overall, whether Ashmore Glass should outsource depends on whether the date problem can be solved rather than on the cost saving **[E]**. The saving is certain, immediate and addresses a genuine deterioration, so doing nothing is not attractive either **[E]**. The risk, though, is concentrated in a few large JIT customers, and concentrated risks are exactly the ones that damage a business badly rather than gradually **[E]**. Ashmore Glass should therefore treat guaranteed delivery dates for its JIT customers as a condition of the contract, and if the provider will not agree, outsource only its general deliveries while retaining a small fleet for those accounts **[E]**

> **[case-study]**
> **Whitlow**
> 
> Whitlow is a commercial laundry in country F, washing linen for restaurants, care homes and gyms. It operates two sites.
> 
> **Table 1: Whitlow site data, 2025**
> 
> |   | **Site A (Elmhurst)** | **Site B (Portway)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Maximum capacity (tonnes of linen per week) | 90 | 60 |
> | Actual output (tonnes per week) | 74 | 26 |
> | Capacity utilisation (%) | 82 | 43 |
> | Fixed costs per week (\$) | 11 000 | 9 500 |
> | Distance from Site A (km) | - | 55 |
> 
> Site B opened four years ago to serve a growing hotel market, but two large hotel customers have since closed. Site B employs 14 people, several of whom have been with Whitlow since it opened.
> 
> The Operations Director, Sam Reilly, proposes closing Site B and transferring its work to Site A, which has spare capacity.
> 
> The Managing Director, Nadia Okonjo, is reluctant. Site B's remaining customers are all within 20 km of Portway and may not accept longer delivery times from Elmhurst. She also notes that a new business park near Portway is due to open next year.

Evaluate whether Whitlow should close Site B in order to improve its capacity utilisation.
parts.solutionMd:
Capacity utilisation is the proportion of maximum possible output a business is actually producing **[K]**. Site B runs at only 43% while carrying fixed costs of \$9 500 a week **[Ap]**. Closing it would remove those fixed costs entirely and concentrate output at Site A, raising utilisation there and lowering the average cost per tonne across the business **[An]**. Since Site B's under-utilisation is caused by customers who have permanently closed rather than by a temporary dip, waiting for that capacity to fill again may simply prolong the loss **[An]**

However, the proposal does not work as stated **[Ap]**. Site A has maximum capacity of 90 tonnes and already produces 74, leaving only 16 tonnes spare, whereas Site B handles 26 tonnes **[An]**. Transferring all the work would exceed Site A's capacity by 10 tonnes a week, so Whitlow would either have to invest in expanding Site A or turn away roughly 40% of Site B's business, losing the revenue that closure was meant to protect **[An]**

Overall, Whitlow should not close Site B on the terms proposed **[E]**. The financial logic is sound in principle, but it rests on an assumption about spare capacity that the figures contradict, and a decision that costs 10 tonnes of weekly business is not a saving **[E]**. The customers within 20 km of Portway compound this, since some would likely leave rather than accept a 55 km delivery distance **[E]**. Whitlow should instead pursue customers from the new business park to fill Site B, and revisit closure in twelve months if utilisation has not improved, by which point it would also know whether expanding Site A is affordable **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Perrin Storage**
> 
> Perrin Storage operates refrigerated warehouses in country M, storing frozen food for producers and supermarkets.
> 
> **Table 1: Perrin Storage data**
> 
> |   | **2024** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Capacity utilisation (%) | 91 | 98 |
> | Storage requests refused (pallets) | 2 400 | 9 100 |
> | Energy cost as % of total costs | 34 | 41 |
> | Equipment breakdowns per year | 7 | 19 |
> 
> Perrin Storage is considering building a third warehouse at a cost of \$4.2 million. It would take 18 months to complete and increase total capacity by 45%.
> 
> The Operations Director, Elena Vasquez, argues the business is turning away too much work, and that breakdowns have risen because the existing refrigeration plant runs continuously with no time for maintenance.
> 
> The Finance Director, Hugo Bram, is cautious. Two of Perrin Storage's three largest customers are on contracts due for renewal within two years, and a competitor has announced its own new facility 30 km away.

Evaluate whether Perrin Storage should build the third warehouse.
parts.solutionMd:
Operating close to or above maximum capacity means a business has little or no slack in its resources **[K]**. Perrin Storage's utilisation has risen from 91% to 98%, and refused storage requests have almost quadrupled from 2 400 to 9 100 pallets **[Ap]**. That refused business is revenue going directly to competitors, and customers turned away once may not return **[An]**. Breakdowns have also risen from 7 to 19 a year because refrigeration plant runs continuously with no maintenance window, and in cold storage a breakdown risks the customer's stock rather than merely delaying it **[An]**

However, \$4.2 million is a large commitment against uncertain demand **[Ap]**. A competitor is opening a facility 30 km away, which may absorb precisely the demand Perrin Storage is currently refusing **[An]**. Two of its three largest customers are also up for renewal within two years, so a substantial share of existing demand is not secure either; the warehouse could open into a market that has both gained a competitor and lost a major customer **[An]**

Overall, the operational case is stronger than the demand case **[E]**. Rising breakdowns are a present and worsening cost that will damage customer relationships whether or not demand grows, so some investment in capacity or maintenance capability is needed regardless **[E]**. The demand justification, by contrast, rests on refused pallets that a nearby competitor may shortly be able to serve **[E]**. Perrin Storage should therefore secure renewal of its two major contracts before committing, and consider a smaller facility that relieves the maintenance problem without betting \$4.2 million on demand it may not hold once the competitor opens **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business might choose to hold low levels of inventory.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason a business might hold low levels of inventory is to avoid the risk of items going out of fashion **[1]**. If a business buys or makes a lot of inventory that customers no longer want, this stock cannot be sold, and the money spent on it is wasted **[1]**. By holding low levels of inventory, the business reduces the amount of stock it could be left with if demand changes suddenly, which lowers this financial risk. This is especially useful for products where trends change quickly, such as clothing or technology **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
>

> 
> AO1
> 
> - Items can go out of fashion, becoming unsold or unused
> - Storage space might be limited
> - Storage conditions need to be suitable to prevent deterioration or damage
> - The business might use a just-in-time (JIT) approach
> - A new business might not be able to afford to hold high levels of inventory
> - The business might carry out specialised work for which there is low demand
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Going out of fashion - if items go out of fashion, the money spent on producing or buying them cannot be recovered through sale, so the business avoids tying up too much cash in stock that could become worthless.
> - Limited storage space - if a business only has a small amount of storage space, it physically cannot hold large amounts of inventory, so it must keep stock levels low to fit within the space available.
> - Storage conditions/damage risk - holding stock for longer increases the risk it will deteriorate or become damaged, so keeping inventory low reduces the amount of stock exposed to this risk and limits potential losses.
> - Just-in-time (JIT) - under JIT, items are made or obtained only when needed for a specific order, so the business avoids the cost of storing and financing stock it does not immediately need.
> - New/small businesses - a new business often has limited start-up capital, so it may not have enough cash to buy and store large amounts of inventory until it becomes more established.
> - Specialised, low-demand work - if demand for the business's product is low or irregular, holding large stock levels would tie up money in inventory that is not used quickly.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Quality Furniture (QF) **
> 
> QF is a public limited company in country S. It manufactures furniture for cafés. The number of cafés in country S has increased by more than 50% over the last 5 years. This has meant that QF has been able to expand and achieve internal economies of scale. However, the growth of the café market has attracted new firms supplying café furniture and increased competition for QF.
> 
> An extract from QF’s income statement is shown in Table 1.1.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Extract from QF’s income statement for 2020**
> 
> |   | \$m |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue | 300 |
> | Cost of sales | 120 |
> | Gross profit | 180 |
> | Expenses | 150 |
> 
> Although QF has been successful so far, Javid, the Managing Director, has identified two problem areas: inventory and human resources.
> 
> **Inventory **
> 
> QF’s inventory includes raw materials, work in progress and finished tables and chairs. QF buys 80% of its materials from country T and there is a long delivery lead time. This means that QF holds a high level of buffer inventory which has a high value.
> 
> **Human resources **
> 
> QF’s production employees are unhappy that they have not received any benefit from the company’s expansion. Profit has doubled over the past three years but employees have not received any pay increases or bonuses. The employees have all been trained by QF and have specialist skills which had ensured that customer expectations were met. However, customers are starting to complain about a fall in the quality of the furniture, which could be the result of the low morale of the employees. Some highly trained employees have left QF to work for competitor firms.

Define the term ‘buffer inventory’.
parts.solutionMd:
Buffer inventory is the minimum level of stock that a business chooses to hold in reserve at all times **[1]**, so that it can continue to meet customer orders even if there are delays or disruptions in the supply of new stock **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The (minimum) level of stocks/components/supplies – a business aims to hold to ensure orders can be met/point at which business re-orders
> - Buffer inventory is the reserve level of stock at which a business re-orders more supplies, held to prevent production or sales being disrupted
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd: Explain why it is important for a manufacturing business to manage its inventory effectively.
parts.solutionMd:
Inventory management means controlling the stock of raw materials, part-finished goods and finished products a business holds, making sure it has the right amount at the right time** [1]**. If a manufacturing business manages this well, it avoids running out of raw materials and stopping production** [1]**, while also avoiding holding too much stock, which ties up money and increases storage costs. This helps the business keep production running smoothly while keeping its costs as low as possible** [1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Inventory management is the process of ordering, storing, using and controlling a business's stock of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods, ensuring the right level of stock is held at the right time.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If a manufacturing business holds too little inventory, it risks running out of raw materials or components, which can halt the production line completely - this leads to lost output, missed delivery deadlines, and potentially lost customers
> - If a manufacturing business holds too much inventory, money is tied up in stock that could otherwise be used elsewhere in the business (e.g. investment or reducing debt), and the business faces higher storage, insurance and security costs
> - Poor inventory management can also lead to stock becoming obsolete, damaged or spoiled (particularly for perishable materials or fast-changing product designs), meaning the business has to write off the cost of that wasted stock, reducing profit
> - Effective inventory management, such as using techniques like just-in-time, helps a manufacturing business keep production running smoothly while minimising the cash tied up in stock - improving both efficiency and cash flow
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'supply chain management'.
parts.solutionMd:
Supply chain management is the process of overseeing the flow of materials, information and finished goods from suppliers through to the final customer **[1]**, in order to keep costs down and deliveries reliable **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Supply chain management is the coordination of every stage from raw material supplier to end customer, so that goods move efficiently and at acceptable cost
> - Supply chain management involves selecting, monitoring and working with suppliers and distributors so that materials and products arrive when required
> - Supply chain management is the planning and control of the movement of goods and materials through all the stages between supplier and customer

> **[exam-tip]**
> A supply chain has two ends, and a definition that mentions only suppliers has covered half of it. The term includes everything through to the final customer, which is why distribution and delivery belong in your answer as well as purchasing. Make sure your sentence travels the whole length of the chain.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Aldworth Carpets**
> 
> Aldworth Carpets manufactures carpets in country N. It buys wool from four suppliers based in three different countries. Last year one of those suppliers delivered late on three occasions, halting production for a total of nine days.

Explain **one** reason why supply chain management is important for Aldworth Carpets.
parts.solutionMd:
Supply chain management is the process of overseeing the flow of materials from suppliers through to the customer **[1]**. Aldworth Carpets buys wool from four suppliers across three countries, and late deliveries from one of them halted production for nine days last year **[1]**. Managing the chain more closely, for example by monitoring supplier reliability and agreeing a reserve, would reduce the chance of production stopping again, so Aldworth Carpets could meet customer orders on time rather than paying wages and factory costs for nine days while machines stood idle **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Supply chain management is the coordination of the flow of materials and goods from suppliers through to the final customer
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Nine days of halted production means fixed costs continue while no output is produced
> - Using four suppliers in three countries multiplies the points at which a delay can occur
> - Monitoring supplier reliability would let Aldworth Carpets identify the weak supplier and replace or supplement it
> - Late delivery to Aldworth Carpets' own customers risks losing contracts, since carpet is often bought to a fitting date
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For "why is this important" questions, the quickest route to the marks is to say what goes wrong without it. Here the case has done the work for you by supplying nine lost days. Name the failure, then follow it to a cost the business actually bears, and the importance proves itself.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 're-order level'.
parts.solutionMd:
The re-order level is the level of inventory at which a business places a new order for more inventory **[1]**. It is set high enough to cover expected demand during the lead time, before the new delivery arrives **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The re-order level is the quantity of inventory remaining at which a fresh order is triggered, calculated to last until the replacement delivery arrives
> - The re-order level is the point on an inventory control chart at which new stock must be ordered to avoid running out
> - The re-order level is the minimum inventory a business allows itself to reach before ordering more, based on usage during the lead time

> **[exam-tip]**
> The re-order level is a trigger, not an amount ordered. It tells a business when to order, while the order quantity tells it how much. Candidates frequently define one and are marked for the other, so make sure your sentence contains the idea of a point at which ordering happens.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Medlock**
> 
> Medlock supplies medical consumables to clinics in country B. Its inventory control chart for surgical gloves shows a maximum inventory level of 8 000 boxes, a re-order level of 3 000 boxes, buffer inventory of 1 000 boxes and a lead time of two weeks.
> 
> Demand has recently risen from 500 boxes per week to 900 boxes per week.

Explain **one** change Medlock should make to its inventory control following the rise in demand.
parts.solutionMd:
An inventory control chart shows the maximum inventory level, the re-order level, the buffer inventory and the lead time **[1]**. Medlock's re-order level of 3 000 boxes was set when demand was 500 boxes a week, so a two-week lead time used 1 000 boxes; at 900 boxes a week the same wait now consumes 1 800 boxes **[1]**. Medlock should therefore raise its re-order level, because at the current level inventory would fall through the 1 000-box buffer before the delivery arrived, leaving clinics without gloves they rely on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - An inventory control chart plots inventory over time, showing the maximum level, re-order level, buffer inventory and lead time
> 
> AO2
> 
> - At 900 boxes a week, a two-week lead time consumes 1 800 boxes, against 1 000 when demand was 500 a week
> - The existing 3 000-box re-order level no longer leaves enough to cover the wait without cutting into the buffer
> - Raising the buffer inventory would give further protection if demand rises again
> - Ordering more frequently, or finding a supplier with a shorter lead time, would reduce the quantity that must be held
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question gives you a lead time and a rate of demand, multiply them before you write anything else. That single calculation, here two weeks at 900 boxes, tells you how much stock the wait swallows and immediately shows whether the current re-order level still works. The arithmetic is the answer; the sentences just explain it.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'Just in Case'.
parts.solutionMd:
Just in Case is an inventory management approach in which a business deliberately holds extra inventory **[1]**, so that it can keep producing or supplying customers if demand rises unexpectedly or a delivery is late **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Just in Case is an approach to inventory in which a business holds spare stock as protection against unexpected demand or supply problems
> - Just in Case involves keeping inventory above the minimum needed, accepting higher storage costs in return for greater security of supply
> - Just in Case is the opposite of Just in Time; stock is held in reserve rather than arriving only as it is required

> **[exam-tip]**
> The name of this method contains a question the definition has to answer: just in case of what? A sentence saying a business holds extra stock has not yet earned the second mark. Name the thing being insured against, whether a late delivery or a sudden rise in demand, and the definition becomes complete.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Frostfield**
> 
> Frostfield produces ice cream in country V. Demand more than triples during the summer months. It is considering moving to Just in Time delivery of cream and packaging, with daily deliveries from a supplier 200 km away.

Explain **one** risk to Frostfield of adopting a Just in Time approach.
parts.solutionMd:
Just in Time means inventory arrives only as it is needed, so very little is held **[1]**. Frostfield's demand more than triples in summer and its supplier is 200 km away, delivering daily **[1]**. If one delivery were delayed by traffic or a vehicle breakdown at the height of the season, Frostfield would have almost no cream or packaging in reserve and would have to stop production at exactly the point when its sales are highest, losing revenue that cannot be recovered once the summer has passed **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Just in Time is an approach in which inventory arrives only as it is needed, so minimal stock is held
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A 200 km daily delivery is exposed to traffic, weather and vehicle failure, any of which stops production
> - Seasonal demand means a stoppage in summer costs far more than the same stoppage in winter
> - Ice cream sales are concentrated in a short season, so lost output cannot simply be made up later
> - Relying on one supplier for a perishable input leaves Frostfield with no alternative source at short notice
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A risk has two halves: something that might happen, and what follows if it does. Answers that stop at "deliveries might be late" have given only the first. Say what the late delivery would force Frostfield to do, and then what that costs, and a one-mark observation becomes a three-mark answer.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Netherby Windows**
> 
> Netherby Windows manufactures double-glazed windows in country K and holds a buffer inventory of 300 glass panes. Its glass supplier is reliable but delivers only once a fortnight, and a broken pane cannot be replaced quickly.

Explain **one** benefit to Netherby Windows of holding buffer inventory.
parts.solutionMd:
Buffer inventory is a minimum level of stock held in reserve in case demand rises or supply is delayed **[1]**. Netherby Windows receives glass only once a fortnight and cannot replace a broken pane quickly **[1]**. Holding 300 panes in reserve means breakages or an unexpectedly large order can be covered from stock rather than halting production for up to two weeks until the next delivery, so Netherby Windows can still meet its agreed installation dates and avoid compensating customers for delays **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Buffer inventory is a reserve level of stock held to protect against unexpected demand or delayed supply
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Deliveries only once a fortnight mean a shortage could halt production for up to two weeks
> - Glass breakages are difficult to replace quickly, so a reserve absorbs them without stopping work
> - Meeting agreed installation dates protects Netherby Windows from compensation claims and reputational damage
> - A reserve allows Netherby Windows to accept an unexpectedly large order rather than turning it away
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Buffer inventory is a form of insurance, so its benefit is measured in what it prevents rather than in the stock itself. Saying a business "has spare stock" restates the case. Identify the specific disruption the reserve absorbs, here a fortnight's wait for glass, and the benefit becomes something the examiner can credit.

parts.problemMd: Analyse the importance of inventory management to a retail business.
parts.solutionMd:
One reason inventory management is important for a retail business is to make sure there is always enough stock to meet customer demand **[K]**. For example, if a supermarket runs out of a popular product, customers who want to buy it will not be able to, and they may go to a competitor instead **[Ap]**. This means the supermarket could lose that sale completely, and if this happens often, customers may stop trusting it to have what they need and shop elsewhere permanently **[An]**. This shows that poor inventory management can directly reduce a retailer's sales revenue and damage customer loyalty over time **[An]** Another reason inventory management is important is to avoid stock becoming out of date or wasted **[K]**. Many retail businesses sell products such as food that have a limited shelf life. If too much stock is ordered and it is not sold in time, it will have to be thrown away **[Ap]**, which means the supermarket has spent money on stock that earns no revenue at all **[An]**. This wasted cost directly reduces a supermarket's profit. By managing inventory carefully, ordering only what is likely to be sold within its shelf life, the supermarket can reduce this waste and protect its profit margins **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > > **Indicative content** > > - Meeting customer demand - effective inventory management ensures a retail business holds enough stock to meet customer demand, including sudden increases such as seasonal peaks. If stock runs out, customers may be unable to buy what they want and could switch to a competitor instead, resulting in lost sales revenue and potential long-term loss of customer loyalty. > - Reducing waste from out-of-date/damaged stock - good inventory management helps a retailer avoid holding stock for too long, especially important for perishable goods that can go out of date or become unsellable. If stock is left too long, this wasted inventory represents a direct cost to the business with no revenue earned, reducing profit margins. > - Controlling storage costs - holding too much inventory increases costs such as storage space, insurance and possible discounting of unsold stock. Managing inventory levels effectively can minimise these unnecessary costs, freeing up cash that would otherwise be tied up in unsold stock, improving cash flow and overall profitability. > - Supplier relationships and delivery reliability - effective inventory management, including good ordering systems and supplier relationships, can help ensure deliveries arrive on time and that the retailer benefits from bulk-buying discounts. parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **benefits to a business of holding high levels of inventory.
parts.solutionMd:
One benefit of holding high levels of inventory is that a business can meet unexpected increases in demand** [K]**. For example, a clothing manufacturer could keep a large stock of finished garments ready to sell** [Ap]**. If a particular style suddenly becomes popular, it would already have enough stock to fulfil the extra orders straight away, rather than losing the sale while more items are made** [An]**. This means it can take advantage of the higher demand to increase its sales revenue, and customers are less likely to be let down, which helps protect their loyalty to the business** [An]** Another benefit is that holding high levels of inventory allows a business to buy raw materials in bulk and benefit from supplier discounts** [K]**. For example, a clothing manufacturer could buy large amounts of cloth** [Ap]** at once rather than ordering small amounts regularly, and store it until it is needed for production. Buying in bulk like this often means suppliers offer a lower price per metre of cloth, which reduces GreenStitch's unit cost of production** [An]**. If GreenStitch can keep its production costs lower in this way, this could lead to higher profit margins on each garment it sells **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

This allows the business to respond quickly to a sudden increase in demand or a special order, avoiding letting customers down; this protects customer loyalty and allows the business to take advantage of the extra sales opportunity, increasing revenue. > - Protection against supply/production disruption - high inventory levels act as a buffer if raw materials are delivered late or if production machinery breaks down. The business can continue selling from its stock of finished goods, or keep production running using buffer stock of components, so customers are less likely to notice any disruption and the business's revenue is protected. > - Stockpiling seasonal products - holding high inventory allows a business to produce goods steadily throughout the year and store them ready for a short period of high seasonal demand, such as toys before a festival period. parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Flight Food (FF) **
> 
> FF is a large secondary sector business that supplies airlines with in-flight meals. Meals are manufactured using batch production. A different variety of meal is made each hour with a five minute changeover time between batches. FF makes use of Just in Time (JIT) to manage inventory wherever possible. Trucks arrive each hour and deliver the materials needed for production.
> 
> The market for airline meals is very competitive. FF uses market segmentation when deciding which meals are most likely to appeal to different airlines. FF must adapt to changes in tastes and the demands of each airline.
> 
> FF is a labour intensive business. The workers are employed with short-term (six month) employment contracts. They are only offered new contracts if they meet their production targets. Table 2.1 shows some production data for FF’s two work teams.
> 
> **Table 2.1: Worker data for FF**
> 
> |   | **Team A** | **Team B** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Number of workers | 100 | 50 |
> | Productivity (per worker per day) | 300 meals | 240 meals |
> 
> The Board of Directors of FF is considering changing the manufacturing process to flow production. This would require purchasing Computer Aided Manufacturing (CAM) equipment and using a capital intensive production process. Production targets would no longer be used for employees because the machinery would be set at a specific production rate.
> 
> Sabrina, the Operations Director, has put forward the following advantages for moving to flow production:
> 
> - more products made each hour
> - lower employment costs
> - improved quality.
> 
> Ben, the Human Resource Director, is worried about the change from a labour intensive process to a capital intensive process.

Analyse **two **possible disadvantages for FF of using Just in Time (JIT) to manage inventory.
parts.solutionMd:
One disadvantage of JIT for FF is the risk of running out of stock **[K]**. > Calderbrook is a medium-sized business in country H that manufactures replacement parts for agricultural machinery. It supplies farm equipment dealers, who fit the parts for farmers during the harvest season. Demand is highly seasonal, with over 60% of annual sales falling in a ten-week period.
> 
> Calderbrook currently uses a Just in Case system, holding substantial inventory of both steel and finished parts. The Finance Director, Anya Bell, has calculated that inventory holding costs reached \$410 000 last year. She argues that this capital is tied up unproductively and wants to move to Just in Time.
> 
> Calderbrook buys steel from two suppliers. One is 40 km away and delivers within a day. The other is overseas and has a lead time of six weeks, but charges 18% less per tonne.
> 
> **Table 1: Selected data for Calderbrook, 2025**
> 
> | Inventory holding cost | \$410 000 |
> |---|---|
> | Value of orders lost through stock-outs | \$95 000 |
> | Lead time, domestic supplier | 1 day |
> | Lead time, overseas supplier | 6 weeks |
> | Share of annual sales in harvest period | 62% |
> 
> The Operations Director, Ravi Chandra, disagrees with Anya. He points out that a farmer whose machine breaks down during harvest needs the part the same day and will buy from a competitor if Calderbrook cannot supply it. Calderbrook has also been approached by two new dealers who want firm assurances on availability before signing.
> 
> The directors must decide before the next harvest season begins.

Analyse **two** advantages to Calderbrook of continuing to use Just in Case rather than moving to Just in Time inventory management.
parts.solutionMd:
Just in Case means holding reserve inventory so a business can continue supplying customers if demand rises or supply is interrupted **[K]**. Calderbrook earns 62% of its annual sales in a ten-week harvest period, and a farmer whose machine has broken down needs the part the same day **[Ap]**. Holding finished parts in stock means Calderbrook can supply immediately during those ten weeks, whereas under Just in Time the part would have to be made or ordered first **[An]**. Since \$95 000 of orders were already lost through stock-outs last year, moving to a system holding even less stock would be likely to increase those losses at precisely the point when most of the year's revenue is earned **[An]** A second advantage is that Just in Case protects Calderbrook against long lead times **[K]**. One of its two steel suppliers is overseas with a lead time of six weeks **[Ap]**. Just in Time depends on short, dependable lead times, which that supplier cannot offer, so under JIT Calderbrook would either have to stop using its cheaper overseas supplier or risk production halting for weeks while an order was in transit **[An]**. Holding steel in reserve allows Calderbrook to keep producing throughout the six-week wait and so to continue buying at 18% less per tonne, which JIT would force it to give up **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance to a hotel of having effective inventory control.
parts.solutionMd:
One important reason inventory control matters for a hotel is that guests expect their basic needs to be met **[K]**, such as meals, clean bedding and towels **[Ap]**. If a hotel does not hold enough food supplies, it may be unable to serve meals guests have booked, which would damage its reputation. However, food also has a limited shelf life, so a hotel must be careful not to over-order or store food incorrectly, as this could cause illness to guests. Because a hotel's reputation depends heavily on the quality of the food served, getting this balance right is essential to keeping guests satisfied and returning in future **[An]**

Another important reason is that hotel demand can be unpredictable **[K]**, so a hotel needs enough inventory to cope with a sudden surge in bookings without letting guests down. At the same time, inventory control is not only about quantity but also how items are stored; food often needs refrigeration and hazardous cleaning materials must be stored safely **[Ap]**, so poor storage methods could cause harm to guests or staff even if enough stock is held **[An]**. This shows a hotel must manage both the amount and the storage conditions of its inventory carefully to protect guest safety and satisfaction **[An]**

Overall, I think effective inventory control is very important for a hotel, but it cannot guarantee success on its own **[E]**. Predicting demand is genuinely difficult; unexpected events, such as a sudden fall in bookings, could leave a hotel holding food and supplies that are never used, wasting money and reducing profit **[An]**. Other factors, such as well-trained staff and good customer service **[Ap]**, may matter just as much as inventory levels in determining whether guests have a good experience. However, because poor inventory control directly risks guest illness, dissatisfaction and wasted cost, I believe it remains one of the most important operational areas for a hotel to manage carefully, even though it should not be seen in isolation from other factors **[E]**

**Thierry’s Kitchen (TK) **

Thierry’s Kitchen (TK) operates in four European countries with its head office in country H. TK was started by Thierry Radelet in 2017, after he gave up a senior management role in a food delivery company to start his own business. Thierry had observed the rise in popularity of delivery of cooked meals to offices and households. He identified a gap in the market for an efficient service, which would focus on high‑quality cooked meals for delivery only. TK grew quickly and converted to a public limited company in 2019. TK now has two kitchens in each of four European capital cities. The eight locations are outside the city centres and each kitchen has the capacity to produce 2200 meals each day. Meals are packaged and then delivered to customers by motorcycle. Thierry works at the company’s head office, attached to TK’s first kitchen location in country H. He visits the other kitchens once every month. Thierry and a team of directors make all the major decisions about the main menu items and new locations. Each kitchen has a manager who is responsible for decisions about inventory management and human resources. TK has financed its growth through retained profits and a loan of \$15 million. Dividend payments to shareholders have been consistently above average for the catering industry. External environment The European countries in which TK operates experienced economic recessions during 2020. There has been economic growth since then. Governments have supported recovering economies with grants and loans to small and medium‑sized businesses, including TK. Social and technological changes have included fewer consumers eating at restaurants. Smartphone apps are increasingly used for online shopping and ordering meal deliveries. More employees are now working from home rather than in offices. The populations of European capital cities include significant numbers of young, professional individuals who earn above average incomes. Marketing TK differentiates its meal service from the increasing number of competitors on the basis of choice, quality and packaging. The menu is varied and includes daily special offers. Consumers are assured of the high‑quality of TK’s meals as it provides a complete service; from sourcing ingredients to cooking, packaging and delivery. TK’s Operations Director has worked closely with a packaging company to research, develop and patent a range of recyclable packaging containers that ensure meals arrive hot and in excellent condition. Marketing is mainly on its website and social media. However, TK’s Marketing Director believes that the monthly distribution of leaflets to businesses and households is a good use of the marketing budget. The average selling price of a meal is \$8. The delivery charge is \$5 per order and the average order is for 3 meals. Innovation Thierry has always ensured that TK is at the forefront of product and process innovations in the food delivery business. The majority of TK’s orders are received through its smartphone app. Thierry and the other TK directors are now interested in trialling automated (driverless) delivery vehicles (ADVs) in country H. The ADVs will be computer controlled and offer fast, low‑cost meal deliveries. ADVs may be ideal for deliveries in city locations. The capital cost of the ADV trial will be \$1.5 million. This could be financed by further bank borrowing or a new share issue.

Operations and human resources TK’s kitchen operations are labour‑intensive. Meals are produced using batch production, but demand for different meals is difficult to predict due to changing food trends. This makes it very difficult to control inventory. Frequently, too much of some menu items is produced leading to food wastage. Recently, following a social media review praising a TK vegan curry meal, demand increased so quickly that the kitchens failed to produce enough. Some customers were disappointed because their orders were not met. Evaluate whether introducing Just in Time (JIT) will be sufficient to solve the inventory problems at TK.
parts.solutionMd:
One key issue is that JIT could reduce TK's current problem of food wastage **[K]**. At the moment, TK's kitchens produce meals in batches and demand is difficult to predict, which has led to too much of some menu items being made and wasted, since many ingredients are perishable **[Ap]**. If TK introduces JIT, it would hold less stock at any time, reducing this wastage and lowering ingredient costs. However, because TK's demand can suddenly spike, as happened when a social media review caused demand for a vegan curry to rise quickly **[Ap]**, holding less stock under JIT could mean TK is even less able to meet sudden demand, repeating the disappointment already experienced by customers **[An]**

A second issue is that JIT would make TK more dependent on reliable suppliers **[K]**. JIT requires more frequent, smaller deliveries, so TK's kitchens across four different countries would need consistently dependable suppliers to guarantee ingredients arrive on time. This is risky for TK because quality is its main USP, as Thierry has said customers judge TK entirely through the food since they never meet staff face-to-face **[Ap]**. If a supplier fails to deliver a specific ingredient under JIT, TK has no backup stock, so a menu item could become unavailable, which would directly damage the reliability and quality TK depends on to compete **[An]**

Overall, I do not think JIT alone will be sufficient to solve TK's inventory problems **[E]**. JIT should help reduce wastage, but TK's core problem is that demand is genuinely hard to predict, driven by factors like weather, trends and social media reviews **[Ap]**, which JIT does not directly fix. Unless TK also improves how it forecasts demand, or uses its marketing and app more closely with operations to manage or smooth customer demand, JIT could simply replace one problem (wastage) with another (unmet orders) **[E]**. Given TK is also considering major new investments such as the ADV trial and the diversification options **[Ap]**, introducing JIT successfully will also depend on TK having the management time, supplier relationships and possibly ERP systems in place to support it properly, rather than treating JIT as a stand-alone solution **[E]**

‘Effective inventory management is the most important function of the operations management department in a manufacturing business.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
Inventory management is important because it affects a manufacturing business's ability to produce and sell its products **[K]**. Holding too little stock can delay production and cause missed customer orders, losing sales and damaging reputation **[An]**. Holding too much stock ties up cash and increases storage costs, reducing profit. This shows inventory management has a direct impact on a manufacturing business's costs, sales and profitability **[E]** However, an operations department is responsible for much more than inventory **[K]**. Choosing a production method, such as job, batch or flow, has a major effect on unit costs and flexibility **[K]**. Quality control is equally important, since poor quality can damage a manufacturing business's reputation as seriously as an inventory problem, because customers link quality directly to the brand **[Ap]**. Decisions about new technology, such as computer-aided design and manufacture, and factory location can also have a significant long-term impact on efficiency and competitiveness, arguably going beyond what inventory management alone can achieve **[An]** This suggests inventory management is one of several important operations responsibilities, not automatically the most important **[E]**. parts.problemMd: Define the term ‘scale of operation’.
parts.solutionMd:
The scale of operation is the size or level of a business's output **[1]**, measured by the resources it uses to produce it **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - the maximum output that a business can achieve
> - using available inputs/resources
> - can increase in the long-term only by using more resources (1)
> - size of business
> - level/amount of output

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Quality Furniture (QF) **
> 
> QF is a public limited company in country S. It manufactures furniture for cafés. The number of cafés in country S has increased by more than 50% over the last 5 years. This has meant that QF has been able to expand and achieve internal economies of scale. However, the growth of the café market has attracted new firms supplying café furniture and increased competition for QF.
> 
> An extract from QF’s income statement is shown in Table 1.1.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Extract from QF’s income statement for 2020**
> 
> |   | \$m |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue | 300 |
> | Cost of sales | 120 |
> | Gross profit | 180 |
> | Expenses | 150 |
> 
> Although QF has been successful so far, Javid, the Managing Director, has identified two problem areas: inventory and human resources.
> 
> **Inventory **
> 
> QF’s inventory includes raw materials, work in progress and finished tables and chairs. QF buys 80% of its materials from country T and there is a long delivery lead time. This means that QF holds a high level of buffer inventory which has a high value.
> 
> **Human resources **
> 
> QF’s production employees are unhappy that they have not received any benefit from the company’s expansion. Profit has doubled over the past three years but employees have not received any pay increases or bonuses. The employees have all been trained by QF and have specialist skills which had ensured that customer expectations were met. However, customers are starting to complain about a fall in the quality of the furniture, which could be the result of the low morale of the employees. Some highly trained employees have left QF to work for competitor firms.

Explain the term ‘internal economies of scale’.
parts.solutionMd:
Internal economies of scale happen when a business's average cost per unit falls as it grows bigger **[1]**. QF has grown a lot because the café market has expanded by 50%, so it now makes more furniture **[1]**. This means QF's fixed costs, like factory costs, are spread over more units, making each unit cheaper to produce **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> **AO1**
> 
> - Economies of scale occur when a business's unit/average costs fall as its output rises
> - Internal economies of scale arise from the growth of the business itself, such as technical, purchasing or managerial economies
> 
> **AO2**
> 
> - QF has grown because the café market in country S has expanded by over 50% in five years, allowing it to increase output and spread its fixed costs over more units, lowering unit costs.
> - As QF's scale has grown, it is likely to gain purchasing economies - buying larger quantities of raw materials from country T, which could reduce the cost per unit bought.
> - QF's growth may allow it to invest in more efficient machinery for furniture production (technical economies), reducing the average cost of making each table or chair.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'economies of scale'.
parts.solutionMd:
Economies of scale are the fall in a business's average cost per unit **[1]** as it grows and produces more output **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The reduction in average/unit cost that a business experiences as it increases its scale of production/output
> - Cost advantages that a business gains as it grows larger, resulting in a lower cost per unit produced

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose a mark by simply writing that "costs fall as a business grows" without specifying that it is the average (or unit) cost that falls. Make sure your definition links the fall in average cost to an increase in the scale of production or output. Simply referring to "costs" in general terms is too vague for full marks.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'offshoring'.
parts.solutionMd:
Offshoring is moving a business activity, such as production or customer service, to another country **[1]**, usually to take advantage of lower costs there **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Offshoring is relocating part of a business's operations abroad, typically to reduce labour or production costs
> - Offshoring means carrying out an activity in a different country from the one in which the business is based
> - Offshoring is the transfer of a business function overseas, whether to the firm's own facility or another organisation's

> **[exam-tip]**
> Offshoring and outsourcing are easily muddled and answering with the wrong one costs both marks. Offshoring is about where the work happens; outsourcing is about who does it. A business that opens its own factory abroad has offshored without outsourcing anything, which is a useful test to apply to your own sentence.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business might decide to reshore its production.
parts.solutionMd:
Reshoring is moving a business activity back to the home country after it has previously been offshored **[1]**. Wage costs in the overseas location may have risen over time, narrowing the cost advantage that prompted the original move **[1]**. Once that saving shrinks, the drawbacks of distance, such as long delivery times and the difficulty of controlling quality from far away, may outweigh what remains of it, so bringing production home can lower total cost even though wages are higher **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Reshoring is the return of a business activity to the home country after a period of offshoring
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Rising overseas wages erode the cost advantage that justified offshoring
> - Long supply chains create delivery delays and tie up cash in goods in transit
> - Quality is harder to monitor at distance, and defects are expensive to correct once shipped
> - Customers may value domestic production, allowing a higher price that offsets higher costs
> - Rising transport costs or new tariffs can make importing less attractive than producing at home
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reshoring is nearly always a response to something that has changed rather than an admission that offshoring was wrong. Strong answers name the change: wages rising abroad, transport costs increasing, or tariffs being introduced. Without that, the answer reads as though the business simply changed its mind.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which globalisation has affected businesses' location decisions.
parts.solutionMd:
Globalisation is the increasing movement of goods, services, capital and labour between countries **[1]**. Reduced trade barriers and cheaper transport mean a business can now produce in one country and sell in many others without facing prohibitive tariffs or freight costs **[1]**. This widens the range of locations worth considering, so a business can choose a site for its costs or its skilled workforce rather than being tied to a position close to its customers **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Globalisation is the growing movement of goods, services, capital and labour across national borders
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Lower trade barriers mean producing far from the customer no longer incurs prohibitive tariffs
> - Cheaper and faster transport reduces the penalty for distance between production and market
> - Businesses can locate where labour or materials are cheapest rather than where demand is
> - Improved communications allow a head office to manage operations in another country effectively
> - Competition from overseas producers puts pressure on firms to find lower-cost locations themselves
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Globalisation changed the size of the shortlist. Before it, a location decision usually meant choosing between sites within one country; now it means choosing between countries. Framing your answer around that shift gives you something concrete to explain, rather than repeating that the world is more connected.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'diseconomies of scale'.
parts.solutionMd:
Diseconomies of scale occur when a business grows so large that its average cost per unit begins to rise as output increases **[1]**, usually because the organisation becomes harder to manage and coordinate **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Diseconomies of scale are the cost disadvantages that arise when a business becomes too large, causing unit costs to rise as output grows
> - Diseconomies of scale occur where further increases in the scale of operations lead to a higher average cost per unit
> - Diseconomies of scale are increases in unit cost caused by the problems of managing, communicating within and motivating staff in a very large organisation

> **[exam-tip]**
> The defining feature is unit cost rising, not the business being large. Plenty of very big businesses have no diseconomies at all. If your definition would still be true of a large, efficient firm, it has not yet identified what makes these diseconomies, so get the rising average cost into your sentence.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** cause of diseconomies of scale.
parts.solutionMd:
Diseconomies of scale occur when average cost per unit rises as a business grows **[1]**. As an organisation becomes larger, communication between departments and between layers of management becomes slower and more easily distorted **[1]**. Decisions then take longer to reach the people who must act on them, and work done on misunderstood instructions has to be redone, so costs rise faster than output does and average cost per unit increases **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Diseconomies of scale are rises in average cost per unit caused by increasing the scale of operations
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Communication slows and messages are distorted as more layers of management are added
> - Coordinating many departments and sites requires extra administrative staff and systems
> - Employees in a large organisation may feel anonymous, reducing motivation and productivity
> - Decisions take longer, so the business responds more slowly to problems and opportunities
> - Duplication of effort between departments wastes resources that a smaller firm would not spend
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the cause rather than the symptom. Writing that a large business "becomes inefficient" restates the term without explaining anything, so no development mark follows. Say what specifically breaks down, whether that is communication, coordination or motivation, and then trace it through to the extra cost.

parts.problemMd: Explain how economies of scale affect a business's unit costs.
parts.solutionMd:
Economies of scale are the cost advantages a business gains as its output increases **[1]**. Fixed costs such as machinery, rent and management salaries do not rise with output, so as more units are produced the fixed cost carried by each unit falls **[1]**. Since average cost per unit is made up of fixed and variable cost per unit, this reduction lowers the total cost of making each item, allowing the business either to reduce its price or to earn more profit on every unit sold **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Economies of scale are the reductions in average cost per unit that come from producing on a larger scale
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Fixed costs are unchanged by output, so spreading them over more units lowers fixed cost per unit
> - Bulk purchasing of materials reduces the price paid per unit of input
> - Specialised machinery becomes worth buying only at higher volumes, lowering the cost of each unit made
> - Lower unit costs allow either a price reduction to win share, or a wider profit margin at the existing price
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The idea underneath this is arithmetic: much the same total cost, divided among more units. Making that explicit, rather than asserting that costs "go down", is what earns the development marks. Name a fixed cost, point out it does not change, and the fall in cost per unit follows on its own.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** factor a business should consider when choosing a location.
parts.solutionMd:
Location decisions involve weighing factors such as site costs, access to customers, availability of labour and transport links **[1]**. The availability of suitably skilled labour is often decisive, because a business unable to recruit the workers it needs cannot operate at full capacity whatever the site costs **[1]**. Choosing a cheaper location without a suitable labour supply may force the business to pay premium wages to attract staff, or to fund relocation and training, which can cancel out the saving on premises entirely **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Location decisions weigh factors including costs, market access, labour availability, transport and government incentives
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A shortage of suitably skilled labour prevents the business operating at full capacity regardless of site cost
> - Premium wages or relocation and training costs can cancel out savings made on cheaper premises
> - Proximity to customers matters most where the product is perishable, bulky or bought in person
> - Transport links determine delivery costs and reliability, particularly for heavy or low-value goods
> - Government grants or tax incentives may make an otherwise unattractive site viable
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Consider" implies weighing one thing against another, so name what your factor is being traded off against. Cheap premises in the wrong place, or a skilled workforce in an expensive city, are both real dilemmas. Showing the tension is what turns a list of factors into an explanation.

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **factors that might determine the relocation of a business.
parts.solutionMd:
One factor is resources **[K]**. A business might relocate to be nearer to raw materials or cheaper labour. This would lower production costs because less money is spent on transporting materials or paying high wages **[An]**. This is common in the textiles industry - many fashion brands produce garments in countries such as Vietnam which has low labour costs **[Ap]. **Over time, this could increase the business's profit margin and make it more competitive against rivals who have higher costs **[An]** Another factor is legal restrictions, like import or export taxes **[K]**. If a business moves its production into the country where it sells its goods, it avoids paying these extra taxes. This means the cost of getting the product to the customer is lower **[An]**, so the business could either reduce its prices to attract more customers or keep prices the same and earn more profit per sale **[An]**. An example of this is Nissan, who set up a production facility in Sunderland, partly so that it was then operating in its key UK market **[Ap]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > > **Indicative content** > > - A business may relocate for resource reasons > > - Moving closer to raw materials or a cheaper labour supply reduces transport and production costs, which could lower average costs and improve the business's competitiveness or profit margins > - Infrastructure can determine relocation > > - A location with better roads, ports or communication networks reduces transport time and distribution costs, meaning goods reach customers faster and more reliably, which can improve customer satisfaction and reduce lost sales > - Legal factors such as import/export taxes or quotas may make it cheaper to relocate production into the target market > > - This removes tariff costs on goods sold there, which could allow the business to lower prices or increase profit margins compared to exporting from its original location. > - Demographic changes, such as a shift in population or a change in the target market's location, may mean demand no longer exists where the business currently operates > > - Relocating closer to where demand now exists could help maintain sales revenue that would otherwise be lost > > Accept any other valid response.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Super Heroes (SH) **
> 
> SH is a leisure (theme) park aimed at 10–18 year olds. It is owned by two companies, X and Y, which started SH as a joint venture. Company X owns many leisure centres and swimming pools. Company Y owns many brands based on superheroes.
> 
> SH employs 200 full-time workers and an extra 50 seasonal workers during the busiest times of the year. The park has 10 large rides which take up 2km<sup>2</sup> of land. There are also many smaller rides, restaurants, toilets and shops. The price of an entrance ticket is \$11 per customer. Table 1.1 shows the costs for SH in 2019.
> 
> **Table 1.1: SH costs for 2019**
> 
> | Total fixed costs (per year) | \$12m |
> |---|---|
> | Variable costs (per customer) | \$3 |
> | Total costs | \$42m |
> 
> One of the larger rides at SH is the Iron Blaster. The number of customers who use this ride has decreased each year for the last three years. This has led the management of SH to consider its options for internal growth.
> 
> *Option 1 – A new virtual reality (VR) ride* 
> This option would involve developing the Iron Blaster into a VR ride. Most of the structure of the Iron Blaster could be used but customers would be given a VR headset to wear during the ride. The cost of developing the VR ride would be \$2m. The Iron Blaster ride would be closed for a three month period during the off-peak season for the development to be carried out. No employees would be made redundant or dismissed.
> 
> *Option 2 – A new hotel *
> SH does not currently have a hotel. It could demolish the Iron Blaster to provide the space to build one. Many of the competitors of SH have a hotel near or within their leisure parks. Hotel customers would pay a high price for a room but have free access to the leisure park’s facilities. Market research suggests that the average hotel customer would spend twice as long in the leisure park than a non-hotel customer. The cost of developing the hotel would be \$15m and take a year to build. All of the employees currently working on the Iron Blaster ride would face redundancy or dismissal.

SH employs 200 full-time workers and 50 extra seasonal workers at busy times **[Ap]**. parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **Merrow Cables**
> 
> Merrow Cables manufactures electrical cable in country D for construction firms and equipment makers. Six years ago it offshored most of its production to country T, where wages were far lower, keeping only a small specialist plant in country D.
> 
> **Table 1: Merrow Cables selected data**
> 
> |   | **2019** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Average factory wage, country T (\$ per hour) | 3.10 | 7.40 |
> | Average factory wage, country D (\$ per hour) | 16.20 | 18.90 |
> | Shipping cost per container (\$) | 1 900 | 4 300 |
> | Time from order to delivery (weeks) | 9 | 11 |
> | Orders rejected for quality faults (%) | 1.8 | 4.6 |
> 
> Merrow Cables' largest customers are construction firms working to fixed completion dates. Two have recently asked whether Merrow Cables can guarantee delivery within four weeks. It cannot.
> 
> The Finance Director, Anouk Baril, notes that wages in country T remain well under half those in country D, and that the offshored plant still produces at a lower cost per metre than the home site could.
> 
> The Production Director, Idris Kane, argues the gap has narrowed sharply, that quality faults have more than doubled, and that Merrow Cables is losing work it would win if it could deliver quickly. He has proposed reshoring around half of production.
> 
> The board will decide next quarter.

Analyse **two** impacts on Merrow Cables of having offshored its production to country T.
parts.solutionMd:
Offshoring means relocating an activity to another country, usually to reduce costs **[K]**. When Merrow Cables offshored in 2019, wages in country T were \$3.10 an hour against \$16.20 in country D, roughly a fifth of the cost **[Ap]**. Labour is a large part of cable manufacturing cost, so producing in country T substantially lowered the cost per metre and allowed Merrow Cables either to quote lower prices or to earn a wider margin **[An]**. Even now, at \$7.40 against \$18.90, country T wages remain under half those at home, so that advantage has narrowed rather than disappeared **[An]** A second impact is on delivery and quality **[K]**. Production is now 11 weeks from order to delivery, and 4.6% of orders are rejected for faults, up from 1.8% **[Ap]**.
