> **[case-study]**
> **Ockley**
> 
> Ockley manufactures laboratory equipment in country B and needs a second production site. Two options are under consideration: a site 60 km from its existing factory in country B, or a site in country N.
> 
> **Table 1: Comparison of the two sites**
> 
> |   | **Country B site** | **Country N site** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Construction and set-up cost (\$m) | 8.4 | 5.1 |
> | Average annual wage per employee (\$) | 34 000 | 11 500 |
> | Distance from Ockley's main factory (km) | 60 | 2 100 |
> | Corporation tax rate (%) | 24 | 12 |
> | Time to obtain regulatory approval for medical-grade equipment (months) | 4 | 19 |
> 
> Ockley's equipment must be certified before it can be sold in its main markets. Around 70% of its customers are in country B and neighbouring countries.
> 
> The Finance Director, Marta Olsen, favours country N. Set-up costs are \$3.3m lower, wages are around a third, and the corporation tax rate is half.
> 
> The Technical Director, Sunil Raman, disagrees. Certification in country N would take 19 months against four, and engineers from the main factory can reach the country B site within an hour to resolve production problems.
> 
> A decision is needed within two months.

Evaluate whether Ockley should locate its second production site in country B or in country N.
parts.solutionMd:
Location decisions weigh costs against access to markets, labour and the ability to operate effectively **[K]**. Country N is markedly cheaper: set-up costs \$3.3m lower, wages around a third of country B's, and corporation tax half **[Ap]**. For a manufacturer, wages of \$11 500 against \$34 000 would reduce unit costs substantially and permanently, and lower tax would raise the profit Ockley retains from every sale **[An]**. Those savings recur every year, whereas the higher set-up cost in country B is paid once, so over a long horizon country N looks the stronger financial choice **[An]**

However, certification in country N takes 19 months against four **[Ap]**. Ockley's equipment cannot be sold until certified, so the country N site would stand idle for well over a year while the loan or investment behind it earns nothing **[An]**. During that time Ockley would be unable to serve growing demand, and competitors could take the customers the second site was built to supply **[An]**

Overall, Ockley should locate in country B **[E]**. The cost advantage in country N is real and substantial, so this is not a straightforward decision, and on a purely financial comparison country N wins **[E]**. What settles it is that 15 extra months of delay applies to a business whose customers are 70% in country B and neighbouring markets, so the cheaper site serves the wrong customers more slowly **[E]**. Proximity matters too, since engineers reaching a site within an hour rather than travelling 2 100 km will resolve production problems far faster in the critical early period. Country N might suit a later expansion, once Ockley has time to absorb a long certification process **[E]**

> **[case-study]**
> **Fenwick Growers**
> 
> Fenwick Growers operates greenhouses in country R, growing tomatoes for supermarkets and wholesalers. A large supermarket chain has offered it a three-year contract requiring roughly triple its current volume.
> 
> **Table 1: Fenwick Growers, current and after proposed expansion**
> 
> |   | **Current** | **After expansion** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Greenhouse area (hectares) | 12 | 38 |
> | Annual output (tonnes) | 4 200 | 13 400 |
> | Employees | 55 | 160 |
> | Average cost per tonne (\$) | 610 | 540 (forecast) |
> | Number of customers | 9 | 4 |
> 
> The expansion would cost \$14m, financed by a bank loan. The supermarket contract would account for 68% of Fenwick Growers' output and runs for three years, after which it is subject to renegotiation.
> 
> The Managing Director, Ines Duarte, points to the forecast fall in average cost per tonne from \$610 to \$540 and to the security of guaranteed volume.
> 
> The Operations Director, Kwame Boateng, is worried. Fenwick Growers would go from nine customers to four, and the loan repayments would continue for far longer than three years.

Evaluate whether Fenwick Growers should expand its scale of operations to take the supermarket contract.
parts.solutionMd:
The scale of operations a business chooses depends on demand, finance available and the cost advantages larger output can bring **[K]**. Expanding would raise output from 4 200 to 13 400 tonnes and cut average cost per tonne from \$610 to \$540 **[Ap]**. That is a saving of \$70 a tonne, and applied across 13 400 tonnes it amounts to almost \$940 000 a year, largely because fixed costs such as greenhouse structures and management are spread across far more output **[An]**. Lower unit costs would also let Fenwick Growers compete more effectively for other contracts, since it could quote prices smaller growers cannot match **[An]**

However, the contract would represent 68% of output and reduce Fenwick Growers from nine customers to four **[Ap]**. If the supermarket does not renew after three years, or renegotiates the price downwards knowing Fenwick Growers depends on it, more than two-thirds of output would need new buyers at short notice **[An]**. The \$14m loan would still be being repaid long after the three years, so the business would carry the cost of the expansion without the revenue that justified it **[An]**

Overall, whether Fenwick Growers should expand depends on how far it can reduce that dependence rather than on the cost saving **[E]**. The economies of scale are genuine and quantified, so refusing the contract has a real cost too **[E]**. But a three-year contract financed by a much longer loan creates a mismatch, and the loss of five customers removes the very outlets Fenwick Growers would need if the supermarket walked away **[E]**. It should therefore seek a longer contract term or a break clause covering the loan period, and expand by less than proposed so it can retain its existing customers as a fallback, accepting a smaller unit cost saving in exchange for a business that survives non-renewal **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one reason **why operational flexibility is important to a large furniture manufacturer.
parts.solutionMd:
Operational flexibility means a business can change how it produces goods to meet different needs **[1]**. For a large furniture manufacturer, this is important because it may get both big orders from retailers and smaller, custom orders **[1]**. Being flexible means it can produce both types without losing the smaller, possibly more profitable, orders **[1]**

>

> - Flexibility allows a large furniture manufacturer to meet small or customised orders as well as large ones, so it does not miss out on potentially profitable one-off or bespoke orders just because it is set up mainly for mass production.
> - Long delivery times can lead to lost customers, so a flexible manufacturer can adjust production to reduce delays and keep customers satisfied.
>

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'Enterprise Resource Planning'.
parts.solutionMd:
Enterprise Resource Planning is a single integrated software system that manages information across all the main functions of a business **[1]**, so that data entered in one area, such as sales, is immediately available to others, such as production and finance **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Enterprise Resource Planning is software linking a business's functions into one system sharing a common set of data
> - Enterprise Resource Planning integrates information on inventory, production, sales, purchasing and finance so all areas work from the same figures
> - Enterprise Resource Planning is a system that replaces separate departmental records with one shared database covering the whole business

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word doing the work here is "integrated". A business with separate systems for sales, stock and payroll has software, but not an ERP. What makes it an ERP is that the systems are one system, so an entry in one function updates the others. Get that idea in and the second mark follows.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which an Enterprise Resource Planning system could improve a business's efficiency.
parts.solutionMd:
An ERP system holds information from every function of a business in one integrated system **[1]**. When a sales order is entered, the production and purchasing departments see the requirement immediately rather than waiting for it to be passed on **[1]**. Materials can then be ordered and production scheduled against actual demand instead of estimates, so the business holds less inventory while being less likely to run short, cutting storage costs and lost sales at the same time **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - An ERP system integrates information across all functions of a business into one shared system
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Sales orders are visible to production and purchasing immediately, so materials are ordered against real demand
> - Lower inventory levels reduce storage costs while shortages become less likely
> - Accurate, shared data on capacity allows production to be scheduled where spare capacity exists
> - Costing and pricing decisions draw on current figures rather than out-of-date departmental records
> - Management sees the position of the whole business at once, so problems are spotted sooner
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> ERP touches almost everything a business does, which makes a general answer very easy to write and worth very little. Choose one function, whether inventory, capacity or pricing, and follow the improvement through in that area alone. A narrow answer developed properly beats a broad one every time.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which artificial intelligence could improve a business's operations.
parts.solutionMd:
Artificial intelligence uses computer systems to find patterns in data and make predictions from them **[1]**. In operations it can analyse records of machine performance to predict when a component is likely to fail **[1]**. The business can then replace that component during planned downtime rather than after a breakdown halts production, avoiding both the lost output and the rushed repair costs that an unexpected failure brings **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Artificial intelligence uses computer systems to identify patterns in data and make predictions from them
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Analysing machine performance data allows failures to be predicted and repairs scheduled into planned downtime
> - Demand forecasting from sales patterns lets production and inventory be planned more accurately
> - Automated visual inspection can identify defects more consistently than human checking
> - Scheduling systems can allocate jobs across machines to reduce changeover time
> - Analysis of delivery and supplier data can identify which suppliers cause the most disruption
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Artificial intelligence is not the same as automation. A robot arm repeating a fixed movement is automation; AI is the system predicting when that arm will need servicing. The marks here go to answers describing something being predicted or learned from data, so make sure yours does more than replace a person with a machine.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** limitation of lean production.
parts.solutionMd:
Lean production aims to eliminate waste, including spare inventory, spare capacity and spare time **[1]**. Because so little slack remains in the system, a disruption such as a late delivery or a machine breakdown cannot be absorbed **[1]**. Production stops almost immediately rather than continuing from reserves, so the business loses output at exactly the point when it has no spare capacity to catch up, and may miss customer deadlines it has already committed to **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Lean production is an approach aiming to eliminate all forms of waste from the production process
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Minimal inventory means a late delivery halts production almost at once
> - Removing spare capacity leaves no means of catching up once output has been lost
> - Heavy dependence on suppliers delivering on time transfers risk the business cannot control
> - Continuous pressure to eliminate waste can be stressful for employees and raise turnover
> - Introducing lean methods requires training and cultural change that take time and money before any saving appears
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The limitation of lean is the flip side of its strength. The slack it removes is exactly what a business would otherwise use to absorb a problem, so efficiency and resilience pull against each other. Framing your answer that way gives you a proper chain rather than a general observation that lean can go wrong.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'network diagram'.
parts.solutionMd:
A network diagram is a chart showing all the activities required to complete a project in the order they must be carried out **[1]**, including which activities cannot begin until others have been finished **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A network diagram maps the activities in a project, their durations and the sequence in which they must occur
> - A network diagram shows the order and dependencies of project activities, allowing the shortest possible completion time to be identified
> - A network diagram is a diagram of activities and nodes representing how the stages of a project relate to one another in time

> **[exam-tip]**
> A list of tasks is not a network diagram. What the diagram adds is dependency: which activities must wait for others and which can run alongside them. That is the whole reason it can reveal a critical path, so build the idea of one activity depending on another into your definition.

This could reduce costly mistakes and wasted materials during manufacturing **[Ap]**, improving the overall quality of the finished product and reducing the chance of customer complaints **[An]**. > **Luxury Hampers (LH)**
> 
> In 2015 Loretta bought LH, an established food hamper business. A hamper is a gift box or basket containing food and drink. Loretta purchased the business for \$500000 using a combination of personal savings and venture capital. Loretta set a short-term objective of profit maximisation and planned for rapid expansion within a five-year period.
> 
> LH buys high-quality food and drink products directly from manufacturers and packages the products into hampers to sell as luxury gifts.
> 
> **Timeline of LH**
> 
> 2015–2017
> 
> Focus on business efficiency improvement using better inventory control and management of costs. 
> Marketing changes from targeting individual customers to targeting national corporate customers. 
> LH develops online marketing capabilities.
> 
> 2018
> 
> Loretta identifies PS (an international luxury gift supplier) as a suitable target for takeover. 
> Loretta prepares a SWOT analysis for LH and PS (see **Appendix 1**). 
> After the takeover, LH uses the brand name of LH nationally, but uses the PS brand name internationally to retain brand awareness.
> 
> 2019–2020
> 
> Investment into rapid development of international corporate customers.
> 
> 2021
> 
> All products now sold using the LH brand. 
> Loretta is asked to present financial data about the impact of the takeover of PS at the annual general meeting (AGM) (see **Appendix 2**).
> 
> 2022
> 
> LH receives increasing numbers of negative online reviews (see **Appendix 3**). 
> Outdated IT systems and quality control procedures identified as problems.
> 
> **Developing an operations strategy **
> 
> In 2023, a cyber-attack corrupted 75% of LH’s IT systems and data. Incomplete supplier data was recovered. However, all customer data was lost. This led to cancelled orders and LH experienced considerable damage to its reputation.
> 
> LH’s shareholders called an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) and Loretta was replaced as Managing Director by Sanjay, the Operations Director.
> 
> Sanjay has identified several problems which need to be solved in both the short and long-term. He considers there are several opportunities to improve LH’s operational efficiency.

Advise Sanjay on an operations strategy for LH to overcome the problems it is experiencing.
parts.solutionMd:
Sanjay should prioritise fixing LH's IT security first. The cyber-attack destroyed all customer data and corrupted 75% of LH's systems, which is a major reason for LH's damaged reputation **[Ap]**, as shown by the negative online reviews. Investing in new, secure IT systems would help stop another attack happening and start to rebuild customer trust **[An]**. However, this kind of investment is likely to be expensive and could take a long time to put in place, meaning LH could keep losing customers to competitors in the meantime **[An]** At the same time, Sanjay needs to deal with the quality control problems shown in the reviews, like wrong hamper contents and poor customer service **[Ap]**. LH could introduce proper quality assurance and try to rebuild a strong supplier base, similar to the reliable national suppliers PS brought to the business **[Ap]**. The problem is that a lot of LH's supplier information was also lost in the cyber-attack, so this could take time to fix properly, and existing supplier contracts may not be easy to change quickly **[An]** A big constraint on Sanjay's plans is LH's financial position **[K]**. Gearing has risen to 85% and the acid test ratio has fallen to just 0.2:1 **[Ap]**, showing LH has very little short-term cash available and is already relying heavily on debt. This makes it risky for LH to borrow even more money to fund a full IT and quality overhaul all at once **[An]** Overall, I would advise Sanjay to focus first on restoring IT security and recovering essential data **[E]**, since this is the most urgent cause of LH's reputational damage and lost trust. Quality control and supplier issues should be tackled in a second phase, once LH's finances allow it, because trying to fund everything immediately would be too risky given LH's high gearing and weak liquidity **[Ap]** **[E]**. **Thierry’s Kitchen (TK) **

Thierry’s Kitchen (TK) operates in four European countries with its head office in country H. TK was started by Thierry Radelet in 2017, after he gave up a senior management role in a food delivery company to start his own business. Thierry had observed the rise in popularity of delivery of cooked meals to offices and households. He identified a gap in the market for an efficient service, which would focus on high‑quality cooked meals for delivery only. TK grew quickly and converted to a public limited company in 2019. TK now has two kitchens in each of four European capital cities. The eight locations are outside the city centres and each kitchen has the capacity to produce 2200 meals each day. Meals are packaged and then delivered to customers by motorcycle. Thierry works at the company’s head office, attached to TK’s first kitchen location in country H. He visits the other kitchens once every month. Thierry and a team of directors make all the major decisions about the main menu items and new locations. Each kitchen has a manager who is responsible for decisions about inventory management and human resources. TK has financed its growth through retained profits and a loan of \$15 million. Dividend payments to shareholders have been consistently above average for the catering industry. External environment The European countries in which TK operates experienced economic recessions during 2020. There has been economic growth since then. Governments have supported recovering economies with grants and loans to small and medium‑sized businesses, including TK. Social and technological changes have included fewer consumers eating at restaurants. Smartphone apps are increasingly used for online shopping and ordering meal deliveries. More employees are now working from home rather than in offices. The populations of European capital cities include significant numbers of young, professional individuals who earn above average incomes. Marketing TK differentiates its meal service from the increasing number of competitors on the basis of choice, quality and packaging. The menu is varied and includes daily special offers. Consumers are assured of the high‑quality of TK’s meals as it provides a complete service; from sourcing ingredients to cooking, packaging and delivery. TK’s Operations Director has worked closely with a packaging company to research, develop and patent a range of recyclable packaging containers that ensure meals arrive hot and in excellent condition. Marketing is mainly on its website and social media. However, TK’s Marketing Director believes that the monthly distribution of leaflets to businesses and households is a good use of the marketing budget. The average selling price of a meal is \$8. The delivery charge is \$5 per order and the average order is for 3 meals. Innovation Thierry has always ensured that TK is at the forefront of product and process innovations in the food delivery business. The majority of TK’s orders are received through its smartphone app. Thierry and the other TK directors are now interested in trialling automated (driverless) delivery vehicles (ADVs) in country H. The ADVs will be computer controlled and offer fast, low‑cost meal deliveries. ADVs may be ideal for deliveries in city locations. The capital cost of the ADV trial will be \$1.5 million. This could be financed by further bank borrowing or a new share issue.

Operations and human resources TK’s kitchen operations are labour‑intensive. Meals are produced using batch production, but demand for different meals is difficult to predict due to changing food trends. This makes it very difficult to control inventory. Frequently, too much of some menu items is produced leading to food wastage. Recently, following a social media review praising a TK vegan curry meal, demand increased so quickly that the kitchens failed to produce enough. Some customers were disappointed because their orders were not met. TK’s Operations Director is investigating the use of lean production techniques, such as Just in Time (JIT), which he believes could improve efficiency. Each kitchen employs a manager and a team of ten full‑time chefs on permanent employment contracts. There are also kitchen assistants, meal packers and delivery drivers who are employed on a range of part‑time and zero‑hours contracts. Workers are under pressure to constantly improve productivity while maintaining high quality. As Thierry always reminds employees ‘the quality of our food is our USP, because we do not see customers face‑to‑face or serve them their meals’. Most TK employees are shareholders in the company. Annual productivity bonuses are paid in TK shares. Kitchen 2 – a problem kitchen Kitchen 2 is one of TK’s kitchens in country J. Kitchen 2 is not performing well because sales have declined over the past six months. The reasons for this are unclear. Kitchen 2 sells TK’s main menu items and has a maximum capacity of 2200 meals per day. The average daily output is 1000 meals but Saturday is the only day when all the meals produced are sold. Evaluate the importance of product and process innovation to the future profitability of TK.
parts.solutionMd:
Product and process innovation has clearly helped TK grow so far **[E]**. Being an early adopter of the smartphone app, which most orders now come through, has helped TK stand out from other delivery companies **[K]**, and its patented recyclable packaging supports its promise of high-quality meals **[Ap]**, which matters a lot since customers never see TK's food being made. This innovation is likely to keep helping TK's future profitability by keeping customers loyal and attracting new ones in a market with growing competition **[Ap] [An]**

However, innovation is not always successful and can carry real risk **[K]**. When a social media review made demand for the vegan curry meal suddenly spike, TK's kitchens could not keep up, and some customers were left disappointed **[Ap]**. This shows that new menu ideas alone do not guarantee more profit if operations cannot support them **[An]**. The planned ADV trial is another example: it could cut delivery costs and support profitability if it works, but it costs \$1.5m and is unproven, so it could turn out to be an expensive failure that TK has to fund through more borrowing, especially as TK already has a \$15m loan **[Ap] [An]**

Innovation's importance to TK's future profitability also depends on other factors **[K]**. Even a great new packaging idea or menu item needs good marketing so customers know about it and needs kitchens with enough capacity and inventory control to actually deliver it, which the vegan curry problem shows is not always the case **[Ap] [E]**

Overall, I think product and process innovation is very important to TK's future profitability **[E]**, because it is central to how TK differentiates itself from competitors in a crowded market **[Ap]**. However, its importance depends on TK also getting its operations right, since the vegan curry example shows that innovation without the ability to deliver on it can actually damage sales and reputation instead of growing profit **[E]**. TK should keep innovating, but also invest in improving inventory and production planning so that new ideas can be properly delivered to customers **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Discuss the importance of operational flexibility and innovation to a multinational car manufacturer.
parts.solutionMd:
Operational flexibility is important for a multinational car manufacturer because it operates in many different countries with different customer needs **[K]**. Being able to change production volumes or adapt models **[Ap]** to suit local tastes means the manufacturer can respond quickly to demand **[An]**, rather than producing cars that customers in a particular country do not want. This can help the business avoid wasted resources and lost sales **[An]**

Innovation is also important, especially in research and development **[K]**. Coming up with new, more cost-effective or sustainable components can reduce production costs and help the car manufacturer build a good brand image, which matters a lot in such a competitive industry **[Ap]** **[An]**. Being flexible and innovative can help a car manufacturer create a unique selling point that helps it stand out from competitors **[An]**

However, how important this is may depend on the country the manufacturer operates in **[E]**, as some markets are more competitive or demanding than others **[K]**. It could also be argued that because most car manufacturers now include lots of innovative features as standard **[Ap]**, it is harder to gain a real advantage just from innovation alone **[E]**. Overall, I think flexibility and innovation are very important for a multinational car manufacturer to stay competitive globally, but they need to be combined with strong marketing and financial management to be fully effective, since production alone does not guarantee success in such a competitive market **[E]**

> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |

> | **1** | - Analysis based on one reason for the importance of operational flexibility and innovation to a multinational car manufacturer |

> 
> - Operational flexibility is the ability of a manufacturer to vary the level of production and range of products in response to consumer demands
> 
>   - For a car manufacturer, this could mean adjusting production volumes or delivery times for specific models, which helps it respond quickly to changes in demand across different countries and avoid over- or under-producing certain models, reducing wasted resources or lost sales.
> - A multinational car manufacturer operates across many countries with different consumer tastes and cultures, so flexible, well-informed management and workers are needed to adapt models or features to local markets
> 
>   - This can help the manufacturer better meet the needs of each market, increasing sales and competitiveness compared with a rigid, one-size-fits-all approach.

> 
>   - Creative thinking in R&D can lead to more cost-effective or sustainable components, which could reduce production costs or improve the manufacturer's environmental image, both important in a highly competitive car market.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'quality'.
parts.solutionMd:
Quality is the extent to which a product meets the expectations of the customers who buy it **[1]**, judged against what they were led to expect rather than against any absolute standard **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Quality means a product is fit for its purpose and satisfies the requirements of the customer buying it
> - Quality is the degree to which a good or service meets customer expectations of performance, reliability and durability
> - Quality is meeting or exceeding the standard customers expect for the price they have paid

> **[exam-tip]**
> Quality is measured against expectations, not against luxury. A budget pen that writes reliably for a year is a high-quality product; an expensive one that leaks is not. Getting the idea of customer expectations into your definition is usually what separates one mark from two.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why quality is important to a business.
parts.solutionMd:
Quality means meeting the expectations of the customers who buy the product **[1]**. A business producing poor-quality goods will face returns, replacements and warranty claims, all of which cost money after the sale has already been made **[1]**. These costs come directly out of profit and are incurred on items the business has already paid to produce, so poor quality raises costs at the same time as it discourages the repeat purchases the business depends on **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Quality is the extent to which a product meets customer expectations
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Returns, replacements and warranty claims are costs incurred after production has already been paid for
> - Satisfied customers repeat purchase and recommend the business, lowering the cost of winning each sale
> - Consistent quality supports a premium price, widening the margin on every unit
> - Poor quality damages reputation, and in the age of online reviews that damage spreads quickly and lasts
> - Fewer defects mean less waste and rework, so more of what is produced can actually be sold
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Most answers say quality keeps customers happy and stop there. The stronger route is to follow quality into costs as well as sales: faulty goods are paid for twice, once to make and once to replace. Showing both sides of the effect gives you a fuller chain than reputation alone.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'quality control'.
parts.solutionMd:
Quality control is the process of inspecting products at the end of production to identify those that do not meet the required standard **[1]**, so that faulty items can be removed before reaching the customer **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Quality control involves checking finished output against a set standard and rejecting or reworking items that fail
> - Quality control is the inspection of products after they have been made, usually by specialist inspectors
> - Quality control means testing samples or all output at the end of the process to prevent defective goods being sold

> **[exam-tip]**
> The distinguishing feature of quality control is where in the process it happens: at the end, once the product is already made. Building that into your definition makes it clear you are not describing quality assurance, and it sets up the drawback questions that usually follow.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** drawback to a business of relying on quality control.
parts.solutionMd:
Quality control involves inspecting products at the end of production to identify faulty items **[1]**. By the time a fault is found the item has already been made, so the materials, labour and machine time used to produce it have all been spent **[1]**. The business must then either scrap the item, losing that expenditure entirely, or pay again to rework it, so the cost of every defect is carried in full even though the fault is caught before it reaches the customer **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Quality control is inspection of finished output to identify items failing to meet the standard
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Faults are found only after materials, labour and machine time have been spent
> - Scrapped output loses that expenditure entirely; reworking it means paying twice
> - Inspection identifies faults but does not reveal or correct the cause, so the same fault recurs
> - Employing inspectors adds a cost that does not itself improve the product
> - Sampling means some defective items can still reach customers between checks
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The problem with quality control is one of timing, not of inspectors being careless. The fault has already been built and paid for by the moment it is spotted. Anchoring your answer in that sequence, made then found, gives you a clear chain to develop rather than a general complaint about cost.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'quality assurance'.
parts.solutionMd:
Quality assurance is a system in which quality is built into every stage of the production process **[1]**, with each employee responsible for checking their own work rather than relying on inspectors at the end **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Quality assurance means setting standards at every stage of production so faults are prevented rather than detected later
> - Quality assurance makes every employee responsible for the quality of their own output as it is produced
> - Quality assurance is a system of agreed procedures applied throughout the process to ensure the product meets its standard

> **[exam-tip]**
> The quickest way to separate assurance from control is to ask who is responsible. Under quality control it is a small group of inspectors at the end; under quality assurance it is every employee, at every stage. Naming that shift in responsibility earns the second mark cleanly.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** benefit to a business of using quality assurance.
parts.solutionMd:
Quality assurance builds quality into each stage of production, with employees checking their own work as they go **[1]**. A fault is therefore identified at the stage where it occurs, rather than after the product has been completed **[1]**. This means the business stops adding materials and labour to an item that is already defective, so less output has to be scrapped or reworked and the amount spent on production that never becomes a saleable product falls **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Quality assurance builds checks into every stage of production, with employees responsible for their own output
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Faults are caught at the stage they occur, before further materials and labour are added
> - Less scrap and rework means a higher proportion of production becomes saleable output
> - Making employees responsible for their own quality can increase motivation and job satisfaction
> - Fewer defects reach customers, reducing returns and protecting reputation
> - Reliable quality can support certification that customers require before placing large orders
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Say where the saving would actually show up. Scrap, rework, returns and warranty claims are all real figures a business tracks, and pointing to one of them makes the benefit concrete. An answer that only says quality "improves" leaves the examiner with nothing to credit as development.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'Total Quality Management'.
parts.solutionMd:
Total Quality Management is an approach in which every employee in the business takes responsibility for quality **[1]**, working towards continuous improvement so that faults are progressively eliminated **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Total Quality Management is a culture in which all employees are responsible for quality and seek continuous improvement
> - Total Quality Management involves the whole organisation aiming to meet customer requirements first time, every time
> - Total Quality Management is an approach that treats quality as the responsibility of every department rather than a single function

> **[exam-tip]**
> Total Quality Management is a continuing approach, not a change a business makes once and completes. Continuous improvement is part of what the term means, so a definition describing a single reorganisation has missed half of it. Get both the whole-organisation involvement and the ongoing nature into your sentence.

parts.problemMd: Define the term 'benchmarking'.
parts.solutionMd:
Benchmarking is the process of comparing a business's own performance or methods against those of the best-performing organisations **[1]**, in order to identify where and how it could improve **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Benchmarking means measuring a business's performance against the standards achieved by the strongest firms in its industry
> - Benchmarking is comparing processes and results with a leading organisation so weaknesses can be identified and addressed
> - Benchmarking involves identifying best practice elsewhere and using it as a target for the business's own performance

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benchmarking always needs something to compare against, so name it. A definition saying a business "measures its performance" describes ordinary monitoring; what makes it benchmarking is the external standard, usually the best performer available. Include the comparator and the purpose of the comparison.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** benefit to a business of benchmarking.
parts.solutionMd:
Benchmarking compares a business's own performance and methods against those of the best-performing organisations **[1]**. Rather than simply revealing that a rival achieves fewer defects, it shows how that result is produced, for example through different training or a different inspection point **[1]**. The business can then adopt a method that is already proven to work elsewhere, which is faster and less risky than developing an improvement from scratch and testing whether it succeeds **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Benchmarking is comparing performance and methods against the best-performing organisations to identify improvements
> 
> AO2
> 
> - It reveals the methods behind better performance, not merely the fact that a gap exists
> - Adopting a proven method is quicker and lower-risk than developing an untested one
> - Comparison sets realistic targets, since another organisation has already achieved them
> - It can identify areas of weakness a business had not recognised as problems
> - Regular benchmarking shows whether improvements are keeping pace with competitors' own progress
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Discovering that you are behind is not itself a benefit; discovering how the leader does it is. Weak answers stop at identifying a gap, which only tells the business something it probably suspected. Push on to what it can now copy or adapt, and the benefit becomes something real.

**Fashion Frames plc (FF) **

FF makes plastic frames for glasses (spectacles) in a factory in country W, in South East Asia. FF sells its plastic frames to wholesale businesses that market well-known brands of plastic frames which they sell globally. The wholesalers reject 7% of the frames supplied by FF because of substandard quality. The FF design team create dynamic styles based on the demands of the wholesalers. Meeting delivery times is very important. FF only delivers 85% of its sales on time. FF needs to improve this percentage. Improving quality Chang, the production manager, aims to reduce the high level of rejects by the wholesalers. He has identified a number of factors which make this difficult including: • employees know that rejected frames can be recycled • production targets are very difficult to meet • problems with suppliers of raw materials • breakdowns with machinery. Chang proposes introducing Total Quality Management (TQM). He thinks this will reduce the number of substandard frames and improve FF’s delivery times. Chang forecasts successful implementation of TQM will also increase output by 10% and average variable cost will fall by 5%. However, Chang is aware that there may be problems with TQM and forecasts can be inaccurate. Table 1 shows information on FF’s output, costs and prices, before TQM is implemented. Table 1: FF’s output, costs and prices Year ending September 2021 Maximum capacity 16 million frames Actual output 14 million frames Average variable cost \$20 Average selling price \$40 Communication challenges FF has a centralised organisational structure with a low degree of delegation. Directors make decisions, department managers plan how to implement these and supervisors give instructions. Employees have little responsibility or control. FF has provided good pay, good conditions of work and security of employment. However, employees are aware that the directors are considering significant changes to working conditions. All employees find it difficult to discuss this with their line managers. Many employees work alone so information is passed on informally and often inaccurately. This uncertainty has begun to lead to dissatisfaction, complaints, higher absence rates and lower productivity. Privatisation of electricity and water industries In country W, state-owned businesses supply all electricity and water. Prices of services in these industries have risen at above the rate of inflation for the last three years. Sometimes, electricity supply is interrupted and FF finds it difficult to obtain information about reconnection. Water quality is variable. The government has announced it intends to privatise these industries in the next three years, to improve these services.

Buying 3D printers 3D printers that make frames for glasses as part of a CAD/CAM process are becoming available. Chang is considering whether FF should invest in this rapidly developing technology. 3D printers have a guaranteed life span of four years but he believes they are probably usable for six years. There is no way of accurately estimating their value after four years. The directors have told Chang that an acceptable accounting rate of return (ARR) is 5%. Chang thinks new 3D printers will increase FF’s long-term profitability. The 3D printers will result in significant reductions in employee costs and waste and substandard reject costs. Maintenance and training costs will, however, increase. Table 2 and Table 3 show some of Chang’s research. He proposes that FF should use product development to design and manufacture metal glasses frames. These would be marketed to wholesalers and directly to businesses who sell glasses with globally recognised brands. FF would have to acquire new skills and equipment in order to design and manufacture metal frames. The marketing manager visited international trade fairs and found that several competitors have research and development (R&D) departments. Strategic choice: enter the Asia Pacific retail market The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) states: ‘My strategic analysis shows that FF must continue with the current business model but should take a new direction as well. My strategic choice is that FF should enter the retail glasses market in the Asia Pacific region. This will mean selling our own glasses in retail shops. We will need to work closely with lens manufacturers. Increased eye strain and higher disposable income are driving the increasing demand for higher value glasses. We could use the Ansoff Matrix to help analyse the link between this business strategy and risk. There are several approaches we could use to enter this new market.’

The CEO illustrates his proposal with Table 4 and Table 5. There are nine stages in the production process, including cutting out plastic sheets, smoothing component parts, attaching them, and final shaping and polishing. Employees only carry out the one task they have been trained for in the production process. The Directors are considering a proposal from Chang to move to team working. A team would be responsible for the whole production of a product and would take all necessary decisions. If successful, FF could possibly reduce the lead-time from order to completion by 60%, inventory levels by 27% and increase productivity by 20%. A change to team working means greater delegation and less centralisation. Control, authority and trust involving directors, managers, supervisors and production employees will have to change. This strategic change must be managed effectively and directors are confident that Chang has the necessary theoretical knowledge. The benefits he identified will only be achieved if he applies the correct techniques to manage the introduction of team working.

Evaluate whether total quality management (TQM) is sufficient to solve FF’s production problems.
parts.solutionMd:
TQM should help FF reduce its 7% reject rate from wholesalers **[Ap]**. Using the idea of "internal customers," each worker on FF's nine production stages would only accept good-quality work from the stage before them **[K]**. This should stop poor-quality frames moving through the whole process, meaning fewer rejects and possibly better on-time delivery, since FF currently only delivers 85% of orders on time **[Ap] **and rework is likely causing delays **[An]**

However, TQM will not fix all of FF's problems **[E]**. Chang identified issues like machinery breakdowns, unreliable raw material suppliers, and unreliable electricity supply in country W **[Ap]**. These are not caused by employee attitudes to quality, so training staff under TQM will not stop a machine breaking down or a supplier delivering poor materials **[An]**. This means some of FF's delivery and quality problems could continue even after TQM is introduced **[E]**

Overall, I do not think TQM alone is sufficient **[E]**. It should help with the reject rate caused by employee behaviour, but FF also needs to fix its supplier relationships, machinery reliability, and electricity supply **[Ap]**. TQM also costs money to train employees, which may not pay off quickly, especially while FF's employees are already dissatisfied about upcoming changes to working conditions **[E]** **[Ap]**. FF should combine TQM with other actions, like reviewing its suppliers and maintenance schedule, rather than relying on TQM alone **[E]**

> The HR Director, Colm Byrne, is doubtful. Employee turnover is 31%, so roughly a third of those trained this year will have left within twelve months. Staff receive one training day a year and have never been asked to take responsibility for quality.

Evaluate whether Redhaven should replace its quality control system with quality assurance.
parts.solutionMd:
Quality assurance builds quality into each stage of production, making employees responsible for their own work, whereas quality control inspects finished output **[K]**. Redhaven currently spends \$315 000 on inspectors and \$740 000 on scrapped and reworked output, over \$1m a year in total **[Ap]**. Because faults are found only at final inspection, every defective box has been fully manufactured before anyone knows, so the material and labour are already spent **[An]**. Catching faults at the stage they arise would cut much of that \$740 000, and reducing inspectors from nine to two would save most of the \$315 000 as well **[An]**

However, quality assurance depends on a trained and stable workforce, and Redhaven has neither **[Ap]**. Turnover is 31%, so around a third of the employees trained at a cost of \$260 000 will have left within a year, meaning that cost recurs indefinitely rather than being a one-off investment **[An]**. With only one training day a year at present and no history of operators taking responsibility for quality, twelve months to embed the change may also prove optimistic, and during the transition Redhaven would be carrying both systems at once **[An]**

Overall, Redhaven should not make the full switch yet **[E]**. The case for quality assurance is strong in principle, and over \$1m of annual quality costs means staying as it is carries a real price too, so this is not an argument for doing nothing **[E]**. The obstacle is that quality assurance relies on the very thing Redhaven lacks, an experienced workforce that stays long enough to apply its training **[E]**. It should therefore address turnover first, and pilot quality assurance on the single line with the most stable staff. That tests the approach at a fraction of \$260 000 and produces evidence about whether it works here, rather than committing the whole workforce to a system a third of them will leave before mastering **[E]**

parts.problemMd: Explain the difference between efficiency and effectiveness in business operations.
parts.solutionMd:
Efficiency means producing output using the minimum amount of inputs — in other words, getting the most from the resources available and keeping unit costs low. Effectiveness means achieving the business's objectives and meeting the needs of customers — producing the right product or service, not just producing it cheaply. A business can be efficient without being effective: for example, a manufacturer might produce large quantities of a product at very low cost, but if customers do not want that product, the business will not meet its sales targets or generate profit. True business success requires both — producing the right output in the most cost-effective way possible

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Efficiency is about producing the maximum output from a given level of inputs - often described as 'doing things right'; it focuses on minimising waste and reducing cost per unit
> - Effectiveness is about achieving the right business objectives and meeting customer needs - often described as 'doing the right things'; it focuses on whether the business is producing what customers actually want
> - The key difference: efficiency is about HOW a business produces its output; effectiveness is about WHETHER that output is the right one
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A business can be highly efficient without being effective - for example, a factory might produce thousands of units at very low cost per unit (high efficiency), but if those units do not meet customer needs or market demand, the business will still fail to achieve its objectives; this shows that efficiency alone is not enough - the business also needs to ensure it is producing the right goods or services for its target market
> - The relationship between efficiency and effectiveness depends on the market a business operates in; a business competing in a volume, low-cost market segment needs both - it must produce efficiently to keep costs down, and effectively to meet the basic needs of price-sensitive customers; however, a business in an exclusive designer market may accept lower efficiency (higher cost per unit) as long as it is highly effective at meeting the expectations of quality-conscious customers
> 
> Accept any other valid response

>

>

parts.problemMd: Analyse the advantages to a business of using mass customisation.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage is that mass customisation helps a business meet the different needs of its customers **[K]**. For example, a trainers company could let customers choose the colour or add their initials to a mostly standard shoe design **[Ap]**. This means customers feel like they are getting a personalised product, even though most of the production process is the same as normal mass production **[An]**. This is likely to increase customer satisfaction and encourage repeat purchases, which can increase the business's sales and market share over time **[An]**

Another advantage is that mass customisation can keep costs relatively low compared with fully bespoke production **[K]**. This is because most of the materials and components used, like the base of the trainer **[Ap]**, are still the same across all versions of the product. This means the business can still benefit from bulk-buying discounts on these shared parts, even though the finished product looks different for each customer **[An]**. As a result, the business can offer variety and charge a slightly higher price without losing the cost advantages of mass production, which should protect its profit margins **[An]**

This increases the business's ability to satisfy a wider range of customer needs, so customers are more likely to buy because the product feels tailored to them, which can increase sales and customer loyalty
> - Cost efficiency - most of the components and materials used in each variation are the same or similar, so the business can still benefit from bulk-buying discounts even though products are customised. This means the extra cost of customisation is lower than fully bespoke production, so the business can offer variety without losing the cost advantages of mass production, protecting profit margins.

This close control over quality helps maintain the standards needed for a luxury product, which may help explain HH's already high gross profit margin of 40%, as customers pay a premium for guaranteed quality.
> - Employee satisfaction and flexibility - with only four skilled staff working closely together, and the ability to make changes during production if a customer requests it, employees produce a finished, unique product from start to finish rather than repetitive tasks. This can increase job satisfaction, helping HH retain highly skilled staff who would be difficult and costly to replace.
> 
> **Disadvantages**
> 
> - High unit costs - job production usually has higher unit costs than batch or flow production because each bag is made individually by skilled staff rather than in volume. This could be a particular problem for HH's planned new range of batch-produced bags for the online market, where there are 15 large competitors and bags must be priced competitively, so high job-production-style costs would not be suitable.
> - Reliance on highly skilled labour - job production depends on staff able to work to a high standard without prescriptive processes, so HH must employ and retain highly skilled specialist staff. This makes HH vulnerable if any of its four skilled employees leave, since replacements may be hard to find quickly, putting pressure on wage costs to retain staff.
> - Slow production time - job production of unique bags can take a long time. This slow speed would not suit HH's planned expansion into online batch-produced bags, where a faster turnaround is likely needed to compete with the 15 large existing businesses in that more price-competitive market.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problemMd: Analyse **two **impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process.
parts.solutionMd:
One impact of increasing automation is that it can lower the business's unit costs in the long run **[K]**. For example, if a food packaging company installs automated machinery to fill and seal its products **[Ap]**, it will need fewer workers to do this job. As the machines create a higher fixed cost but a lower variable cost per unit, the more the business produces, the lower its average cost per unit becomes **[An]**. This means the business could either lower its prices to attract more customers or keep prices the same and earn a higher profit margin, improving its overall competitiveness **[An]**

Another impact is that automation is likely to reduce the number of workers the business needs **[K]**. If the food packaging company introduces machines to do tasks previously done by hand **[Ap]**, some employees may become redundant. This could save the business money on wages in the long run, but making staff redundant can be expensive in the short term due to redundancy payments, and it may lower the morale of the remaining workers **[An]**, who could worry about losing their own jobs. This may increase labour turnover or reduce motivation, which could offset some of the cost savings from automation **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the** **impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the** **impacts on a business of increasing the use of automation in its production process |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of automation |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative Content**
> 
> - Lower unit costs - automating parts of the production process replaces variable labour costs with fixed machinery costs. For example, a food processing company that automates packaging could reduce the number of workers needed per unit produced. As output increases, the fixed cost of the machinery is spread over more units, lowering average cost per unit; this could allow the business to reduce prices or increase its profit margin, strengthening its position against competitors.
> - Increased speed and consistency of output - automated machinery can typically produce output faster and with less variation than manual labour. In a food processing company, this could mean packets are filled and sealed to a more consistent standard, reducing the amount of substandard output that has to be reworked or wasted, which could improve efficiency and protect the business's reputation for quality.
> - High initial capital cost - introducing automated machinery usually requires a large upfront investment to purchase and install the equipment. A food processing company installing an automated packaging line would need significant finance, which could increase its gearing if funded through loans or reduce cash available for other purposes, creating short-term financial pressure before any longer-term cost savings are realised.
> - Workforce reduction and redundancies - increasing automation is likely to reduce the number of workers needed for tasks machines can now perform. For a food processing company, this could mean redundancies among production line staff, involving redundancy payments and potentially damaging morale among remaining employees who fear further job losses, which could increase labour turnover or reduce motivation.
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks on "analyse" questions by simply identifying an impact without developing a chain of reasoning. To reach the higher levels, make sure you explain *why* and *how* the impact occurs, linking cause to effect and then to a further consequence for the business.
> 
> Structure your answer around two impacts and develop each in depth rather than listing several impacts superficially. For example, if you choose "lower unit costs", explain how automation replaces variable labour costs with fixed machinery costs, how this affects average costs as output rises, and what this ultimately means for the business's pricing strategy or profit margins.
> 
> Always apply your answer to a realistic business context - even if the question does not name a specific business, you should create a plausible scenario (e.g. a manufacturer of standardised goods) to demonstrate application skills.
> 
> Avoid spending time discussing multiple impacts; the question asks for **one**, so depth of analysis on a single point is rewarded far more than breadth.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> **NaturaBite Foods (NF)**
> 
> NaturaBite Foods (NF) is a private limited company in country G that produces organic snack foods, including energy bars, dried fruit mixes, and nut butters. NF sells its products to supermarkets and health food stores across country G. NF has built a strong brand with the slogan 'nothing artificial, nothing hidden'.
> 
> NF currently uses flow production to manufacture its products in large quantities. The production manager believes that switching to batch production will allow NF to produce a wider range of flavours and varieties, responding to changing customer preferences. However, the Finance Director has raised concerns about the cost of reorganising the production process.
> 
> NF employs 60 workers in one factory. The Production Manager believes there is significant room to improve labour productivity without increasing headcount. Table 2.1 shows NF's financial data for 2023.
> 
> **Table 2.1: NF financial data 2023**
> 
> |   |   |
> |---|---|
> | Selling price per unit (\$) | 4.00 |
> | Variable cost per unit (\$) | 1.50 |
> | Total fixed costs (\$) | 75,000 |
> | Current annual output (units) | 40,000 |
> | Maximum capacity (units) | 55,000 |

Analyse **two** ways NF could improve its labour productivity.
parts.solutionMd:
One way NF could improve labour productivity is by introducing incentives for its workers, such as performance-related pay linked to output targets **[K]**. At the moment, NF has spare capacity, producing 40,000 units against a maximum of 55,000 **[Ap]**, so there is clear room to produce more with the same 60 employees. If workers are rewarded for higher output, they may work harder and waste less time during shifts **[An]**. This could help NF get closer to its maximum capacity without hiring extra staff, which would spread its \$75,000 of fixed costs over more units and lower the average cost of each item produced **[An]**

Another way NF could improve labour productivity is by redesigning its production process to cut out wasted time and movement **[K]**, following lean production ideas. NF currently uses flow production, and its production manager is already reviewing how production works because of the idea to introduce batch production **[Ap]**. As part of this review, NF could look for delays or inefficient steps in the current flow line and remove them. This would let the existing 60 workers produce more units in the same shift length **[An]**, raising output per worker without needing to spend money on new machinery or extra staff **[An]**

> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the** **impacts on NF of improving labour productivityin its production process |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of labour productivity |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative Content**
> 
> - Training and development - NF's production manager believes there is room to improve productivity without increasing headcount. Investing in targeted training for NF's 60 production workers (e.g. on machine operation, quality control or food hygiene) would help them complete tasks more efficiently and with fewer errors. A more skilled, more confident workforce is also likely to be more motivated, reducing absenteeism and labour turnover; even small efficiency gains across all 60 employees would cumulatively raise output without extra staff, lowering NF's average cost per unit, especially given NF currently has spare capacity to fill (40,000 units against a maximum of 55,000).
> - Automation of repetitive tasks - NF currently uses flow production for large-volume output; introducing automated machinery for repetitive tasks such as packaging or labelling would let the same 60 workers produce more output per shift, freeing staff to focus on higher-value tasks such as quality inspection. This raises labour productivity because output rises without an increase in headcount. However, the upfront capital cost of new machinery is high, so NF's Finance Director - already concerned about reorganisation costs - would need to weigh this against the long-term productivity gains before approving investment.
> - Financial/non-financial incentives - introducing incentives, such as performance-related pay linked to output targets or non-financial rewards, could motivate NF's workers to increase effort and reduce time wasted during shifts. As NF has spare capacity between its current output of 40,000 units and its maximum capacity of 55,000, higher motivation could help NF's existing 60 employees produce closer to this maximum without hiring more staff, spreading NF's \$75,000 of fixed costs over more units and lowering average cost per unit.
> - Redesigning production processes - reviewing and streamlining NF's flow production process to reduce wasted time, movement or waiting between stages (lean production principles) could allow workers to complete more units in the same shift length. This is particularly relevant given NF's production manager is already reviewing production methods (considering a switch to batch production for greater flexibility); removing inefficiencies in the existing flow line could raise output per worker without additional headcount or major capital spend, offering a lower-cost route to improved productivity than automation.
>

Each point should follow a clear structure: identify the way, link it to NF's situation using specific evidence from the case study, and then build a chain of reasoning explaining the consequences for the business
>

> 
> For analysis, avoid simply stating an outcome. Instead, build a logical chain: explain *why* the way would work, *how* it would affect productivity, and *what* the wider implications are for NF. Using connective phrases such as "this means that…", "as a result…" and "which would lead to…" helps signal your analytical reasoning to the examiner.
>

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]** > **Delicious Cocoa (DC) ** > > DC is a co-operative owned by cocoa farmers in country X. It has 500 workers. In 2022, DC produced 2000 tonnes of raw cocoa beans. Productivity is expected to increase by 5% in 2023. Although DC is profitable, it has no retained earnings. > > DC focuses on the triple bottom line as its main objective. The members of the co-operative (farmers) are motivated within the current operation. > > Zara, the Managing Director, has recently completed a workforce plan. She has identified that young people do not want to work on DC’s farms. Their concerns are: > > - lack of investment in training > - most of the work is manual > - lack of control over earnings. > > Ranjit, the Operations Director, has identified an opportunity to create added value by investing in a capital intensive factory. > > The factory will process raw cocoa beans produced by DC’s farms into cocoa butter. Cocoa butter is a premium product and attracts higher profit margins than raw cocoa beans. The processing factory will require a significant capital investment (see Table 2.1). > > **Table 2.1 Data for the cocoa processing factory** > > | | \$ | > |---|---| > | Initial investment:
Land
Machinery
Training | 100 000
150 000
15 000 | > | Average variable costs per tonne | 5 000 | > | Average selling price per tonne | 10 000 | Evaluate whether DC should grow its operations by opening its new cocoa processing factory.
parts.solutionMd:
One important issue is the financial risk of the investment **[K]**. Table 2.1 shows the total cost of the new factory would be \$265,000 (land, machinery and training). DC is profitable but has no retained earnings **[Ap]**, which means it has no spare cash of its own to fund this. DC would need to borrow the money or find external investment, which creates risk because the co-op is owned by farmers rather than shareholders who might expect a quicker return **[An]**. If sales of cocoa butter are lower than expected, DC could struggle to repay this debt, which could reduce the short-term income of the 500 farming families who depend on DC **[Ap]** **[An]**

A second important issue is DC's workforce problem. Zara's workforce plan shows that young people do not want to work on the farms because of a lack of training, mostly manual work, and little control over earnings **[Ap]**. The new factory would include \$15,000 of training and would involve more capital-intensive, machine-based work rather than fully manual farming. This directly addresses two of the three concerns young people have, which could help DC attract and keep younger workers in the future **[Ap]** **[An]**. Without this change, DC risks a shortage of workers as older farmers retire, which would threaten its long-term supply of raw cocoa beans **[Ap]** **[An]**

Overall, I think DC should go ahead with the new factory **[E]**. The financial risk is real, since DC has no retained earnings and \$265,000 is a large sum for a farming co-operative to borrow **[Ap]**. However, DC's own research shows that its current way of working is not sustainable, because young people are turning away from farm work. The factory tackles this problem directly through training and less manual work **[E]**, while also processing beans into a higher-margin product, since cocoa butter sells for \$10,000 per tonne against variable costs of \$5,000 per tonne. This extra profit could help DC repay any borrowing and support its triple bottom line objective **[Ap]** by securing jobs for the community's future, so the long-term benefits are likely to outweigh the short-term financial risk **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
‘In a large computer manufacturing business, the operations department is more important for achieving success than the marketing department.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solutionMd:
The operations department is responsible for turning inputs, such as materials and components, into finished computers that meet the standards customers expect. This includes choosing the best production method, selecting reliable suppliers, and checking the quality of the final product **[K]**. If TechCore's operations department works efficiently, computers will be made to a high standard, at a reasonable cost, and delivered on time. This is important because even if customers want to buy TechCore's computers, poor quality or late production could damage TechCore's reputation **[Ap] **and cause it to lose customers to competitors, no matter how good its marketing has been **[An]** However, the marketing department is also essential, because it identifies exactly what customers want before operations even begins production **[K]**. Marketing research tells TechCore what specifications, features **[Ap]** and price customers expect from a new computer. Without this information, operations could produce computers that nobody wants to buy, wasting resources on unsold stock. Marketing also builds TechCore's brand and communicates why customers should choose TechCore over competitors, which drives the sales that operations then has to fulfil **[An]** This shows that the two departments are closely interdependent **[K]**, and one cannot succeed without the other. If marketing promises features or delivery times that operations cannot actually achieve, customers will be left disappointed regardless of which department is considered more important. In a large business like TechCore, close communication between the two departments is essential to avoid this happening **[An]** It could also be argued that neither operations nor marketing is the most important department in a computer manufacturing business, because the technology industry changes so quickly. Without continuous investment in research and development, TechCore's products could quickly become outdated compared to competitors **[Ap]**, no matter how efficient its operations are or how well its marketing team performs **[An]**. This suggests that innovation may be just as critical to long-term success as operations or marketing **[E]** Overall, I think operations is slightly more important than marketing for a large computer manufacturer like TechCore **[E]**, because even the most effective marketing campaign cannot sustain sales if the actual computers are unreliable, poor quality or delivered late. Marketing can create initial demand, but operations is what allows TechCore to consistently deliver on the promises marketing makes, which is essential for repeat purchases and long-term reputation **[E]**. parts.problemMd: Discuss the view that it is more important for a manufacturer of bicycles to be effective than it is to be efficient.
parts.solutionMd:
One key issue is that being efficient does not guarantee success if a bicycle manufacturer is not effective **[K]**. For example, if CycleWorks produces steel-framed bicycles very cheaply and quickly, this is efficient because it uses fewer resources per bike **[Ap]**. However, if most customers now want lightweight electric bikes because of rising fuel costs and environmental concerns, CycleWorks would be efficient but ineffective, because it is not meeting what customers actually want **[An]**. This could mean CycleWorks produces bicycles that do not sell, wasting the benefit of its low production costs and losing revenue to competitors offering more relevant products **[An]**

However, efficiency is still important because it supports CycleWorks' long-term profitability **[K]**. If CycleWorks uses technology such as computer-aided design and manufacture (CAD/CAM), it may be able to produce a wider range of bicycle designs, such as electric or folding bikes **[Ap]**, while still keeping unit costs relatively low **[An]**. This shows efficiency and effectiveness do not always conflict, and being efficient can actually help CycleWorks stay competitively priced **[An]**. Without reasonable efficiency, CycleWorks may struggle to fund the research and innovation needed to remain effective in a fast-changing market, so efficiency also indirectly supports effectiveness over time **[An]**

Overall, I think effectiveness is more important than efficiency for a bicycle manufacturer like CycleWorks **[E]**, at least in the short to medium term. The bicycle market changes quickly, with growing demand for electric and lifestyle bikes **[Ap]**, so if CycleWorks fails to meet these changing customer needs, efficient production of the wrong product will not generate sales. However, this does not mean efficiency does not matter **[E]**. CycleWorks still needs to control costs to remain profitable and to fund the innovation that keeps it effective in future **[Ap]**. A truly successful bicycle manufacturer needs a balance of both, but when trends are changing rapidly, correctly identifying and meeting customer demand should take priority over minimising costs **[E]**
